## Page 15

Chapter 1

Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to com-
municate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them
a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more.
Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen
if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could
interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models
with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs
work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.

1.1
Why this book?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the world. Large language models that act
change the world in a new way. In order to understand the extent of these changes
it is important for students and researchers of AI to understand both the technology
itself and the applications that are now emerging. This understanding can help us influ-
ence the direction of these developments, perhaps build in safeguards, and, specifically,
it will help us to develop the field further.
This book has been written for the graduate course on agentic LLMs that we teach
at our university. In agentic LLMs two fields of AI research come together: the study
of agents, and the study of large language models. Agents are changing the field of
LLMs, and, conversely, LLMs are changing the field of agents. Although there are
excellent books about LLMs and how they work (such as Jurafsky and Martin \[2025\]),
the ability to act puts agentic LLMs in a class of their own. We think that there is a
need for a course and for a book that explain how agentic LLMs work, and how they
enable things that were not possible before.

1.2
Concepts and Definitions

The strength of the language abilities of LLMs is impressive, they talk just like we do.
Now that LLMs have become agentic, their horizon extends far beyond talking: LLMs

15

## Page 16

16
CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION

have capabilities for reasoning, for using tools such as writing and running code, for
browsing the web to retrieve information, and for interacting with other agents or with
the outside world.
This brings us to two definitions that we use in this book.

Agents perform actions, observe the effect of these actions and use the
feedback they receive from the world to adapt their action policy.

Agentic LLMs are agents that integrate the power of LLMs, such as to
communicate using natural language, write code, or process information.

1.2.1
Agents that Assist, Agents that Interact

The ability to act has increased the relevance and applicability of LLMs in many do-
mains of society. How are agentic LLMs used? In this book, we distinguish two major
classes of use cases for Agentic LLMs:
(1) Agentic LLMs are used to assist their human users in application domains such
as medicine, logistics, and finance (Part IV).
(2) Agentic LLMs are used to interact with each other to perform tasks or function
in simulations of human behavior (Part V).
Many research papers have been published in recent years in both domains. We
will provide overviews of key studies and trends throughout the book.

1.2.2
Agentic Harness

From an engineering perspective, how do we construct agentic LLMs? Agentic LLMs
consist of two elements: (1) the LLM, and (2) a piece of code that is called the harness.

Agentic LLM = LLM + Harness

The harness is a piece of computer code that wraps around the model and controls
how it is called (a horse’s harness helps us guide the power of the noble animal in a
productive direction). The harness performs tasks such as prompt construction, answer
processing, calling external tools, state management, system prompt management, and
skill management. The harness loops through the reasoning, acting, and observing that
are necessary for task completion, without the need for human intervention to guide
the process manually. The agentic harness can thus be seen as a versatile automatic
prompt engineer (Part II, Chapter 6). Importantly, the harness may adapt the behavior
policy of the agent based on feedback on its actions, using reinforcement learning (Part
III, Chapter 9).

1.2.3
Multi-Modal Models

Understanding natural language is crucial for agents that interact with users and the
world around them. However, for many tasks agents must also process other modal-
ities, such as visual information, or other text formats, such as spreadsheets or com-
puter code. As such, the domain of agentic LLMs extends beyond natural language,

## Page 17

1.2. CONCEPTS AND DEFINITIONS
17

Figure 1.1: Recursive self-improvement cycle connecting three categories of agentic
LLM: reasoning, acting, and interacting (in red, corresponding to Parts II, III/IV and
V). Concepts that influence a category are in green.

and includes multi-modal, code, and world models. Therefore, please note that in this
book we use the term LLM pragmatically—depending on the context it can refer to
language-only systems, or it can have a broader scope: large transformer-based model
that processes natural language, computer code, images, tool-commands, or other rel-
evant modalities (Part II, Chapter 7). In cases where the distinction is important, we
flag which variant of the definition applies.

1.2.4
Training Data

Agentic LLMs mark another paradigm shift in LLM engineering, that is related to
machine learning. For a long time, the learning-emphasis in the field of LLMs has
been on learning during model training, but now there is an increasing role for learning
at inference time, when the model is queried.
This has two advantages. First, it creates flexibility and space for dynamic agentic
behavior, as we will see in Chapters 8 and 9. Second, in an era where almost the
entire internet has been used as data for pretraining models \[Sutskever, 2024\], it has
become useful to generate additional, relevant, and high-quality data. By interacting
with the world, agents can generate such new data themselves. Figure 1.1 illustrates
this process. This interaction-data can be used for additional training.
An example of how LLMs are trained on their own agentic actions are vision-
language-action models that learn from robotic action sequences (Chapter 7). Another
example can be found in Chapter 17, where societies of agents allow models to become
more intelligent through interaction, just like humans learn new behaviors and ideas
when they interact with one another.
Thus, in addition to enabling useful applications, another driver of agentic LLMs is
the opportunity to generate more training data, creating a recursive self-improvement
loop. In Figure 1.1 this virtuous cycle of interactive data generation is shown. Shown
in red are the main categories: reasoning (Part II), acting (Parts III/IV), and interacting
(Part V). In green are concepts that influence a category, either directly, or in a feedback
loop.

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION

1.3
Audience and Aim

This book is primarily written for graduate students and researchers in artificial intel-
ligence and computer science. It may also be of interest to students and scholars from
other fields, such as the cognitive and social sciences or humanities, as long as they
have an intrinsic drive to engage with machine learning and technological challenges.
The book’s aim is to introduce and review the advancements of techniques and ap-
plications in the field of agentic LLMs. We discuss the major concepts of agentic LLM
engineering in some depth. We provide references to the scientific literature as well as
links to source code and datasets so that you can experiment with building your own
agents. Note that the field is new, and still very much in motion. A thorough under-
standing of the basics is important in order to be able to follow the latest developments.
Our aim is to provide you with both.
We use this book for teaching the course Agentic LLMs that is part of the Mas-
ter programs Computer Science (AI-track) and Creative Intelligence & Technology at
Leiden University. A website with support material is available (lecture slides, assign-
ments, news).1

Dear reader, we hope that you will enjoy reading this book as much as we did
writing it. Agentic LLM research is a new field, and this book is just as fresh. New
developments occur every day. We very much welcome your feedback and suggestions
for following editions of this book, via the website!

1.4
Prerequisites

This book assumes that you have an undergraduate-level understanding of computer
programming, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and natural language process-
ing.
We assume that you know how to use Python and PyTorch. We also assume that
you understand principles of machine learning, such as the difference between clas-
sification and regression, the difference between a training set and a test set, and the
causes of overfitting and underfitting. You should know classical machine learning
approaches such as decision trees, ensembles, and random forests. You should also
be familiar with concepts of deep learning such as the architectures of artificial neu-
ral networks (fully connected multilayer perceptrons, convolutional neural networks,
and recurrent neural networks), learning by backpropagation, with loss functions (such
as cross-entropy) and activation functions (such as ReLU). We also expect that you
are familiar with reinforcement learning: you should know what a sequential decision
problem is, understand the difference between agent and environment, and know how
to use some policy learning algorithms (such as Q-learning, DQN, PPO, and SAC).
Finally, you should have an understanding of natural language processing: what is
tokenization, what are word embeddings, what is attention, and what is Huggingface.
However, we also believe that if you do not have in-depth knowledge about some
or all of these topics and concepts, you may still find value in reading this book. We
provide brief overviews of essential topics, you will learn about agentic LLMs at a

1.5
Course Structures

We use this book for the graduate course Agentic LLMs at our university. The book
has been written to be both concise and comprehensive: we cover the full breadth of
the field at a level suitable for a graduate course. To allow you to go deeper, we provide
many pointers to the scientific literature, and some advanced topics are covered in the
chapters and sections that are marked with a *.
Different university programs may cover different material (see Table 1.1). The
course that we teach is comprehensive, and consists of 14 lectures: an introductory
lecture, then 3 lectures on part I (language modeling), 3 lectures on parts II (reasoning)
and III (agents), 3 lectures on part IV (tools and assistants), and 3 lectures on part
V (social simulation). The course ends with a final evaluation lecture. Our course
includes as assignments the four case studies, which we grade in an in-person meeting
with the student. We do not have a separate theory exam at the end, the course grade is
the average of the assignment grades.
Although you are of course free to use the book in any way that makes sense in
your situation, we cover two main use cases for agentic LLMs: (1) assistants and (2)
social simulation.
When your program includes a separate in-depth course on LLMs, then a core
program to focus on (1) agentic assistants can include just parts II, III and IV. For the
assignments, we suggest case study 2 and 3.
Alternatively, a core program to focus on (2) social simulation should cover parts
II and III, and part V, using case study 2 and 4 for the assignments.
Both the assistants and the social simulation approach can be augmented with part
I (language modeling), as necessary, depending on how the education program at your
University is structured.
Part VI contains advanced topics. Chapter 19, on synthetic data generation, is suit-
able for the assistants use case, Part IV. Chapter 21, on mechanistic interpretability,
is suitable to go more in depth for Parts I and II, the language and reasoning mod-
els. Chapter 20, on advanced architectures, is also suitable for Part II. Chapter 22, on
cognitive architectures, is suitable for the social simulation use case, Part V.

1.6
Approach, Scope and Overview

Our approach is hands-on. For all new concepts we provide the theoretical background
and we give examples of how to use them in practice. We discuss datasets, training
algorithms, benchmarks, training environments, we provide pseudo-code of important
agent algorithms, and we provide practical case studies to help you learn.
This book is organized in chapters that each cover a comprehensive topic. The
chapters are organized in seven parts.
Part I provides a basic introduction to large language models. Chapter 2 discusses
important natural language processing concepts such as tokenization, embeddings, re-
current neural networks, the attention mechanism, the transformer architecture, and
autoregressive training (the machine learning method that is central to how LLMs
are trained). We also discuss further machine learning methods: supervised learning
and reinforcement learning. Next, in Chapter 3 we discuss in some detail the training
pipeline that is used to train LLMs. We discuss dataset acquisition, pretraining, finetun-
ing, instruction tuning, value alignment, and inference. We also discuss benchmarks
that are commonly used to test the performance of LLMs. In Chapter 4 we discuss
scaling laws and small language models, and we discuss energy consumption. To be
able to use agentic LLMs, you must understand the basics of pretraining and finetuning
a transformer model. In the final chapter of Part I, we help you acquire this experience
with a practical case study where we will guide you to train a transformer model from
scratch.
Part II provides an introduction into the concepts of reasoning, reflection, and world
models, three concepts that are essential elements of (advanced) agentic LLMs. In
Chapter 6 we start with in-context learning, and discuss how the chain of thought
method has enabled LLMs to perform multi-step reasoning in simple math word prob-
lems. We will discuss how LLMs are used to self-reflect on their own in-context learn-
ing, to enhance their reasoning power, using a harness. So far, we have focused on
models that use language. To act in the real world, our agents will also have to un-
derstand image data, and other modalities. In Chapter 7 we go beyond language and
discuss models that understand vision and language, and also models that learn from
decision sequences and know how to perform robotic actions. To act in the world with-
out walking into walls, agents need some understanding of physics. In Chapter 7 we
discuss world models, including their relation to model-based reinforcement learning.
At that point, we will have discussed a multitude of different ways in which the agents
learn and interact with their environment. In Chapter 8 we discuss in more depth how
they learn, and how this learning is a form of metalearning.
Next, in Part III, Chapter 9 provides a historic review of agents in the perspective

## Page 21

1.6. APPROACH, SCOPE AND OVERVIEW
21

of artificial intelligence, and we discuss different agentic interaction styles of agentic
LLMs. Furthermore, in order to act in the world, agents need a form of memory. We
discuss different agentic memory architectures in this chapter. We conclude Part III
with a practical case study, where you can build a self-reflecting agent for challenging
puzzles and games from the BALROG benchmarking suite.
In Part IV we switch gears, from theoretical concepts to practical implementations.
We provide a discussion of the frameworks that have been developed in the commu-
nity to implement agentic LLMs, and for them to use tools to act in the world. Some
are proprietary, but many are open, and can be downloaded from Github. In this part,
we discuss agents that act and perform practical tasks for their users. In Chapter 11
we discuss toolchains, frameworks and APIs that have been developed to implement
agentic LLMs. In Chapter 12 we discuss retrieval augmentation methods and other
methods to search for up to date information that was not available when the LLM was
trained. Chapter 13 provides an overview of practical applications of agentic LLMs.
We discuss applications of LLMs such as shopping assistants, medical assistants, trad-
ing assistants, and assistants that help perform scientific research. In the final chapter
of Part IV we conclude with a practical case study of how to build a medical diagno-
sis agent (also to help you understand its shortcomings, so that you will never blindly
follow an agent’s medical advice).
Part V takes a different point of view: we look at agentic LLMs through a behav-
ioral and cognitive lens, rather than a technical one. After defining and introducing
machine-behavioral research in general, Chapter 15 discusses single LLMs and agen-
tic LLMs in controlled, experimental settings to test their social behavior. Chapter 16
shifts to multi-agent systems, first discussing role-based interactions, where agentic
LLMs are built or prompted to perform a certain role and interact in goal-directed
ways. Next, in Chapter 17 we move to systems comprising multiple agents that in-
teract in open-ended ways and study emergent behaviors, such as cooperation and
norm-enforcement. The case study allows you to experience social agentic behavior
in-depth.
The next part, Part VI, contains more advanced material. Chapter 19 discusses
synthetic data generation. Like all forms of deep learning, LLMs remain to a large
extent a black box, and we discuss techniques that can lift a corner of the veil. Chap-
ter 20 discusses advanced architectures. We discuss transformers that are trained on
decision traces, and looped and recursive LLMs. We also discuss advanced agentic ar-
chitectures: in-context reinforcement learning, self-modifying agents and meta agents.
Chapter 21 focuses on tools from mechanistic interpretability to map patterns of neu-
ronal activity in transformer architectures, allowing to better understand the reasoning
processes of LLMs. In Chapter 22 we review recent literature on behavior and cog-
nition in Agentic LLMs, including advanced questions on Theory of Mind and con-
sciousness.
Finally, in Part VII we draw together the elements of agentic LLMs that are pro-
vided in this book. In Chapter 23 we discuss what agentic LLMs currently can do,
what they still can not do, and we conclude with a vision on what the future of agentic
LLMs might bring.
Note that some of the Chapters and Sections are marked with a *. These contain
more advanced material, that might be better suited for a thesis than for a course.

In this first part we discuss the basics of language modeling and machine learning.
We start with basic principles of how language can be modeled, using tokens and em-
beddings. Next, the attention concept is discussed, a concept that is at the foundation
of the transformer architecture, and the success of large language models. We will also
review two important machine learning techniques: supervised learning and reinforce-
ment learning. In the next chapter, we become more concrete, and discuss the steps of a
typical training pipeline, from pretraining and finetuning to inference. We also discuss
common benchmarks in that chapter. The final content chapter of this first part is about
the large part of large language models: we discuss how performance of LLMs scales
with parameter count, training data and compute, and we delve into efficient models
that benefit from scale while minimizing cost. At the end of the part, we turn to a
hands-on case study, where you will learn how everything comes together when you
create your own tiny large language model from scratch.

Chapter 2

Foundations of Language
Modeling with LLMs


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how natural language can be processed in machine
learning models. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Describe the core concepts of language modeling, including tokenization and
early word-representation methods, and explain what problem each was de-
signed to solve.
• Distinguish the learning regimes used to build a language model—supervised,
autoregressive, and reinforcement—and state what each contributes to the final
model.
• Explain how embeddings represent word meaning as vectors, and predict how
semantically related words are positioned relative to one another.
• Explain how the attention mechanism forms flexible, context-dependent connec-
tions between tokens, and trace how a query, key, and value interact for a given
input.
• Describe how the transformer architecture is built from attention, and identify
its main components.
• Contrast encoder (classification) and decoder (generation) models, and select
the appropriate one for a given NLP task.

2.1
Processing Natural Language

Language is the primary medium through which humans communicate. Language
comes in forms spanning from printed books, digital media to spoken discourse. Lan-
guage research has long been a focal point of multidisciplinary research. Within the
context of artificial intelligence and computer science, language is of particular signifi-
cance: we use it to articulate complex ideas, we formulate algorithms in programming

29

## Page 30

30
CHAPTER 2. FOUNDATIONS OF LANGUAGE MODELING

Figure 2.1: A typical conversation with ELIZA

languages, and we use it to facilitate interaction between software and its users.
For decades, a key aim of AI has been to unlock the ability for machines to under-
stand human-produced language, as is argued by Jurafsky and Martin \[2025\] in their
major textbook of the field. Research in this area is combined in the field of Natu-
ral Language Processing (NLP) and its counterpart, Computational Linguistics.1 In
this chapter, we provide an overview of the complexities of capturing natural (human)
language by computational means, and outline the evolution of various fundamental
techniques over the years for achieving such understanding.
One of the early goals of the fields has been to achieve the dream of practical ma-
chine translation. Since its inception in the 1950’s \[Hutchins, 1999\], human language
processing technology has evolved greatly. Extensive research progress has allowed it
to have a profound impact across industries. This widespread industrial adoption has,
in turn, emerged as a vital driving force for application-oriented development. In NLP,
fundamental theoretical research and practical, real-world utility, go hand in hand. As
a consequence, the application areas have expanded beyond machine translation.
Recently, the impact of language technology on society has truly exploded. We
interact on a daily basis with chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude. We can do so
in multiple languages, and enhanced search engines have been incorporated in many
popular products. However, these developments stand on the shoulders of many earlier
results. A famous early example is ELIZA, the psychotherapist chatbot developed in
1966 by Joseph Weizenbaum \[Weizenbaum, 1966\]. ELIZA was a rudimentary chatbot
based on simple rule-based word substitutions (see Figure 2.1). ELIZA was already
ascribed human-like qualities. Since these early days of rule-based systems for text
processing, where we identify words based on specific delimiters (such as white space),
we have come a long way.

1Originally further apart, the two fields have been growing closer in recent years, one starting from the
linguistic side, the other from the computational side.

2.1.1
Language Understanding and Language Generation

Before considering how computers process language, we will consider how humans
understand language.
A key observation is that communication is a sequential process, and that languages
are shaped accordingly. Words are uttered one at a time, and are also consumed one
at a time. This parallel holds both for human and mechanical processing of language:
language is a sequence of characters (when reading), syllables (when speaking), or
entire words (for early computational models of language).
We will now look deeper into the technology developed for working with natural
language sequences. This technology is categorized as either natural language under-
standing or natural language generation. We will briefly describe both categories.

Natural Language Understanding
Natural language understanding (NLU) focuses
on developing methods for capturing meaning and intent. Approaches and techniques
for NLU map unstructured human language elements onto a structured format such that
a computer can interpret and act upon them. Such techniques can involve several layers
of processing, inspired by linguistic analysis (as visualized in Figure 2.2), as follows:

• Tokenization: determine boundaries between meaningful linguistic elements (such
as words) to be used for further processing.

• Syntactic Parsing: determine the grammatical structure (such as subjects, verbs,
and objects).

• Named Entity Recognition (NER): identify and categorize key entities such as
names, dates, and locations.

• Sentiment Analysis: detect the emotional tone of a text.

• Co-reference Resolution: determine what person or items are referred to in ref-
erential expressions (such as: the computer talked to me).

## Page 32

32
CHAPTER 2. FOUNDATIONS OF LANGUAGE MODELING

• Discourse Analysis: understand how the meaning of a sentence is influenced by
preceding sentences.

One of the primary challenges in NLU is dealing with ambiguity \[Roth, 1998, Liu
et al., 2023\]. Human language is rife with ambiguity. Examples are polysemy (words
with multiple meanings, such as bank) and context-dependent nuances that require
world knowledge to decode correctly. Many more challenges exist; naturally occurring
human language is as rich and complex as humans are.

Natural Language Generation
Natural language generation (NLG) focuses on de-
veloping methods for producing readable, natural-sounding human language. Tasks
range from free-form language generation, to the transformation of structured data or
model representations into realistic utterances.
An important NLG task is language modeling (LM). In language modeling, the
task is to predict the next element in a sequence, given the previous context. Mathe-
matically, this involves assigning a probability distribution over sequences of words.
Traditionally, finding this distribution was achieved using simple count-based models,
often relying on further simplifying assumptions to predict a word based on a fixed
window of preceding words.
Modern approaches use elaborate neural methods that can generate fluent sentences
based on a long context, that often appear meaningful to a human observer.2 Note that
effective language generation requires more than just grammatical correctness; it re-
quires coherence (logical flow) and cohesion (linguistic links). Current NLG systems
use sampling methods, ensembles, and many other mechanisms to balance the creativ-
ity and predictability of the text that they produce, to ensure that the output feels natural
rather than robotic \[Li and Jurafsky, 2017, Dong et al., 2022, Gatt and Krahmer, 2018\].
Techniques for NLG are commonly categorized into two approaches:

• Extractive Generation: Selecting and rearranging existing segments of text (often
used in early summarization tools).

• Abstractive Generation: Generating entirely new sentences from scratch (as mod-
ern models such as ChatGPT do).

Most LLMs use the abstractive approach.
We will now discuss early, fundamental, approaches to language modeling. We
will start by discussing the complexity of language, and then discuss the principle
of distributional representation, tokenization methods, and early language modeling
representations.

2.1.2
Complexity of Natural Language

There are many reasons why natural language can be difficult for a machine to interpret.
Language exhibits subtle nuances that carry meaning or distort it. Capturing the full
nuance of language requires more than understanding its structure. Furthermore, the

2Which is by itself not always difficult to achieve, as we saw in the ELIZA example.

## Page 33

2.1. PROCESSING NATURAL LANGUAGE
33

context in which something is said plays a role in communication. Understanding
goes beyond the words themselves to grasp the intentions, implications, and subtleties
embedded in communication \[Wittgenstein, 1953, Grice, 1975, Krause and Vossen,
2024\]. Below, we introduce topics that are studied in the field of linguistics, each of
which brings about a different view on what language is capable of expressing.

Syntax
Syntax rules govern the structure of sentences. In the study of linguistics,
syntax refers to the set of rules, principles, and processes that regulate the structure of
sentences in a given language. Linguistic syntax examines the underlying logic that
allows a speaker to combine words into well-formed and meaningful sequences. In
English, for example, the most common order is subject-verb-object: in cat bites dog
the verb bites follows the subject cat, indicating that the meaning of the sentence is that
it was the cat that was doing the biting (and not the dog).

Morphology
Morphology is the study of how words change shape depending on
their grammatical function. How words change shape is related to syntax, and the
morphological rules (and their exceptions) depend on the language (family). In the
preceding example sentence, the shape of the verb to bite changed to bites, where the
-s indicates simple present tense (it is happening now, by a singular actor, not by a
posse of felines in ancient times).

Semantics
In linguistics, lexical semantics is the study of the meaning of words. In
natural languages words derive their meaning from their relationship to other words.
For instance, words with nearly identical meanings form synonyms, such as car and
automobile or vanish and disappear; words with opposite meanings form antonyms,
such as hot and cold or buy and sell. Many more relationships exist.
In NLP, computational semantics is the study of how we can represent that mean-
ing efficiently in a computer. A basic approach for storing a sentence in a computer
memory would be to simply use a sequence of indices into a vector of the words of a
language. However, this encoding only records the occurrence of the words, but not
the relationships between the words; the semantics of the words are no longer present
in this naive representation.
Words derive their meaning from their relationship to other words, and we need
a way to efficiently encode these relationships. As we will see later in this chapter,
different solutions have been developed over the years, including the transformer ar-
chitecture and the attention mechanism.

Pragmatics
In addition to the literal meaning of words, humans care about the intent
of the speaker and the context of the utterance. The way language is employed in spe-
cific social contexts determines its effect (meaning is use \[Baker and Hacker, 2008\]).
The study of the implicit, everyday rules humans naturally follow to ensure that our
communication is effective is called pragmatics.
A set of foundational principles are the Gricean Maxims \[Grice, 1975\]: the unspo-
ken cooperative principles that humans use to infer meaning. For instance, the maxim
of quantity states that humans provide exactly as much information as is required for

## Page 34

34
CHAPTER 2. FOUNDATIONS OF LANGUAGE MODELING

the conversation. These maxims shape our communication, and help make our lan-
guage understandable and cooperative. For a machine, interpreting sarcasm, subtext,
or placeholders (e.g., “thingy”) requires knowledge of these rules, beyond adherance
to a static dictionary.

Discourse
Language rarely occurs in isolated sentences; language is structured into
larger units such as paragraphs, conversations, or full documents. The study of dis-
course focuses on how sentences connect to form a cohesive and coherent whole. For
a machine to truly interpret a text, it must be able to track entities across multiple
sentences, a task known as co-reference resolution (e.g., determining whether the pro-
noun it refers to the cat, the dog, or the bite from a previous sentence). Understanding
discourse is vital for complex NLP tasks such as document summarization, machine
translation, and sustaining long-form dialogue.
In addition to these topics, other fields of study exist, such as phonetics (the sounds
of a language that carry additional meaning in human communication), sociolinguistics
(how language varies according to social factors like class or region), lexicography (the
science of compiling dictionaries), and many more.
As this overview may have highlighted, the generation and understanding of natural
languages are large and challenging fields. It is important to realize that language is
not static. Language varies over time, across geographical locations, between different
cultures, and depending on the medium through which it is communicated :-). This
variation makes the creation of language technology a difficult and never-ending quest.
Before we introduce the recent technologies that provide at least a partial answer
to these challenges, we discuss the fundamental assumptions that inspired the modern
turn in NLP.
Representing natural language in a computer is difficult because natural language
is rich and complex. In the remainder of this section, we discuss the principle of dis-
tributional representation, which states that the semantic meaning of a word is driven
by the context that surrounds that word. Next, we will look at tokenization methods:
methods for splitting sentences into words. Finally we will discuss how we can work
with vectors of tokens to arrive at a representation that encodes meaning.

2.1.3
Distributional Representations

How can we teach a machine to understand complex semantic relationships and gram-
matical structures without manually encoding them all? The answer lies in the distribu-
tional hypothesis, a foundational concept in modern NLP. The core idea was articulated
in the late 1950s:

You shall know a word by the company it keeps. (Firth, 1957)

This suggests that the meaning of a word can be inferred from the words around it (con-
texts) in which it typically appears. Words that appear in similar contexts are likely to
have similar meanings. For example, if the words coffee and tea both frequently appear
near verbs like drink, sip, or brew, then a machine may infer that there is a semantic
relationship between them, without explicit definitions or other human-provided infor-
mation.

## Page 35

2.1. PROCESSING NATURAL LANGUAGE
35

Figure 2.3: Illustration of vector arithmetic with word2vec embeddings \[Singerep,
2022\].

To operationalize the distributional hypothesis for computational purposes, we will
rely on linear algebra and turn to a framework known as vector semantics. We represent
words as points in a high-dimensional continuous space. Words with similar meanings
are mapped to points close to each other in this space, and we can measure semantic
similarity using geometric distance measures such as cosine similarity (see Figure 2.3
and Section 2.3.1). Furthermore, we can make modifications to word meaning by doing
vector arithmetic. Early implementations relied on sparse co-occurrence matrices to
construct semantic vectors, where individual words were counted inside their context,
much like other methods described in Section 2.1.5. Modern approaches favor dense,
low-dimensional vectors, often referred to as word embeddings. These representations
are typically learned by training a neural model to predict a word from its neighbors or
vice versa, a breakthrough popularized by the word2vec architecture \[Mikolov et al.,
2013\].
While learning vector-based representations for words is an effective way to capture
meaning, maintaining a distinct vector for every unique word in a language results in
an impractically large vocabulary.
Furthermore, strict word-level approaches struggle to process rare or entirely un-
seen words, as the model has no pre-existing vector for them. Hence, before a model
can assign vectors to linguistic units, we must first determine what those fundamental
units actually are. To address these inefficiencies and handle out-of-vocabulary inputs,
modern methods use a systematic approach to break down raw text into more manage-
able pieces. This process is called tokenization, which we will now discuss.

## Page 36

36
CHAPTER 2. FOUNDATIONS OF LANGUAGE MODELING

2.1.4
Tokenization

Before computers can ascribe meaning to language, they must first have a way to digest
it. Assuming that we already have raw text at our disposal, whether scraped from the
web or transcribed from speech, the immediate challenge is determining how to split
these continuous character strings into meaningful units, or how to split sentences into
words. This process is called tokenization. However, a robust tokenization strategy
must do much more than simply divide sentences by spaces to obtain words; it needs
to be able to handle the nuances of different languages and dialects, parse complex
punctuation, and even account for modern additions like emojis, and fit these into a
vocabulary of fixed size.
This process of segmentation is a key step to many NLP pipelines. While dividing
text might appear straightforward, ambiguities in punctuation complicate the process,
such as in abbreviations (N.L.P. or NLP?). Simple rule-based segmenters frequently
fail against the structural irregularities of natural language. Consequently, there are
different approaches for constructing these units, as shown in Example 1.

Example 1 (Tokenization Strategies). Consider the following sentence:
“Leiden is beautiful in summer.”

Word Tokenization
This approach typically splits text by spaces and punctuation.
\["Leiden", "is", "beautiful", "in", "summer", "."\]

Character Tokenization
This approach breaks the text down into individual characters.
\["L", "e", "i", "d", "e", "n", " ", "i", "s", " ", "b",
"e", "a", "u", "t", "i", "f", "u", "l", " ", "i", "n",
" ", "s", "u", "m", "m", "e", "r", "."\]

Subword Tokenization (e.g., WordPiece)
This approach preserves common words as whole tokens but breaks down com-
plex or rare words into foundational subwords.
\["Lei", "##den", "is", "beautiful", "in", "summer",
"."\]

Word-Level Tokenization
This approach treats each space-separated string as a to-
ken that is unique. While it preserves syntactic structure, it results in impractically large
vocabularies and suffers from the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem, where models fail
on words that were not seen during training.
Large vocabularies are problematic due to the mechanics of one-hot encoding. If
every word 𝑤in a vocabulary 𝑉is represented as a vector x ∈{0, 1}|𝑉|, where only the
index corresponding to 𝑤is 1, the dimensionality |𝑉| scales linearly with the size of the

## Page 37

2.1. PROCESSING NATURAL LANGUAGE
37

vocabulary. As these one-hot vectors will later form the input to our neural networks,
for texts that do not contain all words in a certain vocabulary, we end up creating sparse,
computationally inefficient representations that fail to capture semantic relationships
between words.

Character-Level Tokenization
Pure character-level modeling seems like a clear so-
lution to the problem of increasing vocabularies, and has been explored over the years
\[Mielke et al., 2021\]. Such a method divides text into individual characters, which
restricts the vocabulary to the size of the alphabet, virtually eliminating OOV issues.
However, it significantly increases sequence length and the resulting computational
burden is substantial. Furthermore, because isolated characters lack inherent semantic
meaning, the model must learn word morphology before it can grasp broader linguistic
patterns, increasing training time.

Subword Tokenization
Hence, the current standard for LLMs balances the previous
two methods. It preserves common words as whole tokens while decomposing rare
words into smaller, meaningful components. Notable implementations include:

• Byte Pair Encoding (BPE): An iterative algorithm that begins with individual
characters and merges the most frequent adjacent pairs into single tokens until a
target vocabulary size is reached \[Sennrich et al., 2016\] (e.g., highest →\[high,
est\]). BPE was originally proposed as a data compression algorithm \[Gage,
1994\].

• WordPiece: An iterative algorithm, similar to BPE, that merges pairs based on a
likelihood criterion rather than on raw frequency, aiming to maximize the prob-
ability of the training data \[Wu et al., 2016\].

2.1.5
Early Methods for Language Representation

After tokenization, the next question is how to combine our linguistic units (tokens)
into coherent sentences, that carry meaning? We start with the observation that the
ordering of these units in human language is dictated by strict syntactic and semantic
rules. Now, if our computational approaches would be able to accurately produce sensi-
ble text sequences, then we might say that they possess the same syntactic and semantic
understanding (or at least that they are able to reproduce such understanding).
How can we build mathematical representations that achieve this goal? A core task
in this endeavor is language modeling. Mathematically speaking, a language model is a
function that computes the joint probability of a sequence of words occurring together
in a specific context. By calculating this probability, models can distinguish between a
logical, fluent sentence and a random sequence of tokens. For example, in English, the
sequence the cat sat is significantly more probable than sat cat the because it adheres
to established syntactic rules.
Because written language is sequential, estimating the joint probability of a sen-
tence is inherently a sequence estimation problem. The overarching goal of language

## Page 38

38
CHAPTER 2. FOUNDATIONS OF LANGUAGE MODELING

modeling is to quantify the statistical likelihood that a given sentence, 𝑆, occurs within
a specific language, based on its sequence of constituent words 𝑤1, . . . , 𝑤𝑘:

𝑃(𝑆) = 𝑃(𝑤1, . . . , 𝑤𝑘)
(2.1)

For sentences of arbitrary length, calculating this exact joint probability directly
is computationally intractable, due to the exponentially large number of word combi-
nations in any given vocabulary. To resolve this complexity, we often decompose the
joint probability, using the chain rule of probability. By making specific mathematical
assumptions regarding conditional independence, this decomposition allows the com-
putation to remain tractable for real-world applications \[Jurafsky and Martin, 2025\]:

𝑃(𝑤1, . . . , 𝑤𝑘) = 𝑃(𝑤1)

𝑘
Ö

𝑖=2
𝑃(𝑤𝑖| 𝑤1, . . . , 𝑤𝑖−1)
(2.2)

By maximizing this joint probability, probabilistic models learn to favor grammat-
ically and logically sound sequences. The learned probabilistic distributions effec-
tively reverse engineer the complex, unwritten rules of human language \[Manning and
Schutze, 1999\]. To estimate these probabilities from a segmented text corpus, early
methods relied on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). The simplest approach com-
putes the marginal probability of a word based on its relative frequency in the corpus:

𝑃(𝑤) =
count(𝑤in corpus)
total number of words
(2.3)

To make the computation of these conditional probabilities manageable, researchers
rely on 𝑛-gram models. An 𝑛-gram is a contiguous sequence of 𝑛items from a given
sample of text. Instead of calculating the probability of a word given its entire preced-
ing history, which quickly becomes computationally intractable, 𝑛-gram models apply
the Markov assumption. This assumption states that the probability of the next word
depends only on the preceding 𝑛−1 words, effectively truncating the context. For
example, a bi-gram model (𝑛= 2) approximates the history by looking solely at the
immediately preceding word. The conditional probability is then calculated by taking
the frequency of the two words occurring together and dividing it by the frequency of
the first word alone,

𝑃(𝑤𝑖| 𝑤1, . . . , 𝑤𝑖−1) ≈𝑃(𝑤𝑖| 𝑤𝑖−1) = count(𝑤𝑖−1, 𝑤𝑖)

count(𝑤𝑖−1)
(2.4)

Likewise, a tri-gram model (𝑛= 3) conditions on the previous two words. This
simplification drastically reduces the computational burden and makes it feasible to
estimate probabilities directly from a corpus.
Selecting the appropriate 𝑛involves a critical trade-off. A larger 𝑛captures richer
contextual information and deeper syntactic dependencies, resulting in a model that
generates a more natural language. Yet, increasing 𝑛exponentially exacerbates the
sparsity problem: highly specific word sequences appear far less frequently in the train-
ing data, and the model will increasingly encounter zero probabilities. Conversely, a
smaller 𝑛yields robust, frequent counts but severely limits the model’s understanding
of broader semantic meaning and long-distance dependencies within the sentence.

## Page 39

2.2. MACHINE LEARNING METHODS FOR NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING39

In a standard language model computation, observing an unseen 𝑛-gram results in
a probability of zero, as it nullifies the joint probability of the entire sentence via mul-
tiplication. To mitigate this counterintuitive behavior, total counts are often smoothed.
A common technique is Laplace (or add-one) smoothing, which adds a fictitious count
of 1 to every possible vocabulary item. To maintain a valid probability distribution, the
denominator is adjusted by adding the vocabulary size, |𝑉|:

𝑃Laplace(𝑤) =
count(𝑤in corpus) + 1
total number of words + |𝑉|
(2.5)

These probabilistic and count-based methods ultimately yield a numerical repre-
sentation of language. A strong representation encodes the properties we intuitively
grasp about a word: its meaning, its grammatical function, and its relationship with
other words. In early NLP, these relative frequencies and co-occurrence counts were
structured into vectors, representing words based on their distribution in the text.
While count-based representations are tractable, they result in vectors that are high-
dimensional and sparse, leading to computational inefficiencies and poor generalization
on unseen data. Consequently, modern NLP has transitioned toward learning dense,
low-dimensional vector representations, known as embeddings, using neural networks.
Instead of relying on explicit counting, these models learn continuous representations
as a byproduct of predicting a word from its surrounding context, capturing deeper
semantic relationships in a more efficient format. These modern approaches will be
discussed in Section 2.3. First we will have a brief intermezzo where we review three
important machine learning approaches.

2.2
Machine Learning Methods For Natural Language
Processing

Having established a primer on language representation, we will now turn to the learn-
ing algorithms that allow us to create the large models powering modern AI systems.
LLMs are trained using methods from the broader field of machine learning. While
machine learning is an extensive field of research, understanding LLMs requires fa-
miliarity with three core paradigms, and how they are used in language modeling:
supervised learning, autoregressive learning, and reinforcement learning. We briefly
touch upon these essential methods and refer to standard works for deeper exploration.

2.2.1
Supervised Learning

Supervised learning is the foundation of machine learning. It is named so because
it relies on a set of labels, that must be given beforehand, that supervise the training
process. This approach utilizes a dataset consisting of paired examples and labels,
𝐷= {(𝑥𝑖, 𝑦𝑖)}, to train the parameters 𝜃of a predictive model 𝑓𝜃. The model can be
used to compute an estimate ˆ𝑦for each input 𝑥, denoted mathematically as 𝑓𝜃(𝑥) →ˆ𝑦.
Using the model to compute this estimate is also known as inference, or the forward
pass.

## Page 40

40
CHAPTER 2. ML METHODS FOR NLP

After the forward pass, we can use a loss function L to compute some kind of
difference between the estimate ˆ𝑦and the true label 𝑦. Common examples of loss
functions are the sum of squared-difference loss from statistical regression L = Í
𝑖( ˆ𝑦𝑖−
𝑦𝑖)2, or the cross-entropy loss for classification L = −Í
𝑐𝑦𝑐log( ˆ𝑦𝑐).
The goal of a supervised training algorithm is to minimize the sum of the losses
over the dataset of example pairs by adjusting the parameters. This is done in the
backward pass. Here, the loss function is used to compute an error signal to adjust
the parameters 𝜃of the model 𝑓so that the next forward pass achieves a lower loss
(backpropagation of the error). Minimizing the loss function on the examples from a
data set is a process called training. A single training run of forward and backward
passes over all of the training data is called an epoch (for efficiency reasons, epochs
can be split into training batches).
After training, to see if our model 𝑓𝜃works well—if it generalizes to unseen
examples—it is tested on new examples, that were not part of the training set.
If the accuracy on the training set is high, we say that the model trains well (training
converges). If the accuracy on the test set is also high, then we say that the model
generalizes well and we have achieved our training goal. Informally speaking, if the
accuracy of the model on the training set is high, but on the test set it is low, we say the
model overfits on the training set. This usually means that the model has trained for too
long or has too many parameters, so that it models not only the signal in the training
set but also the noise. If the model has low accuracy on both training and test set, we
say that it underfits. This is most likely due to too short training, or a model that is too
simple (too few trainable parameters) to model the complexities of the data.
Generally speaking, problems with few variables (low-dimensional problems, such
as simple regression) require smaller models (fewer parameters) and less training data
to perform well. Problems with many variables (high-dimensional problems, such as
image classification) require larger models with many millions of parameters (often
deep neural networks) and large training datasets to perform well. Indeed, break-
through performance in image classification \[Krizhevsky et al., 2012\] was only achieved
after the construction of a large dataset with millions of hand-labeled images, Imagenet
\[Deng et al., 2009\].
Supervised learning is the basis of machine learning. Many good text books have
been written about the topic \[Bishop and Bishop, 2023, Goodfellow et al., 2016\]. It is
one of the core techniques in LLM training, for example in supervised finetuning, as
we will see in the next chapter.

2.2.2
Autoregressive Learning

Large language models are trained autoregressively. In this training approach, there is
no dataset of pairs of labeled examples, but there is a lot of (textual) data available.
Autoregressive learning is a form of self-supervised learning, without explicit labels,
using the inherent sequential nature of the data, to predict the next token.
In autoregressive pretraining of language models, our algorithm performs predic-
tions over the dataset where each token 𝑦= 𝑥𝑡is taken as a label for preceding example
tokens x = 𝑥𝑡−1. Autoregressive learning is a core task of modern NLP, and is used in
contemporary model training pipelines \[Radford et al., 2018\] and included in textbooks

2.2.3
Reinforcement Learning

Both supervised and autogregressive learning need a dataset of training data to train
on—they train offline on pre-existing data. However, sometimes no dataset is available,
but we may have access to a function that can tell us when we are in a good state or
in a bad state. In that case, an online learning method called reinforcement learning
(RL) can be used, where an agent performs an action 𝑎to bring an environment from
state 𝑠to the next state 𝑠′, after which the environment reports back the reward 𝑟(𝑠′)
of that new state. (The method is called online because it generates its training data
on the fly, while training.) The agent can then use this reward information to adjust a
𝜃-parameterized behavior policy function 𝜋𝜃(𝑠) →𝑎to know which action to perform
in which state. When the problem at hand is as a sequential decision problem, actions 𝑎
take the system from state 𝑠to another state 𝑠′, and rewards depend on actions taken in
the past (the credit assignment problem: to which actions should rewards be assigned?).
Repeating the state/action/reward process can cause the agent to explore the entire state
space, and learn an optimal policy 𝜋∗(𝑠) of which action to take, for all states.
Note that reinforcement learning, being online, is inherently circular. At the start,
the policy 𝜋has seen few rewards, and has useful information on which action to take
for just a few states. If it would greedily use this information on which good action to
take, it would traverse only a limited part of the environment, and the optimal policy
that it would find would be only locally optimum. To find better optima, it should
explore, and try random actions, ideally to cover the entire state space.
Reinforcement is a form of active agentic learning from feedback from an environ-
ment. A key observation is that it is typically easier to see if an output is good (reward
function), than to create a full new one (labeled dataset). Many reinforcement learning
algorithms have been developed that focus on good exploration methods. Reinforce-
ment learning problems are formally modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP),
consisting of a state representation 𝑆, an action function 𝐴(𝑠), a transition function
𝑇(𝑠, 𝑎) →𝑠′, and a reward function 𝑅(𝑠). Rewards are numeric indications of the
quality of a state, provided by the environment. They can be positive or negative. The
goal of an agent is to find the policy 𝜋(𝑠) of optimal actions 𝑎∗in each state 𝑠. Fig-
ure 2.4 illustrates how a reinforcement learning agent learns a policy with an action
for each state, online, through interaction with the environment, which can compute

## Page 42

42
CHAPTER 2. ML METHODS FOR NLP

functions 𝑇and 𝑅(the environment will answer the agent’s question as to what the
next state is that resulted from its action, and how good that state is).
When the state space is small enough to fit in a computer memory, we can use ex-
act tabular reinforcement learning methods, such as Q-learning \[Watkins and Dayan,
1992\]. For larger problems, function approximation methods are used (deep neural
networks) such as deep Q-learning (DQN) \[Mnih et al., 2015\] or proximal policy op-
timization (PPO) \[Schulman et al., 2017\]. In deep reinforcement learning, the policy
is a parameterized neural network that is trained by backpropagation, as in supervised
deep learning.
Reinforcement learning is the basis of modern reasoning language models. Many
text books have been written about reinforcement learning, such as the seminal work by
Sutton and Barto \[2018\], as well as more educational texts \[Graesser and Keng, 2019,
Plaat, 2020, 2022\]. In LLM training, reinforcement learning is used in reinforcement
finetuning, and in multi-step reasoning, as we will see in Chapter 6. Furthermore,
reinforcement learning formulates machine learning problems in terms of an agent that
tries to learn how to interact in an environment, which fits the agentic LLM setting
nicely. In agentic LLMs, it is used in in-context reinforcement learning for prompt
optimization, in world models, and to model other agent behavior in relation to the
environment, as we will see later in this book.
Reinforcement learning is a popular machine learning approach since we can learn
new environments where we do not have data available. The method finds its own
data. When we consider using reinforcement learning, two questions should be an-
swered: (1) is the problem at hand a sequential decision problem, and, if so, (2) what
is the size of the state space, can we use exact tabular methods, or must we resort to
approximation?
Now that we have discussed the necessary language and machine learning princi-
ples, we turn back to language, to the next step: modeling language.

2.3
Modeling Language

After the basics of language representation and machine learning, we turn to the overar-
ching paradigms used to build computational language modeling capabilities. The de-
velopment of natural language processing is broadly characterized by three paradigms.
Each paradigm represents a fundamental shift in the type of model constructed to cap-
ture language and how the inherent complexity of human language is managed. We
will see that as we move through the paradigms, we incorporate more techniques from
machine learning, leveraging increases in compute power to process more data to train
larger and larger neural networks for language processing. The paradigms are the sym-
bolic, statistical, and neural approaches \[Kautz, 2020, Deng and Liu, 2018\].

Symbolic Methods
Often referred to as Classical AI or rule-based systems, these
early ELIZA-like symbolic approaches rely on explicit, human-defined instructions.
By treating language as a formal system, symbolic models attempt to parse meaning
deductively. While these systems are highly transparent and interpretable by design,

## Page 43

2.3. MODELING LANGUAGE
43

they are brittle, as they struggle using rigid rules (if-then-else) to handle the natural vari-
ation, idiomatic expressions, and ambiguities of real-world language. Scaling symbolic
approaches to larger language tasks requires a labor-intensive, manual enumeration of
many edge cases, which turned out to be unfeasible for all but the smallest problem
domains.

Statistical Methods
To overcome the limitations of rigid rule sets, between 1980-
1990 the field experienced an empirical shift toward probabilistic modeling with the
statistical methods. Instead of relying on explicit syntactic rules, statistical methods
such as hidden Markov models and 𝑛-gram language models leverage large text cor-
pora to compute the likelihood of word co-occurrences. This data-driven approach
scales efficiently and handles linguistic ambiguity and noise far better than its sym-
bolic predecessors. However, because these models typically rely on the Markov as-
sumption, their representation of meaning is inherently limited to local word patterns,
making them ill-equipped to capture long-distance dependencies and broader context.

Neural Methods
After approximately 2010, the contemporary state-of-the-art shifted
to neural networks and deep learning. Rather than using logic or discrete counts, neu-
ral methods represent linguistic units as dense, low-dimensional vectors in a continu-
ous semantic space. Modern architectures, particularly transformers, employ attention
mechanisms to model global context simultaneously across an entire sequence. This
approach yields impressive generalization, high fluency in text generation, and cross-
lingual capabilities. Nevertheless, these advantages come with significant trade-offs:
neural models operate largely as black boxes, sacrificing the interpretability seen in
symbolic methods, and they require large data sets and large computational resources.
The contemporary pipelines for NLP training draw inspiration from all of these
three paradigms. Before describing an example pipeline in the next chapter, we require
a deeper understanding of the core components of these parts, as they are the building
blocks for the systems on which agentic LLMs are based. In the next sections we
will discuss many topics: word embeddings, contextualized embeddings, sequence
modeling, attention, transformers, encoders (such as BERT), and decoders (such as
GPT).

2.3.1
Embeddings

Early models of neural embeddings operationalize semantic understanding of lexical
items by defining a context window, a span of 𝑛words to the left and right of a target
word, and predicting the missing focus word. For the sentence There are two cookies
left on the table, if we set a window of 𝑛= 2, the context words for cookies are are, two,
left, and on. By systematically sliding this window over a large corpus of text, we can
count how many times each word appears in the context of every other word. These
counts form the basis of a co-occurrence matrix, where each row represents a target
word and each column represents a context word. The value in each cell is the number
of times the column word appeared in the context of the row word. For example, the
vector for cherry might have a high value in the column for pie (e.g., 442) and a low

## Page 44

44
CHAPTER 2. ML METHODS FOR NLP

value for computer (e.g., 2). The vector for strawberry would show a similar pattern,
and hence reflect the semantical similarity between the two words.
By representing words as vectors, we place them in a high-dimensional vector space
where each dimension corresponds to a context word. In this space, words with similar
meanings, which share similar contexts, will point in similar directions. This geometric
relationship allows us to measure semantic similarity numerically. The most common
method for this is cosine similarity, which measures the cosine of the angle 𝜃between

Earlier, we argued that count-based vectors result in high-dimensional spaces that
scale linearly with vocabulary size. Since the number of dimensions dictates the com-
putational complexity of downstream models, we wish to keep the dimensionality in
check and instead create dense embeddings. For this, we use the classical word2vec
algorithm \[Mikolov et al., 2013\]. In this approach, a random embedding matrix 𝑊is
initialized and iteratively updated to match the intuition that similar words occur in
similar contexts. This general framework uses two distinct techniques to achieve this:
skip-gram and continuous bag-of-words, as shown in Figure 2.5.
The first, skip-gram, predicts which context words are likely to surround a given
target word. It updates the matrix to ensure that the cosine similarity between posi-
tive samples, which are actual target and context pairs, is high, while driving down
the similarity for negative samples, which are random word pairings. Because skip-
gram treats every target-context pairing as a distinct training observation, it heavily
penalizes incorrect predictions even for infrequent terms. Hence, skip-gram excels at
capturing fine-grained semantic details and produces accurate representations even for
rare words.
The second, continuous bag-of-words (CBOW), performs the reverse operation. It
predicts a single target word based on a combined set of surrounding context words. By
averaging the context vectors before predicting the target, CBOW inherently smooths
over the specific details of individual context words. This distributional smoothing is
the reason for its distinct performance profile: CBOW trains significantly faster than
skip-gram and is highly effective at capturing general syntactic relationships among
frequent words, though it sacrifices some sensitivity to a rare vocabulary.

2.3.2
Shifting to Contextualized Embeddings

Word2vec represented a major leap forward in the creation of high-quality word em-
beddings. However, a major downside is that word2vec results in static embeddings.
This means that a word is mapped to a single vector regardless of its usage (its con-
text). This creates a fundamental problem with polysemy. Consider the word bank in
two different sentences:

1. I need to go to the bank to withdraw some money.

2. The swimmer sat on the river bank.

## Page 45

2.3. MODELING LANGUAGE
45

Figure 2.5: Visualizations of the skipgram (left) and continuous bag-of-words (right)
approaches to constructing word embeddings \[Zhang et al., 2023\].

In a static model, bank has one fixed representation that must average or pick between
these disparate meanings, resulting in a vector that is neither purely financial nor purely
geographical or a weird blend of the two. Modern architectures (such as BERT and
GPT, which are discussed later in this chapter) solve this by producing contextualized
embeddings. Instead of a static look-up table, the model processes the entire sequence.
The resulting vector for bank is calculated dynamically based on the surrounding to-
kens (money, withdraw vs. river, swimmer), allowing the machine to represent the
specific nuance intended by the speaker.

2.3.3
Recurrent Neural Networks

While embeddings are capable of expressing the complex semantics of individual words,
we still need an efficient way to ingest language as a sequence. Training models for
classification tasks, for instance, requires independence assumptions to simplify com-
putational dependencies. We could take a sliding window approach to concatenate
all relevant word embeddings into a single vector to represent a sentence. However,
this rapidly increases the size of the input to any classifier, and does not scale to long
sequences of text.
In humans, the expectation of what we observe next is conditioned on the things
that we have seen (or heard) in the past. Previously, models approximated this intuition
through the independence assumption, as seen in Equation 2.2. Formally, we introduce
additional notation for our input 𝑥occurring in sequence 𝑥1, 𝑥2, . . . , 𝑥𝑡from timestep
1 through 𝑡. In this formulation, predicting the next word can be modeled as 𝑃(𝑥𝑡+1 |
𝑥1, . . . , 𝑥𝑡). Alternatively, we call 𝑥𝑡+1 the prediction 𝑦𝑡for timestep 𝑡.
To effectively observe input in sequences and produce corresponding predictions,
we must incorporate historical context into our models. This means that, in addition
to the current input, we include the previous hidden state from our model. Recurrent
neural networks (RNNs) are networks with such a cycle, where current values depend
on the input as well as the network’s state at a previous timestep. Instead of only
producing a prediction (e.g., a word or token) 𝑦𝑡, we now also keep track of a hidden
state ℎ𝑡. Formally, this is expressed in Equations 2.7 and 2.8. Figure 2.6 illustrate the
architecure of an RNN, and how we can picture its unrolling in time steps.

Figure 2.7: Repeating module of an LSTM (illustration from Chris Olah’s blog \[Olah
et al., 2015\])

ℎ𝑡= 𝑓(Uℎ𝑡−1 + W𝑥𝑡+ bh)
(2.7)

𝑦𝑡= 𝑔(Vℎ𝑡+ by)

This introduces new trainable parameter matrices U, V, W (and subsequent bias terms
b) to make sure our architecture can shape the hidden state and output logits accord-
ingly. RNNs can theoretically process infinite-length sequences, and we no longer need
the Markov assumption to account for a sparsity problem.

Training RNNs is done using backpropagation through time (BPTT), where we un-
roll the temporal dependencies to backpropagate the gradient from time step 𝑡to earlier
ones: 𝑡−1, 𝑡−2, . . . . However, because the gradients for updating the model at a timestep
depend recursively on the previous timesteps, this step is sensitive. Because of the re-
peated matrix multiplications required by the chain rule, this leads to the problem of
vanishing or exploding gradients \[Bengio et al., 1994, Pascanu et al., 2013\]. Control-
ling the flow of information in RNNs is difficult. Information from early timesteps
has relatively little impact on our gradients, compared to more recent information. In
practice, learning salient signals with RNNs is often difficult.

LSTMs
The long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture was introduced to address
the gradient problem \[Hochreiter, 1997\]. An LSTM works by controlling the flow of
information. In an LSTM network, additional gates are added to construct a context
vector, which the network will learn to add and update information to (see Figure 2.7).
Below is the mathematical definition for a single time step 𝑡for the LSTM architecture.
The LSTM maintains two states: a context state (𝑐𝑡) and a hidden state (ℎ𝑡), and uses
gates to control the flow of information:

𝑓𝑡= 𝜎(𝑈𝑓ℎ𝑡−1 + 𝑊𝑓𝑥𝑡)

𝑘𝑡= 𝑐𝑡−1 ⊙𝑓𝑡
𝑔𝑡= tanh(𝑈𝑔ℎ𝑡−1 + 𝑊𝑔𝑥𝑡)

𝑖𝑡= 𝜎(𝑈𝑖ℎ𝑡−1 + 𝑊𝑖𝑥𝑡)

𝑗𝑡= 𝑔𝑡⊙𝑖𝑡
𝑐𝑡= 𝑗𝑡+ 𝑘𝑡
𝑜𝑡= 𝜎(𝑈𝑜ℎ𝑡−1 + 𝑊𝑜𝑥𝑡)

ℎ𝑡= 𝑜𝑡⊙tanh(𝑐𝑡)

In the notation above, ⊙denotes the element-wise multiplication of two vectors, also
called the Hadamard product. Besides LSTMs, there are subsequent variants such
as the gated recurrent unit (GRU) that balance the computational complexity and the
number of trainable parameters \[Cho et al., 2014\].
Recurrent neural networks played an important role in language modeling. For
further explanations of how RNNs, LSTMs, and GRUs, work, see for example Olah
et al. \[2015\], Bishop and Bishop \[2023\], Goodfellow et al. \[2014\].

Encoder-Decoder
So far, we have formulated our task as the language modeling
task: how to predict the next word, given a context of preceding words. However, there
is an alternative task formulation that is useful to introduce.
Consider the problem of machine translation. While this looks like the previous
tasks of predicting token 𝑥𝑡+1 based on inputs 𝑥1, . . . , 𝑥𝑡, we are now dealing with
a sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) problem: we need to process an input sentence
𝑥1, . . . , 𝑥𝑛in one language, and output a translated sentence 𝑦1, . . . , 𝑦𝑚in another.
Why is translation a seq2seq problem? Note that 𝑛and 𝑚can be different from each
other and that translations may not preserve order, as in the English to Dutch translation
example below:

We will celebrate the relief of Leiden (7 words)

Wij gaan Leids Ontzet vieren (5 words)

The encoder-decoder architecture is a powerful framework designed to handle sequence-
to-sequence tasks where the input and output lengths may differ. The encoder and
decoder are two distinct RNNs that work together to map a variable-length input to a
variable-length output. The job of the encoder is to process the input sequence one step
at a time and compress the information into a fixed-length vector, often called the con-

## Page 48

48
CHAPTER 2. ML METHODS FOR NLP

Figure 2.8: Illustration of the Encoder-Decoder architecture

text vector.3 This forces the information into a bottleneck: compressing information
of an input sequence 𝑥1, . . . , 𝑥𝑡into a single hidden vector. However, this process is
difficult to model and there is a loss of information. See Figure 2.8 for an illustration
of the architecture.
The context vector acts as the bridge between the encoder and the decoder. It is the
final hidden state of the encoder that is passed to the decoder as its initial hidden state.
This vector encodes the semantic meaning of the entire source sentence, so the decoder
can begin generating the target sequence accurately. The decoder is a second RNN that
produces output tokens, conditioned on the context vector. Its goal is to generate the
output sequence one token at a time. This continues until a special end-of-sequence
token is generated. This approach works well, in principle. However, forcing a long
input sentence into a single, fixed-length context vector causes information loss (the
bottleneck problem). Moreover, RNNs struggle to remember the beginning of long
sequences by the time they reach the end. These two problems combined prompted the
development of a more dynamic approach for passing information between the encoder
and decoder, which we will discuss next.

2.3.4
Attention

In search for a solution to the bottleneck problem, researchers looked for ways to ef-
ficiently pass information from across the entire sequence into the decoder. During
the generation process, the decoder could then decide which of the parts in the input
sequence were relevant for decoding the next word.
This search has lead to advanced mechanisms for attention \[Bahdanau et al., 2015,
Kim et al., 2017\]. The effect of the attention mechanism is illustrated in Figure 2.9,
where translation performance (in terms of BLEU score \[Papineni et al., 2002\], higher
is better) is plotted. The architecture using the attention mechanism (called RNNsearch,
see Figure 2.9) shows a consistent ability to achieve high translation quality especially
for long sentences. The standard RNN encoder-decoder model (RNNenc) suffers a
sharp drop in performance as sentence length increases.
The intuition behind attention is to include a linear combination of all encoder
hidden states in the context vector, instead of relying on a single final hidden state.
This allows the model to look back at specific parts of the input sequence that are

relevant to the current word being generated. We can control how much focus each
input token 𝑥𝑖receives by adjusting its weight 𝑎𝑖in the linear combination, as shown
in Equation 2.9. Here, c𝑗is the context vector for the 𝑗-th output, and ℎ𝑖represents the

The weights 𝑎(often called attention weights) are not fixed; they are computed
dynamically. A key observation is that we can make use of the hidden states ℎ𝑖, which
are a representation of the semantics of a token or word. We can find out how relevant
one hidden state is to another, by comparing them, for example by computing their
cosine similarity. The softmax-normalized dot product is a common approach:

1. Compare the current decoder state with each encoder hidden state by applying a
similarity function (such as a dot product) to see how well they match.

2. Pass these scores through a softmax function so they sum to 1, effectively creat-
ing a probability distribution over the input tokens.

While attention improved accuracy, the challenge of efficient computation of RNNs
still remained to be solved. Because RNNs process tokens one by one (sequentially),
they cannot take full advantage of modern parallel computing hardware in GPUs. To
be able to scale to large datasets the recurrence should be removed entirely. This
can be achieved by going from a sequential structure to a parallel one with a fixed
context width that processes all tokens in parallel.
This is achieved through self-

types of relationships. One head might learn to look for grammatical structure, while
another learns to look for pronouns, and another for entities. The heads all work in
