2.3.5
Transformers

How can we use the attention mechanism to build an architecture for language mod-
eling? We will now discuss one such architecture, the transformer architecture, intro-
duced in the seminal work by Vaswani et al. \[2017\].
The attention mechanism is the core of the transformer architecture. The original
transformer architecture, shown in Figure 2.10, consists of both an encoder and a de-
coder. The left side of the Figure shows the encoder stack, the right side shows the
decoder stack. Most LLMs are decoder-only transformers.
The Figure shows transformer blocks that each consist of a self-attention module,
a feed-forward network, a normalization layer, and residual connections from input to
output. In most LLMs many transformer blocks are stacked on each other, in layers.
For example, GPT-2 consists of 12 layers or more, depending on the version of the
model.
Let us now have a closer look at the transformer architecture (please refer to the
Figure). The full architecture consists of three main types of elements: embedding,
transformer blocks, and output probabilities:

1. Embedding: First, the input text is tokenized, and projected into low dimensional
embedding vectors. Positional encoding is added to the embedding to preserve

## Page 51

2.3. MODELING LANGUAGE
51

Figure 2.10: Visualization of the Transformer architecture \[Godoy, 2020, Vaswani
et al., 2017\]

word order.

2. Transformer Blocks: The transformer blocks are the main feature of the archi-
tecture. Most models consist of multiple layers of transformer blocks. Within
each layer, each block consists of three elements:

• Self-attention Mechanism: The attention mechanism allows long range
connections between tokens, capturing contextual information and relation-
ships between tokens. Multiple attention heads allow the model to consider
these relationships from different perspectives, for example, for short-range
syntactic links, and for broader semantic context.
For an encoder stack, transformers use self-attention. For a decoder stack,
they use masked self-attention, to prevent looking at the future.

• Multi-layer Perceptron: A fully-connected feed-forward network operates
on each token independently. The attention layer makes connections be-
tween tokens, whereas the MLP can refine each token’s representation.

• Normalization: In most transformer blocks typical deep learning methods
such as normalization, regularization (dropouts), and residual connections
are added, to prevent vanishing or exploding gradients, and to improve sta-
ble training.

## Page 52

52
CHAPTER 2. ML METHODS FOR NLP

3. Output Probabilities: linear and softmax layers transform the processed embed-
dings into probabilities, to make the next-token predictions.

The transformer architecture has two main advantages over earlier methods, such as
RNN and LSTM networks. Attention-based transformers allow (1) large scale parallel
processing, and (2) fine-grained long-range semantic connections—speed and semantic
accuracy.
Transformers have dominated language modeling since their introduction.
Af-
ter large scale high quality training corpuses were created, transformer-based LLMs
achieved impressive performance in question-answering, data-to-text generation, and
application-driven tasks. Researchers have been pursuing increasingly larger models
with promises of even higher capabilities \[Brown et al., 2020\]. In Chapter 4 we will
discuss how to scale performance further.
The transformer architecture is a complex architecture. Excellent interactive tuto-
rials exist online, with more details,4 see also the case study in Chapter 5.

2.3.6
Encoder-only (BERT)

While the original transformer model consists of a combined encoder-decoder struc-
ture, modern models are usually either an encoder or a decoder, as they are found to
have specific empirical strengths.
Let us have a closer look at encoders. Encoders are trained to compress input
data into meaningful representations (embeddings) using techniques such as masked
language modeling (MLM). They are good at NLU tasks such as text classification
and sentiment analysis, while decoders are good at NLG tasks such as text generation,
paraphrasing and summarization.
Encoder-only models are designed to produce high-quality vector representations
(embeddings) of input text. Unlike decoders, which are causal (they can only look
at past words), encoders are inherently bidirectional. In an encoder, every token in a
sequence can attend to every other token simultaneously. This global context allows the
model to build a complex semantic representation of the input. To train these models,
we use masked language modeling. In this process, roughly 15% of the input tokens
are replaced with a special \[MASK\] token. It is up to the model to then learn which of
the tokens from its vocabulary should go in its place. Often the regular cross-entropy
loss is used to update the model. The goal of MLM encoder training is for the model
to use the surrounding context (both left and right) to predict what the masked word is.
Eventually, this forces the model to learn grammar, semantics, and even some world
logic.
To improve learning, in addition to the \[MASK\] token, encoder training typically
includes several special tokens:

• \[CLS\] (Classification): Inserted at the very start. After passing through all
layers, the final state of this token is used as the aggregate representation for the
whole sequence.

4See, for example, https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/

## Page 53

2.3. MODELING LANGUAGE
53

• \[SEP\] (Separator): Used to tell the model where one sentence ends and another
begins, which is vital for tasks such as question answering.

• \[PAD\] (Padding): Ensures all sequences in a training batch are the same length.

The best-known encoder-only model may well be the bidirectional encoder represen-
tations from transformers, better known as BERT \[Devlin et al., 2018\].
Encoder-
only models such as BERT, and its successors RoBERTa \[Liu et al., 2019\] and AL-
BERT \[Lan et al., 2019\], have become popular.
Encoder-only models are quite suitable for transfer learning, where they embed
inputs and are subsequently finetuned on downstream tasks, such as classification for
certain application domains. The pipeline for constructing encoder-only models in-
volves two phases:

1. Pretraining: First train the model on a large corpus of billions of words. It may
learn, for example, that King is related to Man and Queen is related to Woman.
The model does not yet know how to do a specific job yet, it just learns English.
Pretraining is an expensive step, and may take a long time (weeks or months).

2. Finetuning: Second, take the pretrained model and add a small additional classi-
fication layer on top (often called a classification head). Then, the whole model
is trained again on task-specific data (such as spam detection, or sentiment anal-
ysis). Because the model already understands language, it typically only needs
a few thousand examples to become an expert at the new task. Finetuning is a
cheap step, and may take just hours or minutes, whereas starting from scratch on
the specific task would require a large dataset and much training time.

After we have discussed encoder-only models, we will now switch to decoder-only
models.

2.3.7
Decoder-only (GPT)

In language generation tasks, decoder-only models are used. Decoders are trained
to reconstruct data or generate sequences using autoregressive training—they often
generate output one token at a time. This autoregressive dependency, where the next
tokens depend on what has been generated so far, is a form of causal attention. We
cannot use future tokens to derive the best prediction. In an encoder, a word can look
at the words to its right. In a decoder, this is strictly forbidden. We use a look-ahead
mask (often a triangular matrix) that sets the attention scores of future tokens to −∞. If
the model is predicting the word apple in the phrase The boy ate the..., it should not be
allowed to observe the word apple in the training data. The decoder must rely solely on
the preceding context. Subsequently, while encoders use masked language modeling,
decoders use (regular) causal language modeling, as shown in Equation 3.1 in the next
chapter.
As a consequence, when moving from encoders to decoders, the relationship be-
tween pretraining and finetuning changes slightly: decoders learn to predict the next

## Page 54

54
CHAPTER 2. ML METHODS FOR NLP

word in pretaining, and are then fine-tuned with the same loss function, but with an-
other type of data. This allows us to move to in-context learning (ICL) or prompt-
learning: because decoders are trained to continue a sequence, you can simply give
them a prompt (the context), and they will generate the answer without needing any
weight updates. The learn, as it were, from the examples in the prompt \[Brown et al.,
2020\]. The ease of use with which large decoders can be used through in-context
learning, without having to do expensive task-specific training or finetuning, has cre-
ated much interest in ICL.
Decoder-only models, such as the generalized pretrained transformer (GPT) fam-
ily \[Radford et al., 2018, 2019, Brown et al., 2020, Ouyang et al., 2022, Achiam et al.,
2023\], have become quite successful and are now widely used in our society. Many
other models have been developed, both open and closed. Together, the training mech-
anisms that we discussed form the basis of the modern LLM pipeline, which we will
explain in more detail in Chapter 3.

2.4
Concluding Remarks

In this chapter, we have traced the remarkable evolution of natural language processing
from its foundational linguistic roots to the neural architectures that power today’s large
language models. We have argued that human language is inherently complex, defined
by intricate rules of syntax, morphology, and deep semantic and pragmatic nuances.
The breakthrough in modern NLP progressed through a series of paradigm shifts—
symbolic, statistical, neural—delivering building blocks for contemporary language
models that are built on dense embeddings, the attention mechanism, and increases in
scale, for data, model size, and compute power. Encoder models are suitable for NLU,
decoder models are suitable for NLG. Both are trained by pretraining, finetuning, and
decoders allow prompt-based in-context learning.

2.4.1
Open challenges

Although the performance of modern LLMs is impressive, and many useful use cases
exists, important challenges remain. Understanding these challenges is critical for iden-
tifying research gaps and for engineering more robust systems, that are also relevant
for agentic LLMs.

Performance Scaling
Current language modeling assumes scaling laws: better gen-
eralization is achieved through the triumvirate of more parameters, more data, and
more compute. However, further scaling creates significant challenges. Achieving
state-of-the-art performance may require models with billions of parameters, whose
training costs millions of dollars in compute, bringing about a high environmental im-
pact. How to achieve better generalization (the ability to perform tasks that the model
was not trained on) using efficient architectures is an open question. Current research
is exploring model pruning and quantization (both discussed in Chapter 4). Further-
more, synthetic data generation (see Chapter 19) aims to achieve higher generalization

## Page 55

2.4. CONCLUDING REMARKS
55

without more training data, but the sweet spot between model size and generalization
capability remains elusive.

Data Scarcity
The majority of NLP training datasets are built for the English lan-
guage, and so are major benchmarks, such as GLUE (general language understanding
\[Wang et al., 2018\]) or SQuAD (question answering \[Rajpurkar et al., 2016\]). The data
is often accumulated from large web-scrapes. Other high-resource languages, such as
Chinese or Hindi, can also benefit from this approach, while low-resource languages
(such as Dutch or Flemish) lack the digital footprint and the cultural presence that is
necessary to train modern transformers from scratch. Because models inherit the cul-
tural nuances of their training data, non-English speakers often experience degraded
performance or algorithmic bias that favors Western perspectives and linguistic norms.

Multilinguality
Because of the differences in available resources, NLP rarely pro-
vides a generic solution for each language. For instance, translating a model’s success
from English to other languages introduces several linguistic complexities. Other lan-
guages like Turkish, Finnish, or Arabic may be morphologically richer, as they convey
significant information through prefixes and suffixes to verbs or nouns. A single word
in Turkish might correspond to an entire sentence in English. Models that are not
trained on such languages fail to reflect such linguistic richness.
Furthermore, different languages may employ different character sets and scripts.
This leads to problems in handling non-Latin scripts (for example, logographic scripts
for Chinese, or Abjads for Hebrew and Arabic). These languages require new tokeniza-
tion and embedding strategies that lead to sensible subwords.

Language Evolution
Languages are living entities that evolve faster than models can
be retrained. Amongst others, this leads to the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem. Even
with sub-word tokenization (such as byte-pair encoding (BPE) \[Gage, 1994\] or Word-
Piece \[Song et al., 2021\]), models struggle with neologisms, slang, technical jargon, or
names that did not exist at the time of the training cutoff. Furthermore, a model trained
in 2022 may not understand the context of global events or cultural shifts in 2026 (what
is the Gen Z stare?). Creating continual learning systems that update knowledge with-
out forgetting previous information (catastrophic forgetting) is an open challenge \[Wu
et al., 2024\].

Tokenization Beyond Text
The boundary between text and other modalities is blur-
ring as a consequence of the effort to make sense of information outside its traditional
context. A challenge in providing this context is multi-modal representation: repre-
senting images, audio, and video in the same latent space as text. While text is discrete
(words/characters), audio and video are continuous signals that must be sampled and
quantized. Mapping a frame of video or a segment of a waveform to a token that
a language model can process alongside text requires complex architectures like Vi-
sion Transformers (ViT) \[Han et al., 2022\] or Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
(CLIP) \[Radford et al., 2021\]. Chapter 7 will discuss multi-modal models.

## Page 56

56
BIBLIOGRAPHY

Interpretability
Finally, an important open question is how these models work in-
ternally. While we can measure that a model works, we often struggle to explain why
it provided a specific answer. Furthermore, models often fail, or hallucinate, giving
wrong answers in a convincing way. For high-stakes applications such as military, le-
gal or medical NLP, the lack of transparency should be a significant barrier to adoption
of language models. Techniques for interpretable language models, such as mechanis-
tic interpretability, are discussed in Chapter 21.
Beyond these challenges, language modeling faces many other socio-technical chal-
lenges, including ethical alignment, long-form logical reasoning, and many others. As
NLP continues to evolve, these open problems represent a dynamic frontier where solv-
ing one challenges often reveals a host of deeper questions for the next generation of
student, researchers and engineers.

2.4.2
Looking Ahead

In this chapter we have discussed the basics of language modeling, from the early
beginning, to modern decoder models. We are now ready to go deeper into the matter
of agentic LLMs. In the next chapter, we will discuss in more detail how a training
pipeline of a large language model works.

## Page 63

Chapter 3

The Large Language Model
Training Pipeline


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how language models are trained. Specifically, you
will be able to:
• Describe the major stages of a basic training pipeline and explain the purpose of
the individual stage: data acquisition, pretraining, finetuning, preference tuning,
and inference.
• Distinguish pretraining from finetuning, and explain why preference tuning is
applied after, and not before, them.
• Explain how the encoder/decoder distinction shapes which training objective a
model uses.
• Identify common benchmarks used to evaluate language models, and state what
capability each is meant to measure.

3.1
Training Models

The training pipeline of a large language model follows a somewhat standard methodol-
ogy: starting from a model architecture where the parameters are initialized randomly,
we train language capabilities through a process that is called pretraining. During
pretraining, we feed large text corpora to our models, which they are trained on autore-
gressively. The result of this stage is a base model, which is generally not yet suited for
specific, practical applications. Hence, we need to adapt it to a downstream task or pur-
pose. This stage is called posttraining, where we show specific types of additional data
to the model using which we elicit task-specific behavior, such as instruction-following
or classification settings.

63

## Page 64

64
CHAPTER 3. LLM TRAINING PIPELINE

3.1.1
Encoder versus Decoder Models

As we saw in the previous chapter, there are two dominant styles of models. On the
one hand, encoder models are able to create rich contextualized representations based
on input data. However, most of the recent successes are based on the decoder models.
While encoders are better at understanding tasks (classification, sentiment), decoders
excel at generative tasks. Decoder models have grown in size, both in terms of number
of trainable parameters, and the available training data. This leads to models that are
surprisingly capable of generalization to unseen contexts.
Let us have a look in more detail at the relevant steps in the decoder-only training
pipeline.

3.1.2
Pretraining/Finetuning Paradigm

A central feature of the success of current training pipelines is the use of transfer learn-
ing. One of the standard applications of modern transformer models is to take a model
that has been trained on a large, generic dataset, and then retrain it on a new task. The
model is pretrained on the large, generic, corpus, and then finetuned on the new, spe-
cific, task, for which a small dataset is present. Finetuning for the new task is quick,
since the dataset is small, but also since the pretrained weights have been transferred.
The finetuning-training does not have to start from scratch.
This pretraining/finetuning distinction of the transfer learning paradigm is at the
heart of large language model training pipelines. Rather than starting the training from
scratch, the model can reuse already-learned linguistic knowledge in new scenarios,
thus speeding up the training process. Pretraining of large, commercial models may
take months. Usually, the new task is specific (such as question answering in a certain
domain, or sentiment analysis). For the new task, a dedicated dataset will be used to
finetune the model. During finetuning, a subset of the model’s weights are updated
carefully to retain the general linguistic capabilities of the pretrained model, while
gaining an understanding of the new task. Finetuning a model to a new task takes
typically on the order of minutes to hours.

3.1.3
Open and Closed Models

Popular LLMs are OpenAI’s ChatGPT series \[Achiam et al., 2023, Ouyang et al.,
2022\], Meta’s LLaMa family \[Touvron et al., 2023\], Google’s Gemma \[Chowdhery
et al., 2023\] and Gemini \[Anil et al., 2023\], Anthropic’s Claude family, Moonshot AI’s
Kimi, DeepSeek \[Guo et al., 2025\], and Qwen \[Bai et al., 2025\], among others.
There are different degrees of openness between these models. For example, a
model’s training data can be made public, the network architecture of a model can be
disclosed, and the trained weights can be released. However, the companies behind
commercial models seldom publish all elements of their model and training procedure,
as they seek to retain some competitive edge.
In response, the scientific community has developed fully open-source models,
such as BLOOM \[Le Scao et al., 2023\], Pythia \[Biderman et al., 2023\], and OLMo
\[Groeneveld et al., 2024\], to contribute to the collective understanding of how large

Although the models are all based on the transformer architecture, there are small
differences between individual components and their overall layout, for example to
capitalize on hardware differences or specific optimizations developed by their respec-
tive creators. For instance, Google optimized Gemini for their TPU-based compute
infrastructure \[Jouppi et al., 2023\]. We discuss further improvements to the architec-
ture extensively in Chapter 4.

3.2
Training Pipeline

We will now describe in more detail the steps of a standard training pipeline. LLMs are
constructed using an elaborate pipeline with different training phases \[Radford et al.,
2019, Minaee et al., 2024\]. We will describe the phases, as shown in Figure 3.1. The
combinations of individual phases are usually referred to as training recipes, as they
denote the order in which the models were trained. At each phase, a new dataset may
be used, together with a new loss function. Each phase is designed to imbue the model
with a specific capability. This will become clear as we discuss the individual phases.

3.2.1
Acquire Data

The first step in the pipeline is to acquire data. Typically, massive, general-purpose
text corpora are used \[Brown et al., 2020\]. The corpora consist of raw text without
the need for manual labeling. This data is typically aggregated from both curated and
uncurated online sources, then refined through cleaning heuristics to mitigate the effect
of harmful, private, or copyrighted content. The corpora that are used for pretraining
are large. Modern LLMs are trained on a web-scale magnitude of data, often reaching
the scale of trillions of tokens. Some examples of datasets are:

• Common Crawl: a massive, non-profit snapshot of the web containing billions of
pages; alternative sources include https://archive.org. While the size
is unparalleled, the quality of the data is under discussion \[Baack, 2024\]. Many
derivatives, such as C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus) present a filtered subset
of English web text \[Raffel et al., 2020\] to enhance the quality of the data.

### Page links

- [Link 1](https://archive.org)

## Page 66

66
CHAPTER 3. LLM TRAINING PIPELINE

• Dolma 3: a data mixture that is designed to maximize performance across a
diverse suite of tasks. It is used in the OLMo open source/open data project
\[Ettinger et al., 2025, Soldaini et al., 2024\].

• SmolLM3: utilizes a large three-stage training strategy with 11.2 trillion tokens
that dynamically mixes web, math, and code data to optimize reasoning and
knowledge acquisition \[Bakouch et al., 2025\].

Recent research emphasizes that data diversity is as critical as size for improving cross-
domain knowledge and downstream generalization \[Gao et al., 2020\]. The corpus
called The Pile has been specifically created as a heterogeneous corpus. For exam-
ple, models trained on The Pile show significant gains in coding efficiency (Bits Per
Byte, BPB)1 across disparate domains, such as GitHub repositories, medical papers,
and philosophy texts (see Figure 3.2). It is therefore often used as a benchmark, where
successful performance on Pile BPB serves as an indicator of a model’s world knowl-
edge and complex reasoning abilities.
Curation of data for pretraining requires defining complex data cleaning pipelines
that transform raw data from multiple sources into a single collection of cleaned, plain
text documents. Often, this process focuses on quality assurance and safety. The cu-
ration process begins with source prioritization, where the mixture is weighted toward
high-quality sources such as Wikipedia, books, and other known curated sources. Fur-
ther, to ensure the integrity of the corpus, researchers apply noise reduction heuristics
to strip away boilerplate text, navigation menus, and possibly inappropriate content.
Furthermore, de-duplication is performed at both the URL and document levels; this is
essential to prevent the model from memorizing redundant information and overfitting
on repetitive data.
Beyond accuracy, the pipeline must select data that matches safety and ethical con-
straints. This too is commonly implemented through heuristic-based filtering. Fur-
thermore, toxicity-detection systems are implemented to remove hate speech, although
these methods often yield mixed results. A significant challenge in this phase is bias
mitigation, as automated filters can inadvertently flag and suppress legitimate data writ-
ten in specific dialects, such as African American English, leading to the accidental
exclusion of diverse voices from the training set.

3.2.2
Pretrain

The second step in the training pipeline is pretraining the model on the curated cor-
pus, a process that yields a generalist natural language model. This stage uses a self-
supervised transformer approach \[Vaswani et al., 2017\] on the unlabeled text.
In order to acquire internal representations of language, conceptual semantic rela-
tionships, and world knowledge, the model is trained using masked-token cloze-like
tasks. In such tasks the objective is to predict masked tokens conditioned on a preced-
ing context of large corpora of sequences (i.e., representations of text, image patches).
This process is self-supervised (no human-annotated data is required) and is known to

1Bits-Per-Byte is a tokenizer-agnostic metric from information theory that measures the average bits
needed per symbol, reflecting coding efficiency, see also Section 3.3.2.

yield rich representations of language, relations between concepts, and world knowl-
edge, in various forms.
Formally, the language modeling objective maximizes the probability of the tokens
in a sentence U = {𝑢0, . . . , 𝑢𝑛}, based on a window 𝑘of existing tokens (Equation 3.1).
𝐿(U) is the language modeling loss.

log 𝑃(𝑢𝑖|𝑢𝑖−𝑘, . . . , 𝑢𝑖−1; Θ)
(3.1)

Language models estimate these probabilities through trainable parameters Θ, op-
timized via gradient updates. Given that model sizes range from millions to over a tril-
lion parameters, large datasets are required to ensure convergence. During this training
phase, teacher forcing is employed: the model makes a prediction, but the ground-truth
token—rather than the model’s own output—is provided as the input for the next step.
In contrast, during autoregressive generation at inference time, the model must rely on
its own predictions as the input for subsequent tokens. Tokens are created by running
the appropriate tokenizer, as explained in Section 2.1.4.
In pretraining, a key challenge is to ensure that the model learns efficiently and re-
mains stable throughout the trillions of gradient updates. Over time, different strategies
have evolved that aim to keep the training process under control. One such strategy
is curriculum learning. In human learning, we start by learning easy concepts (such
as addition) before we tackle more difficult concepts (multiplication, logarithms). In
language modeling, this idea is used in data mixtures, or data curricula. Rather than
training on all data types simultaneously, researchers select a specific mixture of data
sources to train on first, see the example in Figure 3.3. Creation of mixtures involves
strategically ordering the data according to difficulty. In a training curriculum we start
with easy-to-learn general web crawls, and then shift toward harder high-quality rea-

Figure 3.3: Example data mixtures for training SmolLM3 \[Bakouch et al., 2025\].

Figure 3.4: Training loss for the BERT model using the original architecture (a) and a

soning data (math and code) in later stages. The underlying idea is that this helps the
model converge quicker on more complex logic \[Bengio et al., 2009\].

Other mechanisms for stabilizing training are employed, as training at this scale is
notoriously unstable and prone to loss spikes \[Takase et al., 2025\]. Stability is main-
tained through standard machine learning techniques such as weight decay, layer nor-
malization, and sophisticated learning rate schedulers. The use of specialized optimiz-
ers and the monitoring of gradient norms helps to prevent parameters from diverging
during the intensive pretraining process. An example of how switching embedding
layers can lead to more stable training is shown in Figure 3.4. The left figure shows
the training loss for the 336M and 752M BERT model. While the original architecture
performs well on the 336M model, the modifications in (b) enable stable training with
lower training loss \[Shoeybi et al., 2020\].

3.2. TRAINING PIPELINE
69

3.2.3
Finetune

After pretraining comes posttraining, of which the first important training step is fine-
tuning. LLMs are rarely used in an autocomplete generic predict-next-word setting,
people rather use them to answer questions, give advice and recall information. Fine-
tuning is the process of taking a pretrained model that has already learned general
language patterns, and then train it further on a smaller, more specific dataset. In fine-
tuning, we apply a general model to a specific (narrow) task on a labeled dataset, using
a supervised learning approach. A popular efficient method is low-rank optimization,
which finetunes a small subset of the parameters \[Hu et al., 2021, Wei et al., 2022,
Minaee et al., 2024\].

Supervised Finetuning (SFT)
Finetuning can be applied to many specialized tasks.
The most general models use supervised finetuning to be able to follow instructions
and perform reasoning steps \[Ettinger et al., 2025\]. The supervised finetuning step is
especially important for smaller models, offering an efficient mechanism for significant
improvements in general chat, reasoning, and function-calling capabilities.
Supervised finetuning is also used for more specialized tasks, such as toxicity re-
duction. WildChat \[Zhao et al., 2024\] provides over a million real-world user-ChatGPT
interactions, capturing how humans prompt the LLM with varying complexity and tox-
icity.
For learning reasoning capabilities, OpenThoughts \[Guha et al., 2025\] contains
step-by-step reasoning chains, distilled from advanced models to enhance problem-
solving capabilities in math, science, and coding. Human-obtained data is supple-
mented by synthetic data, which involves generating instructions and responses using
larger teacher models (such as GPT-5) to fill specific data gaps and scale up training
volume \[Zhang et al., 2026\].
Finetuning does not only pertain to general instruction-following or reasoning.
Other tasks can be, for example, translation from one language to another, or question
answering in health-care or customer service. Especially for industrial applications,
where tasks are narrow and models are smaller, finetuning is a fruitful undertaking.
In Chapter 11 we will discuss the use of tools by LLMs, a central aspect of agentic
LLM. The training to use tools also takes place in the supervised finetuning step in the
training pipeline \[Wei et al., 2022, Minaee et al., 2024\].
Furthermore, finetuning is instrumental in establishing a model’s persona and deep-
ening its expertise. For instance, organizations can train models to adopt a specific tone
of voice, for example so that a customer service bot maintains a consistent brand iden-
tity, be that empathetic and formal or witty and casual. Finally, the injection of deep
domain knowledge enables the model to master the intricate terminology and logic
of niche fields, such as industry-specific patent information or debugging proprietary
legacy code.
Ultimately, finetuning transforms a generalist predictor into a specialized expert,
often allowing smaller, more efficient models to outperform larger foundational models
on specific tasks.

3.2.4
Preference Tuning

A problem that surfaced in early models is that training tends to amplify extreme
socially unacceptable texts in the training data and run wild, crowding out moderate
points of view. Since then, an essential step for LLMs to become socially acceptable,
is for pipelines to include a phase in which the model is tuned to behave in socially
acceptable ways. This phase is called preference tuning.
In this phase we align the finetuned model with user expectations (preference align-
ment). The goal of this step is to improve the model to give socially acceptable answers,
prevent hate speech, reduce hallucinations, and improve instruction adherence.
Standard methods for preference tuning include reinforcement learning with hu-
man feedback (RLHF) \[Ouyang et al., 2022\], which trains a reward model to approxi-
mate human values, and direct preference optimization (DPO) \[Rafailov et al., 2024\],
which optimizes the policy directly from preference data. A high-level overview of
RLHF is shown in Figure 3.5. To address the bottleneck of human annotation, modern
pipelines increasingly utilize reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) \[Bai
et al., 2022\], where a stronger model generates the preference signals.
Achieving alignment with human values is not an easy task, and we usually dis-
tinguish between safety alignment, value alignment and preference alignment. In the
latter case, a complication is that preferences are subjective preferences (such as writ-
ing style) that change per person.

Value alignment
On a higher level, value alignment focuses on ensuring that the
model’s underlying principles and worldviews resonate with broad human ethics. Un-
like individual preferences, this involves anchoring the model to high-level concepts
such as fairness, helpfulness, and honesty. In practice, this means the model is gov-
erned by a set of written principles (a constitution) to ensure that it adheres to the
policies set out by the developer.
However, this value alignment usually leads to a trade-off, where optimizing a
model for safety and helpfulness also degrades its performance on other capabilities,
such as factual recall or creativity \[Lin et al., 2024\]. This trade-off is otherwise known
as the alignment tax.

## Page 71

3.2. TRAINING PIPELINE
71

Figure 3.6: Comparison of RLHF (specifically, PPO) to RLVR (specifically, GRPO)
method \[Shao et al., 2024\]

Safety alignment
Safety alignment is the process of setting hard boundaries on model
behavior to prevent catastrophic or harmful outputs. While preference alignment might
focus on tone, and value alignment on viewpoint, safety alignment focuses on adver-
sarial robustness and the refusal of malicious prompts. Example methodologies for
ensuring safety includes red teaming, where models are subjected to rigorous jailbreak
attempts to identify vulnerabilities, and guard railing, where specific refusal boundaries
for high-risk responses are filtered.

Objective alignment
Finally, for domains where objective truths exist, such as math-
ematics or coding, methods known as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
(RLVR) \[Lambert et al., 2024\] are employed. Unlike standard RLHF, RLVR opti-
mizes for objective correctness by leveraging ground-truth signals to robustly improve
reasoning capabilities. Examples include code that compiles, or correct mathematical
solutions. In the latter case, the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm
is often used \[Guo et al., 2025\], a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) that
enhances mathematical reasoning abilities while concurrently optimizing the memory
usage of PPO. It does so by sampling multiple answers from the policy model and
using their relative quality (as assessed by a verifier) to compute the rewards. Instead
of relying on human labels for learning what counts as a good answer, the model gets
direct rewards (+1, or -1) from a deterministic verifier \[Guo et al., 2025, Shao et al.,
2024\], see Figure 3.6.

3.2.5
Infer

The final step in the training pipeline is the inference step. This is the step in which
the trained model is finally used. Here the user finally gets to interact with the model.
Finally, we can use the fruits of our training efforts.
At inference time, we use natural language prompts (instructions and questions) to
obtain responses from the model. Prompting is the preferred way of using LLMs to
have the model answer our questions. Inference results can be sensitive to the way that
a prompt is formulated. The use of certain words, or re-ordering words in the prompt,

## Page 72

72
CHAPTER 3. LLM TRAINING PIPELINE

can influence the answer of the model. This sensitivity has led to prompt engineering
and context engineering, skills that have become important for users of LLMs \[Sahoo
et al., 2024\].
Interestingly, as we discussed in the previous chapter, in decoder models whose
size is beyond hundreds of billions parameters a new learning method emerges: in-
context learning (ICL) \[Brown et al., 2020, Wei et al., 2022\]. In-context learning is
a method where the prompt contains a small number of examples, together with an
instruction. These examples point the model in a certain direction and it uses them
to learn the answer. ICL is a form of within-prompt few-shot learning. ICL is also a
type of learning where no parameters of the model are changed—it is example learning
without parameter training \[Dong et al., 2022\].
In the remainder of this book we will see many examples of the way in which
in-context learning is used, such as in agentic harnesses. Inference-time in-context
learning is a major driver of agentic LLM.

3.2.6
Concluding Remarks

We have now described the phases of a typical LLM training pipeline. Note that the
pipeline that we described is an example of a typical approach, and different models are
trained in different ways. Current modern training pipelines are elaborate, and training
is costly. Innovations to training pipelines are the topic of current research, see, for
example, Guo et al. \[2025\], Du et al. \[2025\].
Being able to obtain predictions quickly is key, and multiple techniques have been
developed to speed up the process. For instance, is is important to strike a balance
between the reasoning effort and response quality. Research into test time scaling
studies this trade-off. A higher inference-time effort costs more compute time, but may
yield a better answer. We discuss these and other optimization techniques in Chapter 4.

3.3
Benchmarks, and Performance

After the pipeline has been used to train the model, we wish to find out how well
the model performs. LLMs are created using a variety of modeling techniques, for
different tasks, on different datasets. As a result, they have often obtained remarkable
capabilities. For example, LLMs perform well on natural language understanding tasks
(GLUE, SQUAD, Xsum) \[Wang et al., 2018, 2019, Rajpurkar et al., 2016, Narayan
et al., 2018\], translation \[Kocmi et al., 2022, Papineni et al., 2002, Sennrich et al.,
2015\], question answering tasks \[Roberts et al., 2020\], and poetry composition \[Zhang
and Eger, 2024\], to name just a few domains. The broad applicability of LLMs shows
their versatility, although the rapid development of the field, as well as ongoing research
efforts, raise many open questions related to the capabilities of LLMs in many domains
and contexts.
We will now discuss benchmarks that are commonly used to test the performance
of our models.

## Page 73

3.3. BENCHMARKS, AND PERFORMANCE
73

3.3.1
Common tasks

Let us have a closer look at some common LLM tasks. The tasks can largely be grouped
under the two language processing categories that we introduced previously: natural
language understanding (NLU) and natural language generation (NLG). Depending
on the category, the exact task formulation, and the underlying data, the performance
metric will differ. We will discuss each separately.
Note that performance is an ambiguous term. In NLP, it is often used in the con-
text of task performance (accuracy), instead of computational performance (speed).
While exact evaluation criteria differ depending on the task, modern evaluation prac-
tices primarily focus on task performance. However, how many of the calls to the LLM
we make, and how quickly we can get responses from the model, is also important to
achieve high scores on contemporary benchmarks, as we will see in later chapters.

3.3.2
Metrics

In order to monitor or report the (task) performance of LLMs, different metrics are
used, depending on the stage of the training that we are in.

Pretraining Metrics
In pretraining, we are mostly interested in knowing whether the
model is able to accurately predict the next word. The standard metric is perplexity,
shown in Equation 3.2. Perplexity measures the model’s uncertainty when predicting
the next token, and is directly related to the cross-entropy loss function. Low perplex-
ity indicates that the model assigns high probability to the correct next tokens. For
perplexity, lower is better.

Perplexity is computed over tokens; adjusting perplexity to stick to word boundaries
needs careful normalization \[Pimentel and Meister, 2024\]. Moreover, even when ad-
justed, it is still tokenizer-specific, as other tokenizers can lead to other subwords and
hence other probability distributions.
As an alternative, bits-per-byte (BPB), shown in Equation 3.3, normalizes the loss
to the byte level, which enables fair comparisons between models that use different
tokenization schemes \[Borgeaud et al., 2022\]. It measures the average number of bits
required to encode a single byte of data.

Posttraining Metrics
In posttraining and inference, when the model is used for prob-
lem solving, generation, or reasoning, we look at the deterministic success rates, based
on ground truth data. Often, tasks are set up in multiple-choice question/answering
formats, where there is a single correct answer. For these types of tasks, we commonly

## Page 74

74
CHAPTER 3. LLM TRAINING PIPELINE

report accuracy, the percentage of questions for which a correct response is given. For
accuracy, higher is better.
In the regular setup, the model needs to provide an answer in one unique attempt.
However, since sampling from a language model is a stochastic process, we may re-
quest additional attempts, and see if the answer is among them. This is formalized in
the Pass@K metric: the percentage of problems solved correctly on the model’s 𝐾th
attempt; higher is better. Common values for 𝐾include 1, 5, 10, 100.

3.3.3
Common Benchmarks

While measuring the performance of LLMs remains an active area of research, many
datasets have become commonplace for reporting their general capabilities. These
datasets are designed to only be used for evaluating the quality of a model, and are
not intended as additional training data. As such, they serve as semi-standardized
benchmarks. Ongoing efforts for moving to field standards, such as MLCommons
\[Thiyagalingam et al., 2022\], show an increasing need for objective and sound evalua-
tion setups.

Data Contamination
Modern benchmarks run a risk of data contamination \[Bal-
loccu et al., 2024\]. As pretraining data increases in size (often a considerable ratio
of the total size of the internet), the line between in- and out-of-domain data becomes
increasingly blurred, especially given that commercial vendors often do not specify the
sources of their training data (either out of commercial interest or for other reasons).
Hence, when we wish to measure true generalization to unseen data, we need to ensure
that the model has not seen the data before (we wish to prevent data contamination).
It is common for benchmarks to host a public, freely accessible dataset for quick
experimentation by developers, but to maintain a private dataset that commercial ven-
dors have restricted access to, to prevent data contamination. Furthermore, in order to
maintain the benchmark’s usefulness into the future, developers often actively update
the samples in the benchmark.
In Table 3.1, we provide a non-exhaustive list of general-purpose benchmarks that
are popular at the time of writing.

3.4
Concluding Remarks

In the field of LLM development, it has become common for commercial LLM devel-
opers (such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Mistral) to publish a tech report
that informs the expert public on how the model behaves across popular benchmarks.
Often, such as tech report is published as a preprint, without going through academic
peer-review, and many details that would be necessary for full scientific reproducibility
(such as data recipe, model architecture) are left out, for commercial reasons. Nonethe-
less, these reports provide useful information to derive insights into what LLMs can and
cannot do.
First, we find that modern LLMs demonstrate a distinct performance hierarchy
across benchmarks, as they have effectively solved broad knowledge tasks, but still

models (such as GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, and Claude 4.5 Opus) have reached, at the

The newest generation of reasoning models (such as OpenAI’s o1, DeepSeek-R1,
and Qwen-3.5) have recently achieved great progress, pushing math and science pass
rates from low percentages to expert levels. Despite these advances, the software en-
gineering SWE-bench remains the ultimate stress test for reliability; while scores have
risen from negligible (¡2%) to respectable levels (40-50% on verified subsets) for top

a real-world repository issue remains a significant hurdle for modern AI.

Open Questions
Open questions about the origin of LLMs capabilities still remain.
As the pipelines have grown complex, both in terms of training (What data matters?

## Page 83

Chapter 4

Scaling Laws and Efficient
Large Language Models


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how performance of language models scales with
data and training effort. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Explain how model performance relates to compute, data, and model size
through scaling laws, and predict the effect of increasing one factor while hold-
ing the others fixed.
• Describe what techniques can be used to develop smaller language models, and
analyze the tradeoff of using smaller models with respect to compute require-
ments and performance.
• Recognize the difference between inference-time compute and training-time
compute.
• Reflect on sustainable language models and the environmental and privacy im-
plications of large-scale deployment

4.1
Scaling Laws: Compute, Data, Parameters

There are three primary factors involved in the training of LLMs: (1) the amount of
compute, (2) the size of the dataset, and (3) the size of the model. Studies have shown
that these three factors relate to the final performance of a model, measured as its loss
on a held-out test set (𝐿). This relation has been found to be both smooth and pre-
dictable. The relationship takes the form of a power law: as any of the three resources
is increased, the loss decreases proportionally to a negative power of that resource. For
instance, doubling the model size might reduce the loss by a factor of 2−𝛼for some
positive exponent 𝛼. Because the behavior is predictable, we can estimate how much
a model will improve (for instance, from doubling the training dataset size) before
committing to an expensive training run.

83

## Page 84

84
CHAPTER 4. SCALING LAWS AND EFFICIENCY

Figure 4.1: Loss on language modeling objective is a function of training compute,
dataset size, and model size \[Kaplan et al., 2020\].

We define these three quantities (𝐶, 𝐷, 𝑁) as follows:

• Compute (𝐶): the total amount of arithmetic performed over the entire training
run, measured in floating point operations (FLOPs). Note that this is a count
of operations in total, not a rate per second. A widely used approximation re-
lates it to the other two quantities as 𝐶≈6𝑁𝐷, since processing a single token
touches each of the 𝑁parameters roughly six times across the forward (twice)
and backward pass (four times).

• Dataset size (𝐷): the total number of tokens the model is trained on. Note that a
token is a subword unit defined by the tokenizer, so the same corpus corresponds
to different values of 𝐷under different tokenizers. The count of 𝐷is the number
of tokens as they are used during the training run. When data is repeated over
several epochs, the repeated tokens still add to 𝐷but may yield diminishing
returns compared to fresh data.

• Model size (𝑁): the number of trainable parameters (weights) in the model ar-
chitecture. This count usually refers only to the parameters that increase when
scaling model depth, and therefore excludes the embedding matrix.

Training large models comes at considerable cost, usually in the realm of tens of mil-
lions of dollars, and up to months of compute time. Scaling laws allow us to predict
whether a model will train well.

4.1.1
Kaplan Scaling Laws

There are different empirical results for scaling laws that are found by fitting a function
to empirical test data. For instance, in Figure 4.1, every point is a trained model on a
fixed dataset with a similar experimental setup, while only changing the three primary
variables 𝐶, 𝐷, 𝑁. In early 2020, Kaplan et al. \[2020\] found how model performance
is related to 𝐶, 𝐷, 𝑁. They estimated, following empirical observations, that the loss
follows independent power laws rekated to the three main variables: 𝐿(𝑁) ∝𝑁−𝛼𝑁
and 𝐿(𝐷) ∝𝐷−𝛼𝐷, with 𝛼𝑁≈0.076 and 𝛼𝐷≈0.095.
The individual power laws can be combined into a single optimizable equation,
shown in Equation 4.1. This relationship was assumed to be generic: it would apply

Specifically, they concluded that as the compute budget 𝐶increases, model size
𝑁should be increased faster than data size 𝐷(𝑁∝𝐶0.73 and 𝐷∝𝐶0.271), leading
to the development of large models such as GPT-3. The negative exponents reflect
diminishing returns: each doubling of model size or dataset size lowers the loss by
only a few percent.
At first glance, this recommendation seems to contradict the exponents themselves:
since 𝛼𝐷> 𝛼𝑁, data scaling reduces the loss faster than parameter scaling for the same
relative increase in compute. The reason is that compute, not the resource itself, is the
constraint: because 𝐶≈6𝑁𝐷, increasing 𝐷consumes compute just as increasing 𝑁
does. This means that 𝑁is with becoming a bottleneck with increasing likelihood.
Hence, once the compute cost for 𝐷is accounted for, allocating additional compute to
𝑁yields a better return than allocating it to 𝐷. This means that the optimal allocation
favors larger models.

Sample efficiency
A separate observation of Kaplan et al. \[2020\] is that larger mod-
els are more sample-efficient. For a fixed number of training tokens, a larger model
reaches a lower loss, and to reach a given target loss it requires fewer tokens and fewer
optimization steps than a smaller one. This effect is visualized in Figure 4.2.

4.1.2
Chinchilla Scaling Laws

In 2022, Hoffmann et al. \[2022\] reevaluated these findings with a model called Chin-
chilla, and found, surprisingly, that most large models at the time were severely un-
dertrained. This discrepancy can be traced back to the methodology of Kaplan et al.
\[2020\]: their optimal allocation was extrapolated from the early, non-converged train-
ing dynamics of many models rather than from runs trained to convergence, which
systematically biased their conclusions toward larger models trained for fewer steps.
The key insight from the Chinchilla study was that for every doubling of the com-
pute budget, both the model size 𝑁and the number of training tokens 𝐷should be
increased in roughly equal proportions (𝑁∝𝐶0.5 and 𝐷∝𝐶0.5). Their rule of
thumb suggests training on approximately 20 tokens for every trainable parameter in
the model to achieve compute optimality. This result has since been reproduced \[Be-
siroglu et al., 2024\] and has been shown to be robust to sizable perturbations \[Schaeffer
et al., 2025\].
In their scaling laws, the loss is modeled as a function of the parameter count 𝑁
and the number of tokens 𝐷that have been trained on, as follows:

so the ratio 𝐷𝑜𝑝𝑡/𝑁𝑜𝑝𝑡stays near a constant value of roughly 20 across many orders
of magnitude of compute. The value is best understood as an empirical calibration an-
chored on real compute-optimal runs rather than a number that results cleanly from the
fitted coefficients. The Chinchilla model itself (70B parameters trained on 1.4T tokens)
sits exactly at 𝐷/𝑁= 20. Table 4.1 shows several well-known models relative to this
rule. Models below the ratio are undertrained (too large for their token budget), while
models far above it are deliberately overtrained to obtain a small model that is cheap
to run at inference time. Earlier flagship models such as GPT-3 and Gopher fall well
below the line (𝐷/𝑁≈1–2): they were made very large but trained on comparatively
too few tokens. It is worth stressing that 𝐷≈20𝑁is optimal only for minimizing the
training loss at a fixed training budget. When a model will later serve many inference
requests, it is often deliberately over-trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter,
trading additional training cost for a smaller model that is cheaper to run at inference
time. LLaMA-3 8B, for instance, is trained on roughly 1900 tokens per parameter. This
deliberate extreme over-training is chosen so that a small model still reaches a low loss,
and is cheap to run during inference.
The picture so far is fairly clean: test loss falls smoothly, monotonically, and pre-
dictably with compute, data, and parameters. However, in practice, various factors
influence our results. We discuss four phenomena that each probe a different edge of
that picture: (1) compute-optimal curves, (2) emergent abilities, (3) inverse scaling,
and (4) grokking.

4.1.3
Compute-Optimal Curve

Computer hardware and energy are finite resources. A practical question is how to split
a fixed compute budget 𝐶between model size 𝑁and dataset size 𝐷to obtain the best
possible model. Scaling laws answer this through the compute-optimal frontier: the
allocation of 𝐶that minimizes the loss.
This frontier is located empirically with the IsoFLOP method \[Hoffmann et al.,
2022\], shown in Figure 4.3. For various model sizes, we choose the number of training
tokens such that the final FLOPs is a constant. The learning rate is adjusted using a
cosine annealing schedule, with the cosine cycle length is set to match the target FLOP
count. We find a clear valley in loss, meaning that for a given FLOP budget there

we show the estimated number of parameters and tokens for an optimal model trained
with the compute budget of Gopher. For a fixed FLOP budget we train several models
of different sizes: a model that is too small underfits, while a model that is too large is
forced to train on too few tokens, so the resulting curve of loss against model size is
U-shaped. Its minimum identifies the compute-optimal model size 𝑁𝑜𝑝𝑡, from which

to each such curve locates this minimum, and repeating the procedure across budgets

This parabola fitting must be done with care, and the simplification introduces sys-
tematic biases in the estimated optimum \[Czech et al., 2026\]. These biases persist
even on noise-free synthetic data and stem from three sources: (1) spacing the sampled
model sizes too coarsely, (2) sampling that fails to locate the true minimum symmetri-
cally, and (3) the genuine asymmetry of the loss surface, which a symmetric parabola
cannot represent. At the scale of Llama-3, they estimate that such biases waste on the
order of $1.4M of compute. As a remedy, they recommend fitting the parametric loss
model 𝐿(𝑁, 𝐷) = 𝐸+ 𝐴/𝑁𝛼+ 𝐵/𝐷𝛽directly—Chinchilla Approach 3, the same form
we used above to derive the 𝐷≈20𝑁rule—with a numerically robust optimizer, rather
than reading the optimum off fitted parabolas.
Complementary views on scaling \[Paquette et al., 2024\] study analytically solvable
models (power-law random features trained with one-pass stochastic gradient descent)
instead of fitting curves to trained models. They find that the compute-optimal expo-
nent is not a single universal constant, but that the data-complexity/target-complexity
plane instead splits into four primary phases (plus three sub-phases), each with its own
exponent governing how 𝑁opt grows with compute. The answer to the question which
allocation rule to apply, and whether a fixed 20 tokens per parameter is even the right
shape, depends on the regime of the problem.

Scaling for finetuning
The preceding works studied how pretraining scales. Do
these scaling laws also govern finetuning? Zhang et al. \[2024\] study this question for
both full-model finetuning, which updates all of the model’s weights, and parameter-
efficient finetuning (PEFT), which freezes the pretrained weights and trains only a

to compute budgeting is that finetuning performance improves more from scaling the
size of the base model than from collecting additional finetuning data, while adding
more trainable PEFT parameters helps little. In practice, a task that underperforms is
usually better served by starting from a larger pretrained model than by enlarging the
adapter or gathering more finetuning examples.

4.1.4
Emergent Abilities

Some of the most interesting phenomena in LLM scaling are emergent abilities: capa-
bilities that are not present in smaller models but that appear suddenly as model size or
compute cross a certain threshold \[Wei et al., 2022\]. Examples include multi-step rea-
soning, few-shot translation, and specialized coding tasks, as shown in Figure 4.4. The
ability to perform a task via few-shot prompting is emergent when a language model
achieves random performance until a certain scale, after which performance signifi-
cantly increases to well-above random.

However, the suddenness of the appearance has been contested. Schaeffer et al.
\[2023\] argue that emergent abilities might be a mirage caused by the choice of evalua-
tion metrics. For instance, in Figure 4.5, we see that while non-smooth discrete metrics
(such as accuracy or exact match) show sharp jumps—they are non-smooth, after all—
underlying metrics (such as the cross-entropy loss or token-level probability) follow a
smooth, predictable power law across scales.

4.1.5
Inverse Scaling

While most tasks improve with scale, some exhibit inverse scaling, where larger mod-
els perform worse or develop stronger biases. This may happen in tasks where a dis-
tractor answer is more probable according to the language modeling objective than the
correct answer, leading larger (and more confident) models to consistently choose the
wrong option \[McKenzie et al., 2023, Michaelov and Bergen, 2023\].

An example of inverse scaling is hindsight neglect, a task that tests whether a bet
was worth taking based on its expected value. In case the expected value is positive,
the model should respond with yes, and in case of a negative expected value it should
respond with no. The situation is as follows. The model is only shown few-shot exam-
ples where the actual outcome always matches the expected value (that is, the bettor
won money when the expected value was positive and lost money when the expected
value was negative). The model is then asked a question about whether it was correct
to take a bet where the expected value and the actual outcome do not match. Hind-
sight neglect tests whether models can correctly generalize from instructions when the
few-shot examples are correctly-labeled but misleading. Repetitive algebra tests how
models respond to simple algebra questions when given a specific pattern of correctly-
labeled few-shot examples. Figure 4.6 shows that models generally start around ran-
dom performance, but fall below random performance at around 1022 training FLOPs.

4.1.6
Grokking

Grokking is a relatively recent paradox in statistical learning theory. This theory holds
that, conventionally, when a large model is presented with a small dataset, it will overfit,
due to memorization of the examples. Grokking, then, occurs when we continue to
train this too-large model, and, after much more training, the model suddenly finds a
generalizing solution \[Power et al., 2022\].
While originally observed on small algorithmic tasks, such as modular addition,
the grokking phenomenon suggests that scaling the number of training steps (over-
training) can lead to qualitative shifts from memorization to understanding, even with-
out increasing the dataset size 𝐷, see Figure 4.7.
The figure shows a data wall that initially limits scaling as the data is running
out \[Villalobos et al., 2024\], but later, after much more training, the model groks a
generalizing solution.
Grokking is relevant to language modeling since we are rapidly running out of high-
quality human text on the internet to satisfy the requirements on data 𝐷of Chinchilla

## Page 92

CHAPTER 4. SCALING LAWS AND EFFICIENCY

scaling for next-generation models. Because of these inherent limits, researchers are
looking beyond simple scaling of 𝐷. As an alternative, we can look at a variety of
these new frontiers: (1) better architectural efficiency (such as Mixture of Experts), (2)
inference-time scaling (such as giving models more compute during inference to think,
as seen in OpenAI’s o-series), or (3) synthetic data generation (Chapter 19).

4.2
Small Language Models

As the requirements for compute and data continue to grow, there is an increasing in-
terest in small language models (SLMs): models that are small enough to run on con-
sumer hardware or even mobile or edge devices while maintaining high performance.
These models are often developed using techniques that optimize for efficiency without
sacrificing too much performance.
To understand the deployment landscape for these models, it is helpful to categorize
common types of compute infrastructure:

• Datacenters: High-performance GPUs (such as NVIDIA H100s) and TPUs, pri-
marily used for pretraining large models and hosting high-throughput inference
APIs.

• Consumer Hardware: Standard desktop GPUs and high-end CPUs, where SLMs
can be affordably finetuned or run locally by individual users.

• Edge Devices: Mobile phones, Internet-of-Things devices, and laptops, which
are increasingly equipped with Neural Processing Units (NPUs) specifically de-
signed for low-power, efficient on-device inference.

To fit models into the latter constrained environments, optimization techniques fo-
cus on speeding up throughput, reducing latency, reducing memory usage, and increas-
ing sample efficiency. The techniques for achieving these goals can be grouped into
two categories: (1) model-centric optimization, which targets the architecture of the
models and their optimization approaches, and (2) data-centric optimization, which
targets the data used to train the models. We will discuss both categories.

4.2.1
Model-centric Optimization

First we discuss the model-centric optimization techniques. We introduce the following
techniques that allow for efficient training of smaller models, while still maintaining
high task performance. Model-centric techniques can focus on pretraining/finetuning
or inference.

4.2.1.1
Reducing Pretraining Cost

Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
Methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation
(LoRA) \[Hu et al., 2021\] allow for adapting a large model to a new task by training only
a tiny fraction (often < 1%) of its parameters \[Lialin et al., 2023\]. The key observation
is that the weight update learned during finetuning has a low intrinsic rank: although

Architectural Innovations
A second family of techniques changes the model archi-
tecture itself so that it is cheaper to run, rather than compressing a fixed architecture
after the fact. Two influential examples are Grouped-Query Attention and Mixture of
Experts.
Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) \[Ainslie et al., 2023\] targets the memory band-
width bottleneck of autoregressive decoding. In standard multi-head attention (MHA),
every query head has its own key and value matrix, which we all need to use for com-
puting attention scores. At the other extreme, multi-query attention (MQA) lets all
query heads share a single key/value head, which shrinks the computation but can hurt
expressive quality and training stability. GQA interpolates between these two: the
query heads are divided into 𝑔groups, and all heads within a group share one key/-
value head. With 𝑔= 1 it is equivalent to MQA, and with 𝑔equal to the number of

## Page 94

94
CHAPTER 4. SCALING LAWS AND EFFICIENCY

Figure 4.9: Illustration of the sparsely gated Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture on
top of a decoder-only transformer \[Zhang et al., 2025\]

heads it is equivalent to MHA, so 𝑔trades quality against memory usage. Often, GQA
is combined with the KV-caching optimizations discussed next in Section 4.2, and it is
now the default attention variant in many open-weight models.
Mixture of Experts (MoE) \[Shazeer et al., 2017\] decouples the total number of
parameters from the compute spent per token. Instead of a single dense feed-forward
block in each layer, a MoE layer contains many parallel “expert” sub-networks together
with a lightweight gating network (router) that activates only a small number of experts
(typically the top-1 or 2) for each token. Because only the chosen experts perform
computation, the per-token cost stays close to that of a single dense block even as the
total parameter count (and hence the model’s overall capacity) grows by an order of
magnitude or more \[Fedus et al., 2022\].
This sparse activation is why models such as Mixtral and many recent frontier sys-
tems can have hundreds of billions of total parameters while activating only a fraction
of them per token. The trade-offs are (1) that all experts must still be held in mem-
ory, (2) that the load must be balanced across experts (often via an auxiliary loss) so
that no expert is over- or under-used, and (3) that routing introduces additional engi-
neering complexity. The MoE architecture is visualized in Figure 4.9, which shows a
top-𝑘routing mechanism, configured with 𝑘= 2, where the gating function selects the
two highest-scoring FFN experts for each token based on the router. The selected ex-
perts are evaluated in parallel, with their outputs aggregated using weighted summation
\[Zhang et al., 2025\].

Knowledge Distillation
A large teacher model is used to train a smaller student
model by encouraging the student to match the teacher’s output distribution \[Gu et al.,
2023, Xu et al., 2024\]. Crucially, the student learns from the teacher’s full soft prob-
abilities (typically softened with a temperature) rather than only the single correct an-
swer. These soft targets carry richer information: for instance, which wrong answers
the teacher considers plausible. This lets the student approach the teacher’s quality at
a fraction of its size. The same idea underpins the synthetic-data generation discussed

## Page 95

4.2. SMALL LANGUAGE MODELS
95

below, where a frontier model effectively acts as the teacher, generating high-quality
training data for a smaller student model.

4.2.1.2
Reducing Inference Cost

Once a model is trained, it can be further optimized for deployment at inference time.
Whereas training-time techniques focus on reducing the cost of producing the model,
inference-time techniques target the cost of using it: the throughput (tokens generated
per second), the latency (time to the first and each subsequent token), and the memory
footprint required to serve a request. We discuss several techniques that are commonly
used to reduce inference cost, which can be applied to both large and small models.

Key–Value (KV) Caching
During autoregressive generation, the model produces
one token at a time, and each new token attends to all previous tokens. Recomputing the
attention keys and values for the entire context at every step is quadratically expensive.
However, when we predict a new token, the context remains the same. Instead of
recomputing the attention values, we can store the key and value vectors of past tokens
in a KV cache and reuse them. This turns per-step attention into a linear-cost lookup.
This is the basic optimization that makes decoding practical, but it comes at a cost: the
cache grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size and quickly dominates
memory usage for long contexts. This problem has motivated both the architectural
choices above (GQA and MQA shrink the cache by sharing key/value heads across
query heads) and dedicated memory-management schemes such as PagedAttention,
which stores the cache in non-contiguous blocks to reduce fragmentation and enable
higher serving throughput \[Kwon et al., 2023\].

Pruning
A more extreme method for reducing model size is to consider removing re-
dundant or less important connections in the neural network \[Ma et al., 2023\]. Pruning
can be unstructured (zeroing out individual weights) or structured (removing entire
neurons, attention heads, or layers); the latter yields concrete speedups on standard
hardware, whereas the former requires sparsity-aware kernels to realize its benefits.

Quantization
Another method of saving memory during inference is to reduce the
size of the matrix that needs to be loaded into memory. Rather than making the ma-
trix dimensions smaller, we can also lower the precision of weights entries (e.g., from
16-bit to 8-bit or 4-bit numbers). This significantly reduces memory usage and speeds
up inference. However, in principle, lower precision means lower performance. The
same idea can also be applied to the KV cache itself to keep long contexts in mem-
ory. Quantization is a frequently used approach \[Dettmers et al., 2022, Dettmers and
Zettlemoyer, 2023, Xiao et al., 2023\].
Alternatively, rather than casting all weights to the same precision, mixed precision
modes have been proposed, with different levels of numerical precision for different
parts of the computation, to balance speed and stability \[Micikevicius et al., 2017\].
This approach may suffer from non-deterministic results due to numerical instabilities
\[Yuan et al., 2025\].

## Page 96

96
CHAPTER 4. SCALING LAWS AND EFFICIENCY

Speculative Decoding
A key technique for optimizing inference efficiency is spec-
ulative decoding \[Leviathan et al., 2023\]. This approach uses a small draft model to
generate multiple tokens quickly, which are then verified in parallel by a larger target
model. This allows for faster inference (up to 2-3 fold speedup) without sacrificing the
quality of the larger model, effectively leveraging the different points on the scaling
curve.

4.2.2
Data-centric Optimization

In addition to model-centric approaches, the literature emphasizes that data quality and
curation are often more important than the size of the dataset when training efficient
models \[Luo et al., 2025\]. Small models can perform well if they are trained on highly
curated, high-quality data. Hence, it is important to create a good data recipe, in ad-
dition to an efficient model architecture. Data-centric techniques broadly fall into two
camps: selecting the most useful parts from a broader pool of data, and generating new
synthetic data where good data is scarce.

4.2.2.1
Data Selection and Curation

Rather than training on all available text, a growing body of work shows that care-
fully choosing which data to train on, and in what proportions, yields better models
for the same compute budget. For pretraining, NVIDIA’s CLIMB framework \[Diao
et al., 2026\] embeds a large corpus into a semantic space, clusters it, and then itera-
tively searches for the data mixture that minimises proxy-model loss. The resulting
ClimbMix dataset (400B tokens) lets a sub-billion-parameter model outperform com-
parable models trained on far larger but unfiltered corpora. The same principle applies
at the finetuning stage: LIMA \[Zhou et al., 2023\] shows that supervised finetuning
on only 1,000 carefully curated prompt–response pairs is enough to produce a strong
instruction-following model, supporting the view that most knowledge is acquired dur-
ing pretraining and that alignment mainly teaches the model a desired response style.

4.2.2.2
Synthetic Data Gathering

When suitable data does not exist, it can be generated. The Textbooks Are All You Need
approach, used for models such as Microsoft’s Phi series \[Gunasekar et al., 2023\],
demonstrates that training on clean, synthetic textbook-quality data can allow a rela-
tively small model of 1.3B parameters to outperform models ten times its size.
Such pipelines typically rely on frontier models to generate the data, combined
with LLM-as-a-judge scoring to filter for the most accurate and educational examples,
and rigorous decontamination to ensure the synthetic data does not leak benchmark
test sets and inflate reported performance. This approach is particularly valuable for
reasoning data: by training on step-by-step reasoning trajectories produced by larger
models, complex problem-solving skills can be distilled into a smaller architecture (see
also Chapter 6) \[Muennighoff et al., 2025, Arora and Zanette, 2026\].

## Page 97

4.2. SMALL LANGUAGE MODELS
