4.2.2.3
Sample-Efficient Learning

Beyond synthetic data, there is an increased research focus on how models can learn
more efficiently from limited, naturalistic data. Initiatives such as the BabyLM Chal-
lenge \[Warstadt et al., 2023\] focus on training models under strict data constraints (e.g.,
10M to 100M tokens). This mirrors the volume of language input a human child re-
ceives during early development, driving innovation in sample-efficient architectures
while providing insights into cognitively plausible language acquisition.

4.2.3
Popular models

Having surveyed improvement techniques, it is useful to look at how popular large and
small models apply them in practice. Models are commonly categorized by their open-
ness: closed-weight (proprietary) models expose only an API, open-weight models re-
lease their trained parameters, and open-source models additionally share the training
data and code. In practice openness is a matter of degree rather than a strict category,
and we may subsequently use an openness index to rate the transparency \[Artificial
Analysis, 2026\]. Most open models can be found on repositories such as Hugging
Face.
Below, we briefly describe some of the most popular open-weight models that are
designed to be efficient enough to run on consumer hardware, and the techniques they
use to achieve this. This is not an exhaustive list, but rather a selection of influential
models that exemplify the trends in efficiency techniques and their scales, at the time
of writing.

Phi series \[Abdin et al., 2024\]. The Phi-series are capable SLMs that are efficient
enough to run locally on mobile devices. The core innovation behind the Phi
models is their data-centric training methodology. Microsoft curates high-quality,
heavily filtered web data combined with synthetic data generated by larger mod-
els. This allows small models (such as the 3.8 billion parameter Phi-3-mini)
to perform well, rivaling the reasoning capabilities of much larger models such
as GPT-3.5 and Mixtral.

Gemma series \[Mesnard et al., 2024\] Google emphasizes that Gemma models inherit
Gemini’s strong generalist capabilities, particularly in text, reasoning, and cod-
ing, while advancing the state-of-the-art for their specific size classes, but little
is known about their training method or data.

OLMo family \[Ettinger et al., 2025\] The OLMo (Open Language Model) family is
developed by the Allen Institute for AI to be a completely open-source model.
The OLMo project open-sourced the full training pipeline, including code and
data: the pre-training dataset (Dolma), the training and evaluation code, train-
ing logs, and intermediate checkpoints. This transparency allows researchers to
study training dynamics, data influences, and algorithmic biases.

Qwen series \[Bai et al., 2023\] The Qwen family represents a high-performing suite of
foundational and instruction-tuned models, ranging from sub-billion dense mod-
els to large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. They are notable for their

## Page 98

98
CHAPTER 4. SCALING LAWS AND EFFICIENCY

multilingual capabilities and performance on mathematics, coding, and logical
reasoning benchmarks.

OpenELM \[Mehta et al., 2024\] Apple’s Efficient Language Model family is designed
to run efficiently on edge devices. The layer-wise scaling strategy uses smaller
latent dimensions in layers closer to the input and widens them closer to the
output. This results in high accuracy for low parameter count.

gpt-oss \[Agarwal et al., 2025\] OpenAI released two open-weight reasoning models
that use an efficient mixture-of-expert architecture, optimized for agentic capa-
bilities.

Mixtral series \[Jiang et al., 2024\] These models popularized Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
(SMoE) architectures in the open-weights ecosystem (e.g., Mixtral 8x7B), al-
lowing for large parameter counts with few active parameters during inference,
to maximize efficiency.

Llama series \[Grattafiori et al., 2024\] Meta’s Llama models have become frequently
used. Trained on large datasets (up to 15 trillion tokens for Llama 3) and rang-
ing from small edge-friendly sizes to large 405B parameter frontier models, they
established the standard for scaling laws in open models and catalyzed an ecosys-
tem of finetuned models and derivatives.

DeepSeek \[Liu et al., 2025\] DeepSeek-V3 is a large Mixture-of-Experts model (671B
total parameters with 37B activated per token) notable for the stability of its
training. It combines Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for a compressed key-
value cache with an auxiliary-loss-free strategy for expert load balancing, and
was trained in FP8 mixed precision, achieving frontier-level performance at a
small compute cost. The line also includes the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning models.

GLM \[Zeng et al., 2026\] Developed by Zhipu AI, the GLM (General Language Model)
family is built on strong reasoning capabilities that are developed early in train-
ing, and retained throughout the training process. Recent iterations are opti-
mized for agentic workflows and software engineering, targeting tool-use and
code-generation performance rather than text completion alone.

Pythia \[Biderman et al., 2023\] EleutherAI’s Pythia is a suite of models (ranging from
70M to 12B parameters) designed to support research into training dynamics
and scaling. Every model is trained on the same data in the same order, with
intermediate checkpoints released per model, enabling controlled studies of how
capabilities, memorization, and biases emerge over the course of training.

BLOOM \[Scao et al., 2023\] BLOOM is a 176B-parameter open-access model pro-
duced by the BigScience collaborative research effort. Trained on the ROOTS
corpus, spanning 46 natural languages and 13 programming languages, it was
among the first large-scale models to prioritize multilingual coverage and full
openness, released under a Responsible AI License.

SmolLM \[Allal et al., 2025\] Hugging Face’s SmolLM is a family of compact models
(135M, 360M, and 1.7B parameters) aimed at efficient on-device deployment,
much like the Phi series. Its performance stems from data curation: it is trained
on the SmolLM-Corpus, which combines high-quality web data, Python code
examples, and synthetically (Mixtral) generated textbooks and stories.

4.3
Inference-Time Compute

The traditional scaling laws focus on the relationship between compute and perfor-
mance at training time. More recent studies shift part of this computational burden
to inference: inference-time scaling (or test-time compute) \[Muennighoff et al., 2025\].
Rather than spending all compute during training, a model is allowed to deliberate
longer at inference time. This is measured by the number of tokens generated or rea-
soning paths explored, in order to produce a higher-quality answer. Hence, optimizing
throughput (tokens/s) becomes of prime importance: the faster tokens can be produced,
the more reasoning a model is able to do during the same amount of time.
Increasing this inference-time budget in terms of tokens can lead to significant
improvements in capabilities \[Du et al., 2024\]; recent work indicates that optimally
allocating test-time compute can allow smaller models to outperform larger ones on
difficult reasoning tasks \[Snell et al., 2024\]. These gains are not guaranteed, however,
and depend on the task and on the specific search or verification strategy employed
\[Stechly et al., 2023\]. Beyond performance, this shift also reframes a broader question
about what kind of systems LLMs are, which we take up in detail in Chapter 6.

4.4
Sustainable Language Models

The large scale of LLM training and deployment has significant environmental and eco-
nomic implications. The energy consumption of AI training and inference is large, and
the subsequent water consumption for cooling comes with a strain on water distribution
pipelines \[Li et al., 2025, Jegham et al., 2025\]. Measuring the energy use and carbon
footprint of training has only recently entered standard reporting \[Ding and Shi, 2024\].
It has been reported that training a single large model can consume as much energy as
hundreds of households use in a year. Training a model such as BLOOM emitted over
50 tonnes of CO2 equivalent when accounting for both dynamic power consumption
and the embodied carbon of hardware manufacturing \[Luccioni et al., 2023\].
As the use of LLMs is increasing in science and society, the total carbon footprint is
increasingly dominated by inference rather than training, especially for models used by
millions of people daily \[ ¨Ozcan et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2022, Samsi et al., 2023\]. This
creates an opportunity: spending more compute during training to create a smaller,
more efficient model (as discussed in Section 4.1) can significantly reduce the long-
term environmental cost of deployment.
As global inference demand scales to billions of daily queries, the cumulative en-
ergy consumption and associated financial cost overtake the initial training investment
\[Faiz et al., 2024\]. Deploying large models at this scale requires a substantial data

## Page 100

100
CHAPTER 4. SCALING LAWS AND EFFICIENCY

center infrastructure, and large electricity and water consumption. Consequently, there
is a strong push toward deploying Small Language Models (SLMs) for sustainable,
large-scale use. By minimizing the parameter and quantization count, SLMs reduce
the memory bandwidth and compute required per generated token, offering a greener
and more economically viable solution.

Privacy and Data Leakage
Beyond environmental concerns, the centralization of
LLMs through cloud APIs introduces privacy vulnerabilities. When users query cloud-
based models, sensitive personal data, corporate intellectual property, or protected
health information must be transmitted to third-party servers. This creates risks of data
leakage \[Aiyappa et al., 2023, Li et al., 2024\], either through unauthorized interception,
adversarial extraction attacks, or the inadvertent memorization and subsequent regur-
gitation of private user prompts by the model \[Chen et al., 2024, Maini et al., 2024, Liu
et al., 2022\].
To mitigate these privacy risks and reduce reliance on cloud infrastructure, devel-
opers can move from API-based inference toward local, on-device inference \[Qu et al.,
2025\]:

• API-Based Inference: API-based inference relies on powerful remote servers.
While this allows access to frontier models with hundreds of billions of parame-
ters, it suffers from network latency, requires constant internet connectivity, and
inherently exposes user data to cloud providers.

• Local Inference: Local inference runs the model directly on the user’s hardware
(e.g., smartphones, laptops, or edge servers). This ensures data privacy because
prompts never leave the device while also eliminating network latency and guar-
anteeing offline availability.

Local inference is constrained by the physical limits of consumer and edge hardware.
For instance, memory and bandwidth are limited. LLM inference is a memory-bound
process. Storing model weights requires significant RAM capacity, while generating
tokens requires a high memory bandwidth. Furthermore, most mobile devices are pow-
ered by a battery. Running intensive matrix multiplications on mobile devices or stan-
dard laptops can lead to rapid battery drain and thermal throttling.
To make local deployment feasible, developers must rely on the inference-time
optimization techniques, such as quantization (e.g., 4-bit) and speculative decoding,
alongside the increasing availability of specialized neural processing units (NPUs) de-
signed for low-power edge AI.

4.5
Concluding Remarks

As LLM use becomes more ubiquitous and the demand for quick responses increases,
the focus in LLM development is shifting towards more efficient solutions. Hence,
the focus on scaling data, compute, and model size purely for raw performance is
transitioning into a focus on scaling for efficiency.

## Page 101

BIBLIOGRAPHY
101

While the fundamental power laws still hold, the focus has shifted from simply
training the largest possible model toward compute-optimal training, inference-time
scaling, and initiatives to develop capable small models that run on consumer and edge
hardware.
The directions that have been discussed in this chapter are complementary rather
than competing: the model-centric techniques (LoRA, GQA, MoE, quantization, distil-
lation) and the data-centric techniques (careful data selection and synthetic generation)
are increasingly combined within a single training recipe.
As we move closer to the data wall, the role of synthetic data and architectural
efficiency are likely to grow in importance, and the ability to do more with less is
becoming a research focus.

Chapter 5

Case Study 1: Building LLMs
from Scratch


What You Will Learn

In this case study you will learn how to train your own model. Specifically, you
will be able to:
• Explain the end-to-end training pipeline of a ChatGPT-style LLM, distinguish-
ing the purpose and mechanics of each stage: tokenization, pre-training, mid-
training, and supervised fine-tuning.
• Configure and train a Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenizer and articulate the
trade-offs involved in choosing a vocabulary size.
• Describe the transformer architecture at a mechanistic level: attention heads,
layer depth, embedding dimensions. You will investigate how these hyperpa-
rameters interact with model capacity and compute budget.
• Evaluate a trained language model on standard benchmarks (ARC-Easy, ARC-
Challenge, GSM-8K) and interpret results critically, including failure modes.
• Critically reflect on the ethical, environmental, and access dimensions of LLM
training, including cost as a barrier to entry and data curation as a values-laden
choice.
• Access and navigate the information related to open-access LLM models. This
includes reading model cards, training reports, reading code related to training
LLMs, and other types of hub entries.

5.1
Building a Chatbot

We will work through a practical case that covers the full lifecycle of a modern ChatGPT-
style language model. We use nanochat,1 a minimal, single-codebase, full-stack im-
plementation of an instruction-following LLM, released by Andrej Karpathy in April

1https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat

111

### Page links

- [Link 1](https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat)

## Page 112

112
CHAPTER 5. CASE STUDY 1: BUILDING LLMS FROM SCRATCH

2025. Unlike his earlier nanoGPT, which covered pre-training only, nanochat imple-
ments the complete training pipeline: a Byte Pair Encoding tokenizer, pre-training on
web text followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on benchmark datasets, an inference
server, and a chat web UI.
The code uses mostly pure Python with minimal dependencies, and therefore is
easy to use and extend. The codebase comprises roughly 8,000 lines of Python and a
small amount of Rust.2

The performance of nanochat is striking: a GPT-2-capable LLM (which cost ∼$43,000
to train in 2019 \[Radford et al., 2019\]) for only $48 (∼2 hours of 8xH100 GPU node).
While this compute is not exactly commonplace for standard student projects at a uni-
versity, we can scale down the experiment to make it suited to a hands-on course as-
signment. It is important to realize that every gradient update and every design deci-
sion is visible, from raw bytes to a working chat assistant. We will take you trough the
nanochat pipeline across four tasks that you should all perform.
Because GPU budgets on a course are limited, you will train a small model (depth 4,
depending on availability, see Section 5.3); you will then reflect on what may happen
at larger scale using some theory and the published (nanochat) benchmarks.

5.2
Background: Karpathy’s nanochat

The case study will give you direct, hands-on experience with every stage of the modern
LLM training pipeline, from input text to a deployed chat assistant. This experience
will ground the theoretical concepts from Chapters 2–4 in concrete, debuggable code.
nanochat is configured out of the box to train a compute-optimal model by set-
ting a single complexity dial: --depth, which specifies the number of transformer
layers.
All other hyperparameters—embedding width, number of attention heads,
learning rate schedule, training horizon, weight decay—are derived automatically in
a near-optimal way. This keeps the configuration space manageable while preserving
the full educational value of understanding what each parameter does.
The training pipeline proceeds with the by now hopefully familiar stages, which
are briefly described next.

Pretraining
The model is trained on approximately 6 billion tokens drawn from
CLIMBMix \[Diao et al., 2026\], a clustering-based iteratively bootstrapped data mix-
ture corpus. A depth-24 (∼1.4B-parameter) model trains to a validation loss of 2.41
(0.717 bits-per-byte) in roughly 4 hours on a 4×H100 node compute cluster.

Supervised finetuning (SFT)
Starting from the pretrained checkpoint, the model is
finetuned on a mixture of instruction-following and reasoning data: SmolTalk \[Ben Al-
lal et al., 2024\] (460K general-purpose conversations), MMLU (multiple-choice knowl-
edge questions, 3 epochs), GSM-8K (grade-school mathematics, 4 epochs), identity

2If that number sounds large, it is worth noting that the corresponding proprietary systems run to millions
of lines. Nanochat is aimed to be a small self-contained version.

## Page 113

5.3. EXPERIMENT PREPARATION
113

conversations, and synthetic spelling tasks—approximately 1.1 million training exam-
ples in total. Note that the cross-entropy loss is computed only on assistant tokens, not
on user prompts, mirroring the InstructGPT training procedure \[Ouyang et al., 2022\].
Before each training stage, a BPE tokenizer is trained on 2 billion characters using
a Rust implementation, producing a vocabulary of 32,768 tokens in under one minute.
A web inference server and a lightweight JavaScript chat UI are included out of the
box, allowing immediate interaction with your trained model.

Supplementary resources
Two freely available courses provide complementary per-
spectives on the material in this case study. The Hugging Face LLM Course \[Hug-
ging Face, 2022\] introduces the transformers, datasets, tokenizers, and
accelerate libraries, and the Hugging Face Hub through which most open-weight
models are distributed and evaluated today. Mathieu Labonne’s LLM Course \[Labonne,
2023\] provides a practitioner roadmap covering pre-training data curation, parameter-
efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA), preference alignment (DPO, PPO, GRPO), quan-
tization (GGUF, GPTQ), and production inference serving (vLLM, TGI). Together
these resources situate nanochat within the broader open-source LLM ecosystem and
are referenced explicitly in Tasks 3 and 4. You are also free to browse around for ad-
ditional resources. It is strongly recommended to link and reference sources in your
report where needed.

5.3
Experiment Preparation

Repository
Clone the course repository and read the README carefully before
writing any code.

Listing 5.1: Cloning the nanochat repository

1
git clone git@github.com:karpathy/nanochat.git

Compute
No dedicated compute is necessary. You may use your own laptop (with a
GPU), or a larger computer. The experiments are planned so that each run completes a
maximum of approximately 8 hours. For pretraining, use a --depth 4 configuration;
--depth 2 is acceptable only if your hardware does not permit the larger model. Do
not attempt depth ≥12 unless you have some serious hardware.

Logging
nanochat logs training loss, validation loss, and bits-per-byte at configurable
intervals to your terminal, and additional functionality for reporting and saving infor-
mation during the run is available. It is therefore wise to enable structured logging to a
.jsonl file from the start. Retrofitting logging after a run is painful. You may want
to experiment with the logging file formats. We recommend using a service such as
wandb.ai before training full models.

5.7
Task 3: Mid-Training and Supervised Finetuning

5.7.1
What to Do

Recall that nanochat only performs two training stages: pretraining and SFT. However,
in the book, we discussed that additional stages in the form of mid-training can help
the model perform better. In this task, you will implement a new mid-training stage by
modifying scripts/chat sft.py. The goal is to separate reasoning adaptation
(mid-training) from instruction following (SFT) and measure the effect empirically.

Stage 1 — Mid-training
Modify the train tasks list in chat sft.py so that
it contains only reasoning and knowledge tasks: MMLU and GSM-8K. Remove all
other conversational and spelling data. Run chat sft.py from your pre-trained
base checkpoint and save the resulting checkpoint.

Stage 2 — SFT
Modify chat sft.py again so that train tasks contains only
SmolTalk. You will also need to make a small change so the script loads your Stage 1
checkpoint rather than the base pre-trained model. Inspect the load model call in
chat sft.py as a starting point.4 Run chat sft.py from your Stage 1 checkpoint
to proceed with SFT after mid-training.
After each stage, evaluate with scripts/chat eval.py on ARC-Easy, ARC-
Challenge, and GSM-8K.
Sanity check: Before running Stage 1, inspect the data: print the first few rows of
the MMLU and SmolTalk datasets to understand their format and content. Make sure
you are able to answer: how many training examples does each dataset contribute, and
what does a single training example look like?

5.10
Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have used nanochat as a window into the complete LLM training
pipeline. You have trained a BPE tokenizer, observed a transformer learn from web
text, adapted that model to follow instructions, evaluated it on standard benchmarks,
and deployed it as a chat assistant.
The gap between your depth-4 model and the frontier will be obvious, because we
don’t expect you to have access to datacenter-grade compute capabilities. However,
the experiments are, in theory, scalable: rerunning at higher depths and with additional
data resources should lead to more capable models, as predicted by the scaling laws.
After completion of Assignment 1, you have essentially trained a full LLM by yourself,
and you will be better equipped for future experiments where an increased scale is
necessary.

This part is about the brains of our agents, and how they use them to learn. The
previous part showed us how a basic next-token LLM is trained. In agentic models typ-
ically more advanced reasoning and multi-modal models are used (which we continue
to call LLM). In this part we will discuss these more advanced models, why they are
needed, and how they are trained and used.
The first chapter of this part introduces reasoning models. Originally LLMs could
not solve simple reasoning problems, and the chain of thought concept caused a major
leap forward in this field. We will discuss math word problems, chain of thought
prompting, and in-context learning. We will see models that use self-reflection to try
to improve their own behavior. Self-reflection loops led to the development of agentic
harnesses for LLMs.
In the following chapter we go beyond language: we will see that the transformer
architecture also works for vision and action domains. We will discuss various kinds
of World Models, models that allow agents to act more intelligently in their interaction
with the world.
In the last chapter of this part, we introduce the concept of metalearning, a paradigm
that is present in many of the types of learning that we see in agentic LLMs. We will
discuss what metalearning is, and why it is a challenging form of machine learning.

What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how language models can solve more complex prob-
lems through multi-step reasoning. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Describe the chain of thought concept: how we can use in-context learning to
guide the LLM to take intermediate steps in answering a query, and thus provide
better answers to more complex queries.
• Describe how reasoning methods have increased the power of LLMs greatly,
and why this power is essential for agentic LLMs to act realistically in the real
world.
• Write your first agentic harness: a small algorithm that calls the LLM with
different prompts. The agent harness manages the prompts and the replies from
the LLM.
• Explain self-reflection: LLMs can be called in different roles by the harness,
for example, to evaluate an answer, or to generate subproblems. The LLM is
reflecting to improve its own answers.
• Understand the role that is played by memory: how the harness keeps track of
the state of the agent, and how this state is used by the harness to manages the
prompts.
• Use the concept of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards:
where
inference-time reasoning results are used for finetuning.

6.1
In-Context Reasoning

As we noted Chapter 3, in large models, beyond hundreds of billions of parameters, a
new kind of learning has emerged in LLMs. It is called in-context learning (ICL) or
prompt-learning \[Brown et al., 2020\]. It is an important learning method, which we
will discuss in more detail in this section. Then, we will discuss common benchmarks,
and the chain of thought method for multi-step reasoning.

125

## Page 126

126
CHAPTER 6. MULTI-STEP REASONING IN LLMS

6.1.1
In-Context Learning

In-context learning \[Dong et al., 2022\] occurs not at training time, but at inference time,
from examples that are provided in the LLM prompt, when the model is used to answer
questions. These examples cause the decoder model to access relevant knowledge
stored in the LLM. Because of this rich knowledge, in-context learning finds accurate
results with few examples, which is why it is a so-called few-shot learning method. The
few-shot learning is made possible by the large size of the model, containing rich and
varied knowledge on many topics.

Learning, not Training
A main difference between in-context learning and finetun-
ing or pretraining is that in-context learning does not change the parameters of the
transformer. Since no model-parameters are changed at inference time, it is not a pa-
rameter training method; however, since it does learn an answer from provided ex-
amples, it is a learning method. A consequence is that ICL has the disadvantage of
forgetfulness: since model parameters remain unchanged, all learned information is
lost between LLM calls. To share information between LLM calls, previous results
must be added to the prompt of the next call, in the context window, as extra learning
examples.

Context Window
How does in-context learning work? The part of an LLM in which
the prompt is written is called its context window. The decoder model learns inside
this context window, from the examples that are provided in the prompt. A point to
note is that all examples that the answer is learned from must be provided together in
the context window—they should fit in the prompt. Typically, the size of the context
window is limited to a few thousand tokens, and only few examples can be provided:
all ICL is able to perform is few-shot learning. This becomes problematic when the
amount of information that we wish to learn from grows, since the context window is
typically limited in size. We might say that in-context learning suffers from long-term
memory loss.

Example
In in-context learning, a prompt, consisting of a few pieces of demonstra-
tion context, is concatenated with a query question, which is given to the context win-
dow of the language model \[Liu et al., 2023\]. The model will then generate the answer
by performing a forward pass through the model. For example, when the task is emo-
tion recognition in a social media post, I missed the bus today, can be followed by I felt
so \[
\], and the model could answer with bad. Alternatively, for translation, we could
follow I missed the bus today, by French: \[
\] to request a translation. The prompt
contains background information that is recognized by the model, selecting the desired
model context.

Few-shot Learning and the Holy Grail of Machine Learning
In-context learning
works when language models contain enough knowledge, allowing them to generalize
on the (few) examples provided in the prompt. The user provides a few relevant exam-
ples in the prompt, in order to prime the LLM to select the right background knowledge

## Page 127

6.1. IN-CONTEXT REASONING
127

for answering the prompted instruction. Contexts that contain a few examples are said
to perform few-shot learning. Contexts that contain only instructions, with zero exam-
ples, are said to perform zero-shot learning.
ICL is a form of few-shot learning that caused much excitement among researchers.
In traditional machine learning, a model 𝑓is trained on dataset. To achieve high ac-
curacy on complex problems, the datasets must contain many examples. Traditional
machine learning is a form of many-shot learning, requiring many (expensive) training
epochs to train the parameters of the model. In-context learning, on the other hand,
is cheap, requiring just a few examples followed by a single forward pass through the
decoder model (since the expensive training has been done in the pretraining phase).
Few-shot learning is something of the holy grail of machine learning: a model that
generalizes, cheaply.

Practical Considerations and Prompt Engineering
In-context learning further has
the practical advantage of convenience: we can perform ICL on an LLM that runs
commercially in the cloud, from our smartphone, without going through the difficulty
of finding a computer to train a large model on.
Although prompts provide a user-friendly interface to LLMs, the success of in-
context learning tends to be quite sensitive to the way a prompt is formulated or when
different examples are provided. Prompt-learning is brittle, and a new field called
prompt engineering has emerged to help human users to learn how to make LLMs do
what we want them to do \[Radford et al., 2019, Wei et al., 2022a, Giray, 2023, Sahoo
et al., 2024\].
In most LLMs the context window is provided with hidden prompts, the system
prompts, to specify a particular role for the model, to prevent the use of swear words,
and, in chatbots, to have a short history of previous search results, to allow for more
naturally flowing conversations.
In-context learning has spawned much further research. One of the areas is multi-
step reasoning, which is the topic of this chapter. Reasoning used to be an area where
LLMs performed poorly. For example, LLMs failed at simple math exercises. To bet-
ter understand this application domain we will introduce a few reasoning benchmarks.
Then we will discuss an in-context learning method that greatly improved the perfor-
mance of reasoning by LLMs.

6.1.2
Multi-step Reasoning Benchmarks

Progress in artificial intelligence is measured by benchmarks. The research on multi-
step reasoning with LLMs started with easy (grade school) math word problems. Specif-
ically for the study of such easy reasoning the GSM8K benchmark was composed
\[Cobbe et al., 2021\]. GSM8K was created with the aim of providing high quality prob-
lems, of high diversity and moderate difficulty, in natural language. It consists of 8500
human-written math problems and solutions. Language models struggled to achieve
good performance on this dataset before chain of thought was introduced (see the next
section). Here is an example of a typical math word problem:

Problem: Romeo bakes 4 trays with two dozen batches of cookies in a

## Page 128

128
CHAPTER 6. MULTI-STEP REASONING IN LLMS

week. If these cookies are shared amongst 16 people equally, how many
cookies does each person consume?
Answer: 4 × 2 × 12/16 = 6.

The GSM8K benchmark, although it may look easy to us, turned out to be difficult
for LLMs. When it was introduced, the state of the art LLM GPT-3-175B achieved a
rather low accuracy of around 15% \[Wei et al., 2022b\]. Other benchmarks of similar
math word problems are the SVAMP varying structures benchmark \[Patel et al., 2021\],
the ASDiv dataset of diverse math problems \[Miao et al., 2021\], the AQuA dataset
of algebraic word problems \[Ling et al., 2017\], and the MAWPS benchmark \[Koncel-
Kedziorski et al., 2016\].
Later, benchmarks for other tasks were introduced, to assess LLM reasoning abil-
ities in other fields of reasoning. For example, benchmarks have been developed on
advanced mathematical questions (AIME \[Codeforces, 2024\]), computer code compre-
hension (Spider \[Yu et al., 2018\], transcoding (translating a program in one computer
language to another) \[Roziere et al., 2020\]), robotic movement (Alfworld \[Shridhar
et al., 2020\], kitchen tasks \[Ahn et al., 2022\]), puzzle solving (Game24 \[Yao et al.,
2024\]), creative writing \[Yao et al., 2024\]), board games (Checkmate problems \[Yang
et al., 2024\], MineCraft \[Fan et al., 2022\]), and webpage navigation (WebShop \[Yao
et al., 2022a\]). Further relevant benchmark studies also focus on games and planning
problems \[Ruoss et al., 2024, Paglieri et al., 2025, Wen et al., 2025a\].
The goal of benchmarks is to be able to clearly compare the performance of differ-
ent approaches. However, it can be difficult to directly compare different benchmarking
results, since there may be differences in the way the experiments were conducted. See
Kamoi et al. \[2024\], Shojaee et al. \[2025\] for a critical discussion of challenges in
benchmarking LLM reasoning.

6.1.3
Chain of Thought Prompting

Around 2022, regular LLMs of the time performed poorly on simple math word prob-
lems. Interestingly, the standard Chapter 4 approach to improve performance of LLMs
by scaling up the size of the LLM, did not solve the problem \[Rae et al., 2021\]. The
problem appeared to be somehow fundamental in nature, and researchers went looking
for a different approach.
The LLM architecture is a transformer-based decoder. Given a certain input, it
is designed to produce a single token. LLMs are next-token predictors. When we
prompt such a decoder to produce an answer, it does as it is instructed to: it provides
an answer quickly—any answer. But that is not how humans work towards an answer
in a mathematical reasoning problem, we divide the question into a sequence of steps
to solve (4 × 2 × 12/16 = 6). Thus, for the LLM, what we should do instead is to
prompt it to follow a well-chosen sequence of intermediate steps, answer those, and
thus work towards the final answer, just as a student is taught to break down a complex
problem into smaller steps, and to also provide the reasoning steps when answering a
problem in school—Don’t just tell me the answer, but tell me how you arrived at the
answer. Children are taught in school to break down a big problem into a sequence
of small steps, when solving a mathematical problem. Similarly, we should guide the

Thus, our few-shot prompt should contain examples of intermediate reasoning
steps, instead of only examples of the final answer. This question was studied by Wei
et al. \[2022b\], amongst others, who introduced the chain of thought approach. Fig-
ure 6.1 illustrates how the approach works, in addition to related approaches, that it
inspired.
The way to instruct an LLM to generate intermediate steps is to manually write a
prompt consisting of specific reasoning steps to answer the task (for example, calculate
how many balls are in the container, or in how many pieces the pie was cut). Indeed,
when Wei et al. \[2022b\] tried this approach, and the LLM was prompted to rephrase
information from the question as intermediate reasoning steps in its answer, the LLM
performed much better than when it was prompted to produce a single answer. The ex-
ample from the chain of thought paper is shown in Figure 6.1. When shown the longer
example prompt, the LLM follows the longer example when answering the question
(Few-Shot CoT). On GSM8K, the chain of thought approach showed a large increase
in accuracy, from 16% to 47%.
The idea that, when prompted, an LLM can be made to follow step-by-step instruc-
tions, has caused much excitement and has opened up further research on multi-step
reasoning with LLMs. Chain of thought (CoT) has become a standard prompting ap-
proach in LLMs since.
In the original paper the prompts were hand-written by the researchers for the in-
dividual types of problems. Kojima et al. \[2022\] go a step further. They show that
the addition of a single task-independent sentence (Let’s think step by step) also sig-
nificantly improves performance for many problems. Since this text does not contain
problem-related elements, it is as a form of zero-shot learning. Figure 6.1 compares

the approaches (second and third column). Experiments further show that with this
addition significant performance gains are also achieved on other reasoning bench-
marks, including arithmetic, symbolic, and logical reasoning (achieving 70% accuracy
on GSM8K when self consistency (see next section) is also included, using the newer
PaLM LLM \[Wang et al., 2022\]).
The chain of thought idea itself is inspired by Scratchpad \[Nye et al., 2021\], by
other earlier work where natural language steps are generated for arithmetic reasoning
\[Ling et al., 2017, Cobbe et al., 2021\], and by the use of formal languages for rea-
soning \[Roy and Roth, 2016, Chiang and Chen, 2018, Amini et al., 2019, Chen et al.,
2019\].

6.1.3.1
Self Evaluation

LLMs are not perfect, and errors in results occur. When multiple reasoning steps are
generated, errors accumulate. To prevent the errors from getting out of hand we should
pay extra attention to the evaluation of results. We will now review approaches to re-
duce error accumulation, either by examining the model, or by evaluating intermediate
reasoning steps.
When LLMs are prompted to perform CoT reasoning, they perform a sequence
of steps. Performing multiple steps makes them sensitive to mistakes and vulnerable
to error accumulation \[Weng et al., 2022, Xiao et al., 2023\]. Several methods have
been developed to prevent error accumulation. One approach is to create a new model
to separately evaluate the results. Weng et al. \[2022\] propose an automated approach
using evaluation by the same LLM, called self verification. The LLM is prompted to
use the conclusion of the chain of thought reasoning chain as a condition for solving
the original problem and then compare the answer, going back to the original question.
The LLM is given variations of its own conclusion and is instructed to choose the one
with the highest similarity to the original question.
A popular related approach is self consistency \[Wang et al., 2022\]. Self consistency
is an ensemble approach (a well-known machine learning technique to make a strong
learner by running multiple weaker learners \[Sagi and Rokach, 2018, Breiman, 2001\]).
Conventionally, the answer of an LLM query is extracted from the decoder network by
greedily following the path with the highest logit values. In self consistency, greedy
single-path decoding is replaced by majority voting over a wider sample of paths. By
sampling diverse reasoning paths, evaluating them, and selecting the most consistent
answer among them, self consistency effectively asks the LLM to perform the same
query multiple times, and takes the majority-vote of the internal decoding paths of
the transformer model. Self consistency works because complex reasoning problems
typically have different reasoning paths that lead to the correct answer. Figure 6.2
provides an example of the approach.
Self consistency has been evaluated on arithmetic reasoning, on commonsense rea-
soning and on symbolic reasoning, with a variety of LLMs, including GPT-3. Self
consistency typically improves the performance of chain of thought by a further 10-20
percentage points. Self consistency is often used in combination with chain of thought
in modern LLMs.

6.1.3.2
Code Generation for Validation

Another approach to improve the accuracy of a sequence of reasoning steps is to switch
from a natural to a formal language. The advantage of a formal language is that it is
less ambiguous than a natural language. Examples are computer languages, such as
Python, or mathematical logic.
LLMs have been quite successful in generating computer code from natural lan-
guage prompts. Chen et al. \[2021\] introduced Codex, a GPT model that was trained
on publicly available code in the repository GitHub. Codex is able to generate correct
programs from descriptions in natural language, such as commentary strings. Sub-
sequently, the use of a formal language for reasoning has become a popular approach.
Many approaches generate the reasoning steps in Python, so that the code can be evalu-
ated by a compiler, debugger, or interpreter. Human programmers, when writing code,
typically follow a cycle of writing some code, compiling and executing it to look for
errors, and then using the feedback to improve the code. This approach is followed,
for example, in self debugging \[Chen et al., 2023\]. It follows the same steps of code
generation, code execution, and code explanation. Self debugging is able to identify
mistakes in its own code by investigating the execution results, and can also provide an
explanation of the generated code, in natural language.
Another approach, program aided language \[Gao et al., 2023\], uses the LLM to
generate Python and then use an interpreter to evaluate the result. In this approach
the problem is translated into small pieces of Python code, that can then be executed
by an interpreter to solve the problem. Figure 6.1 (fourth column) illustrates the pro-
gram aided language approach. When the evaluation of the reasoning steps is offloaded
to the Python interpreter, decomposing the natural language problem into executable
code-steps remains the only task for the LLM. Gao et al. \[2023\] provide extensive ex-
perimental evidence showing the synergy between the neural LLM and the symbolic
interpreter. Experiments were performed on 13 mathematical, symbolic, and algorith-
mic reasoning tasks, achieving more accurate results than much larger models of the
time (for example, program aided language reported 72% on GSM8K and 93% on
Penguins).

6.1.3.3
Evolving code generation prompts

The work on verification with formal languages has lead to several works that generate
working code tuned for solving specific problems automatically, without human feed-
back. Romera-Paredes et al. \[2024\] introduced FunSearch, an approach that integrates
formal methods and LLMs to enhance mathematical reasoning and code generation.
FunSearch uses a genetic approach with multiple populations of candidate solutions
(programs), which are evaluated using a function depending on the problem specifica-
tion. After evaluating the generated programs from the starting prompt, a new prompt
is created, in an iterative fashion, combining a selection of sampled programs sorted
according to their evaluation score, and the LLM is requested to generate a new pro-
gram. Another work leverages evolutionary computation methods to generate and op-
timize evolutionary algorithms \[van Stein and B¨ack, 2024\]. This approach, LLaMEA
(Large Language Model Evolutionary Algorithm), utilizes LLMs to design and opti-

## Page 133

6.2. SELF-REFLECTION AND STATE
133

mize evolutionary algorithms. The approach uses LLMs to generate initial algorithmic
structures, which are then refined through mutation and selection. Accuracy improve-
ments on the Black-Box Optimization Benchmark (BBOB) \[Hansen and Ros, 2010\]
are reported of 11 percentage points.

6.2
Self-Reflection and State

In-context learning has emerged as a powerful new few-shot learning method. When
our few-shot examples specify reasoning steps, we can improve the capabilities of
LLMs even more.
In this section we will look at some of the limits of in-context learning, and we will
look at ways to extend the limits. We will first discuss the question of state and memory.
We will look at how state can be passed between separate invocations of LLMs, at long
context windows, and at the question if LLMs are good at solving problems for which
they have to manipulate state.

6.2.1
LLMs are Memory-less Functions

In-context few-shot learning exploits the capabilities of LLMs to retrieve knowledge,
conditioned by the prompt.
The instructions and examples are provided, and the
transformer architecture finds the answer (next token) in its vast model of (𝐾,𝑉)-
parameters. With chain of thought prompts, the LLM is conditioned on few-shot rea-
soning steps that are specified in the prompt.
In-context learning uses the LLM in a functional way, where all input to the LLM
is provided in the prompt. The model 𝑓finds the answer 𝑎for the input prompt 𝑝:

𝑓(𝑝) →𝑎.

In principle, LLMs do not retain information between LLM calls (model parameters
remain unchanged, and there are no global variables with history). If we wish to refine
our request, and we wish to carry state information from the previous call to the next,
then all such state must be specified by the user in the new prompt 𝑝′. The model itself
has forgotten all about the previous answer.
For a chatbot, repeating the entire conversational history in each new question
would be a cumbersome and unnatural way of conversing. In human conversation
our conversation partners do remember what was last said, without us having to ex-
plicitly repeat their last sentence (although, when interviewing politicians, journalists
sometimes use this method to try to keep them on message). Commercial chatbots
overcome this problem in part using system prompts, by invisibly providing the output
of the previous LLM call to the prompt for a new LLM query. However, the principle
remains that LLMs are good at finding associative next-token answers for a prompt, but
not at all at remembering answers and manipulating the state of variables as we know
them from general computer programming languages. As no parameters are changed,
LLMs do not remember in-context state between calls.

## Page 134

134
CHAPTER 6. MULTI-STEP REASONING IN LLMS

Figure 6.3: Tic Tac Toe is a Simple Board Game, in which State is important

6.2.2
Retrieval Augmentation and Long Context Windows

The LLM-memory problem goes deeper. All information for the query must be spec-
ified in a context window. The size of this context window is limited, which funda-
mentally limits the amount of information that can be communicated to the LLM for a
query. This limitation is a problem when a large text (such as a book) is to be summa-
rized. Furthermore, in Section 20.2.1 we will discuss in-context reinforcement learning
methods, that work by storing full episode histories in the context window. In short,
methods are needed to pass more information to the LLM.
One of the earliest methods to extend the amount of information at inference time
is retrieval augmentation for generative AI (RAG). RAG lets the LLM place a call to
external data, such as a corporate database, or to Wikipedia \[Lewis et al., 2020\]. RAG’s
use is also in reducing factual hallucinations and providing access to time-sensitive
information, such as financial or logistics data. RAG will be discussed in Chapter 12.
For passing longer texts to the model, LLMs have been developed with longer con-
text windows. With the standard transformer architecture, the compute requirements
scale quadratically with the size of the context window, and linear architectures are
being developed \[Ren et al., 2024\]. Another solution is to compress the information
in the context window, for example using semantic compression \[Fei et al., 2024\], by
chunking the information \[Wang et al., 2023, Zhou et al., 2025\], or by recursive meth-
ods \[Zhang et al., 2025\]. Devising novel memory architectures for LLMs is an active
area of research \[Yan et al., 2025\].

6.2.3
LLMs and Stateful Problems

LLMs perform poorly at solving problems in which state must be managed \[Wong
et al., 2025\]. This occurs for example in planning problems in which the current state
has to be remembered accurately, even in simple board games such as the one shown in
Figure 6.3. LLMs tend to mix up the states, and to provide plausible sounding answers
that may be correct for games that it has seen in its training corpus, but that are wrong
for the actual board state at hand \[Paglieri et al., 2025, Ruoss et al., 2024\].
Many approaches have been tried to improve reasoning with state, often inspired by
reinforcement learning and planning algorithms \[Wong et al., 2026\]. To see how LLMs
can be used to solve these stateful problems, we discuss how the memory-less nature

## Page 135

6.2. SELF-REFLECTION AND STATE
135

of LLMs makes them suffer from a problem known as the knowing-doing gap. Other,
advanced, methods have been developed to allow LLMs to deal better with stateful
problems. Chapter 20 will discuss these advanced approaches.

Knowing-Doing Gap
In addition to the lack of state between LLM calls, there is
another memory-related problem, in the internal execution by the LLM of certain tasks.
This problem has been named the knowing-doing gap. This gap describes the cu-
rious phenomenon where an LLM is able to generate a correct textual description to
solve a problem, even the correct algorithm, but is not able to execute this algorithm
correctly \[Paglieri et al., 2025\]. When you ask an LLM how to solve a certain prob-
lem, it can promptly provide the right algorithm in executable Python code. When
one subsequently asks it to actually solve this problem, the LLM does not correctly
follow the algorithm that it just generated. More often than not, errors start appear-
ing between state changes of the variables in the algorithm that it generated \[Paglieri
et al., 2025, Ruoss et al., 2024\]. Note that faithfully executing algorithmic code step by
step, tracking values in registers, is not what the attention-based transformers in LLMs
were designed for at all—they were designed to simulate natural language processing
through a form of associative memory \[La Malfa et al., 2024\].1

In addition to the knowing-doing gap, there is another state-management problem.
Prompting an LLM to play the first few moves of a board game against itself may
show a game in which pieces on the board magically (dis)appear between moves. The
model does not recognize that the moves that it plays that may have been good in
certain situations, do not fit the current board position, and even decorates these wrong
moves with a plausibly sounding reason in a chatty conversational style. LLMs have
difficulty reliably managing the state transition of a variable that goes from one value to
another value. Individual values tend to be forgotten or mixed up. Additional text can
be inserted into the prompt to instruct the model to carefully track values of variables
before making a next step \[La Malfa et al., 2024\], but this is a cumbersome and error-
prone solution.
Both the knowing-doing gap and the disappearing-pieces problem can be circum-
vented by calling an external interpreter to execute an LLM-generated algorithm. This
strategy is sometimes taken by commercial chatbots. It is a smart, practical, solution,
since, in addition to being able to correctly execute Python code, the Python interpreter
will do so more efficiently than an LLM.
Chapter 20 will discuss other approaches that address state and memory in the
transformer architecture.

6.2.4
Agentic Harness for Prompt Improvement

In addition to resorting to externally executing generated code, other methods have
been developed to deal with memory and state. In this section, we will go agentic,
and introduce small external algorithms to explicitly manage state and prompts. Such

1Note further that the human mind sometimes has the same problem: we can easily describe an algorithm
for long division, but when asked to compute 12345/42, we may make mistakes—computers are good at
this, but not humans, and also not LLMs.

## Page 136

136
CHAPTER 6. MULTI-STEP REASONING IN LLMS

an algorithm is called a harness. The harness may also call the same LLM in different
roles, with different prompts for each role, for example, for generation or for evaluation
of states. We start with prompt management based on search algorithms.
When the LLM is called in different roles, for example to critique (evaluate) its own
performance (that it just generated), the LLM can be said to perform self-reflection.
This somewhat anthropomorphic term is often used in the literature for these approaches.
Exactly what (not who) is doing the self-reflecting, the LLM, or the agentic harness, is
a matter for debate.

6.2.4.1
Search-based Prompt Optimization

We will now discuss search-based inference-time decision methods. These are in-
context learning methods that go beyond chain of thought. Chain of thought explores
a single line of reasoning steps, where each step has a single successor step. Search-
based methods explore multiple options at each step, creating a tree of possibilities.
When we wish to examine a tree of possible reasoning steps, then we need a method
to keep track of the state of which step we have seen, what the best answer so far was,
and which steps should still be further examined. As we have seen, LLMs are not terri-
bly good at keeping track of state, whereas conventional computer algorithms, such as
small pieces of Python code, are. Such an algorithm will decompose the problem into
a search tree, where multiple alternative steps are generated that can be searched mul-
tiple steps into the future (see Figure 6.6 on page 138). The algorithms call the LLM
as a subroutine prompting it to perform requested tasks, such as action selection and
reward evaluation. Then, backtracking can be performed by the algorithm, allowing
alternative steps to be tried. This control algorithm is external to the LLM. It wraps
around the LLM, keeping track of state, managing the prompts, shielding it from the
outside world (and shielding the outside world from LLMs that mess up state). The
control algorithm is called a harness.
We start our discussion of control strategies with depth-first and breadth-first search
\[Cormen et al., 2022\]. Tree of thoughts \[Yao et al., 2024\] uses breadth-first or depth-
first search to dynamically follow different reasoning steps.2 Both the generation (red)
and the evaluation (green) part in tree of thoughts are performed by prompting the
LLM, see Figure 6.4. Together, the two LLM prompts with the external control, al-
low systematic exploration of the space of reasoning steps, performing look-ahead and
backtracking.
Tree of thoughts (ToT) has been used on planning-based puzzles, such as the Game
of 24. In this game, 4 numbers are give, and the task is to reach the number 24 by using
the arithmetic operators (+−∗/) in between the numbers. For example, for the numbers
4 9 10 13, a solution would be (10−4)∗(13−9) = 24. Tree of thoughts first generates a
position with the propose prompt: Input 4 9 10 13; Possible next steps:
to which the model answers by generating possible next step thoughts. These are then
evaluated by the model with an evaluation prompt including chain of thought examples.
Figure 6.5 shows a possible prompting sequence from the original paper.

The authors compare their approach to traditional linear chain of thought with self

Tree of thoughts is an elegant approach, adding two of the simplest possible search
structures on top of an LLM. The sequence of prompts is easy to follow, and finding
and correcting mistakes is also easy.
The two search methods of tree of thoughts follow a fixed expansion policy. Next,
we will discuss more advanced learning-based approaches, that may perform better, at
the cost of higher algorithmic complexity.

6.2.4.2
Self-Reflection

Many approaches have been devised that use the LLM in more than one role. Such
approaches are generally called self-reflective approaches. The LLM is used not just to
evaluate a prompt, but also to generate new reasoning steps, and often to refine them.
The field of self-reflection is young and new approaches are being developed regu-
larly. We will present four such approaches: self refine, ReAct, reflexion, and buffer of

3A similarly named approach is graph of thoughts \[Besta et al., 2024\]. Graph of thoughts allows more
general reasoning graphs, providing a formal framework, where the different elements can then be specified
manually.

## Page 139

6.2. SELF-REFLECTION AND STATE
139

Figure 6.7: Self Refine Architecture \[Madaan et al., 2023\]

thoughts. These approaches use the LLMs in different ways, using schemes inspired
by reinforcement learning to let the LLMs improve themselves.

Self Refine
The first approach is self refine \[Madaan et al., 2023\]. This approach aims
to improve answers from feedback. The LLM generates an initial output and provides
feedback for its answer, using the LLM to refine itself, iteratively. The LLM is thus
used to improve its own answers, see Figure 6.7. Self refine prompts the LLM in three
ways: (1) for initial generation, (2) for feedback, and (3) for refinement, following a
greedy reasoning chain. Self refine reportedly improves significantly over regular chain
of thought, on benchmarks such as dialogue response generation, code optimization,
and constrained generation. This approach does follow a linear, greedy, reasoning
chain, where a single successor is tried in a state (it does not explore a tree, as in ToT).

ReAct
Generalizing the greedy approach, we can use LLMs to examine multiple op-
tions per state. A notable approach that combines reinforcement learning and LLMs is
ReAct \[Yao et al., 2022b\].4 ReAct uses chain of thought prompt-learning as part of a re-
inforcement learning framework that also uses external knowledge sources (Wikipedia)
and finetuning; for error reduction, grounding, and for reducing hallucination. The
framework allows hand-written prompts. On two interactive decision making bench-
marks (Alfworld and WebShop), ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learn-
ing methods by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively.

Reflexion
The ReAct work has been developed further. Reflexion \[Shinn et al., 2024\]
creates AI agents that learn by reflecting on failures and enhance their results, inspired
by the way that humans do this.5 Reflexion uses three prompts for the LLM: actor, eval-
uator, and reflector. The reflexion harness incorporates explicit memory between LLM
calls. For trajectory generation it has a short-term memory, and for storing experience
information it has a long term memory. This approach addresses the state management
problem of regular LLMs using memory in the external algorithm. Reflexion works as
follows: (1) an actor model generates text and actions, (2) an evaluator model scores

5https://github.com/noahshinn/reflexion

the outputs produced by the actor, and (3) a self-reflection model generates verbal rein-
forcement cues to assist the actor to self-improve (see Figure 6.8). For the actor, chain
of thought and ReAct can be used. Reflexion has been evaluated on decision-making,
reasoning, and coding tasks. Improvements of 10-20 percentage points are reported
\[Shinn et al., 2024\].

Buffer of Thoughts
Another approach is buffer of thoughts \[Yang et al., 2024\],
which goes a step towards metareasoning \[Gao et al., 2024\]. It introduces a meta-
buffer that stores high-level thought-templates. Thought-templates are derived from
a variety of tasks. Buffer of thoughts uses a problem distiller that stores high-level
thoughts distilled from different problems in a meta-buffer, which is actively managed
for capacity. Figure 6.9 compares the buffer of thoughts approach to other approaches
such as chain of thought and tree of thoughts. Buffer of thoughts outperforms other
methods in puzzles such as Game of 24 (by 11%) and checkmating (by 51%). Thought
templates are related to metacognition (thinking about thinking) \[Didolkar et al., 2024\].

Critique and Prompt Sensitivity
The concept of self-reflection is not without pit-
falls and criticism. To start, the basic idea of asking a model to refine its results begs the
question why the model did not give the better answer in the first place. Next, studies by
Huang et al. \[2023\], Shojaee et al. \[2025\] find methodological issues with some of the
studies, such as the use of data labels that reveal the answer, second refinement prompts
that unintentionally reveal more information than the initial prompts, and the use of the

## Page 141

6.2. SELF-REFLECTION AND STATE
141

Figure 6.9: Buffer of Thoughts \[Yang et al., 2024\]

same LLM for agent and environment. In one reproducibility study performance did
not exceed that of chain of thought with self consistency \[Huang et al., 2023\]. LLMs
are sensitive to how a question is formulated in the prompt. Self-reflection is still a
young and active field of research, with an appealing premise, but many open ques-
tions.
The approaches that we have presented potentially make many LLM calls, which
can become expensive and slow. Finding the optimum approach for your problem may
require quite some experimentation. In Chapter 10 we will discuss a practical case
study where we will get hands-on experience with self-reflection methods. Please keep
the preceding critique in mind.

6.2.4.3
Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

The focus of this chapter is on in-context learning. In-context learning occurs at in-
ference time, and no parameters are trained or changed. Finetuning occurs at training
time, and does change the parameters of the model. In this section we will, however,
briefly talk about a mix of finetuning and in-context learning, we will be mixing train-
ing and inference.
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards refers to an algorithmic approach
for training language models on tasks with verifiable outcomes such as mathematical
problem-solving and instruction following. Especially for reasoning problems, such
as math word problems and coding, inference-time chain of thought results have been
found to significantly improve models when they are used for finetuning.
RLVR is an improvement over reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF),
dispensing with the need for human feedback. In many domains, such as mathematics,
a simple function exists to check if an answer is correct, without the need for human
feedback. RLVR leverages the existing RLHF objective but replaces the reward model

## Page 142

142
CHAPTER 6. MULTI-STEP REASONING IN LLMS

with a verification function. RLVR samples completions from a policy model given a
set of prompts, and verifies their correctness using a deterministic function. If correct,
the reward is positive, otherwise it is 0. This reward is then used to train against us-
ing PPO \[Schulman et al., 2017\] (a standard reinforcement learning algorithm), as in
RLHF.
An influential approach of this type was proposed in the development of DeepSeek-
R1 Guo et al. \[2025\]. This method distinguishes itself from external reasoning ap-
proaches by emphasizing the model’s self-generated reasoning steps. It learns the steps
through reinforcement learning, integrating data generation and training in a single
loop. Lowering the supervised data requirements to train LLMs, DeepSeek’s method-
ology leverages reinforcement learning to enable models to evolve reasoning skills
autonomously. By starting with a base model and applying reinforcement learning, the
system identifies and reinforces effective reasoning patterns. DeepSeek uses group-
relative policy optimization (GRPO), which calculates advantages with group-based
scoring \[Shao et al., 2024\].
One of the key features of DeepSeek’s approach is the emergence of sophisticated
reasoning behaviors during finetuning, such as reflection and exploration of alternative
problem-solving methods \[Mercer et al., 2025\]. These behaviors arise spontaneously as
a result of the model’s interaction with the reinforcement learning environment, rather
than being pre-programmed, and without external self-reflection loops. For example,
DeepSeek-R1-Zero learns to allocate more thinking time to problems by reevaluating
its initial approach. This autonomous approach of learning to reason may lead to more
stable and adaptive reasoning LLMs.
One of the successes behind GRPO is its focus on applications for which verifiable
rewards exist, allowing reinforcement learning methods to be used. The focus on ver-
ifiable rewards has been quite successful, and reinforcement learning with verifiable
rewards (RLVR) methods are often used in finetuning LLMs \[Lambert et al., 2024\].
RLVR methods such as GRPO are typically used dynamically, where an inference
time chain of thought query is used to answer a query from the training set to finetune
the model. Thus, test time inference is used for finetuning. The impressive results of
DeepSeek \[Guo et al., 2025\] have made GRPO \[Shao et al., 2024\] and RLVR \[Lam-
bert et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2025, Wen et al., 2025b, Yue et al., 2025\] highly popular
finetuning methods.

6.3
Concluding Remarks

In the preceding pages we have seen how the reasoning capabilities of language models
can be improved. The best-known approach is chain of thought, which is a prompt-
engineering method that shows an LLM to provide a multi-step reasoning when it is
answering a question, just like we are taught in school when we are shown how to solve
math exercises. More elaborate prompt improvement algorithms have been introduced,
from depth-first search, via self-reflection, to inference-time reinforcement learning
methods. Advanced training methods such as RLVR combine inference-results with
finetuning, achieving strong training results.

## Page 143

6.3. CONCLUDING REMARKS
143

6.3.1
Brittleness

We have discussed many different algorithmic approaches to create an agentic harness.
There are multiple reasons why there are so many. First, the field of agentic LLM is
still young, many challenges exist, leading to many new solutions.
Second, the methods are quite brittle. Small changes in prompts, a comma here
or there, sometimes make the difference whether an approach works or not. Small
changes in hyperparameters, such as the temperature of your model, or even using a
different seed of a random number generator, may have large effects. Changes to the
memory management method of the agentic harness, or using a different LLM, may all
have a large effect on performance.
This may feel like a unsatisfactory state of affairs. Indeed, the field is young, and it
will take some years before methods have stabilized. In your experiments, you should
keep in mind to always do multiple runs, with different seeds, different models, and dif-
ferent hyperparameter settings. This will help you better understand how your solution
works in different circumstances.

6.3.2
Thinking, Fast and Slow

To conclude this chapter we will discuss reasoning in LLMs in a broader perspective.
In the history of AI, two approaches, or schools of thought, can be seen: symbolic AI
and connectionist AI. Symbolic AI roughly corresponds to the idea that intelligence
is best modeled as the manipulation of symbols via the rules of logic. Connection-
ist AI studies whether intelligence emerges spontaneously out of interactions between
connected elements (be they neurons, cells, ants, humans, or robots). Symbolic AI
draws on mathematics, connectionist AI on biology. As we already saw in Section 2.3,
both schools have developed useful methods, and both schools have seen important
successes (such as search algorithms and reasoning, or deep learning and LLMs).
In 2011 Daniel Kahneman published the book Thinking, Fast and Slow in which
the terms System 1 and System 2 were used to distinguish human thought into intuitive,
fast, thinking, and deliberative, slow, thinking \[Kahneman, 2011\]. These terms have
become popular in artificial intelligence, where fast thinking is linked to associative
lookup and slow thinking to multi-step reasoning. At inference time, zero-shot LLMs
think fast (System 1 thinking). Inference-time step-by-step methods (either through
longer prompts or with an agentic harness) perform deliberative slow thinking (System
2 thinking).
LLMs are based on the connectionist AI tradition (System 1). The use of tools
at inference time enhances the LLM part with knowledge retrieval or processing tools
from the symbolic AI tradition (System 2).
We should note that whereas researchers sometimes humanize LLMs and their ca-
pabilities, LLMs only perform next-token prediction. LLMs are not even close to be-
ing human. By generating more tokens to form an answer (reasoning step-by-step),
the token-path from the prompt to the final answer becomes longer. The reason that
this leads more often to correct answers, might be because it takes smaller steps into
the direction of the answer, making the correct answer more plausible with every step
in between—not that it is similar to the way humans are taught to solve the problem.

## Page 144

144
BIBLIOGRAPHY

Reasoning is narrowing down probabilities such that the correct answer becomes more
probable to generate, independent of interpretations related to human cognition \[Guo
et al., 2025\].

6.3.3
Conclusion

In this chapter we have discussed how LLMs can solve language tasks by next-token
prediction, and solve tasks that require multi-step reasoning. We have discussed ways
to manage complex reasoning structures.
Most methods are in-context methods, efficient and easy to use since the prompts
that guide the reasoning are readable by the user. We have introduced the rule of
an agentic harness for prompt improvement and memory management. We have also
touched upon methods that use pretraining and finetuning, not just for the language
part, but also for integrating multi-step reasoning. These methods thus train models for
decision making, beyond pure next-token prediction in language models.
There has been much activity in the creation of such richer models, adding visual
reasoning, decision making, and actions to become an integral part of the LLMs. In
the next chapter we will look deeper into these pretrained and finetuned multi-modal
models.

## Page 151

Chapter 7

Vision, Action and World
Models


What You Will Learn

Agents act in a world that consists of more than language. In this chapter you
will learn how transformer-based models can gain world knowledge in modalities
beyond language. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Describe the architecture of vision-language models, or VLMs, (mostly) trans-
former models that consist of a language and a vision part. VLMs are highly
successful, for example in generating realistic fake images, and film clips.
• Understand how vision-language-action models work. VLAs are also trained on
robotic action. VLAs help improve the generality of robot behavior.
• Explain why agents benefit from world models: models that have learned some
physical aspects of the world around us, preventing agents from attempting to
walk through walls.

7.1
Multi-modal Vision Language Models

Many decisions involve vision. As we will see in this section, the transformer archi-
tecture is also able to learn tokenized visual patterns. Models that are pretrained on
both language and visual data are called vision-language models, or VLMs. VLMs
typically consist of (1) a language part, (2) a vision part, and (3) a part that combines
both embeddings.
We will discuss various architectures of these vision-language models. For each
type of model we will describe the task, the architecture of the model, and the algorithm
with which it is trained. We will see impressive results.
Computer vision has a long and successful history in AI. Deep learning has been
successful in image recognition tasks, long before the breakthroughs in natural lan-
guage processing \[Krizhevsky et al., 2012\]. Can these two successful fields be com-

151

## Page 152

152
CHAPTER 7. VISION, ACTION AND WORLD MODELS

Figure 7.1: A Question in a Visual-Question Answering Tasks might be: What is the
mustache made of?

bined? This is not a trivial question, since the two fields are based on deep learning
architectures that re quite different: image processing is based on convolutional neural
networks that work well on two-dimensional rectangular grids of pixels, and language
processing on transformers that work well on one-dimensional sequences of tokens.
As we will see, architectures have indeed been developed for combining the two
fields, to the extent that most frontier models are now VLMs.

7.1.1
Tasks

Let us first discuss the types of tasks that vision-language models must solve, and list
some of the popular benchmark suites. For understanding, the models can be tested on
visual question answering tasks (VQA), to see if the models have acquired some tex-
tual understanding of visual images. A related, but generative, task is that of captioning
problems, where models have to generate a textual descriptions of images. Addition-
ally, models may be tasked to do image generation.
Let us have a look at some example tasks. For Figure 7.1, a VQA question could
be: What is the mustache made of? and the system should answer: Bananas. Other
typical VQA questions are to count the number of certain shapes of a certain color in a
certain part of an image (to answer questions such as: Is there a red block in the upper
corner of the table in this scene?). The tasks can be quite diverse, and there is a range
of popular benchmarks such as MOSAIC \[Burda-Lassen et al., 2025\], GLOBAL-RG
\[Bhatia et al., 2024\], CultureVQA \[Nayak et al., 2024\], FoodieQA \[Li et al., 2024\],
and MaRVL \[Liu et al., 2021\].
In captioning problems, a model could be prompted to provide a caption for the
scene in Figure 7.2, which shows a happy dog standing in the ocean. Note that vari-
ations may be equally valid, such as a wet dog, a cold dog, or a dog with a red collar
standing in the ocean. Popular benchmarks are MS-COCO \[Lin et al., 2014\], nocaps,1

and, for video, MSR-VTT \[Xu et al., 2016\], and VATEX for traditional, short-caption

1https://nocaps.org
