7.1. MULTI-MODAL VISION LANGUAGE MODELS
153

Figure 7.2: A Captioning Task, possible Caption: A happy dog is standing in the ocean

evaluation \[Wang et al., 2019\]. Newer benchmarks have been developed that focus on
detailed, multi-faceted descriptions: DetailCaps \[Dong et al., 2024\], VDC \[Chai et al.,
2024\], and CapArena \[Cheng et al., 2025\].
Typical applications of VLMs are summarization, image generation, search and
retrieval, image segmentation, and object detection.
The Massive Multi-discipline
Multi-modal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark (MMMU) for Expert AGI is
a comprehensive benchmark for vision-language models \[Yue et al., 2024\].

7.1.2
Architecture

Now that we have seen the types of tasks that VLMs are tested on, how could we design
a model to perform these tasks?
Language, when modeled as a sequence of tokens, is a sequential (1 dimensional)
problem domain. Vision, when modeled as a grid of pixels, is a rectangular (2 dimen-
sional) problem domain. Correspondingly, the deep learning architectures for the two
applications are different. For language, the transformer architecture is used, finding
sequential patterns, and for imaging, the convolutional neural network is used, find-
ing 2-dimensional patterns. It is therefore not obvious what architecture a multi-modal
vision-language model should have. Indeed, it was unclear if a VLM would work at
all.
Research first focused on the question if the transformer architecture would also
be able to work on image processing (in addition to the conventional convolutional
neural networks, CNN). Special vision transformers and tokenization schemes were

## Page 154

154
CHAPTER 7. VISION, ACTION AND WORLD MODELS

Figure 7.3: Architecture of a VLM (after LLaVa \[Liu et al., 2023\], image from Hug-
gingface)

developed that worked well in image processing \[Dosovitskiy et al., 2020\].
Then, an architecture was needed to combine the language and image embeddings,
and to generate language. In general, the architecture of a VLM consists of an image
encoder (either a CNN or a specially tokenized vision-transformer) and a text encoder
that are connected to an embedding projector to align image and text representations
(often a dense neural network), connecting to, finally, a text decoder (a transformer).
Figure 7.3 illustrates this architecture, using LLaVa as an example \[Liu et al., 2023\].
The connection between the visual embedding and the textual embedding is made by
a network that projects the visual embedding to another embedding, to allow unified
reasoning by the model. The projector network is often a dense neural network (multi-
layer perceptron, MLP).
More elaborate architectures have been developed, and the architecture of state of
the art VLMs can become quite complex, consisting of multiple transformer modules.
As an example, Figure 7.4 shows the generative Stable Diffusion architecture \[Esser
et al., 2024, Weng, 2021, Yang et al., 2023\].

7.1.3
Learning Algorithm

Now that we have seen the tasks and the architecture of VLMs, it is time to look at
the type of learning algorithm that is used by the models. The different encoders and
projectors allow the VLM to be trained. The training algorithms should align and fuse
the knowledge from both the visual and the language encoders. The VLM can then
correlate the image and text information so that the model can analyze the query and
provide an answer based on the two modalities. The literature reports a variety of
approaches for training the VLM.
OpenAI’s CLIP \[Radford et al., 2021\], which stands for contrastive language-
image pretraining, uses contrastive learning. Contrastive learning is a form of self-
supervised learning, creating supervisory signals when there are no such labels in the
dataset. The idea is to push dissimilar data points apart and pull similar data points
together in an embedding space. Contrastive learning maximizes the similarity of rep-
resentations for positive pairs (such as similar forms of the same image) and minimize
the similarity for negative pairs (images of different objects).

## Page 155

7.1. MULTI-MODAL VISION LANGUAGE MODELS
155

Figure 7.4: Architecture of Stable Diffusion \[Esser et al., 2024\]

Another approach is to use masking. Here the VLM learns to predict randomly
obscured parts of an input text or image, just as it is used in language model training.
The model learns to reconstruct the hidden pixels in an image given an (unmasked)
caption. An example is FLAVA, or foundational language and vision alignment, which
uses a vision transformer as image encoder and a transformer for its language encoder
and multi-modal projector \[Singh et al., 2022\].
VLM’s are also used in a generative style, to generate an image based on a text
prompt. Popular text-to-image models often use diffusion models \[Ho et al., 2022,
Yang et al., 2023\]. Well-known examples are Google’s Imagen \[Baldridge et al., 2024\],
Midjourney, OpenAI’s DALL-E \[Betker et al., 2023\] and Stability AI’s stable diffusion
\[Esser et al., 2024\]. DALL-E 2 uses a diffusion model conditioned on CLIP image
embeddings. Figure 7.5 shows DALL-E’s well-known surrealistic avocado armchairs.
Pretraining vision language models from scratch is expensive, and since a VLM
consists of a language model and a vision model, we could try to see if it is possible
to build a VLM out of one or two existing models, that have already been pretrained
before. Both a pretrained LLM and a pretrained vision encoder can be used, to which a
mapping network can be added that projects the visual embedding to the textual input
space of the language model. An example is LLaVA, which stands for large language
and vision assistant. LLaVa uses the Vicuna language decoder and the CLIP ViT visual
encoder, and their outputs are merged into a shared dimensional space using a linear
projector \[Liu et al., 2023\].
Many vision language models have been developed. VLMs tend to perform well
on benchmark tasks and they are often used for decision making in agents. VLMs

Figure 7.5: DALL-E: Avocado Armchairs

Figure 7.6: Flava Pretraining Image-Text Dataset Examples \[Singh et al., 2022\]

have become so popular that many current open and commercial LLMs are VLMs:
DeepSeek-VL2, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o, Llama 3.2, NVLM, Qwen 2.5-VL.

7.1.4
Results

Let us take a look at how well VLMs perform at captioning and image generation by
looking at some of the examples that are reported in the literature.

Vision language models have produced imaginative and inspiring results ranging
from visual question answering, object detection, image captioning to text-to-image
generation. An example of the test dataset that is used in Flava is shown in Figure 7.6.
The successor of DALL-E 2, DALL-E 3, focused on training on highly descriptive
generated image captions, yielding even more impressive results \[Betker et al., 2023\].
Some of the prompt following image generation capabilities of DALL-E 3 are shown
in Figure 7.7. Figure 7.8 shows examples from stable diffusion (based on the rectified-
flow diffusion models).

7.2
Decisions & Vision Language Action Models

To act, agents must make decisions, and to make decisions, different options must be
weighed. As we will see in this section, we can train transformers on episodes of states,
actions and rewards {(𝑠, 𝑎, 𝑟)} (see also Section 20.1.2). These models are trained on
sequences of language, vision, and robotic actions. Vision-language-action models,
VLAs, (Figure 7.9) are trained to output robot API commands, which are a special
type of language: the language of commands to steer robotic movement.
The task of a VLA is to understand a visual scene, and, when given a textual com-
mand, instruct a robot arm to perform an appropriate action, depending on what the
model sees through the camera. These models have shown impressive results of robots
generalizing to unseen situations, successfully performing tasks.

7.2.1
Tasks

The main task of VLAs is to perform instructions in the real world, and to do so in a
general way, in a changing environment. When a robotic manipulation model has been
trained to pick up a set of red pencils, and the task changes to pick up blue pencils,
then it would be nice if the model generalizes, and we do not have to assemble a
new training set involving blue pencils and re-train the model again from scratch. We
also want our model to recognize objects, and recognize when an object is oriented
differently, has moved, or the lighting changes. The model should know how to use a
robot arm to manipulate objects, and how to perform different actions. See Figure 7.10
for an example, taken from the CLIPort paper \[Shridhar et al., 2022\].
The hardest task for VLAs is to combine these scenes, objects and actions to ma-
nipulations that are complicated combinations of what the model has seen during train-

## Page 159

7.2. DECISIONS & VISION LANGUAGE ACTION MODELS
159

Figure 7.10: Example from CLIPort: put the gray letter E in the left letter E shape hole
\[Shridhar et al., 2022\]

Figure 7.11: Another Example from CLIPort: sweep the beans into the blue zone
\[Shridhar et al., 2020\]

## Page 160

CHAPTER 7. VISION, ACTION AND WORLD MODELS

ing, and to generalize to unseen combinations. Especially long-horizon navigation
through complex, changing, environments (perhaps even outdoors) is a complex chal-
lenge \[Shridhar et al., 2022\].
In realistic human-robot interaction settings, collecting additional demonstrations
is often infeasible. To perform high-level tasks, such as in Figure 7.11, the VLA must
be able to recognize objects, their poses, and segmentations of instances. The model
must also be able to understand language, and relate the meaning of language to the
meaning of visual objects and to the meaning of robotic actions.
As we will see, language provides an intuitive interface for specifying goals and
for transferring semantic concepts across tasks. Furthermore, the work on VLMs has
shown how to semantically connect different kinds of embeddings.

7.2.2
Architecture

Now that we have seen the task and the challenges, let us look at possible model ar-
chitectures. Again, they can become quite complex. The transformer architecture is
well suited to learn patterns in sequential data, as the results on natural language show.
Intuitively, this suggests that transformers may also work well to model sequential deci-
sion problems, the type of problems that are often solved in reinforcement learning for
robotic action, as we discussed in Section 2.2.3 (and further in depth in Section 20.2.1).
These problems consist of a state, from which actions cause the system to enter a new
state, which has actions, etc. The transformer architecture is well suited to model these
problems.
Early work on decision transformer (DT) \[Chen et al., 2021, Janner et al., 2021\]
showed that on offline (static) reinforcement learning problems, the GPT architecture
was indeed able to learn optimal policies. The decision-pretrained transformer (DPT)
Lee et al. \[2023\], Wang et al. \[2024a\] showed that the basic transformer architectures
can be pretrained and finetuned on decision traces. Section 20.1.2 discusses decision
traces further.
Following pioneering work on CLIPort \[Shridhar et al., 2022, 2020\], VLAs are
often built on VLMs, where the robotic commands are used as regular language tokens.
Let us have a closer look at some representative models.
The goal of Mobility VLA \[Chiang et al., 2024\] is navigation. This VLA is created
by combining a long context VLM with topological maps, as illustrated in Figure 7.12.
Mobility VLA is used on a problem category of navigation tasks called multi-modal
instruction navigation with demonstration tours (MINT). In this dataset, an environ-
ment prior is provided through a previously recorded demonstration video. The model
consists of a two-level VLA that combines the environment understanding and com-
mon sense reasoning of long-context VLMs with a low-level navigation policy based
on topological graphs. The high-level policy is created by combining user instructions
from a long-context VLM that finds the goal frame in a demonstration video. Then, a
low-level policy starts at this goal frame to traverse a topological graph to generate the
robot action instructions at every timestep.
LM-Nav \[Shah et al., 2023\] uses a different architecture, based on existing models.
It takes as input a set of raw observations from the target environment and from free-
form textual instructions. From this, it derives an action plan using three pretrained

## Page 161

7.2. DECISIONS & VISION LANGUAGE ACTION MODELS
161

Figure 7.12: Mobility VLA Architecture: Long Context VLM and Topological Maps
\[Chiang et al., 2024\]

Figure 7.13: Three-LLM Architecture of LM-Nav \[Shah et al., 2023\]

models: a language model (LLM) for extracting landmarks, a vision-language model
(VLM) for grounding, and a visual-navigation model (VNM) for execution (not unlike
the topological map previously discussed). Together, these models enable LM-Nav to
follow textual instructions from visual observations without any finetuning. Figure 7.13
shows an illustration of the approach.
Google’s RT-2 \[Brohan et al., 2023\] uses a different approach. The idea of RT-2 is
to leverage knowledge from the web to inform robotic control: the robot should learn
how to act from watching videos. A standard vision language model is finetuned both
on textual robotic trajectory data and on Internet-scale vision-language tasks, such as
visual question answering. Robotic actions are expressed as regular text tokens and are
incorporated directly into the training set in the same way as natural language tokens,
as shown in Figure 7.14. A similar approach is taken by Magma \[Yang et al., 2025\].
Magma is pretrained on heterogeneous datasets spanning from images and videos to
robotics data. However, in Magma the actionable visual objects in images are labeled
by special tokens (Set-of-Mark) for action grounding. Similarly, object movements
(such as the trace of human hands or robotic arms) are labeled by Trace-of-Mark to
ease action planning. Figure 7.15 provides an illustration.
Finally, a VLA called 𝜋0 \[Black et al., 2024\] stresses the reinforcement learning
approach by using a pretrained late-fusion vision-language model, as well as a diverse

by adding a separate action expert that produces actions via flow matching, for fluent
manipulation skills. The resulting model can either be used directly to perform tasks
based on a prompt, or be further finetuned on higher-quality data to enable complex
multi-stage tasks, such as folding multiple articles of laundry or assembling a box (see
Figure 7.16).

7.2.3
Learning Algorithm

The model architecture of most VLAs is based on VLMs, in some cases augmented
with navigation map data. The robotic action commands are typically encoded as
regular text commands. Likewise, for pretraining and finetuning typical LLM self-
supervised learning algorithms are used, similar to VLMs and decision transformers.
Sometimes existing pretrained models are used, to reduce the training expense.

7.2.4
Results

Various VLA models have been created that achieve impressive zero-shot results, gen-
eralizing behavior to unseen situations. Chiang et al. \[2024\], Brohan et al. \[2023\], Yang
et al. \[2025\] are examples of VLA models for robotic action, achieving complex tasks
such as navigation, table top manipulation, or even folding laundry \[Black et al., 2024\].
VLAs have shown impressive and imaginative results, where robots were able to
generalize at inference time without the need for retraining. A survey of VLAs can be
found in \[Ma et al., 2024\].

7.3
World Models, Physics, and Planning

To a VLM, an image consists of pixels without a deeper intrinsic meaning. However,
agents that interact with the world need knowledge about physical aspects of that world.
The models need an understanding of what is physically possible, so that agents do not
walk through walls, as they still sometimes do in video games.
World models help agents understand the world, allowing them to act effectively
in the physical world, taking actions that make sense. Originally, LLMs are language
models. We can converse with them in natural language, and they necessarily contain
some knowledge of the world, but they were not specifically trained to have a wide and
deep understanding of worldly affairs. Some researchers argue that in order for agentic
LLMs to be truly successful, and for LLMs to reach a high level of general intelligence,
research into world models should be strengthened \[Sutton et al., 2022, Matsuo et al.,
2022, LeCun et al., 2022, Klindt et al., 2026\].
Agents and robots that act in the world need a rudimentary understanding of the
physics of the world. One of the challenges for training an LLM is to ground its un-
derstanding of the physical world and of the possible robotic actions into reality. One
way to do this is to learn an agentic model of the world (environment) from feedback
on actions.
The term world model has been used in AI in other contexts. Most notably, it
refers to the model in model-based reinforcement learning \[Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018,
Moerland et al., 2023, Sutton, 1991\] (see next section). This model contains a local
copy of some knowledge of the environment, based on the interactions it has had with
the environment, to be used to improve the action policy. The world model contains
an efficient, compressed, learned representation of the world \[Hafner et al., 2019, Plaat
et al., 2020\]. The representation of a world model is often called an abstract or latent
representation, to contrast it with the regular representation of the real world in the
environment. World models are often trained to contain knowledge about physics and
certain spatial properties, that puts restrictions on the agent’s actions. The precise
contents of the world model depends on the domain in which the agent operates.
Note that in a just few chapters we have progressed from understanding language
to understanding the world. The goal of a large language model is to understand some
semantics of natural language from statistical patterns in text, to be used for question
answering and translation. The goal of a world model is to understand causal relations
in the laws of physics, to be used to simulate future world states for our agent. Quite
some new technology is necessary to go from LLM to agentic LLM.
We start with a look at how world models are currently used in agentic LLM.

7.3. WORLD MODELS, PHYSICS, AND PLANNING

7.3.1
Tasks

World models should encapsulate knowledge of the world, so that an agent can per-
form meaningful actions. The actions should be grounded in the physical world. For
example, the model should understand the limitations of the joints of a robot arm that
it is commanding; a navigational agent should understand some physics, such as the
concept of gravity, of distance, and that walls are solid objects; a financial agent should
understand the consequences of a negative bank balance. Often this is the type of in-
formation that humans take for granted, and we are surprised when an agent fails to
understand such basic things about the world in which it operates. VLMs that are only
trained on pixels may miss the semantic meaning of a specific texture, whether it is a
garment, smoke, or a wall.
Standard pretrained LLMs already contain some useful world knowledge. They
learn acceptable textual behavior using reinforcement learning with human feedback
(RLHF), and acceptable mathematical and coding behavior using reinforcement learn-
ing with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Some early approaches use LLMs as pretrained
world model without any finetuning. A natural way to learn about the physics of the
world is through interaction: agents can learn acceptable physical behavior through a
reinforcement learning-style reward function.
The goal of world models in model-based reinforcement learning is to improve
the sample efficiency of learning from interaction, by planning with the world model
instead of sampling from the real world. This is especially useful when interacting with
the world is more expensive than performing a simulation, as will often be the case in
agentic LLM. In the approaches that we will discuss, LLM world models use methods
from model-based reinforcement learning (see Section 7.3.5). Currently, world model
approaches in LLM are quite diverse. To show which tasks world models are used for
in LLMs, we will discuss three examples: WorldGPT, WebDreamer, and WorldCoder.

WorldGPT
The goal of WorldGPT \[Ge et al., 2024\] is to solve visual question
answering and embodied planning tasks, including audio-video question answering.
WorldGPT learns a world-VLM from videos. It uses a latent space VLM with external
knowledge bases and long-term memory.

WebDreamer
The goal of WebDreamer \[Gu et al., 2024\] is to improve efficient
learning of Web-interaction tasks, such as e-commerce. WebDreamer enables web-
agents to simulate actions before execution, and thus be faster and more sample effi-
cient (by not having to act in the real web to gather experience). WebDreamer is a
model-based reinforcement learning approach in a web-world. (The name is derived
from Dreamer, a series of influential model-based reinforcement learning latent dy-
namics models \[Hafner et al., 2019, 2020a, 2023\].) Typical tasks are to find products
on e-commerce sites. It does so by training a small model from a large model, allowing
efficient simulation.

WorldCoder
The goal of WorldCoder \[Tang et al., 2024\] is also to improve sample
efficiency, but the approach is different. WorldCoder improves efficiency by gener-
ating the dynamics model (transition function and reward function) in interpretable

Python code, which is then used in a standard model-based reinforcement learning de-
sign. The generated Python code executes more efficiently than LLM inference does.
WorldCoder is used in grid-tasks (Sokoban, see Figure 7.17) and domestic task plan-
ning (AlfWorld, see Figure 7.18).

7.3.2
Architecture

The purpose of a world model is to add semantic meaning to observations—actions
having consequences—something that LLMs and VLMs may struggle with. When
does a pixel belong to a floor to walk on (restrict 𝑦movement) and when is it part of
a wall to stop you (restrict 𝑥movement)? A reward function provides feedback infor-
mation on which actions are good, and which are not. Thus, world model architectures
often use a reinforcement learning setting, in which an action policy is trained from
feedback rewards. We can think of a world model as a VLM with a policy learner
inside.
WorldGPT, WebDreamer, and WorldCoder use different architectures for their world
model, which we will now discuss in more detail.

WorldGPT
WorldGPT is based on a standard LLM, Vicuna-7B-v0.4 It performs
reasoning in latent space, following the model-based reinforcement learning approach.
The goal of WorldGPT is to be a simulator of realistic dynamics of the world—the
transition and the reward function in reinforcement learning. To do so, the architecture
helps synthesize multi-modal instruction instances, using a special architecture. At
the core WorldGPT follows the common VLM architecture with a central LLM, and
a multi-modal encoder and a decoder. To help the model synthesize multi-modal in-
structions, a cognitive architecture is added to help with specialized or long-term tasks.
The architecture adds memory, knowledge retrieval, and context reflection. The con-
text reflection is built on Q-former \[Li et al., 2023\]. See Figure 7.19 for a diagram of
the architecture.

WebDreamer
WebDreamer is aimed at web-interaction. It distills a large model,
Qwen-70B \[Bai et al., 2025\], into a small 7B model. The small model is then used for
simulating actions with the world model, before acting in the “real” web-world. It uses
model predictive control (MPC) as planning approach \[Garcia et al., 1989, Schwenzer
et al., 2021\] for decision making about website actions, re-planning at each interaction
step. WebDreamer leverages LLMs as world model and as value function. The LLM
implements both the simulation function (sim) and the scoring function (score), see
Figure 7.20. Furthermore, following \[Koh et al., 2024\], the LLM is used for candidate
action generation (in addition to sim and score). The authors employ a two-stage ap-
proach: first sampling top-𝑘actions, and then using the LLM to self-refine unnecessary
actions for simulation.

WorldCoder
WorldCoder is a model-based agent that builds a Python program to
represent its knowledge of the world. WorldCoder creates a transition function of the
world in executable Python code, see Figure 7.21. WorldCoder uses program synthe-
sis. In reinforcement learning, problems are formalized as MDPs, consisting of a state
representation 𝑆, action function 𝐴, transition function 𝑇, and reward function 𝑅(see
Section 7.3.5). WorldCoder uses an LLM to generate Python code for action, transi-
tion and reward functions for a task, as well as for the state representation, which is
then used in a model-based reinforcement learning approach. This code is checked
and improved, in an iterative self debug refinement process \[Chen et al., 2023\], see

## Page 169

7.3. WORLD MODELS, PHYSICS, AND PLANNING
169

Section 6.1.3.2. This process repeats until the program produces the correct output.
Note that in WorldCoder the learned model is symbolic (the transition function
is represented as computer code), where in regular deep reinforcement learning the
model is a neural network. At inference time, WorldCoder is efficient, since no LLM
calls occur that require forward passes through a large network, only interpretation of
the transition and reward function Python code.
In regular model-based LLM approaches, the LLM simulates the world, in World-
Coder the LLM builds a simulation of the world, for later execution. At inference time,
the Python interpreter executes the transition function, where in ReAct, an LLM rea-
sons about the world state. For planning problems, the symbolic approach is better
suited, since LLMs struggle with planning during inference (see Section 6.2.3).

7.3.3
Learning Algorithm

We will now discuss the pretraining and finetuning algorithms that the different ap-
proaches use.

WorldGPT
WorldGPT acquires an understanding of world dynamics by pretraining
and finetuning on millions of videos across various domains. Vicuna-7B-v0 is used
as the base LLM. Pretraining then uses a language-centric encoder to obtain a uni-
fied representation of the multi-modal state. For multi-modal decoding, special tokens
are inserted into the LLM’s vocabulary. Training starts uni-modal, and progresses to
cross-modal. For finetuning, a special cognitive reinforcement architecture is used with
a dataset with fine-grain sequential state-transition sample annotations from more than
10 million videos. As mentioned before, the cognitive architecture consists of mem-
ory, knowledge retrieval, and context reflection. Through finetuning, agents acquire
specialized knowledge by finetuning on synthetic multi-modal instruction data.

WebDreamer
The WebDreamer approach aims to learn dynamics suitable for model-
based reinforcement learning. First the pretrained Qwen-2-VL vision language model
\[Wang et al., 2024b\] is used to initialize the Dreamer-7B model, which is then further
finetuned on 3.1 million interaction examples. The data synthesis pipeline consists of
(1) random walks over the web, where the model autonomously interacts with web
pages through actions such as typing for search and clicking, and (2) synthesis, where
Qwen2-VL-72B generates textual descriptions of state changes based on visual snap-
shots before and after the actions. WebDreamer simulates possible future states for
each action over a finite horizon (replanning and retraining according to the model
predictive control (MPC) approach, a reinforcement learning approach for adaptive
retraining that is used in engineering and control problems).

WorldCoder
WorldCoder uses program synthesis to learn to make a transition func-
tion, the function that computes the next state of the world. WorldCoder then performs
planning-actions using that coded world model. It initially performs random explo-
ration to initialize a dataset of environmental interactions; it updates its world model
using a program synthesis algorithm, generates the code, and then performs planning.

## Page 170

170
CHAPTER 7. VISION, ACTION AND WORLD MODELS

Different planners are possible, from depth-limited value iteration (in simple domains)
to MCTS (for more complex domains) \[Browne et al., 2012\].

7.3.4
Results

We will now look at the results of the three approaches.

WorldGPT
The WorldGPT model is evaluated with a multi-modal state transition
prediction benchmark. WorldGPT is effective, and understands and predicts the dy-
namics of complex real-world kitchen and cooking scenarios accurately.
The system is also evaluated as a world simulator, showing that it can generalize to
unfamiliar domains. In one experiment, WorldGPT is 30 times faster then traditional
diffusion-based methods on audio-video question answering tasks \[Ge et al., 2024\].

WebDreamer
WebDreamer also performs well. It is reported to surpass GPT-4o
performance on web interaction tasks. Substantial performance improvements are re-
ported over reactive baselines, on which it is 4-5 times more efficient than tree search.
WebDreamer performs well on the sandbox environment VisualWebArena, and also
on real-world websites (Online-Mind2Web and Mind2Web-Live), where tree search
methods are difficult to implement and deploy. Moreover, on online benchmarks, us-
ing Dreamer-7B, the approach achieves performance comparable to GPT-4o. On real-
world websites, WebDreamer outperforms the reactive baseline with a relative gain of
42% and 24%, respectively.

WorldCoder
For WorldCoder results are reported on grid worlds and on task plan-
ning (AlfWorld). WorldCoder is more sample-efficient than model-free reinforcement
learning, and more compute-efficient compared to ReAct-style agents that try to per-
form in-context planning by the LLM.
Generating world knowledge as computer code by LLMs brings advantages. It
allows prior world knowledge embedded in the LLM to improve code generation, as
existing solutions to published problems may well have been seen during pretraining.
The code can also be transferred across tasks by reusing pieces of old programs. Fur-
thermore, the results are human readable, allowing the world knowledge to be inspected
by humans by reading the generated code.
Though promising for planning problems, a limitation of the WorldCoder approach
is inherent to the computational difficulty of planning problems. Problem instances that
are difficult to solve with dedicated solvers are also difficult to solve for WorldCoder
solvers. The transition function that is generated by the LLM is unlikely to be better
than those designed by expert human researchers.
So far, the synthesized code aims to reproduce the transition and reward functions.
For future work, self reflection and metalearning approaches may be able to improve
performance further.

7.3.5
*Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

World models are being used successfully in agentic LLM. An extensive literature ex-
ists on world models in model-based reinforcement learning. At the end of this chapter,
we will now provide a brief overview of world models in model-based reinforcement
learning, in order to provide more context for the use of world models in LLM.

An influential early model-based approach is Dyna \[Sutton, 1991\]. Influential re-
cent works are \[Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Hafner et al., 2020b\]. Two modern surveys
are Moerland et al. \[2023\], Plaat et al. \[2023\].

In reinforcement learning, agents learn how to act in an environment by sampling
rewards from actions that are executed in the environment.

7.3.5.1
Model-free Reinforcement Learning

In regular reinforcement learning an optimal agent policy is learned model-free: the
best actions for all states are learned directly from interaction with the environment
(see Figure 7.22), without the help of an extra model of the environment. Regular
reinforcement learning is formally described as a Markov decision process, with four
functions {𝑆,𝑇, 𝐴, 𝑅}: a function 𝑆(𝑜) →𝑠to represent the state of the system for
observation 𝑜, a function 𝑇(𝑠, 𝑎) →𝑠′ that transitions from one state to the next state
using an action, a function 𝐴(𝑠) →𝑎that returns an action for a state, and a func-
tion 𝑅(𝑠) →𝑟that assign a reward value (positive or negative) to a state. The goal
of reinforcement learning is to use the MDP to learn an optimal policy 𝜋∗(𝑠) →𝑎∗,
the function that returns the best action for each state that the MDP can be in. Thus,
a reinforcement learning problem consists of four functions 𝑆, 𝑇, 𝐴, and 𝑅, and the
goal of the agent is to find the optimal policy 𝜋∗(𝑠) with the highest expected cumu-
lative reward. The agent does not have access to 𝑇and 𝑅, functions that reside in the
environment. Regular, model-free, reinforcement learning is also called direct rein-
forcement learning. The direct method naturally has high sample complexity: policy
improvement requires sampling, and large MDPs require many samples for the policy
improvement process to converge (Figure 7.22).

7.3.5.2
Model-based Reinforcement Learning

In direct reinforcement learning, sampled information is not retained by the agent, but
forgotten, and each policy improvement requires a new sample. Interaction by the
agent with the outside environment is often expensive, for example for a robot acting
in the real world, whose joints wear out. In this case it would be beneficial to find ways
to reduce the sample complexity. We should try to improve the policy without having
to sample as much from the environment.
A straightforward idea is not to throw away the samples, but to store them in a
buffer, and also sample from that buffer of older interaction results, or, slightly more
advanced, to train a local surrogate model 𝑀= ( ˆ𝑇, ˆ𝑅) of the environment dynamics.
When we have trained this local dynamics model, we can also sample from the model,
cheaply, in addition to sampling the environment, expensively (see Figure 7.23).
These methods are indirect methods, since, in the last methods, where a local dy-
namics model is built up by the agent, the policy is learned indirectly (through a local
model) from the environment.
Using a local dynamics model is called model-based reinforcement learning. The
dynamics model consist of local estimations ˆ𝑇and ˆ𝑅by the agent, estimates of the real
𝑇and 𝑅that are known only to the environment. Model-based reinforcement learning
has been successful in some applications, such as Go \[Silver et al., 2016\], Diplomacy
\[Bakhtin et al., 2022\], StarCraft \[Vinyals et al., 2019\], and showing learning across
domains \[Hafner et al., 2020b\].
Model-based reinforcement learning also connects to planning, a classic field in
symbolic artificial intelligence, that looks ahead into the future, simulating different
possible worlds using the efficient latent representation, without having to act in the
real world.

7.3.5.3
Dimension Reduction

In deep model-based reinforcement learning, the local dynamics models are also called
world models \[Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018\]. In this context world models reduce high
dimensional observation spaces to lower dimensional state and reward spaces, that can
then be used in model-based reinforcement learning methods to efficiently improve
policy functions. The idea behind world models is that in most high-dimensional en-

## Page 173

7.4. CONCLUDING REMARKS
173

vironments there are elements that are less important, such as, in a video game, trees
in the background that never move, that have little or no relation to the value of the
agent’s actions. The goal is to abstract away these unimportant elements of the input
space, reducing the effective dimensionality of the state space.

7.3.5.4
Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture

The joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) is proposed by LeCun et al. \[2022\]
and further refined in Assran et al. \[2023\]. The goal of JEPA is to predict future states
in an abstract, compressed representation (latent space) rather than trying to recreate
raw sensory details or pixels. This goal is similar to the dimension-reduction goal of
a world model in model-based reinforcement learning. Where model-based reinforce-
ment learning uses learns a local transition model supervised by rewards, JEPA is a
self-supervised representation learning framework. JEPA is trained via self-supervised
observation (watching videos or images) to map context embeddings to target embed-
dings without rewards or explicit actions. Model-based reinforcement learning ex-
plicitly incorporates actions, rewards, and control optimization to maximize the return
\[Lim et al., 2026\]. JEPA and reinforcement learning are close, JEPA can be used as
a perception engine (world model) for reinforcement learning or planning algorithms,
for example to guide robotic control \[Destrade et al., 2025\].

7.3.5.5
Agentic World Models

In the context of model-based reinforcement learning, LLMs can be used in two differ-
ent ways. We can use a pre-trained (static) LLM as world model ( ˆ𝑇, ˆ𝑅) in model-based
reinforcement learning (LLM4MBRL). Often this approach uses a tree search or MCTS
planning. In this approach, the LLM is used to help reinforcement learning.
Alternatively (model-based) reinforcement learning settings can be used to train
LLM world models (MBRL4LLM) with feedback from world-interaction. Now, the
LLM has become adaptive, either through an adaptive harness, or by posttraining the
model itself, as in a VLA. This approach is also known as agentic world models, and
holds much promise for agents to better understand their environment, to act in more
realistic ways. In this approach, reinforcement learning is used to help agentic lan-
guage modeling. This is an active area of research, see, for example, Zuo et al. \[2026\],
including their references.5

7.4
Concluding Remarks

Transformers can be trained on tokenized language data, but also on other tokenized
data. In this chapter we have seen different model architectures for different modal-
ities. Architecturally, the models were quite different. However, most models are

5There is a third connection between reinforcement learning and language modeling. Model-free rein-
forcement learning is also used inside the LLM training pipeline, for finetuning, as in RLHF and RLVR.

## Page 174

174
BIBLIOGRAPHY

transformer based, and tokenization approaches have been devised for a surprising dif-
ference in modalities. Let us review the different types of models to see what they have
in common:

• Large language models (LLM) are transformers that are pretrained on tokenized
natural language.

• Vision language models (VLM) are models that consist of a transformer that is
trained on tokenized vision data (or a diffusion model, or a convolutional net-
work) and a transformer trained on tokenized natural language, whose embed-
dings come together in a joint decoder.

• Decision transformers (DT) are transformers that are trained on tokenized (𝑠, 𝑎, 𝑟)-
episodes of decision paths (see Section 20.1.2).

• Vision language action models (VLA) are models that consist of a vision-language
architecture that are also trained on tokenized (𝑠, 𝑎, 𝑟) episodes of robotic actions.

• World models are models that consist of a vision-language architecture that are
also trained on tokenized (𝑠, 𝑎, 𝑟) episodes of real world actions or decisions.

There are other types of models that we have not discussed in this chapter. For example,
a large music model (LMM) is a transformer that is pretrained on tokenized musical
sequences (which can be either symbolic music (score sheets) or a soundtrack) \[Yuan
et al., 2025\].
This chapter was devoted to advanced models for agents. We discussed language
models that were pretrained and finetuned on vision and action. These models under-
stand more of the world, allowing agents to achieve impressive generalization results.
We have seen how the LLM, originally a language model, is becoming a world model,
a term that is borrowed from the field of model-based reinforcement learning.
At this point it might be good to look back on what we have seen so far. The
first part of the book explained how to pretrain models self-referentially for language.
Then, Chapter 6 explained how in-context learning emerged, and how it can be used
for inference time multi-step reasoning and self-reflection. This chapter discussed pre-
training and finetuning methods to yield multi-modal world models of the environment.
Together, pretrained language, inference time reasoning, and finetuned world models
enable agents more and more to act intelligently and achieve tasks in the world for their
users.
We have now discussed many different modalities and training methods. In the next
chapter we will take a step back and reflect on how agents can learn in a stable manner,
while they are also acting in the world that they learn from.

## Page 181

Chapter 8

Metalearning


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn about metalearning. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Recognize the different levels of learning that are used in LLM pipelines.
• Understand the connection between in-context learning, few-shot learning and
metalearning.
• Create a metalearning system that consists of an inner learning loop and an outer
learning loop.
• Recognize the moving-target problem: why it is challenging to achieve stable
learning in a dynamic metalearning system.

8.1
Why Metalearning?

As we have seen, the self-reflecting LLM approaches are powerful, but getting the
training processes to converge can be a challenge. In agentic LLM, learning occurs
at multiple levels, and sometimes at the same time. In machine learning, algorithms
that learn at multiple levels are said to perform metalearning. Metalearning is often
described as learning to learn, for example, learning which prompt works better for
a certain task. Metalearning can be a powerful concept, but sometimes the different
learning levels interfere, and learning stops.

To help us understand why our LLM multi-level learning algorithms sometimes do
not work, we will look deeper into metalearning. In this chapter we will discuss how
we can improve the stability of dynamic, feedback-rich, metalearning approaches.

The term metalearning is used for multi-level learning algorithms. Metalearning
algorithms learn to learn, to quickly solve examples of new, unseen, tasks, that the
model has not trained for.

181

## Page 182

182
CHAPTER 8. METALEARNING

8.1.1
Deep Learning is Slow

Metalearning has a long history in machine learning (see, for example, Schmidhuber
\[1987\], Hospedales et al. \[2021\], Huisman et al. \[2021\]). It is inspired by human learn-
ing, since humans are said to be able to learn how to learn. Another reason for its
development, is speed.
The problem is that regular deep learning is slow. Neural networks for typical
deep learning tasks are large, with millions or billions of parameters, and training them
requires large datasets, often with millions of examples. Training times for training
a network from scratch are long, from hours to months, and only when special par-
allel parallel hardware (GPU) was employed, did deep learning become successful
\[Krizhevsky et al., 2012\].
At this point, researchers started dreaming about few-shot learning, methods that
would achieve high accuracy by training on just a few examples.

8.1.2
Achieving Few-shot Learning

In machine learning, some algorithms are better suited for certain types of problems
than others. Furthermore, most training algorithms have elements that can be tuned
for performance, such as the learning rate, momentum, the initialization scheme of the
parameters, or, for a multi-level algorithm, even the choice of the underlying train-
ing algorithm. These elements are called hyperparameters, and they govern how the
algorithm learns. Would we be able to learn them?
Different types of problems require different hyperparameter settings. For example,
for a smooth dataset, a high learning rate may work well, or a local search algorithm,
but for a peaky dataset a lower learning rate works better, or a global search algorithm.
The point is that the best hyperparameter configuration in machine learning depends
on the task to be solved, and that, crucially, this configuration can be learned. Learn-
ing such hyperparameters of the algorithm for different tasks is called metalearning.
(In contrast, the learning of the regular parameters of the model is now called base
learning.)
The aim of metalearning is to create algorithms that learn certain tasks faster. In-
stead of using a generic algorithm that is not adapted to the task, starting from scratch,
we should use a learning algorithm whose hyperparameters are first matched to the type
of task to be solved. The metalearning approach is to first learn from a set of related
tasks how to configure the learning algorithm, learning to learn a certain set of tasks
faster.
When we have learned the hyperparameter configuration for such an adapted algo-
rithm, we may hope to be able to achieve few-shot training: being able to train on just
a few examples, while still achieving high accuracy on examples from a new test task.
Metalearning achieves few-shot learning by starting the training not from scratch, but
from related knowledge.
Metalearning consists of a (hyper) training loop around a (base) training loop. In
classical (non-neural network) machine learning, common hyperparameters are the
learning rate, or algorithm selection, where different learning algorithms are tested
on training tasks \[Brazdil et al., 2022\]. In deep learning, the initialization of the neural

## Page 183

8.2. INNER/OUTER LOOP
183

network weights is often used \[Finn et al., 2017\].
In agentic LLM, we have also encountered learning at different levels (and we will
continue to discuss multi-level learning in the next chapter). It is useful for us to study
the theory and insights of the metalearning literature.

8.2
Inner/Outer Loop

As any supervised learning approach, metalearning consists of (1) a meta-train phase,
training on a variety of related tasks, and (2) a meta-test phase, testing on a new, un-
seen, task, to see how well it generalizes to this new task. The goal is to improve
generalization by learning a hyperparameter setting of the training algorithm that work
well on a wide variety of training tasks.
The process of training the parameters of a model is implemented as an optimiza-
tion loop, in which a loss-function is used to compute a difference between training
examples and current model-estimates. The training algorithm loops over the dataset,
each time adjusting the parameters of the model, with the goal to minimize the sum of
the loss.
The learning-to-learn concept consists of two loops: an inner training loop to op-
timize the model’s parameters, and an outer training loop to optimize the algorithm’s
hyperparameters. The inner loop optimizes parameters over the examples of one task,
the outer loop optimizes hyperparameters over the set of tasks of an application domain.
Each base-learning task T𝑖has a dataset 𝐷𝑖and a learning objective, the loss func-
tion L𝑖. Thus T𝑖= (𝐷𝑖, L𝑖). Each dataset consists of pairs of input-examples and
labels 𝐷𝑖= {(𝑥𝑗, 𝑦𝑗)}, and is split into a training and a testset 𝐷𝑖= {𝐷𝑖,𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑛, 𝐷𝑖,𝑡𝑒𝑠𝑡}.
On each training dataset a parameterized model ˆ𝑓𝜃𝑖(𝐷𝑖,𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑛) is estimated, with a loss
function L𝑖(𝜃𝑖, 𝐷𝑖,𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑛). The model ˆ𝑓is approximated with an algorithm that is gov-
erned by a set of hyperparameters 𝜔. The particular hyperparameters vary from algo-
rithm to algorithm, but frequently encountered hyperparameters are the learning rate
𝛼, the initial parameters 𝜃0, and algorithm constants.
The inner loop optimizes the base-parameters 𝜃, and the outer loop optimizes the
hyperparameters 𝜔to find the best performance on the set of base tasks with the ap-
propriate test data:

The inner loop optimizes 𝜃𝑖within the datasets 𝐷𝑖of the tasks T𝑖, and the outer loop
optimizes 𝜔across the tasks and datasets. The outcome of the meta optimization is a
set of optimal hyperparameters 𝜔★.
After metalearning has finished, we have a hyperparameter set (tuned algorithm)
that works well for a set of tasks in an application domain, and we can assume that it
will generalize well, after training on just a few examples of a new task, scoring high
accuracy on testing an unseen example.

## Page 184

184
CHAPTER 8. METALEARNING

Transfer Learning
There is an important connection between metalearning and trans-
fer learning. Transfer learning pretrains the neural network on a single task, and then
performs a transfer of the weights to a quick finetuning phase. Transfer learning can
thus be regarded as a single iteration of a network-initialization-based metalearning
approach: transfer learning is metalearning with just one base learning task.

8.3
LLM and Metalearning

In the field of LLM, we encounter metalearning in many places. A common metalearn-
ing approach is to initialize the model parameters to earlier learned knowledge, so that
they may train faster on a related task. This is transfer learning, that we find in ev-
ery standard LLM training pipeline, in the pretrain/finetune phases, where we take the
pretrained parameters and finetune them further for a specific task. Metalearning is
repeated finetuning, and large language models are a prime example of a metalearning
training pipeline that achieves that major goal of machine learning: few-shot learning.
In-context learning was one of the major breakthroughs of machine learning \[Brown
et al., 2020\].
When we go to agentic LLM, few-shot learning occurs in many other places as well.
We will discuss both static and dynamic forms of metalearning. In static metalearning,
weights in inner loops are not influenced by other loops. In dynamic metalearning,
they are.

8.3.1
Static LLM Metalearning

We start by reviewing some examples of static LLM metalearning.

8.3.1.1
Pretraining Pipeline

The regular LLM training pipeline is a good example of an elaborate, multi-phase,
transfer learning scheme. It achieves good zero-shot performance, in the sense that it
can answer many regular queries accurately—where was Mozart born?—based on the
pretrained and finetuned knowledge.
The different phases in the pipeline are the inner optimization loops, and the choices
of which weights to transfer, and the manual choices of how to finetune in the subse-
quent phases, can be considered as the outer loop hyperparameter choices.
This is a static form of metalearning, since the weights, once trained in a phase, are
not influenced by training results of later phases. Weights are stable between phases of
the pipeline. The pipeline is a purely sequential training process.

8.3.1.2
In-Context Learning

Going beyond zero-shot learning, in-context learning is a form of few-shot learning
where a few training examples are provided by the user, prompting the LLM to infer
a better answer. The pretrained model is the inner loop, the examples in the prompt
guide the outer loop.

## Page 185

8.3. LLM AND METALEARNING
185

This is a static form of metalearning, since the values of the weights of the model
are not influenced by the examples in the prompt.

8.3.1.3
Chain of Thought

Regular in-context learning provides facts as few-shot examples; it is content-focused.
Chain of thought provides process-steps as few-shot examples, it is process-focused.
Again, the pretrained model is the inner loop, the examples in the prompt guide the
outer loop, and the weights of the model are static.

8.3.1.4
Static Metalearning is Stable

The regular LLM pipeline consists of transfer learning phases (inner loops), that run in
sequence. Once an inner training loop has converged, that phase is not run again. The
pipeline is a form of static metalearning. (The results of finetuning are not fed back
into the pretrainer again, nor is the pretrainer ran with adjusted hyperparameters based
on the finetuning results. The different training phases can not interfere.)
In contrast to static metalearning, there is also dynamic metalearning, where differ-
ent iterations do interfere.

8.3.2
Dynamic LLM Metalearning

In agentic LLMs different forms of dynamic metalearning are used. In dynamic met-
alearning the iterations are run concurrently, and can have destabilizing effects on each
other’s convergence process.
In previous chapters, we have discussed self-reflection, and RLVR. These are ap-
proaches where an inner loop can be changed by an outer loop, and results of one inner
loop may affect another inner loop. We have created a moving training target. This
may cause unstable divergence of the training process. Training results may also ap-
pear brittle: they react greatly to small changes in input values or hyperparameters,
such as different random seeds, different prompt reformulations, or even changes in
the length of the metalearning process itself. Furthermore, hallucinating tendencies of
the base LLM may be amplified when the same model is used in different roles, such
as for correction and for generation.
Let us discuss the examples of dynamic metalearning in agentic LLM.

8.3.2.1
Self-Reflection

In self-reflection (Section 6.2.4.2) an agentic harness performs prompt management,
calling the LLM in different roles, such as, to evaluate a state, and to refine an answer.
In metalearning terms, the model is the inner training loop, and the harness the
outer loop. Although the model itself is static, it is called with different prompts, and
the answers of the model are used by the harness to produce new prompts. Therefore,
the prompt results (outer loops) start interfering, and may interact in non-linear and
non-intuitive ways.
Furthermore, when the same model is used for different roles, imperfections (bi-
ases, hallucinations) may be amplified.

## Page 186

186
CHAPTER 8. METALEARNING

8.3.2.2
RLVR

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR, Section 6.2.4.3) is a popular
training scheme for code and math applications, where inference-time reasoning results
are used for finetuning at training-time.
In metalearning terms, finetuning is the inner loop, and inference-time reasoning
is the outer loop. RLVR uses outer loop results in the inner loop, feeding inference
results into the training phase, mixing two learning processes. Care should be taken
to prevent that inference time errors, which are used as truths, are amplified in the
finetuning/inference loop.

8.4
Stabilizing Dynamic Metalearning

Unstable training occurs when inner/outer interference is under-damped. When this
happens, oscillation between inner loops and outer loops may grow larger, instead of
dying out.
This problem can be mitigated by increased damping, or by decoupling the time
by which different inner loops move. For example, the learning rates of one of the
loops may be reduced, or the parameters of some of the inner loops may be kept stable
for a longer time than the other loops. Another idea is to use a mixture of model
types or sizes, such as in Mixture-of-Experts \[Jiang et al., 2024\]. A student/teacher
setup deliberately uses a stronger and a weaker model for the different roles. By using
different models, we may hope to dampen hallucinations and interference between
inner loops.
In general, when metalearning misbehaves, we should aim to create more diversity,
to stimulate exploration, and to prevent greedy behavior that leads to local optima or
divergent training. These solutions often require much experimentation to build up
intuition about the problem. Debugging agentic LLMs can be challenging.

8.5
Concluding Remarks

As we have seen, we can understand LLM-training as a form of metalearning. Regular
LLM training is a form of transfer learning, and inference-time reasoning and training,
as is used in agentic LLM, use even more metalearning ideas. Although dynamic
metalearning approaches (such as self-reflection) are a powerful concept, care should
be taken since interference between inner and outer loops may destabilize the training
process. This may happen unexpectedly, in agents that were previously behaving.
When we use a trained model in our agent that interacts with the world, and that
agent is also trained using feedback from this interaction, then the model can be re-
garded as the base learner (inner loop) and the interaction with the world can be re-
garded as the metalearner (outer loop). All the preceding caveats for in-pipeline met-
alearning also apply for out-of-pipeline metalearning. Only now, when interacting with
the real world, the consequence of errors may be more severe.
Related fields of online machine learning, such as deep reinforcement learning,
also suffer from the unstable training and the moving target problem. The field of deep

## Page 187

BIBLIOGRAPHY
187

reinforcement learning has introduced many stabilization techniques, such as replay
buffers and target networks \[Mnih et al., 2015, Hessel et al., 2018\]. These methods
typically try to decouple the periodicity of the two learning processes, often by slowing
down one of them. A similar approach is introduced in Hierarchical Reasoning Models
(HRM) \[Wang et al., 2025\]. HRM consists of a two-layer metalearning approach. Here,
too, the learning is stabilized by learning at two different speeds.
Knowledge of such stabilization methods is useful when designing agentic LLM
solutions. In the next part we will provide an overview of the different interaction
styles by which agentic LLM interact with the world. The styles go from static to
dynamic.

We have now discussed the foundations of LLMs and agents. We have seen how
language and tokenization works, we have seen how LLMs are trained and finetuned,
and we have seen how advanced reasoning models reason and self-reflect. We have
looked at different learning modalities, from language, vision, and action. We have
also looked at the intricacies of metalearning.
We have now arrived at the heart of agentic LLM, where we will review the differ-
ent interaction styles of LLM agents. This part consists of one content chapter and one
practical chapter. First we will review the five agentic interaction styles that we have
seen so far, and we discuss the importance of memory. Then, in the practical chapter,
we will discuss a hands-on case study where many of the techniques of this part come
together. You will be invited to create a self-reflective LLM agent that can play typical
AI-games such as TextWorld and NetHack.

Chapter 9

Interaction Styles for Agentic
LLMs


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn about different agentic interaction styles and agentic
memory. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Recognize three different historic types of agents in AI, and how they connect to
current agentic LLMs.
• Recognize five different agentic LLM interaction styles.
• Understand the importance of memory in agentic LLMs, and recognize different
agentic memory architectures.

9.1
Agents in AI

Agents play a central role in artificial intelligence, and we will first discuss some of the
background of agents in AI.

9.1.1
Agents Act and Adapt in their Environment

In artificial intelligence, entities that act in the world are called agents. They are the
AI equivalent of humans acting in the world. In the agent concept, AI researchers try
to capture what they perceive to be the essence of what humans do—understanding
intelligence by building it.
Agents are autonomous software systems that act in an environment. They (1)
have goals, they (2) perceive their environment, they (3) make decisions, they (4) take
actions to achieve their goals, and, most importantly, they (5) learn from experience.
Agents should adapt to new information in order to achieve their goals better, or, in
reinforcement learning terms, agents improve their action policy.
Traditional computer programs are deterministic, they predictably follow pre-set
instructions (this makes computers so useful to do things from accounting to control,

193

## Page 194

194
CHAPTER 9. INTERACTION STYLES FOR AGENTIC LLMS

in which predictability is paramount). LLM agents, in contrast, are less deterministic,
and less predictable. They learn, and change their behavior from time to time. They can
autonomously reason, plan, and perform tasks using tools to perform simple workflows
for users in areas such as coding, customer service, and data analysis. (They also
hallucinate, make mistakes, and generally are unpredictable and undependable. In that
respect, LLM agents are more like humans than computers.)
Agents have been studied for quite some time in artificial intelligence. It is useful to
distinguish three types of agents: (1) robotic assistant agents, (2) belief-desire-intention
agents, and (3) swarm agents.

9.1.1.1
Robotic Assistants

First we discuss agents that are robotic assistants. This view on AI agents is from the
field of engineering: agents perform human-like tasks for humans. An agent is a tool to
more easily achieve routine tasks. An example is a welding robot in a factory, an auto-
pilot in an airplane, or a self-driving car that has to find a safe route in an unpredictable
environment.
Further examples of such agents are virtual assistants, such as Alexa and Siri, or
coding assistants such as CoPilot that help software developers become more produc-
tive, or customer service bots that help customers navigate the maze of rules of a com-
pany to achieve goals such as filing a complaint or getting a refund. Robotic assistant
agents can have significant reasoning abilities \[Dorri et al., 2018\], and LLMs are in-
creasingly used for such assistants \[Plaat et al., 2025\].

9.1.1.2
Agents with Beliefs, Desires, and Intentions

Another view on AI agents is rooted in the field of cognitive science. Here the goal
is for agents to model human cognitive processes, and agents have beliefs, desires
and intentions (BDI). Cognitive science studies human thinking processes. AI agents
can be used to implement cognitive models, and experiment with models of thinking:
is the model able to reason logically, to cooperate with human players in a game of
Bridge, to deconstruct a theater play by Shakespeare, to compose music, or to have
self-awareness? Cognition may take many subtle forms, such as interpreting sensory
input, guiding physical actions, and empathizing with others.
Originally, BDI agents come from the tradition of logic reasoning. They are imbued
with goals, which they pursue through actions. The literature in this field sees actions
as a way to achieve the goals of an agent \[Rao et al., 1995, Georgeff et al., 1998\].

9.1.1.3
Swarm Agents

A third view on AI agents stresses interaction patterns between large numbers of small
agents. Where the previous multi-agent systems consisted of few, complex, agents that
act and think—agents that could assist, or agents with beliefs, desires and intentions
(BDI)—this approach studies flocks and swarms of many, simple, agents. Now the em-
phasis is on emergent collaborative behavior, behavior that emerges at a scale beyond

## Page 195

9.1. AGENTS IN AI
195

the reasoning of the agents themselves. Can a swarm offer protection against a preda-
tor? What are the prerequisites for collaboration to occur? When is a society peaceful,
when is it at war? What is a super-organism \[Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010, Wilson
and Sober, 1989\]?
Swarm agents come from the connectionist tradition of embodied AI \[Brooks,
1990\]. The agents communicate, and researchers are often interested in the emer-
gence of large scale behavioral patterns such as cooperation and communication. A
well-known swarm algorithm is ant colony optimization \[Dorigo et al., 2007\], and a
well-known software environment to study such patterns is Netlogo \[Wilensky and
Rand, 2015\].1

Multi-agent systems and agentic LLMs are suitable for the study of all three types
of approaches: agents as tools, agents as cognitive entities, and agents that help us
study how to achieve peaceful societies (or how to conquer another). Part IV of this
book is dedicated to agents as tools, and Part V is dedicated to cognition and agent
societies.

9.1.2
Agentic LLMs as Reinforcement Learning Agents

The study of the behavior of intelligent agents has a long tradition in AI. A central
aspect of agent behavior is how agents learn in their environment. Mechanisms by
which agents learn from feedback are studied in reinforcement learning \[Sutton and
Barto, 2018\] and multi-agent reinforcement learning \[Wong et al., 2021\].
In the next section we will discuss five interaction styles that we see in agentic
LLM. As preparation for this overview, we will provide a formal basis for agents that
interact in the world using the language of reinforcement learning.
Figure 9.1 shows a reinforcement learning system that consists of an agent and an
environment. In this system, the agent interacts with the environment through actions,
and the environment responds with the new state of the system and a reward value,
indicating how good the new state is.
The agent can learn from these reward values, and note which actions are favorable
and which are unfavorable in each state. The goal of the agent is to find the optimal
behavior for the environment, and thus, the best actions in each state. The agent uses
the rewards to reinforce its notion of the best actions in each state, and thus learn a
function of optimal behavior. This function, mapping each state to an action, is called
the behavior policy, denoted as 𝜋. The optimal policy is denoted as 𝜋∗. If the agent
learns through deep learning, then the policy is parameterized by the weights 𝜃of a
neural network.
The world in which the agent operates is represented by the environment. The
agent takes actions and changes the state of the environment. The environment has a
probabilistic transition function that computes the new state whenever an action has
been performed by the agent. The environment also computes a corresponding reward
for the new state. Thus, the environment is modeled with two functions: a transition
function 𝑇and a reward function 𝑅.

discuss and illustrate the different agentic styles.

9.2
Learning Mechanisms in Agentic LLMs

The field of agentic LLM is new, and the previous chapters have shown many different
approaches in which LLMs have been used in an agentic setting. In this section we
will review the approaches that we have seen so far in this book. We distinguish the
approaches based on their prompting method and their training method.
We will describe five styles of interaction that fit agentic LLMs. Table 9.1 sum-
marizes the five agent styles. We focus on the way that the LLM is prompted by the
harness at inference time, and how it is trained. All prompting styles can yield useful
agentic assistants and interaction partners, that act in realistic ways, for certain do-
mains. The more elaborate prompting styles have been developed in the pursuit for
better performance in more challenging domains.
The first column of the table gives the name of the agentic interaction style, from
query to reinforcement finetuning. The second column lists the type of prompting of
the styles, from a simple static instruction prompt without any examples, to a dynamic
reinforcement learning prompt. The third column shows the training method of the
LLM, whether it is pretrained or finetuned or both. The fourth column gives a concrete
example of the interaction style (with references to the literature).

9.2.1
Agentic Interaction Styles

We will now discuss the interaction styles. In the first three agent styles the prompt of
the LLM is static. The prompt is written by the user and does not change.

9.2.1.1
A. Query Prompt

The first interaction style is interacting with the LLM by giving it a simple instruction.
Figure 9.4 shows this interaction style. It simply consists of an instruction written by
the user. For example, Lily missed the train. She felt very ... to which the model hope-
fully responds with something like angry, or sad. The prompt is purely a query, without
any training examples. The learning style is zero-shot learning, instruction only. The
LLM is able to correctly answer many such queries because it has been pretrained on
a large corpus of text, which may provide an answer to many of the queries that users
may ask. The model has also been finetuned for instruction answering. Examples of
this interaction style are the early LLMs, such as GPT-2 \[Vaswani et al., 2017\].

9.2.1.2
B. In-Context Learning

Next, we turn to in-context learning. For machine learning, in-context learning is an
exciting new type of learning, in addition to supervised and reinforcement learning. In
a large language model in-context learning often achieves good results with just a few
examples, achieving one of the main challenges of the field of machine learning.
Compared to interaction style A, in-context few-shot learning is a more involved
interaction style. In-context learning occurs when the user provides a few examples
along with the query. In doing so, the user conditions the decoder model to activate the
correct part of the large amount of knowledge that is represented in its parameters.
Figure 9.5 shows an illustration of a prompt that fits this interaction style. An
example from the literature of this interaction style is GPT-3. The paper that introduced
in-context learning is Brown et al. \[2020\]. An example of a few-shot prompt is: Fill in
the dots: the sea-la mer, oysters-huitre, the window-la fenetre, cheese-... to which the
model hopefully responds with fromage.
Note that in-context learning only emerges when the model is large enough. Orig-
inally, in-context learning emerged in models with around 100 billion parameters. At
that size, the model was rich enough for the few prompt examples to activate the right
parts of the model. As our LLM methods improve, this boundary keeps shrinking.

9.2.1.3
C. Chain of Thought

Next, we turn to another famous method, chain of thought learning \[Wei et al., 2022\],
Figure 9.6, top. This method was developed, as we saw in Chapter 6, to address the
weakness of LLMs in solving simple math word reasoning problems. A disadvantage
of the original chain of thought approach is that a new prompt has to be written by the
user for each new reasoning task at hand. A subsequent development was the zero-shot
chain of thought prompt, Figure 9.6, bottom. Kojima et al. \[2022\] found that adding
the generic sentence: Let’s think step by step to prompts already improves performance
on many benchmarks, although often not by as much as a hand-written task-specific
prompt. As in the previous interaction style, chain of thought is an in-context few-
shot learning method, although now the examples in the prompt are a few examples of
the steps that the model should take before it provides its answer—whereas previously
they were examples of facts. These steps help the model arrive at the right answer,
following a multi-step reasoning chain. The examples are not examples of answers
to activate parts of the model, but of steps on how to arrive at the answer. Example
prompts for few-shot and zero-shot chain of thought have been shown in Figure 6.1 on
page 129.
Again, as with in-context learning, chain of thought only works in models of suffi-
cient size, and again, this size is getting smaller as our understanding of LLM methods
increases and models are being finetuned for chain of thought. Furthermore, it is possi-
ble to transfer the learned reasoning methods from a large model to a model with orders
of magnitude fewer parameters, by distillation \[Li et al., 2023\].

9.2.1.4
D. Self-Reflection Harness

The preceding agentic interaction styles all used a single static prompt, achieving en-
couraging performance on many benchmarks. To perform well on planning problems,
or other problems where state must be tracked, a reasoning style is needed where
prompts are optimized, searching through options in a tree of possibilities.
We will now discuss two interaction styles where the LLM prompt is dynamically
manipulated by a small algorithm that is external to the LLM. This algorithm is called
a harness. The first style is in-context (LLM parameters are not changed), while the
second style (in the next subsection) also uses finetuning of the model.
These interaction styles are dynamic. As we saw in the previous chapter on met-
alearning, a challenge of dynamic methods is to achieve a stable learning process.

When training targets are changing, learning algorithms may diverge, and extra care
is needed to achieve convergence. Achieving predictable high performance with self-
reflection is still an area of active research.
The first dynamic prompting methods that we discuss emerged out of the need to
model more complex reasoning structures, that go beyond the straight line sequence
of steps of chain of thought. First, simple search algorithms were introduced (tree of
thoughts). Next, full fledged dynamic prompting methods were introduced to manage
prompt development (ReAct, reflexion, self refine). Often, the harness of these meth-
ods introduced short-term and long-term memories to remember state between LLM
invocations.
An interesting aspect of these methods is that the LLM is used in different roles,
for which it is called with different types of prompts. The original role of the LLM in
chain of thought tasks is to evaluate the answer in each reasoning step. This evaluation
prompt is now augmented with a different type of prompt, to generate a new reasoning
step. Sometimes a third type of prompt is added, whose task is to improve the prompt
itself. Thus, a single model is used to self-reflect on itself through different prompts,
managed by an external harness.

9.2.1.5
E. Reinforcement Finetuning Harness

Up to now, all learning was in-context, the model provided answers based on examples
provided in the context. The parameters of the LLM were not changed. Although ICL
is easy to use, it limits learning. If we wish the model to adapt more profoundly to
a certain environment, if we wish the model to remember what it learned at inference
time, then it helps if the parameters can change. We call approaches that use this
method reinforcement finetuning. RLVR is a well-known example.

Figure 9.8 provides an illustration, where the trainable model parameters are indi-
cated as 𝜓. Note that the only difference with Figure 9.7 (bottom) is the introduction of
the 𝜓parameters. In ReFT the LLM parameters 𝜓change, they are finetuned based on
the rewards from the dataset. We should interpret the figures such that where learning
at inference time was in-context, this has now changed, since we allow finetuning of the
parameters 𝜓. In the traditional LLM training pipeline, finetuning is a stage that comes
before inference. However, for many important applications, such as math reasoning or
coding, chain of thought multi-step inference-time roll-outs produce accurate rewards
that can be used for finetuning. Therefore, in reinforcement finetuning, the model is
used to produce training targets at inference-time, that are then used to finetune the
parameters of the same model—finetuning at inference-time. Reinforcement finetun-
ing blurs the line between inference and finetuning, where supervised finetuning has a
clear separation between training and inference.

In LLM training there are three main training/inference moments: (1) pretrain-
ing, (2) finetuning, (3) testing (inference). Self-reflection (Style D) does reinforcement
learning at inference time. In style E, reinforcement finetuning, we do not do reinforce-
ment learning at test time (3), but at finetune time (2). In agentic LLM, this interaction
style allows the LLM to learn from agent interaction with the world.

For the dynamic agentic styles D and E, care must be taken to achieve stable con-
vergence. As of this writing, few works have been published that report on such results.
