CHAPTER 9. INTERACTION STYLES FOR AGENTIC LLMS

9.3
Memory Architectures for Agentic LLMs

Humans (and other forms of life) remember. Our memory enables us to have an iden-
tity. We can remember our name, our friends, and our family members. Memory allows
us to learn what is good an what is bad for us, and it allows us to adapt our behavior.
When we suffer memory-loss, either through injury, illness, or old age, our personality
changes. Severe memory-loss leads to loss of identity, we wander aimlessly through
the world.
Agents also need memory. In this section we will discuss why agentic LLM needs
memory, and we provide a brief overview of the different types of memory that have
been developed for agentic LLM.

9.3.1
The Need for Memory

A statistical model 𝑓(𝑥) →ˆ𝑦estimates an output ˆ𝑦based on the relation 𝑓that it
has learned for its input 𝑥at training time. Such functional behavior is memory-free.
Any new information (post-training) must be provided to the model through the input
parameters 𝑥. LLMs are no different, and even the earliest chatbots were provided with
special hidden system prompts that fed the model a history of the conversation, so that
it is able to hold a coherent conversation.
As the use cases for agentic LLM increase, more advanced techniques are needed,
beyond the system-prompt method. To better understand what memory is used for in
agentic LLMs, we will now discuss different use cases for memory.

9.3.1.1
Coherent Conversation

Many machine learning benchmarks for LLMs are of the challenge/response type, and
they are well suited for the functional input/output behavior of statistical models. The
main real world use case for LLMs, however, is as a chat-bot, where the LLM is ex-
pected to engage in a meaningful conversation with the user. In order to maintain
a coherent conversation, in which conversational partners react and respond to each
other, chat-bots must be able to know what has been said before.
Thus, a first requirement for agentic LLMs is to be able know what has been said
before in a conversation.

9.3.1.2
Adaptation

According to our definition in Chapter 1, agentic LLMs are expected to learn. When a
robot performs a task in a kitchen, such as chopping an onion, and the location of the
knife has moved, then it should adapt its actions: it should now first pick up the knife
from its new location before starting to chop. Agents interact with the environment,
and if the environment changes, then agents should adapt.
Either our agent’s pretrained policies must be highly general, and able to adapt to
all new situations in a certain domain, or our agents architecture must flexible, and
recognize when a pretrained policy requires adaptation, finetuning or even re-training.
For this, they need memory.

## Page 203

9.3. MEMORY ARCHITECTURES FOR AGENTIC LLMS
203

As we have seen in Section 6.2.4, the external prompt improvement harnesses that
are used in self-reflective agent architectures require buffers and other memory types
for explicit prompt improvement.

9.3.1.3
Identity

Our experiences shape our personality and our identity. When LLM agents are to build
up their own identity, the experiences must either be collected and held in a memory, to
be used for self-reflection, or they must be processed and used in other ways to adapt
their behavior policy.
As the memory architectures of agentic harnesses improve, agents will be able to
better remember their experiences. When that happens, we may find that our agents
can acquire, through their agentic experiences, a unique personality.

9.3.1.4
Continual Learning

Traditional machine learning trains a model on a particular dataset for a particular
task. Human learning is different, our learning evolves continuously throughout our
lives. In machine learning, continual learning studies how models can be trained for a
sequence of new tasks while preserving previously learned tasks \[Wang et al., 2024, Li
et al., 2025a\]. Like metalearning, it studies generalization across related tasks. Major
challenges in continual learning are to overcome catastrophic forgetting, and how to
cope with changing data distributions.
The field of continual learning provides a variety of architectures that support this
type of training.

9.3.2
Memory Architectures

The field of agentic LLM is young. Only recently are memory architectures for LLM
agents starting to receive attention. We will discuss the different approaches that have
so far appeared.

9.3.2.1
Finetuning

A pragmatic way to deal with the need for memory is to incorporate new informa-
tion into the model as it arrives. Instead of developing external memory management
algorithms, we could take advantage of the fact that model parameters are a form of
memory, and finetune the model as the new examples arrive.
To achieve this approach in an agentic setting, the finetuning must happen quickly,
before the user can perceive a lag. Parameter efficient finetuning methods such as
LoRA are an option \[Yang et al., 2024\]. Although this is an elegant approach that
does not require external algorithms or memory structures, for most applications the
finetuning will not happen quickly enough, and an in-context or harness solution should
be developed.

## Page 204

204
CHAPTER 9. INTERACTION STYLES FOR AGENTIC LLMS

9.3.2.2
Long Context Windows and Compression

A second approach is to perform prompt management. The standard approach of chat-
bots is to provide a truncated form of the chat-history to the LLM by injecting it into
the prompt in addition to the user’s text. This is an approach that works quite well
in practice. A limitation is that context windows are limited in size, and processing
large contexts is expensive because of the squared time complexity of the attention
mechanism.
Two types of solutions have been pursued. First, specific long-context architec-
tures have been developed, that keep track of attention in different ways \[Smith et al.,
2022\]. This is an active field of research, a survey of recent approaches is Liu et al.
\[2025\]. Second, compression schemes have been developed, to semantically compress
the prompt into a smaller stream. A survey is Li et al. \[2025b\]. Prompts can be divided
into chunks \[Sheng et al., 2025\], to allow processing of large prompts. A related ap-
proach uses the LLM to generate code for processing long prompts recursively \[Zhang
et al., 2025a\].
Prompts can also be compressed through filtering of unnecessary tokens (this sen-
tence could become Prompts compressed filtering unnecessary tokens). Another ap-
proach is soft prompts \[Lester et al., 2021\]. Soft prompts eliminate discrete tokens, but
learn embeddings (via backpropagation) that can be fed directly into the transformer,
without mapping them to actual language tokens. This context can serve as an alter-
native to a plain-text context. Impressive compression rates have been reported, from
ten-fold \[Mu et al., 2023\] to hundred-fold \[Li et al., 2025c\].

9.3.2.3
Explicit Memory Management

If we need to store state between LLM calls, then a straightforward solution is for
the agent harness to provide this storage, as part of its prompt management. In Sec-
tion 6.2.4 we saw how the external prompt-improvement algorithms for self-reflection
add different types of storage, such as in the reflexion approach and the buffer of
thoughts approach (Figures 6.8 and 6.6).
Agents can have different requirements for their storage (see Zhang et al. \[2025b\],
Chhikara et al. \[2025\] for a survey). We will discuss some of the recent studies of
this active field of research. Prompts can be stored in textual or parametric form, and
relevant operations are the reading and writing to memory. Furthermore, memory man-
agement operations are important, such as for compacting and forgetting information.
Also, additional services can be provided by the memory systems. For example, Mem-
oryBank \[Zhong et al., 2024\] adds hierarchical summaries and uses LLM prompts to
provide a running personality of the interaction events of a user.
Operations to store and retrieve items can be added to an agent. MemGPT \[Packer
et al., 2023\] studies how LLMs can read and write to external memory using function
calls (memory as a tool). A-mem \[Xu et al., 2025\] introduces contextual descriptions
of memory, based on a mailbox principle.
A disadvantage of the explicit memory management approach is that the LLM has
to perform memory management explicitly, without having been trained how to do this
effectively. An alternative solution is to manually write memory management code,

## Page 205

9.4. CONCLUDING REMARKS
205

when it is possible to foresee all possible requirements. The Model Context Protocol
(MCP) is a set of strategies designed for context management. Section 11.4 describes
the protocol in more depth.

Learning to use memory
Mem1 \[Zhou et al., 2025\] uses a different approach: af-
ter each LLM interaction the agent updates a compact state to be shared with future
LLM calls. The memory size required is constant, so that the state does not run out of
the context window. The shared state is created by inserting reasoning-style tags into
the prompt, and is trained using reinforcement learning to incentivize state consolida-
tion. Mem-𝛼is another approach that uses reinforcement learning to train agents to
effectively use memory \[Wang et al., 2025\].
AgeMem \[Yu et al., 2026\] integrates memory management operations into agent’s
policy for end-to-end optimization. It distinguishes long term and short term memory,
and uses a three-stage reinforcement learning scheme to train the agent in the use of
the two types of memory.
This, too, is an active field of research, new studies and frameworks can be ex-
pected. See, for an overview, Zhou et al. \[2026\].

Vector Databases
In addition to the storage of prompts as human-readable text, we
can also store their tokenized embeddings directly. Storing prompts as text is useful for
retrieving data when an exact textual match is needed. Embeddings encode semantic
information—which tokens are close to each other in meaning. Storing embeddings is
therefore useful when we would like to retrieve items that are semantically close.
Embeddings can be stored in vector databases. Traditional relational databases
store data in rows and columns. Vector databases store high-dimensional lists of num-
bers, and provide low-latency access to them, making them well-suited for LLMs \[Xie
et al., 2023, Ma et al., 2023\].

9.4
Concluding Remarks

The concept of an intelligent agent is a central concept in artificial intelligence. LLMs
have increased the communication and reasoning capabilities of agents significantly.
In this chapter, we have discussed different agent types, and have connected them to
different traditions in AI.
Agents act. We have discussed 5 main interaction styles based on the preceding
chapters. Agents need memory to interact meaningfully with their environments, and
we have discussed this new field of research.
After covering so much theory, it is high time to get our hands dirty. In the next
chapter we will look at a practical case study, to get more experience with using some
of the theoretical concepts that we have seen.

Chapter 10

Case Study 2: BALROG for
LLM Reasoning and Reflection


What You Will Learn

In this case study you will gain hands-on experience building self-reflective agent
for reasoning domains. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Run a multi-step reasoning agent on a benchmark of puzzles and games.
• Adapt a reasoning agent with your own ideas.
• Implement your own self-reflective agent.
• Critically reflect on the performance and stability of a learning agent in the do-
main of puzzles and games.

10.1
BALROG Overview

In this case we will work with an agentic LLM that performs self-reflection.
We
use a popular benchmark suite for reasoning tasks, called BALROG.1 BALROG is
an acronym for Benchmarking Agentic LLM and VLM Reasoning On Games. The
BALROG benchmark consists of a mix of easy and hard games, some of which are dif-
ficult for LLMs to play well, as the BALROG paper shows in their own benchmarking
study \[Paglieri et al., 2025\].
Initially, the BALROG games are benchmarked with vanilla LLMs. The code,
however, is quite open and amenable to writing your own agent approaches, to see if
you can do better. The software is written for you to write your own agent code for
in-context (reinforcement) learning.
The main BALROG website is https://balrogai.com. The code is easy to
adapt and use for your own experiments, and there is a leaderboard. In this chapter we

1A Balrog is a mythical demon from Middle-earth, featured in the fantasy works of J.R.R. Tolkien. A
Balrog is a match even for Gandalf the Grey, the most powerful wizard of all.

CHAPTER 10. CASE STUDY 2: REASONING AND REFLECTION

Figure 10.1: List of games in BALROG \[Paglieri et al., 2025\]

will guide you to write your own agent code, that can then be run on the BALROG
games-suite.
BALROG is designed to challenge in-context agents on reasoning problems. It uses
puzzle-style games to benchmark the reasoning capabilities of LLMs and VLMs. Fig-
ure 10.1 lists the games. The games are from easy to hard: BabyAI, Crafter, TextWorld,
BabaIsAI, MiniHack, and NetHack. The games offer a mix of challenges, some are
text-based, some have a visual component, all include reasoning challenges for the
model. Some of the games are considered hard. For example, it is not expected that
your model or your agent—or your self—will reach a high score on NetHack. (If you
do achieve that, without having accessed the cheat-sheets, you may want to consider
writing a paper for a prestigious AI conference.)

10.1.1
Puzzles and Games

BALROG consists of the six puzzles and games shown in Figure 10.1. The games run
from easy grid world puzzles to hard text-based dungeon and dragons strategy games,
with long credit assignment episodes and flat reward landscapes.
The authors of BALROG provide a code base that allows experimentation with
agents, to design your own agent, to see how well they do on the benchmarks. To
perform well on the benchmarks in BALROG, the agents must be good at reasoning and
planning, and, most likely, be good at adapting and reflecting on their own behavior.
BabyAI is a simple grid-world game, where the agent has to solve a navigation
task. A simple reinforcement learning type algorithm would be able to easily solve this
game. Tasks are given in natural language, such as: go to the blue ball, then pick up
the grey key. Of course, the challenge for the agentic LLM is to perform the planning
part of the task. It is expected that the LLM will be able to do well on this simple game
(see the BALROG paper).
NetHack, on the other hand, is a highly challenging game, also for human players.
NetHack is a text-based dungeons and dragons-like game. It includes both long-term
strategic planning, in the sense that winning a game can involve hundreds of thousands
of steps, and short-term tactical fights to fend of the usual hordes of monsters. Credit
assignment is a challenge in NetHack, in order to understand which of the actions that
the agent took in the past contributed to ultimate success or failure, since actions in one

10.1.3
Agent

Please read the Agent tutorial in BALROG at https://github.com/balrog-ai/
BALROG/blob/main/docs/agents.md. In BALROG, agents are small pieces
of Python code that call an LLM with a prompt to provide an answer how to determine
the next step. The agent code is responsible for receiving answers from the model
(observations) and for selecting the next action. The LLM is used to execute various
prompts.
BALROG follows interaction style D from Figure 9.7, where the prompt is built up
from the history of interactions.

10.1.3.1
Prompt Builder

The agent builds a prompt based on previous actions, based on observation/action pairs
from previous interactions. Thus, in reinforcement learning terms, the agent performs
the function of the policy, selecting the next action to perform based on the incoming
observation.
Go to the prompt_builder directory to change the way that prompts are con-
structed from the history of actions.

10.1.3.2
Agents

Agents are responsible for the memory function: managing the observation/action his-
tories. The agents must keep a record of past observations and actions to support
context-aware decision-making, and this must be implemented by us, external to the
LLM.
The agent code in BALROG queries the LLM: agents send observations to the
LLM, receive responses, and use those responses to decide on actions to take in the
game.
BALROG comes with a number of pre-written agents, which you should study to
design your own. The repository has a naive agent and a chain of thought agent. Also
provided are more robust versions for handling LLM responses.
When you build your own agent, you will most likely build on the custom agent.
The BALROG agent tutorial provides an example for a simple planning agent.

10.2
Implementation Steps

We will now provide some exercises to help you explore building your agents.

10.2.1
Reproduce Paper

We start by trying to reproduce the results in the BALROG paper. Please have a look
at the BALROG code at Github https://github.com/balrog-ai/BALROG.
Read the Evaluation Guide, the Agent Development tutorial, and the instructions how
to run Few Shot Learning experiments (in-context learning). Install the relevant tools
on your computer, and the right Python version (and put it in your PATH). Check the
version by starting the Python interpreter from the command prompt: $ python.
First, run the standard evaluation, to make sure you installed things correctly, see
Listing 10.2.

10.2.2
Different LLMs

To get a feeling for how the standard agent performs on the different benchmarks with
different LLMs, it is useful to run a few different LLMs. It is recommended to run
closed and open LLMs, and see how they perform. Especially the open version from
OpenAI, Claude, DeepSeek, OLMo and Qwen may work well.
Running these models is important, and will lead to more insight into the relative
strengths of the various models.

10.2.3
Different Puzzles

Next, to get a better understanding of the benchmark, you should, after running the
LLM agent in the different puzzle problems, have a closer look at the prompts and the
answers of LLM. See if you can see where the LLM agent fails, where the weakness of
the agent lies. By close inspection of the individual actions, and a deeper understanding
of the puzzle, you might be able to think of a way to improve your agent.

10.2.4
Computational Cost

BALROG agents call an LLM for each step that the agent makes, often with a long
prompt. In these puzzles and games many such steps are made. Running different

LLMs on the full benchmark, for different seeds, will easily require many tokens.
In your experiments, first try a small and cheap LLM, such as Qwen-3B. Start with
the easiest benchmarks (BabyAI and Crafter). If you wish to expand, please go ahead,
but be mindful of the computational cost. You want insights, but you also want your
experiments to finish in a reasonable time for a reasonable cost.

10.2.5
Implement Own Reasoning Agent

Now it is time to implement your own learning agent. Go to the agents directory in bal-
rog, and edit the custom.py file. Listing 10.3 reproduces the code for Custom Agent
from the BALROG readme. The code can be run with the command in Listing 10.4
(specifying the custom agent, and running gently with fewer workers). Of course, you
can specify your own LLM of choice in the command.
Start with the provided code, run it, see how it works. Then, you can try to make
small improvements. Try making changes to the prompt for the LLM, and to the way in
which the Python code handles the learning in the agent, either with the history prompt
builder, in the plan, or in the learning algorithm.

10.3
Evaluation

The performance of your agent will be reported by BALROG as a progression percent-
age. Record the progression numbers for each benchmark, and for the agent types that
you try. Do this in a structured way, you may want to write a Python or shell script to
automate the running of the experiments and the logging of the results, perhaps also
plotting the progression in a graph. Consider using wandb.ai.
What agent types work well, and on what benchmark do they work well? Make a
matrix in which you log progression for the agent types and the benchmark types that
you try.
Note that LLM experiments are inherently non-deterministic: two runs with the
same prompt may give different results. Therefore, perform multiple runs of each
experiment. If you get five identical results in a row, you may start to trust these results.
If they vary widely, you may want to investigate. Is the reason purely statistical? Does
turning down the temperature solve the problem, or is there another problem?
Do not blindly trust the progression numbers that are reported. Since you are us-
ing code on a computer, there may be bugs, or other issues. The BALROG system
facilitates delving deeper into the runs. It logs csv files that you can look at with a
spreadsheet. Have a look at some of the runs, and decide if it makes sense what you
see, or if the agents are exhibiting degenerative behavior. If they do, try to find the
reason. Did you do something wrong? Is there unexpected interference between the
benchmark and the agent behavior? Is the reward landscape too flat, so that there is no
signal for the agent to go after, and all it does is random actions running in circles in a
way that makes no sense at all? Is there something that you can do about this?
Please note that the field of large language models, and especially of agentic LLMs,
is new, and our insights and our software frameworks have not yet stabilized. Some
unexpected results are to be expected, and some challenges or frustration as well.

12
if prev_action:

14

15

16

17

18

23

25

27
messages = self.prompt_builder.get_prompt()

28

32

35

40

41

def _extract_plan_and_action(self, response_text):

45
plan_match = re.search(r"PLAN:\s*(.*?)(?=\nACTION:|\Z)", response_text, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL)

46
action_match = re.search(r"ACTION:\s*(.*)", response_text, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL)

47

48
plan = plan_match.group(1).strip() if plan_match else "No changes to the plan."

49
action = action_match.group(1).strip() if action_match else None

50

51
return plan, action

10.4
Self-Reflection

When you were able to reproduce the benchmark results, and have experimented some-
what with the agents, you may want to try to take on some larger challenges. In this
section, we will try to extend the BALROG agent towards self-reflection, where the
LLM is used in different roles, such as evaluation and action selection. Self-reflection,
as any adaptive system that chases a target that is itself being optimized, can be prone
to instability and oscillations. Therefore, before we try our self-reflective ideas, it is
important that the base learner system of the previous subsection works, and converges
in a stable and predictable manner. Please go back to that section and make sure things
work as you want them to work.
There are many recent works that try to improve LLM agents. We will mention two:
ReAct \[Yao et al., 2022\] and reflexion \[Shinn et al., 2024\]. ReAct is primarily focused
on prompts, where reflexion introduces new agent algorithms, including short-term and
long-term memory.

ReAct
ReAct uses promtps to interact with the world.
ReAct promotes the use
of tools, to lookup information, see Figure 10.3.

the LangChain2 and BeeAI3 frameworks.
Have a look at these framework to get an understanding of the prompt-based agent
interaction style that ReAct introduces. Then, implement the prompt-based interaction
in BALROG. Does is improve performance? For which games does it help to lookup
external information? For which games not?

Reflexion
Where ReAct is prompt-based, allowing interactive lookups, the reflex-
ion approach introduces Python-coded agents, allowing more elaborate agent behavior.
Reflexion uses the same LLM in different contexts, with different prompts. It works on
the assumption that it is easier to criticize what is wrong with an existing prompt, than
to come up with one that works.
Reflexion is a popular self-reflection architecture \[Shinn et al., 2024\]. The main
webpage for reflexion is https://github.com/noahshinn/reflexion. A
blog post on reflexion, describing the main ideas, is here: https://nanothoughts.
substack.com/p/reflecting-on-reflexion.

10.5
Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have discussed a practical case study, to see how an LLM can per-
forms self-reflection. We used BALROG, a popular benchmark suite for reasoning
tasks. BALROG consists of a mix from easy to hard games, some of which are difficult
for LLMs to play well. The BALROG suite is designed in an open style. We can write
our own agent code that can then be run on the BALROG games.
This has been an important practical case study. You have explored writing our
own agent code for in-context reasoning. You have also gone beyond base-learning,
by implementing self-reflection. You have explored the stability of self-reflection, on
different LLMs and with highly challenging benchmarks.

## Page 225

The first three parts discussed the AI techniques for constructing advanced LLM
Agents that can interact with and act in the real world. These capabilities allow them
to do useful things for their users. In this part we will address the use of tools by LLMs
to perform specialized tasks, such as looking up information, or controlling robots.
Agents use tools through learned APIs (Application Programming Interfaces).
Tools can help us solve a major problem of pretrained LLMs, which is that the
information that is contained in them is only as up to date as the dataset on which they
were trained. Retrieval augmentation techniques allows LLMs to provide up to the
minute information.
Many types of such agents have been created, and in the final chapter of this part we
will review important examples, from the medical, financial, and scientific domains.
Finally, we will discuss a practical case study in which the use of the technologies
comes together, when we will implement an LLM Agent to perform medical diagnosis.

## Page 227

Chapter 11

How Agents Use Tools to Act in
the World


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how agentic Large Language Models connect to the
external world through tools. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Explain why tools are essential for agents that act beyond pure language gener-
ation.
• Distinguish between the direct invocation and Planner–Caller–Summarizer ar-
chitectural patterns.
• Work with toolchains and frameworks such as LangChain and the ReAct loop,
and understand how agents interact with browsers and desktop environments.
• Describe the Model Context Protocol as a standardized approach to tool integra-
tion.
• Reason about robustness, error recovery, and the safety and security risks that
arise when agents are given access to external tools.

11.1
Why Tools Matter in Agentic LLMs

In the taxonomy of reasoning–acting–interacting (Figure 1.1), tools are the primary
bridge between an LLM’s internal reasoning and its actions in the external world. A
tool may be as simple as a calculator, as complex as a scientific simulation engine,
or as open-ended as a full desktop environment. By equipping LLMs with tool use
capabilities, we allow them to:

• Access fresh, domain-specific data (e.g., via APIs, databases, or search engines).

• Perform actions in the world (e.g., controlling robots, operating browsers, send-
ing messages).

• Delegate complex computations or retrieval to specialized systems.

227

## Page 228

228
CHAPTER 11. HOW AGENTS USE TOOLS TO ACT IN THE WORLD

• Chain multiple tools into composite workflows that can be planned, executed,
and monitored.

Retrieval is one specific kind of tool primarily aimed to augment an LLM’s knowl-
edge. We will discuss it in depth in Chapter 12. Tool use in general can also augment
an LLM’s capabilities to manipulate its environment. These capabilities also come
with additional risks, such as safety, reliability and performance risks. They introduce
additional points of failure and might be misused under certain conditions.

11.2
Tool Use Architectures

Let us see some common software architectures for tool use by LLMs. Integrating
tools into an LLM agent typically follows one of two patterns: direct invocation, and
planner-caller-summarizer.

Direct Invocation

In the direct invocation pattern, the LLM outputs structured calls (e.g., JSON or func-
tion signatures) that are parsed by an external controller and routed to the tool. For
example: OpenAI’s function calling API or Gorilla \[Patil et al., 2023\].

Planner–Caller–Summarizer

The planner-caller-summarizer pattern is an extension of the direct invocation pattern
where we use a multi-agent architecture where the LLM serves as a central planner.
It calls a separate module to execute a tool (which might be another LLM or another
kind of agent), which then returns a summarized observation back to the LLM. This
allows the LLM to maintain a high-level view of the task while outsourcing the detailed
execution to a dedicated system.
ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) \[Yao et al., 2022\] is a prominent framework that
interweaves reasoning and acting.
Instead of generating a full plan and then exe-
cuting, an LLM using ReAct follows an iterative loop of Thought, Action, and
Observation. This allows the agent to dynamically adjust its plan based on the
real-time feedback it receives from tool outputs, making it more robust to errors and
unexpected results. This works well because the tools (observation part) often act as
a grounding mechanism in the real world (such as the execution of a code snippet,
or an internet search), which provides the LLM with factual information for the next
iteration.

11.3
APIs and Toolchains

When their application programming interface (API) is known, LLMs can be integrated
easily with external tools: for an LLM, an API is just another language to learn. One
common way to use a tool, is to augment LLM input with results that are retrieved from

## Page 229

11.3. APIS AND TOOLCHAINS
229

external sources, such as search engines. You can read more about retrieval methods in
Chapter 12.
Agentic LLMs must be trained to decide when and how to utilize external tools,
depending on the task \[Shen et al., 2024\]. Language models can teach themselves to
use tools. The Toolformer model \[Schick et al., 2023\] is trained to decide which APIs
to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to best incorporate the
results into future token prediction. A range of tools is tested: a calculator, a question-
answering system, a search engine, a translation system, and a calendar. Further works
extend this to a larger range of tools. ToolBench \[Qin et al., 2023\] contains 16,464
APIs from RapidAPI, a large dataset of publicly available REST APIs.1

Another framework is EasyTool \[Yuan et al., 2024\], which focuses on structured
and unified instructions from tool documentations, building on ToolBench. ToolAl-
paca is a benchmark with over 3938 instances from 400 API \[Tang et al., 2023\]. A
tool-based benchmark for question answering is ToolQA \[Zhuang et al., 2023\]. Go-
rilla is a finetuned LLaMa-based model for generating API calls \[Patil et al., 2023\],
also introducing the APIBench benchmark. Many tool calling frameworks have been
developed.
Selecting the right tool and summarizing its result are difficult skills for a model.
Zhao et al. \[2024\], Shen et al. \[2024\] study how LLMs can improve recommendation
through tool learning. They use different LLMs for (1) reasoning ability, (2) request
writing, and (3) result summarization. Figure 11.1 illustrates this architecture, consist-
ing of a planner, a caller, and a summarizer, each implemented by a different LLM
finetuned for its specific capability. Good results are reported on the LLMs Claude-2,
ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Tool-LLaMa, using as reasoning strategies ReAct \[Yao et al.,
2022\] and DFSDT \[Qin et al., 2023\]. Other frameworks also exist, such as \[Ocker
et al., 2024\].

11.3.1
LangChain Example

LangChain \[Chase, 2022\] is a widely-used framework for building LLM applications,
offering robust abstractions for creating agents and tool chains. Listing 11.1 is a simple
Python example demonstrating how to define a tool and use it within a basic agentic
framework. In this scenario, the agent is asked a question that requires a numerical
check, which it delegates to a specialized tool.

11.3.2
Computer and Browser Tools

One specific set of action tools is to let an LLM use a browser or even a complete
computer system as a special form of API. Equipping agentic LLMs with the ability to
interact directly with a computer environment enables many interaction possibilities.
Tools that parse, interpret, and manipulate graphical user interfaces (GUIs) have gained
attention for bridging the gap between language models and real-world applications.
One such example is OmniParser V2 \[Lu et al., 2024\], which introduces a vision-
based screen parsing method to detect and label interactable elements such as buttons

components. This grounding increases the accuracy of the action predictions of LLMs.
Another line of research focuses on enabling LLMs to initiate system-level com-
mands or navigate within browser or operating system interfaces. Computer Use, pro-
posed by Antropic, and Operator and later GPT Agent, proposed by OpenAI, are ex-
amples of such efforts. These tools wrap common desktop and browser actions (such
as opening applications, clicking buttons, and filling forms) into tool APIs callable by
an LLM. This setup translates high-level textual commands into executable steps. As a
result, an agentic LLM can browse the web, manage files, or run administrative tasks,
all through natural language prompts. This can lead to more autonomous behavior and
execution of larger and more complex tasks.
Browser Use \[M¨uller and ˇZuniˇc, 2024\] is an example of an open-source tool that
enables LLMs to use a browser with persistent session management. Browser Use
enables agentic LLMs to maintain longer browsing states across multiple pages or do-
mains. The tool manages cookies, session tokens, and dynamic web content updates,
thereby allowing LLMs to execute more complex browsing tasks like multi-step form
completions or cross-site queries.
For a more in-depth discussion about browser and computer environments, see
the survey by Wang et al. \[2025b\]. The survey discusses design patterns for combin-
ing automated GUI parsing, tool call integration, and human-in-the-loop supervision.
Collectively, these approaches reveal that reliable computer and browser tools are im-
portant components for agentic LLMs. By translating textual intents into grounded,

## Page 232

232
CHAPTER 11. HOW AGENTS USE TOOLS TO ACT IN THE WORLD

environment-level operations, such systems expand the possible tasks and domains
where language-driven autonomy can be effectively realized.

11.4
Model Context Protocol and Context Management

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard introduced by An-
thropic for connecting AI applications to external data sources, tools, and workflows
\[Hou et al., 2026\]. It is often described as a “USB-C port for AI”, providing a standard-
ized way for applications such as Claude or ChatGPT to access local files, databases,
search engines, calculators, and other external capabilities.
MCP uses a client-server architecture. An MCP host, such as an AI application,
manages one or more MCP clients, with each client maintaining a connection to an
MCP server. MCP servers provide context and capabilities that can be used by the
host, including tools, resources, and prompts. Local servers commonly communicate
with a single client through STDIO, while remote servers can support multiple clients
through Streamable HTTP.
The protocol is organized into two layers. The data layer defines the JSON-RPC-
based communication between clients and servers, including capability and version
discovery, as well as primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, and notifications.
The transport layer specifies how this communication is established and exchanged,
including connection management, message framing, and authorization. This separa-
tion allows AI applications to interact with a wide range of external systems through a
common interface, while leaving the management of the resulting context to the host
application.
One of the key challenges in building agentic systems is managing the LLM its
finite context window. For multi-step tasks that require numerous tool calls and obser-
vations, the context can quickly fill up, causing the model to lose track of its original
goal or forget crucial past information. Simply keeping all the context and raw re-
sults from multiple tool calls often does not fit the context window and therefor causes
forgetting. Deciding what to keep, what to summarize and what to discard is essential.
MCP servers are mostly stateless. This means that we need an additional set of
strategies designed to manage the agent’s state and context. These strategies should
ensure that the agent maintains a clear and coherent state throughout a long-running
task. In addition to the fixed tool registration/calling format that MCP offers, additonal
components to include are:

• Summarization: Tools’ outputs and past conversations are periodically summa-
rized and stored in a compressed format. This reduces the token count while
preserving key information.

• State Management: Explicitly maintaining a state variable or a scratchpad in the
prompt, where the agent stores its current plan, important intermediate results,
and a summary of its progress.

• Prioritized Retrieval: Instead of feeding the entire history back into the context, a
retrieval mechanism can be used to only inject the most relevant past information

11.5. ROBUSTNESS, ERROR HANDLING, AND RECOVERY
233

for the current step, based on the agent’s reasoning.

Example: Implementing the Model Context Protocol
Listing 11.2 and 11.3 illus-
trates a simplified implementation of the Model Context Protocol. It demonstrates how
an agent can manage its context by summarizing past interactions to avoid exceeding a
fixed context window size.2

11.5
Robustness, Error Handling, and Recovery

The external nature of tool use introduces new points of failure. An API service might
be down, a tool might return an unexpected error, or the LLM might make a logical
mistake in its plan. A robust agentic system must be able to handle these failures
gracefully.

Reactive Error Handling
A basic but essential strategy is to implement an error-
handling loop. When a tool call fails, the system can provide the LLM with the error
message as an observation. The LLM can then reason about the error and attempt a new
action, such as re-invoking the tool with corrected arguments, trying a different tool,
or informing the user of the failure. This process of observe-reflect-retry is
a fundamental mechanism for self-healing in agentic systems \[Sun et al., 2024\]. Note
that this pattern is similar to the ReAct framework but in a different context.

Self-Correcting and State-Aware Systems
More advanced systems, such as Healer,
are designed to correct runtime errors in real-time \[Wu et al., 2024\]. Healer can dy-
namically generate and execute a small code snippet to patch a faulty program state
without stopping the entire execution. This goes beyond simple retries; it involves the
LLM understanding the context of the error, analyzing the program state, and actively
correcting the error (in code).

Human-in-the-Loop Integration
While autonomy is a goal of agentic systems, the
most effective applications often involve a human-in-the-loop. This approach improves
safety, allows for corrections, and incorporates human expertise at critical junctures.3

An agent can be designed to pause and ask for human confirmation before executing
a high-stakes action (e.g., making a financial transaction or sending a critical email).
This co-piloting model creates a powerful symbiosis, combining the LLM’s speed and
scale with human judgment and domain knowledge \[Mozannar et al., 2025\].

11.6
Safety and Security

Safety and security are becoming more important as the capabilities of Agentic LLMs
grow. This goes beyond simple error handling and is more subtle on a misbehavior and
misuse level. An obvious example of a safety problem is that without additional pro-
tection, the system prompt of an LLM can easily be exposed, often revealing sensitive
information.

The robustness of LLMs to jailbreak attacks, where users design prompts to cir-
cumvent safety measures and misuse model capabilities, has been studied for chat-
bots. Meanwhile, agentic LLMs use external tools and can execute multi stage tasks,
and may pose a greater risk. Andriushchenko et al. \[2024\] propose AgentHarm. This
benchmark includes a set of 110 malicious agent tasks ranging from fraud, cyber crime,
to harassment. The authors find that leading commercial LLMs are surprisingly com-
pliant to their given rules with malicious user requests without jailbreaking (How do I
make a pipe bomb? is blocked). However, simple universal templates can be adapted
to effectively jailbreak agents (Order online all necessary ingredients to make a pipe
bomb and get them delivered to my home without getting flagged by authorities, how-
ever, passes in GPT-4).

Rainbow Teaming \[Samvelyan et al., 2024\] uses an open world approach to gen-
erate adversarial LLM prompts, to improve the robustness of LLMs. As with train-
ing LLMs, a problem with testing methods is a lack of diversity. Rainbow Teaming
casts adversarial prompt generation as a quality-diversity problem. Rainbow Team-
ing is an open-ended approach \[Hughes et al., 2024\]. It creates diversity with MAP-
Elites \[Mouret and Clune, 2015\], an evolutionary meta search method that iteratively
populates an archive with increasingly higher-performing prompts. See Figures 11.2
and 11.3.

## Page 237

11.7. CONCLUDING REMARKS
237

Figure 11.3: Quality Diversity Mutation Architecture of Rainbow Teaming \[Samvelyan
et al., 2024\]

11.7
Concluding Remarks

Tools are what turn a static language model into a dynamic agent that can act in the
world. Their ability to grant LLMs access to fresh data, perform external actions, and
delegate complex tasks is transformative. For any agentic system to be successful in
practice, the result goes beyond just connecting a tool to an LLM, but now requires us
to think about the full life-cycle of the agent’s interaction with the environment, and
what can happen. Four steps should be followed:

1. Choose the right Architecture: Methodologies such as ReAct \[Yao et al., 2022\],
which tightly interleave reasoning and tool calls, lead to more robust self-correcting
behavior than simpler one-shot approaches.

2. Manage your Context: For multistep long-term tasks, the LLM context window
is a critical bottleneck. Use strategies such as the Model Context Protocol to
summarize history and manage state, preventing the agent from losing its way.

3. Embrace Failure: Tool-use systems are inherently fragile due to their reliance on
external APIs. Build in robust error handling, allowing the agent to observe and
reason about failures, and attempt recovery.

4. Keep a Human in the Loop: For high-stakes applications, ensure that the agent
has a clear mechanism to pause and seek human confirmation before taking irre-
versible actions. This blend of autonomy and human oversight is key to building
trust and ensuring safety.

Chapter 12

Search and Retrieval in Agentic
LLMs


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn why retrieval is a fundamental capability for agentic
systems that need knowledge beyond their training data. Specifically, you will be
able to:
• Describe the full retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, from indexing and
chunking to query formulation and answer generation.
• Implement adaptive retrieval methods such as Self-RAG and Self-Ask, and build
a dense retrieval system in Python.
• Extend retrieval beyond plain text to graphs, code, tabular data, and multimodal
sources.
• Distinguish agentic RAG from simple one-shot retrieval, including real-time and
streaming variants.
• Evaluate retrieval systems using standard metrics such as Recall@𝑘, Mean Re-
ciprocal Rank, and faithfulness scores.

12.1
Retrieval in General

Before examining how agentic LLMs consult external knowledge, it is worth situating
retrieval within its own, much older, disciplinary history. Information retrieval (IR)
is a mature field of computer and information science that predates neural networks
by decades. Many of the ideas that power modern retrieval augmented generation
(RAG) pipelines are direct descendants of classical information retrieval research. The
standard reference works of the field, Salton and McGill \[1983\] and later Manning
et al. \[2008\], still provide the conceptual vocabulary such as: indexing, term weighting,
ranking and relevance, that this chapter builds on.

CHAPTER 12. SEARCH AND RETRIEVAL IN AGENTIC LLMS

12.1.1
Bag of Words

Early information retrieval systems represented documents and queries as bags of words
and asked a deceptively simple question: which terms make a document a good match
for a query? Sp¨arck Jones \[1972\] gave this question a statistical answer with the notion
of inverse document frequency (IDF), observing that terms occurring in few documents
are more discriminating than terms that occur almost everywhere. Weighting terms by
how frequently they occur in a document (term frequency, TF) and how rare they are
across the collection (IDF) yields the TF-IDF family of weighting schemes, still one of
the most widely deployed representations in production search systems.
Term frequency counts how often a term 𝑡occurs in a document 𝑑:

TF(𝑡, 𝑑) =

where 𝑓𝑡,𝑑is the raw count of 𝑡in 𝑑. Inverse document frequency, following Sp¨arck Jones
\[1972\], down-weights terms that occur in many documents:

IDF(𝑡, 𝐷) = log

(12.2)

where 𝐷is the document collection. Combining the two gives the classic TF-IDF
weight of term 𝑡in document 𝑑:

TF-IDF(𝑡, 𝑑, 𝐷) = TF(𝑡, 𝑑) × IDF(𝑡, 𝐷)
(12.3)

12.1.2
Vector Space Models

Salton et al. \[1975\] formalized this idea into the vector space model, representing every
document and query as a vector in a high-dimensional term space and ranking docu-
ments by their cosine similarity to the query vector. The vector space model established
a pattern that persists directly into today’s dense retrievers (Section 12.3): reduce doc-
uments and queries to points in a shared geometric space, and let distance or similarity
stand in for relevance.
More formally, in the vector space model, each document 𝑑(and query 𝑞) is repre-
sented as a vector of term weights, ®𝑑= (𝑤1,𝑑, 𝑤2,𝑑, . . . , 𝑤𝑛,𝑑), typically using TF-IDF
weights (Eq. 12.3). Relevance is then approximated by the cosine similarity between
query and document vectors:

sim( ®𝑞, ®𝑑) = cos(𝜃) =

(12.4)

Documents are ranked by decreasing sim( ®𝑞, ®𝑑). This same operation, cosine simi-
larity between two learned vectors, reappears in dense retrieval (Section 12.3), the
only difference being how the vectors are obtained. Where the vector space model
used raw term co-occurrence, modern dense retrievers such as dense passage retrieval
(DPR) \[Karpukhin et al., 2020\] use learned neural embeddings, but the underlying ge-
ometric intuition is unchanged.

Two further developments bridge classical and modern retrieval. First, Robertson and
Zaragoza \[2009\] developed the probabilistic relevance framework, which treats re-
trieval as a problem of estimating the probability that a document is relevant to a query
given its term statistics. This framework produced BM25 Robertson et al. \[1994\], a
term-weighting and ranking function which ranks document 𝑑for query 𝑞as:

BM25 remains the sparse-retrieval baseline referenced throughout the hybrid retrieval

problem that motivates dense and semantic retrieval today.

𝑘
(12.6)

retains only the 𝑘largest singular values in Σ𝑘, producing a rank-𝑘approximation of 𝑋.
Documents and terms are then represented in this reduced 𝑘-dimensional latent space,
where semantically related terms and documents lie close together even without exact
term overlap.
The final bridge from classical IR to the neural retrieval methods used through-
out this chapter is the emergence of learned, dense vector representations of words.
Mikolov et al. \[2013\] showed that simple neural network architectures, trained to pre-
dict a word from its context, produce continuous word embeddings that capture rich
syntactic and semantic regularities. This work, together with the encoder architectures
that followed, supplied the representational building blocks on which dense retrieval,
DPR-style bi-encoders, and ultimately retrieval-augmented generation are built.
Retrieval, in other words, is a decades-old discipline concerned with a single endur-
ing question: given a query, which pieces of a large collection are actually relevant to
it? What has changed with the arrival of LLMs is not the question but the stakes: mod-
els now consult retrieved evidence not merely to rank documents for a human reader,
but to condition their own generation. We will now discuss why that shift matters.

## Page 244

244
CHAPTER 12. SEARCH AND RETRIEVAL IN AGENTIC LLMS

12.2
Why Retrieval Matters for Agentic LLMs

Building on this foundation, large language models introduce a new reason to care
about retrieval. LLMs are frozen snapshots of world knowledge. The LLM’s parame-
ters can not contain information that was generated after the corpus was fixed. LLMs
struggle when tasks require timely, proprietary, or long–tail information that was absent
at pretraining time. Retrieval augmentation mitigates these limits by consulting exter-
nal sources at inference time and conditioning generation on the retrieved evidence.
Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) methods have been developed to integrate
data from external knowledge bases with the pretrained knowledge stored in the pa-
rameters of language models. Most RAG approaches work at inference time, although
some can work during finetuning or even pretraining. Most RAG approaches work on
unstructured (textual) data sources. These text documents are indexed to increase effi-
cient access, and they can be organized and a knowledge graph can be created. Finally,
database-type query optimization is often performed, where queries can be expanded
or complex queries can be split into sub-queries \[Cong et al., 2024\].
This simple idea, popularized by early systems such as REALM \[Guu et al., 2020\],
DPR \[Karpukhin et al., 2020\], and RAG \[Lewis et al., 2020\], has grown into a rich
design space spanning indexing, query planning, re-ranking, citation and attribution,
and continuous data refresh. Recent surveys synthesize the landscape and evaluation
practices \[Gao et al., 2023b, Huang et al., 2024, Yu et al., 2024, Sharma et al., 2025,
Peng et al., 2024\].

When to retrieve.
Retrieval is most beneficial when: (1) the task is knowledge-
intensive (definitions, entities, numbers, references), (2) the domain shifts rapidly (news,
prices, docs), (3) transparency is required (with citations), or (4) models must respect
strict source-of-truth constraints (compliance portals, internal wikis). In agentic set-
tings, retrieval can be interleaved with tool use and planning (see Chapter 11).

12.3
Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipeline

A practical RAG system typically implements the following seven stages:

1. Indexing: The indexing phase is the first step. This step involves: Taking all raw
source material, such as HTML pages, PDFs, tables, or code, and converting
it into clean, consistent text. Keep important structure as metadata (headings,
anchors, timestamps, authorship). Break content into chunks with meaningful
boundaries (e.g., sentences or sections) and small overlaps so context isn’t lost.
Create two types of searchable representations: sparse ones, like BM25 (a classic
term-matching method) or SPLADE \[Formal et al., 2021\] (a more modern vari-
ant that expands terms), which are good for exact keyword matches; and dense
ones, which are embeddings that capture meaning for semantic matches. Storing
both lets the system find exact matches (IDs, numbers) and semantic matches
(paraphrases, synonyms) in the same search.

## Page 245

12.3. RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION PIPELINE
245

2. Query Construction: Turn the user’s question into one or more precise search
queries. This can involve rewriting the question for clarity, breaking complex
questions into sub-questions (multi-hop), adding related terms (query expan-
sion), or even generating a hypothetical answer to use as a search target (HyDE)
\[Gao et al., 2023a\]. For structured data sources, generate specific queries such as
SQL or graph lookups. The aim is to make the search engine understand exactly
what to look for.

3. Candidate Retrieval: Use the constructed queries to pull in potentially relevant
chunks from the index. Dense retrievers (e.g., DPR \[Karpukhin et al., 2020\],
Contriever \[Izacard et al., 2022\]) match by meaning; sparse methods (BM25,
SPLADE) match by exact terms; hybrids combine both. To search quickly at
scale, use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes like HNSW \[Malkov
and Yashunin, 2020\] or IVF-PQ \[J´egou et al., 2011\]. For code or images, use
specialized encoders. This step is about casting a wide net without losing focus.

4. Re-ranking: Take the pool of retrieved candidates and reorder them by relevance
using more accurate but slower models, like cross-encoders (BERT, MiniLM).
Late-interaction models such as ColBERTv2 \[Santhanam et al., 2022\] balance
quality and speed. This ensures that top results are the ones most likely to answer
the question.

5. Context Assembly: Remove duplicates, ensure coverage of different aspects of
the query (diversity), and prefer recent or domain-relevant sources. Bundle the
selected passages, along with their metadata (source, URL, date), into a con-
text package to feed into the LLM. This gives the model a curated, trustworthy
information set.

6. Grounded Generation: Ask the LLM to generate the answer using the provided
context, with citations for each claim. If evidence is insufficient, the model
should abstain or ask for clarification. Some systems, such as Self-RAG \[Asai
et al., 2023\], decide on the fly whether to retrieve more information. The focus
is on answers that are both correct and well-supported.

7. Attribution and Logging: Show the sources alongside the answer so readers can
verify claims. Log the entire process including queries, retrieved documents and
versions, for debugging, evaluation, and compliance. This makes the system
transparent and auditable.

A straightforward RAG system follows the seven-step pipeline outlined above. List-
ing 12.1 shows Python-style pseudo-code for this process. The function takes a user
question, rewrites it into one or more search queries, retrieves and re-ranks candidate
passages, assembles a context window and finally generates an answer while tracking
which passages were used. We will go into more details below.

## Page 246

246
CHAPTER 12. SEARCH AND RETRIEVAL IN AGENTIC LLMS

1
# Input: question q, search index, and number of passages k

2
def rag_answer(q, index, k=8):

3
# 1. Construct search queries (possibly decompose multi-hop questions)

4
queries = rewrite_question(q)

5
# 2. Retrieve candidate passages from the index

6
candidates = retrieve(index, queries, k=200)

7
# 3. Re-rank with a cross-encoder or late-interaction model

8
ranked = rerank(candidates)

9
# 4. Assemble a context window from the top-k passages

10
context = assemble(ranked\[:k\])

11
# 5. Generate an answer conditioned on the context and provide citations

12
answer, citations = generate_answer(q, context)

13
return answer, citations

Listing 12.1: High Level Flow of a Basic RAG Setup

12.4
Adaptive Retrieval Methods

Traditional RAG systems retrieve a fixed number of passages regardless of whether
any retrieval is actually needed. This always–on strategy simplifies engineering but can
hurt both efficiency and accuracy. Recent research explores adaptive or gated retrieval
strategies that teach the model to decide when to search and how much evidence to
consult. These methods align with the self-reflection ideas introduced in Section 6.2.4:
rather than blindly ingest retrieved text, the language model introspects about its own
confidence and triggers retrieval only when it recognizes a knowledge gap.
Concretely, Asai et al. \[2023\] propose Self-RAG, which trains a single model to
generate answers, request retrieval, and critique its own outputs using special reflection
tokens. When the model’s draft answer is uncertain, it emits a <RETRIEVE> token
to call the search tool and incorporates the retrieved passages in the next step. Experi-
ments show that this learned gating improves factuality over static RAG while avoiding
unnecessary calls.
A more lightweight approach is Self-Ask \[Press et al., 2022\], where the model
decomposes a complex question into simpler sub-questions, issues them to a search
tool, and uses the answers to compose a final response. Self-Ask can be combined
with planning agents, enabling models to interleave reasoning, tool calls, and retrieval.
Graph Toolformer \[Zhang, 2023\] extends this idea by training a policy to insert search
queries into a program graph. At inference time the LLM dynamically decides whether
to retrieve from a text index, a knowledge graph, or a database, based on the current
state of reasoning.
Beyond these specific examples, adaptive retrieval can be implemented in several
ways:

• Confidence-based Gating: The model estimates its uncertainty (e.g., from en-
tropy or calibration metrics) and triggers retrieval when confidence falls below a
threshold.

• Iterative Retrieval: Rather than pulling all evidence at once, the system retrieves
a few passages, reasons about them, and then decides whether additional rounds

## Page 247

12.4. ADAPTIVE RETRIEVAL METHODS
247

of search are needed. This approach is useful for multi-hop questions.

• Query Planning: An agent decomposes the user query into sub-tasks, dispatches
them to different tools (search, database, calculator), and integrates the results.
Retrievers are called only when the plan requires external knowledge.

• Learning to Retrieve: Reinforcement learning or supervised finetuning can teach
the model to emit <RETRIEVE> tokens at appropriate times. Self-RAG is one
instantiation; other methods explore training retrieval policies end-to-end with
the generator.

Adaptive retrieval reduces latency and cost by avoiding unnecessary searches, and it
often improves answer quality by focusing attention on missing knowledge. Designing
effective gating policies, however, requires careful evaluation (see Section 12.7) and
may demand additional supervision during training.

12.4.1
Adaptive Retrieval via Self-RAG and Self-Ask

The Self-RAG framework of Asai et al. \[2023\] teaches the model to request retrieval
on demand by emitting a special <RETRIEVE> token during generation. The pseudo-
code in Listing 12.2 sketches how such a loop operates. The model maintains a growing
context and alternates between generating output tokens and pulling in new evidence
when needed.

1
# Input: question q, search index, and trained Self-RAG model

2
def self_rag_answer(q, index, model):

3
context = \[\]

4
output_tokens = \[\]

5
# Generate tokens sequentially

6
for token in model.generate_stream(q, context):

7
if token == "<RETRIEVE>":

8
# Model requests more information

9
new_docs = retrieve(index, rewrite_question(q), k=5)

10
context.extend(new_docs)

11
else:

12
output_tokens.append(token)

13
if token == "<END>":

14
break

15
return detokenize(output_tokens)

Listing 12.2: High Level Pseudo-Code Demonstrating Self-RAG

It should be noted that for Self-RAG to work, the foundation model should be
trained or fine-tuned to produce the <RETRIEVE> token. Self-Ask \[Press et al., 2022\]
on the other hand is not dependent on the language model. Self-Ask decomposes a
complex question into simpler sub-questions, retrieves evidence for each and synthe-
sizes the final answer. The following high-level pseudo-code shows one way to imple-
ment this strategy:

12.4.3
Query Rewriting and Expansion

Effective retrieval often starts with transforming the original question into a form that
the index can match. Large language models can act as query re-writers by paraphras-
ing, expanding acronyms, adding synonyms or even producing a hypothetical answer

## Page 249

12.5. GRAPHS, CODE, TABULAR DATA
249

to use as a pseudo-query (the HyDE technique).1 Listing 12.5 sketches a simple func-
tion that calls an LLM to produce multiple rewrites and expansions and then merges
the results into a set of search queries.

1
def rewrite_question(q, n_variants=3):

2
"""

3
Use an LLM to generate alternative phrasings and hypothetical answers.

4

5
:param q: The user question.

6
:param n_variants: Number of rewrites to generate.

7
:return: A list of expanded queries.

8
"""

9
variants = \[q\]

10
# Ask the model for paraphrases and clarifications

11
paraphrases = llm.generate(\["Rewrite: " + q\] * n_variants)

12
variants.extend(paraphrases)

13
# Ask the model to guess an answer (HyDE) and use it as a pseudo-query

14
guess = llm.generate(\["Answer briefly: " + q\])\[0\]

15
variants.append(guess)

16
# Optionally add entity aliases from a knowledge base

17
aliases = lookup_aliases(q)

18
variants.extend(aliases)

19
return variants

Listing 12.5: A Simple Example of Query Rewriting

In practice, the rewrite question function might call an API such as Ope-
nAI’s gpt-5 to generate paraphrases and hypothetical answers, then use a thesaurus
or entity-linking tool to add aliases. Query expansion improves recall but can also
introduce noise.

12.5
Beyond Text: Graphs, Code, Tabular Data and
Multi-Modal

While most RAG systems operate over unstructured text, many agentic applications
require reasoning over structured data, source code, or images. Extending retrieval
beyond plain text opens up new opportunities but also introduces modeling challenges.

Graph-RAG
A knowledge graph encodes entities as nodes and relations as edges.
Building a lightweight graph over the corpus allows the retriever to follow links (e.g.,
works for, located in) rather than relying solely on bag-of-words similarity. The GraphRAG
survey formalizes a three-step workflow: graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval,
and graph-enhanced generation \[Peng et al., 2024\]. Indexing extracts entities and rela-
tions from text, canonicalizes them and builds neighborhood structures. Retrieval then
expands the query through the graph to find related nodes and associated passages; this

1HyDE stands for Hypothetical Document Embeddings and generates a plausible answer which is then
embedded and used to retrieve supporting passages \[Gao et al., 2023a\].

## Page 250

250
CHAPTER 12. SEARCH AND RETRIEVAL IN AGENTIC LLMS

supports global reasoning and disambiguation. Finally, the generation model can use
the graph structure to organize facts into a coherent narrative and avoid contradictions.

12.5.1
Graph-based retrieval example

GraphRAG systems represent knowledge as a graph of entities and relations and use
graph traversals to retrieve relevant nodes \[Peng et al., 2024\]. A lightweight imple-
mentation can be built with the networkx library. In the example in Listing 12.6 we
construct a small knowledge graph and implement two simple retrieval primitives: (1)
get the immediate neighborhood of an entity, and (2) find the shortest path between two
entities. These operations can support multi-hop reasoning.

1

2

3
def build_knowledge_graph():

4

5

6

7
G.add_node("Nobel Prize", type="award")

8
G.add_node("Physics", type="field")

9
G.add_node("1921", type="year")

10
# Add edges representing relations

11
G.add_edge("Albert Einstein", "Nobel Prize", relation="received")

12
G.add_edge("Nobel Prize", "Physics", relation="category")

13
G.add_edge("Nobel Prize", "1921", relation="year")

14
return G

15

16
def neighbours(G, entity):

17
"""Return all outgoing neighbours of an entity."""

18
return list(G.successors(entity))

19

20
def shortest_path(G, source, target):

21
"""Return the sequence of entities on the shortest path."""

22
try:

23
return nx.shortest_path(G, source, target)

24
except nx.NetworkXNoPath:

25

26

27
# Example usage

29

30

31

Listing 12.6: An Example of Graph-based Retrieval Primitives in Python

In a full GraphRAG system the graph nodes would store pointers to the original text
passages, and the retrieval procedure would return both the sequence of nodes and the
associated passages to the LLM. Graph-guided retrieval can reduce hallucinations by
grounding reasoning in explicit edges and by encouraging consistency between related
facts.

## Page 251

12.5. GRAPHS, CODE, TABULAR DATA
251

Code-RAG
Source code has a rich syntax-structure. The semantics of source code
differs from natural language. For code retrieval to be effective, it should index at the
function or module level, including signatures, docstrings, abstract syntax trees (ASTs)
and dependency graphs. Models such as CodeBERT \[Feng et al., 2020\] learn joint
embeddings for code and natural language; they support tasks like natural-language
code search, code summarization, and documentation generation. In Code-RAG, the
retriever can fetch relevant functions, APIs and test cases, and the re-ranker can use
code-aware cross-encoders or graph neural networks to prioritize exact matches. Re-
trieved code snippets, comments and dependency metadata are then provided to the
LLM, which can answer questions, suggest fixes, or generate new code while citing
the source files. Evaluation should consider correctness of the code, type safety and
adherence to dependencies.

12.5.2
Code retrieval example using ASTs and embeddings

Retrieving source code requires understanding its syntax and semantics. An easy ap-
proach is to embed code snippets and natural language queries with a pretrained model
such as CodeBERT \[Feng et al., 2020\]. Another complementary approach is to parse
the code into an abstract syntax tree (AST) and search its structure. The example in
Listing 12.7 demonstrates both: we embed functions with CodeBERT for semantic
search and use Python’s ast module to extract function definitions and docstrings for
indexing.
This example indexes the functions in an imported module and performs a cosine
similarity search between the query and the encoded source code. In practice one might
combine code embeddings with lexical features (identifiers, comments) and incorpo-
rate AST-based matching to handle structural queries (e.g., find all functions that call
a specific API). Code-aware retrieval is essential for agentic systems that need to read,
execute or modify existing code during tool use.

12.5.3
Multi-modal and heterogeneous sources

Tabular and other heterogeneous documents
Existing RAG approaches face criti-
cal limitations when applied to heterogeneous documents, comprising both textual and
tabular components \[Yu et al., 2025\]. A primary challenge is Structural Information
Loss. When tabular data is linearized or chunked for text-based RAG, its inherent rela-
tional structure, the interdependence of rows and columns, is compromised. This loss
of structure impedes the LLM’s ability to perform accurate multi-hop heterogeneous
reasoning. This indicates that merely converting non-textual data to text is insufficient.
To address these challenges, hybrid frameworks such as TableRAG \[Yu et al., 2025\]
have been proposed, that unify textual understanding and complex manipulations over
tabular data.
TableRAG employs SQL programming and execution to treat table-related queries
as indivisible reasoning units, thereby enhancing both computational efficiency and
reasoning fidelity. Similarly, MixRAG \[Zhang et al., 2025\] has been shown to signif-
icantly improve retrieval performance for heterogeneous document RAG, which de-
mands joint retrieval and reasoning across textual and hierarchical tabular data.

Multi-modal RAG
Many knowledge bases contain tables, figures, diagrams, audio
and video. A straightforward approach is to extract any textual content using OCR
and treat the remainder as plain text. A richer approach stores embeddings for images
or other modalities (e.g., CLIP or ViT representations) and pairs them with captions
and context. Queries can be encoded jointly across modalities, allowing the system to

agent might retrieve a plot and its caption to answer a data-analysis question, or an
educational agent might fetch diagrams from a textbook.
Multi-modal RAG remains an active research area. Challenges include cross-modal
alignment and efficient indexing of high-dimensional embeddings. Furthermore, non-textual
evidence should be properly grounded in the generated answer.

12.6
Agentic RAG: Beyond Simple Retrieval

While traditional RAG systems augment LLMs with external knowledge, they are often
passive, relying on a static, pre-defined pipeline. A significant and recent advancement
is the concept of Agentic RAG, which integrates autonomous AI agents directly into
the retrieval-augmented generation pipeline \[Singh et al., 2025\]. This paradigm shift
moves RAG from a mere tool to an active, intelligent, and agent-driven process. Agen-
tic RAG systems are characterized by their ability to dynamically manage retrieval
strategies, iteratively refine contextual understanding, and adapt workflows to meet
complex task requirements.
Agentic RAG represents a more sophisticated form of a retrieval loop, where the
LLM agent itself is responsible for orchestrating the retrieval process. This differs from
simpler RAG methods by embracing a continuous feedback loop that is fundamental
to advanced agentic systems. Rather than a single-shot query transformation, the agent
can actively refine its queries based on intermediate results and ongoing interaction.
This approach addresses the limitations of conventional RAG systems, which are of-
ten constrained by static workflows and lack the adaptability required for multistep
reasoning and complex task management \[Singh et al., 2025\].

12.6.1
Key Components of Agentic RAG

Agentic RAG frameworks typically incorporate several key components that enable
their dynamic behavior:

• Dynamic Query Generation: The agent formulates queries based on its current
understanding of the task and the retrieved context, allowing for more precise
and effective searches. This can include query expansion, decomposition, or
rewriting in response to initial retrieval failures.

• Iterative Refinement: The agent evaluates the quality of the retrieved informa-
tion and, if necessary, initiates a new retrieval cycle with a refined query. This
iterative process ensures that the final response is grounded in the most relevant
and accurate information.

• Autonomous Tool Use: The agent can select and use a variety of tools, includ-
ing different retrieval models (e.g., dense vs. sparse), ranking algorithms, and
external APIs, to optimize its retrieval strategy. See Chapter 11 for additional
information on how an agent can use tools.

• Self-Correction and Reflection: The agent can assess its own output for accuracy
and completeness. If it detects a hallucination or an unsupported claim, it can
trigger a new retrieval and reasoning process to correct the error.

The rise of Agentic RAG indicates a shift in the role of RAG in LLM systems. Retrieval
shifts from a passive data lookup to an active, intelligent capability that is integral to the
agent’s cognitive functions, allowing for more sophisticated, adaptive interactions with
external knowledge sources. This shift is crucial for developing robust and reliable
LLM agents capable of handling complex, real-world tasks.

## Page 255

12.7. EVALUATION
255

12.6.2
Real-Time and Streaming RAG

While traditional RAG systems are effective for static data, they are often not designed
for applications that require continuous, real-time information. This section looks into
the architectural considerations and challenges of RAG systems that operate on contin-
uously updating, high-throughput data streams. Examples of such streams are found
in news feeds, social media, or financial markets. For streaming data, simply query-
ing an updated static index no longer suffices. Retrieval now involves dynamic index
management and continuous knowledge assimilation.
In traditional RAG systems, designed for static data, preprocessing is slow, and
unsuitable for real-time analysis \[Zhu, 2025, Sankaradas et al., 2025\]. How should
we maintain data freshness and semantic coverage under memory budgets and high
data ingestion rates? Methods such as StreamingRAG \[Sankaradas et al., 2025\] try to
overcome these issues with knowledge graphs that evolve dynamically in real-time.
LLM agents for dynamic domains such as medicine, logistics and finance, must
have access to real-time, continuously updated information. Static RAG would yield
obsolete or inaccurate information in such fast-changing environments. In many agen-
tic applications real-time RAG is necessary for advanced, timely, and reliable informa-
tion.

12.7
Evaluation

Evaluating a retrieval-augmented system is more difficult than evaluating a stand-alone
language model because both the retriever and the generator contribute to the final
answer. Good evaluation should separate these components and also judge their joint
behavior.

Retrieval metrics
For a given query, we compare the retrieved passages to a set of
gold documents. Standard metrics include:

1. recall@k (Eq. 12.7) and precision@k (Eq. 12.8), the fraction of relevant docu-
ments retrieved among the top 𝑘

2. mean reciprocal rank (Eq. 12.9) and mean average precision, which capture
ranking quality

3. normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) (Eq. 12.10), which weights
higher ranks more heavily

BEIR presents a heterogeneous benchmark of 18 datasets covering tasks like question
answering, fact checking and entity retrieval; their experiments show that late-interaction
and re-ranking models improve zero-shot performance but at increased cost \[Thakur
et al., 2021\].
KILT evaluates knowledge-intensive tasks under a unified Wikipedia snapshot and
measures both task performance and provenance, encouraging models to cite the pas-
sages they used \[Petroni et al., 2021\].

Generation metrics
Once context is assembled, we must assess the quality of the
generated answer. Automatic metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore are of
limited use because there is often no single ground-truth answer. More appropriate
are faithfulness and helpfulness. Faithfulness is often measured via entailment mod-
els. It works as follows for generated output 𝑦and retrieved context 𝑥(Eq. 12.11):
check whether every claim is supported by the cited passages, for example via natural
language inference models or quote checking.

Faithfulness = # outputs entailed by context

Helpfulness (or utility) indicates whether the answer satisfies the user’s information
need. To measure this, often human evaluation or specialized LLM-based evaluators
are needed. In interactive settings latency and cost are also important.
Helpfulness is based on human or model scoring:
