where score is a Likert-scale or pairwise preference judgment.

Joint evaluation and new metrics
A key challenge is to evaluate retrieval and gen-
eration separately. For example, a system may retrieve irrelevant documents but still
guess the right answer, or retrieve perfect evidence but fail to use it. Recent work
therefore proposes unified evaluation frameworks. The Auepora process recommends
reporting separate retrieval and generation scores and then to combine them into a
holistic measure \[Yu et al., 2024\]. RAGAS and similar toolkits provide automated

## Page 257

12.8. CONCLUDING REMARKS
257

pipelines that compute context recall, answer correctness, and citation accuracy using
small models. When we evaluate adaptive methods (Section 12.4), we also need to
measure the trigger decisions: how often does the model retrieve when it should, and
how often does it skip retrieval unnecessarily?

Attribution and freshness
In many applications the model must cite its sources and
avoid outdated information. Claims can be aligned with evidence by attribution tests.
Such tests use natural language inference and ensure URL–answer consistency. Fresh-
ness metrics measure whether the answer reflects the most recent valid sources. This
metric can also quantify version drift.
Attribution and freshness are especially important for time-sensitive domains like
finance or medicine.
A good system design is based on careful evaluation. When we find high retrieval
recall but low faithfulness, then better re-ranking is needed. Similarly, high faithful-
ness but poor helpfulness may indicate insufficient context coverage. To support error
analysis and auditing, evaluations should be accompanied by transparent logging of
queries, retrieved passages and model outputs.

12.8
Concluding Remarks

Retrieval is an essential element of any agentic LLM system that needs to provide up-
to-date information. Large language models are static snapshots of knowledge; RAG
helps them stay up to date, transparent and grounded. Effective RAG requires careful
engineering across indexing, query planning, retrieval, re-ranking, context assembly
and grounded generation, along with adaptive techniques that let the model decide
when and how to search. We have also seen how retrieval can be extended beyond
plain text to graphs, code and multimodal assets. For building trustworthy systems,
rigorous evaluation is essential.

Operational considerations
In production systems the retriever is a living service,
not a one-off script, and it should be maintained carefully. Crawlers, webhooks and
document pipelines should continuously ingest new data. Be careful to track versions
and deprecations, and maintain per-entity timelines to prefer recent facts. Your system
should apply access control lists at retrieval time and redact personally identifiable
information during indexing. Latency and cost matter: cache embeddings and top-
𝑘results, reuse retrieval across conversational turns, compress context with extractive
summarization, tune 𝑘and chunk sizes per domain, and re-rank only the top candidates.

Practical suggestions
When you create a RAG system, start with a hybrid approach:
combine a strong dense retriever with BM25 or SPLADE and re-rank the top hundred
hits with a cross-encoder before sending six to twelve passages to the LLM. Be careful
to chunk your corpus thoughtfully, for example using 300–500 token windows with
10–15 % overlap and preserved headings and tables, also attach timestamps or other
metadata. For query writing, craft your queries carefully. Rewrite complex questions,

## Page 258

258
BIBLIOGRAPHY

decompose multi-hop queries, expand entity aliases and enforce domain filters. For
transparency, always require citations. If, however, the evidence is weak, ask follow-up
questions, or else abstain.
Finally, use evidence-based system design, measure what you build. You should
track retrieval recall, groundedness, timeliness and cost. A further suggestion is to
experiment with re-rankers. For debugging, you should log system traces.

Integration into agentic AI
Retrieval is an integral element of agentic LLMs, it is
used in planning, self-reflection, and while acting in the real world (see Chapter 13).
Agentic pipelines can call the retriever dynamically based on the model’s confidence
or plan, as in Self-RAG and Graph Toolformer. They can query different data sources
such as text, graphs, code and images, and leverage the strengths of each. The line
between the model and its memory therefore blurs: RAG becomes part of the agent’s
cognitive loop.

Further Reading
For in-depth exploration, consult the surveys on RAG, evaluation
and graph-based methods \[Gao et al., 2023b, Huang et al., 2024, Yu et al., 2024, Sharma
et al., 2025, Peng et al., 2024\]. Foundational works include REALM, DPR and the orig-
inal RAG formulation \[Guu et al., 2020, Karpukhin et al., 2020, Lewis et al., 2020\].
The GraphRAG, evaluation and agentic RAG communities are evolving rapidly; fol-
lowing their latest papers and benchmarks is the best way to stay current.

Chapter 13

From Tools to Assistants:
Real-World Applications


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how agentic language models are deployed as prac-
tical assistants across real-world domains. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Describe how assistants go beyond question answering to plan, retrieve informa-
tion, invoke tools, and adapt their behavior over time.
• Compare assistant architectures across domains including shopping, medicine,
aviation, scientific research and coding .
• Explain why high-risk domains impose stricter requirements around safety,
transparency, and regulatory compliance and how agentic designs respond to
these demands.
• Critically evaluate assistant behavior and reflect on the ethical implications of
deploying agentic systems in socially consequential settings.

13.1
Agentic LLMs as Assistants

LLMs have moved from text generators to active assistants. They combine reasoning,
retrieval, and tool use to perform actions in the real world. Assistants are the practical
(software) form of agentic LLMs: systems that interact, plan, and learn from feed-
back. Assistants are where reasoning meets reality: they turn language models into
collaborative actors in the world.
An assistant links perception, reasoning, and action. Through APIs and external
tools, it can converse, execute tasks, and adapt to a specific context. These systems not
only support users but also create valuable human-AI interaction data that we can then
use for further developments and training the next generation of models.
This chapter reviews the main types of assistants. We start with conversational
systems and their evolution toward multi-modal, tool-aware interfaces. Next, we dis-

263

## Page 264

264
CHAPTER 13. FROM TOOLS TO ASSISTANTS

Figure 13.1: AssistGPT system architecture \[Neszl´enyi et al., 2024\]

cuss domain-specific assistants in medicine, finance, and trading. Finally, we look at
scientific assistants for reasoning and discovery.

13.2
Conversational Assistants

The first application domain is in general conversational situations, such as helping
with meetings by taking meeting minutes, acting as meeting chair or general adminis-
trative assistant.
In this type of application, the LLM basically serves to make the interaction be-
tween human and computer more natural and streamlined \[Neszl´enyi et al., 2024,
Oluwagbade, 2024\]. For example, the AssistantGPT system \[Neszl´enyi et al., 2024\]
is a general purpose administrative assistant, designed for deployment in an educa-
tional or corporate setting. Furthermore, it supports remote work environments such as
Teams and Slack. AssistantGPT supports a diverse range of operations, including web
searches, API interactions via OpenAPI, voice conversations, and command execution
through the shell. The system consists of an LLM with access to various tools such as
a planner, and memory (see Figure 13.1).
These conversation and meeting assistants have been shown to improve agile soft-
ware development team meetings \[Cabrero-Daniel et al., 2024\]. They created favor-
able results for preparation and live assistance during Scrum meetings, although some
testers remarked that LLM interventions felt unnatural and inflexible.
Other examples include LLM agents in a collaborative learning classroom setting
where the LLM agents improved overall collaboration between participants \[Wei et al.,
2024b\]. Another study \[Bastola et al., 2023\] reports improved work efficiency in a
collaborative task scheduling experiment including conversational assistants.
A slightly different type of assistant is the thinking assistant. This assistant tries

## Page 265

13.3. SHOPPING ASSISTANT
265

to improve human reflective thinking for difficult decisions, by asking instead of an-
swering \[Park and Kulkarni, 2023\]. Similar initiatives have recently appeared from the
large LLM vendors, such as Study mode in OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini
applications.
Conversational assistants have mostly evolved from regular pretrained LLMs, some-
times finetuned for a particular domain. Some approaches use a specialized multi-
LLMs approach, specializing LLMs for different sub-tasks, or orchestrating a single
LLM with different prompt sequences focusing on different sub-tasks.

13.3
Shopping Assistant

In this section we examine how language-based assistants can be applied in the e-
commerce domain. Our goal is to highlight the principal components, architectural
choices and domain-specific challenges in this domain.

What does a shopping assistant do?
A shopping assistant is a conversational sys-
tem built on an LLM that helps users navigate online shopping tasks. It can help in
understanding product needs, comparing alternatives, recommending items and com-
pleting purchases. Such a system typically complements the underlying LLM with
domain-specific modules, including retrieval of up-to-date product information, API
access to product-catalogs, integration with recommender engines and reasoning (e.g.,
via chain of thought) over user requirements, attributes and constraints.

Key ingredients
Because general-purpose LLMs lack built-in awareness of e-commerce
concepts (brands, categories, product hierarchies, user purchase behavior), building a
capable assistant requires several augmentations:

• Retrieval Augmentation: dynamically fetch product metadata, pricing, availabil-
ity from external sources.

• Tool / API Invocation: the assistant may call search, filter, ranking tools to inter-
act with product databases.

• Domain Finetuning or Instruction Tuning: adapt the LLM to the shopping con-
text (branded language, attribute reasoning, user intents).

• Structured Reasoning: add chain of thought prompting or explicit reasoning
steps. This helps the model compare products, evaluate trade-offs (e.g., price
vs features) and align with user preferences.

Benchmarking shopping-assistants
To study how well models cope with shopping-
specific tasks, researchers have developed benchmarks. For example, the Multi-task
Online Shopping Benchmark dataset (ShopMMLU) \[Jin et al., 2024\] defines 57 tasks
grouped into four skills: concept understanding, knowledge reasoning, user-behavior
alignment and multi-linguality.
It draws on real-world e-commerce data (Amazon
product catalogs, sessions and reviews) and evaluates how well an LLM can handle

## Page 266

266
CHAPTER 13. FROM TOOLS TO ASSISTANTS

aspects like brand-model recognition, reasoning about product compatibility, session-
based recommendation tasks, and multilingual queries. Another example is the LLaSA
system (large language and E-commerce shopping assistant) \[Zhang et al., 2024a\]
which is trained via an instruction dataset (65,000 samples) dubbed EshopInstruct. Af-
ter instruction-tuning on shopping tasks, LLaSA competes on the ShopBench bench-
mark and achieves strong results, showing that adaptation significantly improves per-
formance in this domain.

Practical Recommendations
The following principles are important for building
shopping assistants:

• A capable assistant merges natural-language understanding and domain reason-
ing. It should know what noise-canceling headphones under 200 euro with ¿
20 h battery means, and be able to translate this into product attributes and user
constraints.

• Domain-specific data matters: off-the-shelf LLMs work to some degree, but fine-
tuning or instruction-tuning on shopping tasks significantly lifts performance.
LLaSA \[Zhang et al., 2024a\] shows this in practice.

• Evaluation must reflect the domain. Accuracy in understanding product attributes
or generating queries is less relevant than whether the assistant can align with
user behavior, handle multi-step sessions and support multilingual users.

• Tool and retrieval integration is important. The assistant must act as an interface
to product systems, not just as a pure language model. This introduces additional
complexity (API design, latency, freshness of data and handling integration er-
rors).

• Consider ethics and trust. In shopping, recommendations carry commercial, pri-
vacy and bias implications. These issues should be assessed before deploying
such a system in production, through questions such as: which brands are shown,
is user history handled correctly, and how transparent is the reasoning.

Challenges and open questions
Even with recent progress, shopping assistants face
several non-trivial challenges. First, handling long interaction trajectories (browsing,
refining queries, switching intents) is still difficult for LLM agents. Second, updating
product knowledge in real-time (new models, price changes, availability) remains a
major engineering pain-point. Third, explaining and justifying recommendations to
users (why this product vs another) is under-explored in LLM-based assistants. Finally,
cross-lingual behavior and multilingual product queries increase complexity (shopping
contexts span languages and regions).

13.4
Flight Operations Assistant

Language-based assistants are also applied in aviation operations, a domain that ex-
tends beyond consumer booking and moves into planning and decision support.

## Page 267

13.4. FLIGHT OPERATIONS ASSISTANT
267

Booking and travel-planning
One of the simpler applications is a conversational
booking assistant, similar to the shopping assistants in the previous section. For exam-
ple, Manasa et al. \[2024\] present a system built on LLaMa 2 with RAG to interactively
help users book flights. The assistant is fine-tuned on flight-booking data, and con-
nects to current flight information via retrieval. User testing achieved strong marks for
capturing user preferences and guiding the booking process efficiently.
Notice how this use-case remains relatively shallow in operational complexity. The
assistant deals with structured user intents (I want to fly from A to B on date D), retrieval
of up-to-date product data, preference elicitation and generation of responses. It does
not (yet) deeply engage with, say, dynamic air-traffic constraints or safety margins.

Operational decision support
Moving to more demanding settings, LLM-based as-
sistants are being proposed for actual flight operations. We discuss two examples.
In a study by Zhou et al. \[2024\], the arrival-slot-allocation problem (i.e., deter-
mining in which sequence arriving aircraft should land) is formulated as a language
modeling task. The authors encode the scheduling inputs and outputs as tokens and
fine-tune an LLM to generate conflict-free landing sequences. Their experiments show
that the model can reduce conflict rate and total delay time even for airports where
traditional methods struggle.
Another operational problem is planning under environmental hazards. Tabrizian
et al. \[2024\] use chain of thought to support routing or flight plan generation under
wind-hazard constraints. Here, the assistant’s task is no longer simply book a flight
but it has to reason about constraints (wind, routing, aircraft performance) and propose
operationally feasible plans.

Key recommendations
These studies illustrate several important aspects of agentic
systems with LLMs:

• Tool/Backend Integration: in operational assistants, the LLM must not only con-
verse but also interface with flight-databases, weather feeds, routing engines
and slot-allocation systems. This means implementing tool invocation, retrieval
pipelines and decision logic.

• Reasoning under Constraints: these assistants must handle combinatorial or schedul-
ing constraints, generate plans, and deal with real-time uncertainties (such as
weather, runway availability). The arrival-slot example is a good example, where
the LLM must reason about dynamic sequencing.

• Domain-specific Data and Finetuning: the standard pretrained LLM lacks priors
about aviation operations. The systems above are finetuned or prompted specif-
ically for the domain. A dataset of domain-tasks, prompts, expected outputs are
evaluation metrics tailored to the domain are necessary.

• From Conversational Agent to Autonomous Planner: while booking assistants
remain user-driven (the user asks, the assistant helps), operational assistants in-
creasingly take on planning roles. The assistant should handle requests such as

## Page 268

268
CHAPTER 13. FROM TOOLS TO ASSISTANTS

here are constraints, propose a schedule or route. This change raises issues of
trust, verification and explainability.

• Evaluation in Real Contexts: the evaluation of operational systems often involves
more than does the assistant answer the user?, but also measure aspects such as
conflict rate, delay time, and sequence efficiency. For example, the arrival-slot
LLM study measured total delay and conflict rate.

13.5
Medical Assistant

Medicine is one of the most active application domains for LLM-based assistants
\[Thirunavukarasu et al., 2023, Clusmann et al., 2023, Mehandru et al., 2024\]. Recent
studies report that LLMs can outperform trained physicians on diagnostic tasks \[Goh
et al., 2024\] and exceed human medical scribes in clinical note generation \[Yuan et al.,
2024\]. Other evaluations confirm these strengths, while also identifying systematic
weaknesses in specific clinical scenarios \[Panagoulias et al., 2024\].
Agentic architectures are increasingly used to address regulatory, ethical, and us-
ability requirements. Sudarshan et al. \[2024\] present an agentic workflow for gener-
ating patient-friendly medical reports that comply with the 21st Century Cures Act.
Their system uses reflexion (Section 6.2.4, \[Shinn et al., 2024\]) to iteratively improve
clarity and correctness before information is released to patients.
Other studies explore the use of LLM agents for broader clinical support. Qiu
et al. \[2024\] identify applications ranging from clinical workflow automation to multi-
agent diagnostic support, although concerns remain regarding accuracy, completeness,
and hallucinations. A scoping review by Ullah et al. \[2024\] emphasizes that medical
domain knowledge and ethical constraints are essential when training and fine-tuning
such systems.
To mitigate common failure modes, Das et al. \[2024\] propose an agentic retrieval-
based architecture in which the LLM acts as a planner rather than a direct answer
generator. The agent coordinates specialized tools to retrieve and synthesize evidence
from trusted medical sources, reducing hallucinations and lost-in-the-middle errors.

High-risk application domain
Medicine is a high-risk application domain, where
incorrect or biased outputs can have direct consequences for patient safety. As a result,
medical AI systems are subject to strict regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI
Act, which classifies many medical uses of AI as high-risk. Transparency, fairness, and
accountability therefore play a central role, both in clinical practice and in academic
research on medical LLMs. These concerns motivate increased interest in methods that
go beyond post-hoc explanations and aim to understand model behavior at a deeper
level. We return to this topic in the chapter on mechanistic interpretability (Chapter
21), where techniques for analyzing and controlling internal model representations are
discussed.

Medical education
In medical education, agentic systems are used to simulate re-
alistic training environments. Wei et al. \[2024a\] introduce a multi-agent copilot that

## Page 269

13.6. TRADING ASSISTANT
269

Figure 13.2: Medical Education Copilot \[Wei et al., 2024a\]

supports case-based learning and clinical reasoning practice (Figure 13.2). For system-
atic evaluation of medical retrieval-augmented generation, a dedicated benchmark is
provided by Qiao et al. \[2024\].

13.6
Trading Assistant

A further specialized domain is financial trading. Already many (non-LLM) algorithms
are used in financial organizations for trading decisions. The interest in agentic LLMs
in the financial world is large \[Ding et al., 2024\].
InvestorBench is a benchmark for financial trading systems \[Li et al., 2024\]. FinA-
gent is a tool-augmented multimodal agent for financial trading \[Zhang et al., 2024b\].
It contains a market intelligence module, which is able to extract insights from multi-
modal datasets of asset prices, visual representations, news and expert analyses. The
system can also perform query retrieval and performs reflection in a low-level module
for technical analysis and in a high-level module to analyze past trading decisions.
FinRobot is an agentic LLM for financial analysis, to assist human traders. \[Yang
et al., 2024a\]. FinRobot can provide document analysis and generation and market
forecasts for individual stocks. FinMem is an agentic LLM framework devised for
financial decision-making \[Yu et al., 2024\]. It features a layered memory system and
adjustable character design for the trading agent. FinMem is inspired by the generative
agents framework by Park et al. \[2023\] (see Section 17.2.1 and Case Study 4).
So far, most financial market machine learning has focused on single agent systems.
An approach called TradingAgents uses a multi agent system to replicate real-world
trading firms’ collaborative dynamics \[Xiao et al., 2024\]. TradingAgents simulates
LLM-powered agents in specialized roles such as fundamental analysts, sentiment an-
alysts, technical analysts and traders with varied risk profiles. The outcome of the

## Page 270

270
CHAPTER 13. FROM TOOLS TO ASSISTANTS

system is a buy or sell advice to a human manager. A simulation showed that it outper-
formed baseline models.

Evaluation
Financial trading is a challenging field of research. The competitive in-
terests in financial trading are high, and there is a natural tendency to keep strong
research findings private, which creates a tension with the principles of openness and
transparency of scientific research.
Furthermore, despite the abundance of available numerical data in the field, there
are relatively few benchmarking studies that compare different agentic LLM approaches
on the same data. A recent benchmarking study found methodological flaws in some
financial LLM studies, such as selecting short evaluation periods with positive market
trends or leakage of test in training data \[Li et al., 2026\].

13.7
Automated Scientific Discovery

The workflow of scientific experimentation is relatively standardized in certain fields
of science. For example, in machine learning, (1) ideas are generated, (2) a hypothesis
is formulated, (3) an experiment is designed, (4) datasets are acquired, (5) experiments
are performed, (6) results are interpreted and (7) a report is produced. This standard
workflow has attracted researchers to experiment with agentic LLMs for performing
scientific research, see Eger et al. \[2025\] for a survey.
Google and OpenAI have both released Deep Research agents. These agents can
perform multi-step research tasks, such as synthesizing online information. They are
built with a reasoning LLM and use retrieval augmentation for finding information
sources. The systems are able to create scientific research papers that look impressive,
but are often not error-free.
AI Scientist \[Lu et al., 2024\] is a framework to automate the process of scientific
discovery, from idea generation to paper writing, including a review process. Users
must specify a topic and provide an experimentation template and indicate datasets.
The authors report experiments in three areas of machine learning: diffusion modeling,
transformer-based language modeling, and learning dynamics, with promising results.
To improve idea generation and reviewing, the agent accesses open sources. Current
limitations include limited experiments, incorrect implementation if ideas, and visual
errors when the paper is produced. On the other hand, rarely are entire results halluci-
nated. Nevertheless, results of the AI scientist are recommended to be taken as hints of
promising ideas, worthy of a follow up study \[Lu et al., 2024\].
Building on top of the AI scientist idea, the Agent Laboratory was proposed \[Schmidgall
et al., 2025\], an open-source framework that employs specialized LLM-based agents to
accelerate the full research cycle. Unlike the AI Scientist, Agent Laboratory is explic-
itly designed as a co-pilot for human researchers, complementing rather than replacing
human ideation. The framework consists of three main phases: literature review, ex-
perimentation, and report writing. Each phase is executed by dedicated agents, such
as the PhD, Postdoc, and Professor agents, coordinated through a structured pipeline.
The system integrates two specialized components: mle-solver, responsible for au-
tonomously generating, testing, and refining machine learning code, and paper-solver,

## Page 271

13.8. CODING ASSISTANTS AND GENERAL ADVANCES
271

Figure 13.3: SWE-Agent for Software Engineering \[Yang et al., 2024b\]

which produces a complete research report in LATEX format based on the experimental
results. Both solvers employ iterative refinement, self-evaluation, and reward-based
scoring to improve code and report quality across cycles.
Evaluation results demonstrate that Agent Laboratory can autonomously generate
complete research projects, including executable code and publication-ready reports,
at a fraction of the computational cost of comparable systems (approximately $2.33
per paper using the gpt-4o backend). Human-in-the-loop or co-pilot mode further
improves research quality and usability, with participants reporting high satisfaction
and continued use intentions. Nonetheless, human oversight remains essential, as au-
tomated self-evaluations tend to overestimate research quality compared to human re-
viewers.

13.8
Coding Assistants and General Advances

SWE-Agent (short for software engineering agent) \[Yang et al., 2024b\] aims to auto-
mate the process of software discovery, to help agents to autonomously use computers
to solve software engineering tasks. SWE-agent introduces tools to create and edit code
files, navigate through software repositories, and execute computer programs. Experi-
ments on coding benchmarks such as HumanEvalFix achieve high success rates of over
80%. This success is attributed to the interactive design of the agent (see Figure 13.3).
MLGym \[Nathani et al., 2025\] follows the popular Gym reinforcement learning
framework \[Brockman et al., 2016\]. Gym provides a standardized interface between
environment and agent. Introduced in 2016, it accelerated the development of rein-
forcement learning algorithms, facilitating progress in the field. Taking further inspira-
tion from SWE-agent (such as file editing capabilities) the MLGym work shows how
the process of scientific discovery can be modeled as an interactive process. Applica-
tions are discussed in fields ranging from data science, game theory, computer vision,
reinforcement learning, to natural language processing. Experiments are reported with
commercial LLMs (OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic).
Most LLM-based assistants, including research and coding assistants, depend on
pre-defined tools, limiting their autonomy and scalability. Toolmaker \[W¨olflein et al.,
2025\] addresses this limitation by enabling agents to create new tools directly from sci-
entific papers and their code repositories. Given a task description and GitHub URL, it
installs dependencies, configures a reproducible Docker environment, and implements

## Page 272

272
CHAPTER 13. FROM TOOLS TO ASSISTANTS

a working Python tool through iterative self-correction and error diagnosis. The system
was evaluated on TM-Bench (also introduced in W¨olflein et al. \[2025\]), a benchmark
of 15 real-world scientific tasks across medicine, biology, and AI. Toolmaker achieved
80% task success. Its closed-loop design allows agents not only to use but also to au-
tonomously build new tools, marking a step toward self-extending research assistants
and adaptive scientific workflows.
While systems such as Agent Laboratory and Toolmaker focus on the capabilities
of individual agents, The Agent Company \[Xu et al., 2024\] provides a comprehensive
benchmark to evaluate how LLM agents perform in realistic, work-like environments.
It simulates a small software company where agents must complete professional tasks,
ranging from software development and project management to finance and human
resources, using standard digital tools like browsers, terminals, and communication
platforms.
The benchmark includes 175 tasks designed to test multi-step reasoning, tool use,
and collaboration with simulated colleagues powered by LLMs. Each task is divided
into checkpoints that measure both full and partial completion.
Experiments with
twelve foundation models, including GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini, and Llama, reveal that
even the strongest current systems can autonomously complete only about 30% of
tasks. Failures often come from weaknesses in communication, long-horizon planning,
and navigation of complex user interfaces.
By introducing a reproducible, self-hosted environment that mirrors a modern work-
place, The Agent Company offers a critical stress test for evaluating the maturity of
agentic LLMs. It highlights both the rapid progress and the persistent limitations of
current systems, underscoring that while digital work automation is within reach, truly
autonomous collaboration remains a major research frontier.

13.9
Concluding Remarks

This chapter has shown how agentic LLMs have been used as assistants, interacting
with the real world. Assistants move beyond passive question answering toward active
collaboration in domains such as dialogue, flight operations, medicine, education and
scientific research. They plan, retrieve information, invoke tools, reflect on outcomes
and adapt their behavior over time. Agentic LLMs therefore shift the role of language
models from isolated reasoning engines to participants in broader socio-technical sys-
tems.

Domain sensitivity and risk
Not all assistants operate under the same constraints.
High-risk domains such as medicine and aviation demand strong guarantees on safety,
robustness, transparency and fairness, and are shaped by regulatory frameworks such
as the EU AI Act. In these settings, agentic designs increasingly rely on retrieval, plan-
ning, verification and human oversight rather than on end-to-end generation. Academic
research mirrors these concerns, with growing emphasis on evaluation, bias analysis
and interpretability as first-class design objectives rather than afterthoughts.

## Page 273

BIBLIOGRAPHY
273

Practical advice
When building assistants, grounding (real-world evaluation) is im-
portant. Use architectures where agents retrieve evidence, justify actions and defer to
humans under uncertainty (human in the loop). Treat tools as modular components
with explicit contracts and failure modes. Log decisions, plans and intermediate states
to enable debugging and auditing. In high-stakes domains, we suggest to design for
graceful degradation; an agent asking for clarification or abstaining is preferable to
confident error.

Outlook
The future of agentic assistants lies in tighter integration between reasoning,
learning and control. Progress will require richer cognitive structure, continual adap-
tation from interaction and stronger guarantees around safety and ethics. These goals
connect directly to advances in interpretability and transparency. In later chapters, par-
ticularly in mechanistic interpretability (Chapter 21), we return to techniques that aim
to open the black box and better understand how agentic LLMs represent goals, plans
and decisions internally.

What You Will Learn

In this case study you will gain hands-on experience building a multi-agent system
for a high-stakes application domain. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Implement a hospital diagnostic workflow with planner and executor agents
communicating through a shared context.
• Integrate trained machine learning classifiers as tools within an agentic pipeline.
• Replace rule-based planners with a language model and evaluate the impact on
routing and diagnostic accuracy.
• Assess system performance using classification and routing metrics, separating
planner errors from executor errors.
• Critically reflect on the limitations, risks, and ethical considerations of deploy-
ing agentic systems in medical settings.

14.1
Scenario Overview

This case study focuses on building and extending a simplified multi-agent hospital
simulation using a shared context inspired by the Model Context Protocol (MCP, Chap-
ter 11) \[Hou et al., 2026\]. The case study is designed to provide hands-on experience
with agentic architectures in a high-risk domain, highlighting coordination, planning,
evaluation, and safety considerations.
You will simulate a diagnostic workflow in a hospital setting. Patient cases are
processed by agents that interact exclusively through a shared context:

• Planner agents decide which diagnostic pathway(s) should be followed.

14.3.2
Step 1: Understanding and Running the Baseline

The baseline implementation, 1 basic mcp.py, uses three rule-based planner agents,
each hard-coded to a specific disease. Before running anything, read the code carefully.
It implements three components that recur throughout this case study:

• Shared context (MCP-like layer). A central data structure that stores incoming
patient cases, assigned diagnostic tasks, and diagnostic results. All agents inter-
act only through this shared context, never directly with one another, mirroring
the shared-state coordination pattern discussed for the Model Context Protocol
in Section 11.

• Planner agents. Each rule-based planner reads unassigned cases, decides (using
a fixed rule) whether its disease domain applies, and creates a task in the shared
context.

• Executor agents. Each executor reads tasks assigned to its specialty, runs the
corresponding trained ML classifier from Step 0, produces a prediction, and
writes the result back into the shared context.

Run the baseline simulation and observe how a single patient case flows through
the system: from arrival, through planning and task creation, to execution and logging
of the result.

Analysis questions
Assess how realistic this baseline setup is. How well is perfor-
mance evaluated? What assumptions are implicit in the way patients and diagnoses are
handled?

14.3.3
Step 2: Replacing the Rule-Based Planners with an LLM
Agent

In the second part, 2 llm mcp.py, the three rule-based planners are replaced by a
single LLM-based planner agent. This is a substantially harder task for the planner:
each patient case now combines features drawn from all three datasets into one record,
and is converted into a textual description using the provided make case text func-
tion, which you are not permitted to modify. The LLM planner must read this com-
bined, textual case description and decide, without hard-coded rules, which diagnostic
pathway or pathways apply.
Your tasks are to:

## Page 280

280
CHAPTER 14. CASE STUDY 3: MULTI-AGENT DIAGNOSIS

• implement a function that calls a real LLM (e.g., via Ollama for a local model,
or the OpenAI or Gemini APIs) to obtain the planner’s decision for a given case;

• implement the step() method of the LLMPlannerAgent, so that it selects
one or more diagnostic pathways together with a primary diagnosis for each case;

• handle malformed or unparseable LLM outputs gracefully, rather than letting the
simulation crash on a single bad response; and

• log every planner decision, together with the case it was made for, so that planner
behavior can be analyzed after the run.

Because the planner now has to infer relevance from unstructured text rather than from
a fixed rule, this step should give you direct experience with the reliability problems
that arise when an LLM is placed in a decision-making role: parsing failures, in-
consistent formatting, and disagreement between the LLM’s routing decision and the
dataset’s ground-truth label.

A working LLMPlannerAgent, a short note on which LLM you
used and how you accessed it (local vs. API), and the logged planner decisions for
a full simulation run.

14.4
Evaluation

You must evaluate both components of the system, and keep the two evaluations sepa-
rate:

• Model (executor) performance: assess executor predictions using confusion ma-
trices and standard classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) for each
disease.

• Planner performance: evaluate the LLM’s triage quality using precision and re-
call of routing decisions (did the case get sent to the right disease pathway or
pathways?) and primary-diagnosis accuracy (did the planner correctly identify
the main concern?).

In your report, clearly separate errors due to incorrect routing (a planner error) from
errors due to incorrect model predictions (an executor error). A case can fail for either
reason independently: a well-routed case can still be misclassified by the executor, and
a correctly-classifiable case can be missed entirely because the planner never routed it
to the right pathway. Reporting only an end-to-end accuracy number would hide this
distinction and is not sufficient for this case study.

tation. You do not need to write a narrative essay; concise, direct answers are sufficient,
and you should be prepared to elaborate on your reasoning verbally.

14.6
Concluding Remarks

This case study brought together several threads from earlier parts of the book: agent
roles and coordination (Part III), tool use and the Model Context Protocol (Chapter 11),
and the evaluation methodology needed to separate planning errors from execution er-
rors in a compound agentic system. By first building a rule-based baseline and then
replacing its planners with a single LLM-based planner, you have seen directly how
much harder planning becomes once it depends on an LLM’s interpretation of unstruc-
tured, textual case descriptions rather than a fixed rule.
The medical framing was chosen deliberately: it is a domain where the cost of an
overconfident, unexplainable error is high, and where questions of abstention, human
oversight, and auditability are core design requirements. The same coordination pat-
tern applies well beyond healthcare, to any agentic system where a language model is
responsible for routing decisions that other, more specialized components then act on.

In the previous parts we have examined agentic LLMs primarily through a technical
lens: architectures, training procedures, reasoning strategies, tool use, and applications
in various domains. In this part we shift gears. Rather than asking how agentic LLMs
work and can be built, we ask how they behave, socially. As agentic LLMs are increas-
ingly deployed in social contexts (as assistants, collaborators, tutors, etc.), their behav-
ioral inclinations start to matter practically. It has real-world consequences whether,
for example, an agent tends to cooperate or defect in strategic situations, whether it
responds to politeness, or whether it can track another agent’s belief-states in a multi-
agent simulation.
Most research that we discuss in this part builds on methods originally developed
to study humans and other animals, addressing strategic behavior, social etiquette, em-
pathy, personality, and other traits. We end each chapter with a short reflection on the
general question whether such methods can be productively applied to AI.
In the next and final part, we go deeper into questions of LLM inner workings and
the potential emergence of various forms of cognition, or even consciousness.
