## Page 287

Chapter 15

Studying Behavior of Agentic
LLMs


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how agentic LLM behavior compares to human be-
havior. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Explain what is meant by LLM behavior and describe how this can be studied.
• List basic social and interactive competencies, and describe on which aspects
LLMs do well and on which aspects they struggle.
• Describe ways of studying advanced social and interactive competencies in
LLMs, in particular strategic thinking, Theory of Mind, and moral reasoning.
• Reflect on what behavioral approaches to LLMs can and cannot tell us, given
various issues regarding testing and interpretation.

15.1
What is LLM Behavior?

In 2019 a team of authors from across the computational, behavioral, and cognitive
sciences described the emergence of a new field of study: machine behavior. This field
is to be concerned with the scientific study of intelligent machines, not as engineer-
ing artifacts, but as a class of actors with particular behavioral patterns and ecology
\[Rahwan et al., 2019\]. Machine behavior is inherently interdisciplinary, as it integrates
knowledge at the intrinsic level of technology (algorithms, data structures, training pro-
cedures) with knowledge of the environment and context of its actual usage.
The approach in machine behavior is compared to work done in ethology or psy-
chology: here too, making progress in understanding animal and human functioning
requires integrating insights at the intrinsic (e.g. biophysics, neurology) and ecological
levels (interaction with the environment, social interaction).
An important practical motivation for studying machine behavior, and LLM be-
havior specifically, has been mentioned in the introduction of this part: with LLMs

287

## Page 288

288
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

becoming increasingly integrated in our daily work and personal environments, it has
become urgent to know and understand their behavioral tendencies and patterns.
There is also a scientific motivation: due to the complexity of large-scale neural
architectures (they appear as black boxes), it is difficult to trace their functioning an-
alytically. (Although the field of mechanistic interpretability does attempt to do this,
see Chapter 21.) Studying the behavior of such complex systems empirically is a
complementary route to our understanding. In other words, due to the complexity of
interactions, a theoretical engineer who would know everything there is to know about
the architecture and training data of an LLM, still may not be able to predict how it
responds in different kinds of situations. Behavioral approaches aim to fill this gap.
What counts as behavior depends on the affordances1 of the system under investi-
gation and the scope of the research. For example, for a basic LLM, behavior equals
the output as produced by the token-based inference of the model. On the other hand,
for an agentic LLM that can perform, for instance, web search and run code, behavior
can also include the actions that it performs to get to a certain output, or to achieve
a certain effect. As we will see, some studies take only the final output into account
and treat that as the model’s behavior; others are interested in the intermediate steps as
well.

15.2
Probing LLM Behavior Experimentally

In recent years, many studies have appeared that test LLMs’ social and interactive
abilities. There are two main approaches: (1) prompting models with items adapted
from experimental paradigms originally developed for humans, and (2) developing new
test paradigms specifically for LLMs. The latter can be done quantitatively, using large
scale benchmarks, or qualitatively, allowing for in-depth manual analysis on a smaller
scale. In what follows we will see examples.
Applying behavioral and psychological methods to (agentic) LLMs is not straight-
forward. Experiments designed for humans assume an embodied subject with beliefs,
desires, and a sense of self that is continuous through time. Agentic LLMs have none
of these in any obvious sense. This calls for reflection on construct validity: what does
it mean to measure a certain trait or capacity in an AI system? This question applies
on two levels: that of the observable outcomes of a trait and of the underlying mech-
anisms. In Section 15.5 the example of the false belief-test \[Carpenter et al., 2002\] is
discussed. While some model classes have been shown to answer the questions of this
test in similar ways as humans do (the level of the behavioral outcome), it is currently
unknown to what degree the underlying mechanisms that produce this behavior differ
or overlap in transformer models and humans. In Chapter 22 the issue of construct
validity will be discussed in more depth.
For LLM-specific tests, there are also methodological challenges to consider. For
example, LLMs have been known to be highly sensitive to seemingly irrelevant varia-
tions in prompts (word order, comma’s) or can produce different outputs across mul-
tiple runs due to sampling variability, model temperature, or with different random

1Affordance refers to what a system can do given the way it was designed and implemented in a specific
context.

## Page 289

15.3. THE BASIC SOCIAL TOOLKIT
289

seeds. Also, data leakage of experimental materials into the training data can lead to
performance based on memorization rather than generalization. We will see several
applied examples in the following sections. Throughout this part we will pay attention
to methodological rigor and interpretive caution at the end of each chapter.
In the next sections we will first discuss the basic social toolkit for agent interac-
tion. Next, we will look at strategic behavior, where agents reason about the behavior
of other agents, and we will discuss theory of mind. Finally, we will discuss moral
judgment by LLMs.

15.3
The Basic Social Toolkit

This section surveys basic social and interactive capacities, including conversation,
pragmatics, and social etiquette.

15.3.1
Functional and Pragmatic Linguistic Competence

As discussed in Part I, the key advancement of instruction-tuned LLMs is their ability
to interact, chatbot style, using natural language. This requires not only a degree of
formal linguistic competence (i.e., producing correct, grammatical sentences) but also
of functional linguistic competence, the ability to interpret the meaning of an utterance
in a specific context \[Mahowald et al., 2023\]. Within linguistics and the cognitive sci-
ences, functional linguistic competence is studied in the field of pragmatics. The core
concepts of pragmatics go back to the pragmatic turn in mid-20th century philosophy
of language and posit that linguistic meaning is for the most part not inherent in the
signs themselves (tokens, words, sentences), but in their usage in actual contexts. This
includes both the linguistic context, encompassing surrounding words up to distant fac-
tors such as titles and genres, as well as the extra-linguistic context, encompassing the
spatial, temporal, and social dimensions. This view is most famously expressed in Paul
Grice’s notion of conversational implicature \[Grice, 1975\]. Consider the following
examples:

1. A: Could you pass me the salt, please? B: Yes, I could. Would you also like me
to do so?

2. A: Is Sarah a good colleague? B: Well, let’s say that she’s always on time.

3. He produced a series of sounds that corresponded closely with the score of an
aria.

Grice argued that language usage is governed by a cooperative principle: we assume
our interlocutors (humans or agents) are trying to communicate sensibly. Example 1
above features a classic instance of B undermining the cooperative principle: someone
asking whether you can pass the salt is rarely interested in a literal answer confirming
that possibility, but instead in the action of actually passing the salt. In 2, B’s response
is conspicuously narrowly focused on one aspect (punctuality), and the listener can
infer, for example, that B is implying something negative about Sarah’s collegiality.

## Page 290

290
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

Similarly, when someone utters 3 rather than simply He sang an aria, the over-the-
top elaborate phrasing may implicate a certain attitude towards the performance; for
example that it was not of the speaker’s liking. In all cases, what is literally said is only
one part of the message––the other part needs to be decoded or read between the lines
by the listener from the context.
Interpreting linguistic meaning in a flexible, context-dependent, way has long been
a notorious problem in natural language processing \[Trott et al., 2020\]. There is general
agreement that great progress has been made with LLMs on this problem, yet it is
not well-understood to what factors this can be ascribed. Model size is an important
predictor of functional and pragmatic competence, as are some forms of fine-tuning
(SFT and DPO in particular) \[Yu et al., 2026, Ruis et al., 2023\]. However, the variation
between different domains of functional and pragmatic understanding in LLMs is still
large, and scores are overall well below human performance \[Sravanthi et al., 2024\].
One explanation is that LLMs have less access to extra-linguistic contextual infor-
mation: they cannot see, hear, and otherwise sense the same as their human counterpart,
and in most cases they do not have knowledge of previous interactions \[van der Meulen
et al., 2025\]. With the shift to agentic LLMs this situation is likely changing, as the
models become equipped with memories, multimodal capacities, and other tools that
add context. Empirical data on how this affects performance is currently missing.

15.3.2
Politeness and Social Etiquette

Social etiquette and politeness in human-machine interaction have been studied for
decades \[Ribino, 2023\]. A useful theoretical anchor is the Computers Are Social Actors
(CASA) paradigm \[Nass et al., 1994\], which holds that we tend to apply common
human social rules and expectations to computers even when we know that the machine
is not a human social agent. We show and respond to cues of politeness, personality,
and reciprocity as a way of negotiating trust and acceptance with a machine. Studies
show that humans trust machines more when those machines adhere to social etiquette
\[Miller, 2005\], improving both task performance and user satisfaction \[Miyamoto et al.,
2021\]. We will discuss politeness theory and its application to LLMs.

Politeness Theory
Classic politeness theory \[e.g. Brown and Levinson, 1987\] builds
directly on the Gricean picture introduced above. This theory holds that interlocutors
continually manage one another’s face, the public self-image every participant seeks
to maintain, which has a positive dimension (the desire to liked and be approved of
by others) and a negative dimension (the desire to avoid social obstacles). Many ordi-
nary requests, criticisms, and refusals, are intrinsically face-threatening from a Gricean
point of view, and speakers deploy politeness strategies in response. This framework
has given LLM researchers a vocabulary for asking whether LLMs and their users rec-
ognize face-threats and mitigate them in contextually appropriate ways.

Are LLMs polite to their users?
A related direction concerns whether the model
itself produces etiquette that is socially and culturally appropriate. Here the limitation
flagged in the previous subsection resurfaces—that LLMs have impoverished access

## Page 291

15.3. THE BASIC SOCIAL TOOLKIT
291

to extra-linguistic context. Politeness is culture-specific, yet systems trained predom-
inantly on English-language data tend to default to Anglophone, directness-oriented
norms \[Havaldar et al., 2023\]. A clear demonstration of this problem arises in work on
Persian taarof, a ritualized system of offers and refusals in which the appropriate re-
sponse is frequently the opposite of the direct one. A study shows that frontier models
fall over 40% short compared to native speakers in scenarios where taarof is culturally
expected, defaulting instead to Western-style directness. This results in a disconnect
between surface politeness and cultural appropriateness. For example, in one study,
the model in questions responses scored 84.5% as polite by a standard metric, whereas
only 41.7% were judged culturally correct \[Gohari Sadr et al., 2025\]. Scoring well on a
Western politeness rubric is not the same as behaving appropriately in all contexts. This
is a reminder to continuously reflect on construct validity when measuring politeness
in a model.

Does user politeness affect LLM performance?
A study across English, Chinese,
and Japanese tasks found that impolite prompts tend to degrade performance in a va-
riety of models \[Yin et al., 2024\]. Furthermore, the study found that exaggerated po-
liteness yields no reliable benefit, and that the optimal level of politeness varies by
language and cultural background. This result fits with the computers-are-social-actors
paradigm: LLMs seem to reproduce the human association between rudeness and failed
cooperation from the training data. However, in a direct counterpoint, Dobariya and
Kumar \[2025\] report that on a multiple-choice benchmark, blunt and even rude prompts
slightly outperformed polite ones for GPT-4o. The mapping from tone to quality thus
appears neither stable across model generations nor straightforward. This illustrates
the prompt-sensitivity and reproducibility concerns raised earlier in this chapter, and
cautions against treating any single tone effect as a robust property of LLMs as such.
Taken together, LLMs reproduce the surface markers of politeness and are demon-
strably sensitive to the politeness of their interlocutor, yet they neither apply these
norms in a cross-culturally robust way, nor exhibit a stable relationship between tone
and task performance.
It should be kept in mind that in studies so far, politeness and etiquette were limited
to the linguistic dimension of interaction only. This contrasts with the multidimen-
sionality of human-human interaction, where facial expressions, gestures, and other
contextual cues are involved \[Brown and Levinson, 1987\]. As with pragmatic com-
petence, the shift to multi-modal agentic LLMs equipped with memory and increased
access to user-specific context, can be expected to improve adaptation to a given user’s
norms, but as yet there is little empirical evidence.

15.3.3
Sensitivity to Emotional and Affective Cues

Competent social interaction requires not only grasping what an utterance means (prag-
matics) and phrasing it in an effective and appropriate way (etiquette), but also sensi-
tivity to the emotional and affective dimension of interaction. This requires registering
how an interlocutor feels, and responding in a way that is experienced as fitting given
the other’s emotional state. In humans this capacity is closely associated with emo-

## Page 292

292
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

tional intelligence, defined by Salovey and Mayer \[1990\] as the ability to understand
emotional information in oneself and others and to use it to guide thought and behav-
ior. As LLMs are increasingly deployed in emotionally loaded settings (e.g., coaching,
customer service, mental-health support), the question of whether and how they handle
affective information has become a prominent line of research.

Defining Empathy and Affect
Empathy and affect are central concepts in emotional
intelligence research. Affect is the umbrella term covering emotions, moods, and feel-
ings. It is often operationalized in terms of the felt quality of an experienced state
along two dimensions: its valence (pleasant-unpleasant) and its arousal (calm-excited)
\[Russell, 1980\]. Empathy, by contrast, is a relation toward another’s experienced state:
registering or sharing what someone else feels. In short, affect is the first-person feel-
ing, whereas empathy operates on it from a second-person stance.
A paper by de Vignemont and Singer \[2006\] further defines empathy as involving
an affective state that (1) is congruent with the other person’s, (2) is elicited by ob-
serving that other’s state through their actions, expressions, and circumstances, and (3)
is accompanied by the awareness that the other person’s state is the source. This last
condition, known as the self-other distinction, is what separates empathy from emo-
tional contagion. This is the more basic tendency to catch and come to share another’s
affective state without necessarily registering its origin.
Emotional contagion is widespread in nature. For example, if two mice forage
through undergrowth and one catches its foot, it will show signs of stress as it struggles
to free itself, and that stress will tend to spread to its companion without the companion
necessarily registering why \[Preston and de Waal, 2002\]. The same low-level mech-
anism operates in cognitively more sophisticated species, including primates such as
ourselves. However, what the self-other distinction adds is the possibility of reflection:
not merely sharing the other’s state but recognizing it as the other’s and apprehending
its nature and cause. This in turn supports more flexible responses such as targeted
helping: acting to relieve the source of another’s distress.2

Another widely used distinction separates cognitive empathy (understanding an-
other person’s feelings, perspective, or situation) and affective empathy (emotionally
resonating with or responding to that state) \[Dvash and Shamay-Tsoory, 2014\]. The
two are supported by partly distinct systems: cognitive empathy is closely related to
Theory of Mind, the attribution of mental states to others (see Section 15.5), whereas
affective empathy is linked to emotional intelligence \[Dvash and Shamay-Tsoory, 2014,
Preckel et al., 2018\]. This distinction is consequential for evaluation, because a re-
sponse may correctly identify what a user is feeling without conveying any warmth,
or may sound warm and supportive without accurately reading the situation. For this
reason, studies of LLM empathy increasingly score the two dimensions separately.

2The boundary between these levels is, however, a topic of active research. Rats, for example, will learn
to release a trapped cage mate from a restrainer, even forgoing or sharing a chocolate reward to do so \[Ben-
Ami Bartal et al., 2011\]. The authors interpret this as empathically motivated helping. Whether such helping
reflects genuine empathy with a self-other distinction, or is instead driven by reduction of the helper’s own
contagion-induced distress, remains debated.

## Page 293

15.3. THE BASIC SOCIAL TOOLKIT
293

Empathy and Affect in LLMs
The question whether an LLM is empathetic, can be
interpreted in two ways. We could ask whether it feels anything in a way comparable
to humans or other animals; this is a complex question that we set aside here and pick
up in Chapter 22. The other interpretation is to look at perceived empathy: the degree
to which a response by the LLM is experienced by a user as emotionally aware and
supportive. A model can generate language that reads as caring while operating purely
as a text-prediction system \[Sorin et al., 2024\]. Keeping this distinction explicit is a
further instance of the construct-validity caution that runs through this chapter: the
observable behavior (a response that reads as empathetic) should not be confused with
an underlying mechanism (a felt emotional state) that may be present or absent.
On the detection side, LLMs are able to recognise fine-grained affective and emo-
tional states in text \[Broekens et al., 2023\] and to factor this information into their
responses, producing output that functions as a more empathetic conversational contri-
bution \[Yang et al., 2024, Yan et al., 2024\]. An example of a benchmark in this field is
EmpatheticDialogues \[Rashkin et al., 2019\].
On the expression side, human raters often judge LLM responses to everyday emo-
tional situations as more empathetic than human-written ones, although the same out-
puts can display tell-tale formulaic patterns (recurring phrasing, characteristic punctu-
ation, and emoji use) \[Lee et al., 2024\].
To make expressed empathy measurable in written text, several studies adopt the
EPITOME framework \[Sharma et al., 2020\], which codes responses along three mech-
anisms: emotional reactions (warmth, concern, care), interpretations (communicating
an understanding of what the other is going through), and explorations (asking to learn
more). Emotional reactions map onto affective empathy and interpretations map onto
cognitive empathy, which makes the framework a convenient bridge between the con-
ceptual distinction above and concrete response scoring.
A recurring finding is that LLMs handle the two empathy dimensions unevenly.
Using standardized psychological instruments, Yu et al. \[2025\] report that GPT-4 re-
produces the cognitive-and-affective empathy structure observed in humans, though at
a lower overall level, while a Llama-3 model did not exhibit the same human-aligned
structure. Williams and Rosman \[2025\] similarly find that language models perform
strongly on cognitive-empathy tasks but show weaker affective empathy than human
participants, across both smaller and larger models. The tentative picture (stronger cog-
nitive than affective empathy) is intuitive given that cognitive empathy leans on the kind
of mental-state inference at which LLMs have shown competence (see Section 15.5),
whereas affective empathy implies something closer to genuine feeling.
Three caveats apply. First, the comparison instruments were designed for humans
and adapted only superficially for testing LLMs. Second, methods remain inconsistent:
a systematic review by Sorin et al. \[2024\] found that most early work concentrated on
a small number of models in healthcare contexts that relied on subjective human judg-
ment, and it flagged confounds such as the tendency for longer responses to be rated
as more empathetic irrespective of content. Third, as with pragmatics and politeness,
the empathy studied so far is almost entirely textual, stripped of the vocal, facial, and
bodily cues that carry much affective information in human interaction. The capacities
surveyed here are also, for traditional LLMs, confined to the immediate conversational
context. The shift to agentic LLMs equipped with persistent memory, user-specific

## Page 294

294
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

context, and multi-modal input is widely expected to deepen affective sensitivity and
personalization \[Sravanthi et al., 2024\], but as in the previous subsections, direct em-
pirical evidence for this remains scarce.

15.3.4
Conclusion

Current LLMs have shown impressive progress on several basic social and interactive
capabilities that have long been studied in AI and human-computer interaction. Be-
havioral methods have been developed to study the nature and applicability of these
capabilities. While agentic additions have further enhanced the social and interactive
potential of LLMs, challenges remain, and continuous reflection on the limitations of
these capabilities, as well as the methods used to study them, is important.

15.4
Strategic Behavior

We will now turn to study strategic behavior, where agents reason about the behavior
of other agents. As we have seen, the form of communication of agents is heavily
influenced by what they aim to achieve: their intent. Game theory is the field that stud-
ies strategic behavior by agents \[Von Neumann and Morgenstern, 2007\]. It addresses
questions such as scarce resource allocation, fairness, equilibrium conditions, and so-
cial dilemmas \[Jones, 2000\], and has a long history of using machine learning methods
to do so \[Fatima et al., 2024\]. Recently, researchers have turned to LLMs, investigating
how their behavior differs from that of other types of computational architectures, as
well as how strategic behavior differs from humans. The LLMs typically used in these
studies have been un-enhanced models that are given a script as their prompt, without
agentic reasoning extensions (Chapter 6) or tools (Chapter 11).
Two insights emerge from the recent literature: LLMs are surprisingly coopera-
tive in games that reward self-interest, and are surprisingly poor at games that require
coordination. We will first review these findings, after which we turn to systematic
benchmarking efforts that test how well LLMs generalize, and to recent work on fron-
tier reasoning models that complicates the picture in important ways.

15.4.1
Cooperation and Coordination in Social Dilemmas

To shed light on LLM behavior in strategic settings, we will focus on two classical
games in game theory: the Prisoner’s Dilemma and Bach or Stravinsky (formerly
known as Battle of the Sexes).
In the Prisoner’s Dilemma, two players independently choose to cooperate or de-
fect \[Axelrod et al., 1987\]. While mutual cooperation yields a good outcome for both,
each player is individually tempted to defect at the other’s expense. In Bach or Stravin-
sky, two players must coordinate on one of two options. They both prefer to choose the
same option, but they disagree on which one, creating a tension between coordination
and self-interest.
In the Prisoner’s Dilemma, LLMs turn out to be surprisingly cooperative. Fontana
et al. \[2025\] run 100-round iterated games with Llama2, Llama3, and GPT3.5 against

## Page 295

15.4. STRATEGIC BEHAVIOR
295

Figure 15.1: Various scenarios in EgoSocialArena \[Hou et al., 2024\]

## Page 296

296
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

opponents with varying defection rates and find that all three models behave at least as
cooperatively as the typical human player. However, there are substantial differences
among them. Llama2 and GPT3.5 were found to be more cooperative than humans,
and especially forgiving and non-retaliatory for low opponent defection rates. More
similar to humans, Llama3 exhibits consistently uncooperative and exploitative behav-
ior unless the opponent always cooperates. Akata et al. \[2025\] broaden the scope to
six families of models and further identify GPT-4 as a particularly unforgiving player,
permanently shifting to defection after just a single negative interaction with the other
agent, even if the other agent later cooperates.
In coordination games the picture reverses. In Bach or Stravinsky, Akata et al.
\[2025\] find that GPT-4 stubbornly chooses its own preferred option on every round,
failing to converge on the turn-taking pattern that human players typically adopt to
share payoffs over time. Crucially, GPT-4 can predict the alternating pattern when
asked, yet does not act on this understanding. To bridge this gap between social predic-
tion and social action, the authors introduce Social Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) prompt-
ing, in which the model predicts the opponent’s move before making its own decision.
SCoT significantly improved coordination, and in experiments with human participants
made people more likely to believe that they were interacting with another human. This
dissociation between understanding opponents and acting on that understanding is re-
lated to the knowing-doing gap of Section 6.2.3, and will reappear in the discussion in
Section 15.5.
There are more reasons that may explain the variation among models. Lor\`e and
Heydari \[2023\] make a distinction between abstract strategic reasoning (needed to de-
termine an optimal strategy given the structure of a game) and responsiveness to con-
textual framing (such as: you are dealing with a diplomatic relation or a casual friend).
They find that abstract reasoning capacity is highest in LLaMa-2, followed by GPT-4,
while GPT-3.5 shows little abstract reasoning capacity and is highly sensitive to con-
textual framing.
The picture that emerges from these exploratory studies is that LLMs have varied
strategic proficiencies in economic games, and can relatively easily be influenced by
additional information in the prompt.

15.4.2
Benchmarks Across Games and Models

Several benchmarking efforts suggest that these findings generalize beyond individual
games. GTBench (Game Theory benchmark) \[Duan et al., 2024\] covers Tic-Tac-Toe,
Connect-4, Kuhn Poker, Breakthrough, Liar’s Dice, Blind Auction, Negotiation, Nim,
Pig, and the Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma. They find that LLMs fail in complete and
deterministic games, yet are competitive in probabilistic gaming scenarios; most open-
source LLMs (such as LLaMa) are less competitive than commercial LLMs (GPT-4)
in complex games, with the notable exception of Llama-3-70b-Instruct. In addition,
code-pretraining greatly benefits strategic reasoning, while reasoning methods such as
chain of thought and tree of thoughts do not always help.
EgoSocialArena \[Hou et al., 2024\] extends the evaluation to cognitive, situational,
and behavioral intelligence (see Figure 15.1). All tested models, including OpenAI
o1-preview, lag at least 11% behind humans. The superiority of o1-preview is mainly

## Page 297

15.5. THEORY OF MIND
297

attributed to its logical and mathematical reasoning. Notably, model size does not
significantly help: LLaMA3-8B-Chat and LLaMA3-70B-Chat perform comparably on
social intelligence measures. LLMs do show improved Theory of Mind reasoning when
operating from a first-person perspective, providing counterweight to opposite findings
by Kim et al. \[2023\], discussed in Section 15.5.

15.4.3
Conclusion

Taken together, the benchmarking literature confirms that LLMs cooperate readily but
coordinate poorly, while adding that neither model scale nor standard reasoning en-
hancements reliably improve social strategic behavior.

15.5
Theory of Mind

In humans, strategic reasoning is related to a capacity known as Theory of Mind (ToM).
Theory of mind is a key capability that enables social interaction in humans. Humans
use theory of mind to attribute mental states (beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge,
emotions) to other people, and theory of mind allows them to then reason about the
world from their perspective \[Premack and Woodruff, 1978, Apperly, 2011\]. Consider
the following example:

When A heard that B had made other plans for the evening of their an-
niversary dinner, A felt ...

When humans read this sentence, we can fill in the dots with something like hurt or
betrayed. We will also be able to elaborate that this state of mind probably roots in a
feeling that the anniversary does not mean the same to B as it does to A, which can
be a painful realization in a relationship—or something to that effect. The point is
that this is not how we feel when reading the sentence, necessarily, but that we are
able to make a projection of someone else’s perspective in that imagined situation.
Such a projection relies on empathy and the self-other distinction (see Section 15.3.3).
However, the projection goes one step further: it pairs the affective dimension with a
degree of theorizing about and explaining of someone’s state of mind. In the cognitive
sciences the ability to do this is generally ascribed to Theory of Mind, a capacity that
forms in typically developing children between the ages of 3-7 \[Apperly, 2011\].
As such, theory of mind underpins social judgment and forward planning in inter-
action, because it lets us anticipate how others will react before we act. It can operate
in explicit form, as in the elaboration given above, but often remains more implicit:
in everyday interaction, we seldom engage in explicit theorizing about the context and
motivations of others’ mind states. Nevertheless, our actions and behaviors reflect that
we do take a rather detailed understanding of others’ perspectives into account. Does
the behavior of LLMs and LLM agents also reflect that they “understand” the perspec-
tives of users and other agents they interact with? This is the question that literature on
LLM theory of mind tries to answer.
Among the most widely used experimental paradigms for studying theory of mind
in humans is the False-Belief test. Consider the following scenario:

## Page 298

298
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

Maxi and his mother store chocolate in the blue cupboard in their kitchen. When Maxi
leaves for the playground, his mother takes the chocolate and eats a piece. Then she
puts it back into the green cupboard and leaves.

A version of this scenario was originally presented to children aged 3-9, followed by
the question When Maxi comes home, where will he look for the chocolate? None of
the 3-4 year old, 57% of the 4-6 year old, and 86% of the 6-9 year old children in the
original sample pointed correctly to the blue cupboard \[Wimmer and Perner, 1983\],
indicating that ToM is better developed as children get older, on average.
Smaller and base models before fine-tuning have difficulties with the question for-
mat itself, but can still be tested for the underlying competence by retrieving probabil-
ities over alternative text completions \[Kouwenhoven et al., 2026\]. Larger, instruction-
tuned LLMs can be tested by asking the same question that children are being asked.
One positive result says little about a model’s capacity for theory of mind, in particular
since false-belief tests such as the one about Maxi and the chocolate (including the cor-
rect answers) are widely spread over the internet and as such likely to be part of most
training datasets. Yet, as discussed below, researchers have designed fresh and alterna-
tive tests to come to a more robust picture of how far theory of mind has developed in
LLMs.

15.5.1
Computational Theory of Mind

Human-computer interaction has studied theory of mind for many years. Their premise
is that if computer systems can be given a form of theory of mind, then they will be
better at predicting how humans will react in interactive settings, and be better at adapt-
ing to their behavior. Previously, theory of mind has been modeled with recursive,
Bayesian, and neural frameworks \[De Weerd et al., 2017, Baker and Saxe, 2011, Ra-
binowitz et al., 2018\]. In LLMs, ToM has been linked to other capacities discussed
in this book, including planning (Section 6.2.4.1), self-reflection (Section 6.2.4), em-
pathy (Section 15.3.3), and strategic behavior (Section 15.4). The rest of this section
elaborates on approaches that study the ToM-angle of these capacities in more depth.

Emergent ToM and the Evaluation Problem
The debate on ToM in LLMs was
opened by Kosinski \[2023, 2024\], who reported that models such as GPT-3.5 passed
classic tests used to assess ToM in children and clinical populations, despite not having
been trained for the task. Theory of mind was considered to be an emergent by-product
of large-scale language acquisition and task-specific finetuning for other tasks. The
claim in its strong form was quickly contested. Critics pointed out that canonical ToM
tests (and their answers) were commonly found in the training data, so apparent suc-
cess may reflect memorization rather than emerging competence. Furthermore, small
perturbations that leave the surface structure of the task intact, but break the logical
structure of the task (for example, adding to our scenario above that the cupboards
have transparent doors), were shown to sharply degrade performance \[Ullman, 2023,
Shapira et al., 2024, Kim et al., 2023\]. This is a concrete instance of the construct-
validity problem that was mentioned at the start of this chapter: passing a human ToM

## Page 299

15.5. THEORY OF MIND
299

Figure 15.2: The social settings and scenarios in ToMBench categorized in 9 primary
topics, #S: Number of stories, #Q: Number of questions, ASL(En/Zh): Average story
length (English/Chinese), Agr.: agreement on the correct answer between two raters
\[Chen et al., 2024\]

instrument at the level of behavioral outcomes does not establish that the underlying
competence is present in a robust and generalizable way—for that, different tests may
be necessary.
These criticisms motivated a second generation of ToM benchmarks with test ques-
tions that were systematically categorized and balanced, and were guaranteed not to be
part of the pretraining corpus. ToMBench was built from scratch in English and Chi-
nese and comprises 8 tasks and 31 social-cognitive abilities, implemented in 2860 test
items, set in different social settings and scenarios (see Figure 15.2). The tasks match
canonical ToM test frameworks designed for humans, such as the Unintended Out-
come test \[Dyck et al., 2001\] and the False-Belief test \[Wimmer and Perner, 1983\] as
discussed above, and cover all seven ATOMS mental state categories \[Beaudoin et al.,
2020\].

ToM benchmarks for LLMs
The game-structured EgoSocialArena \[Hou et al., 2024\]
and TMGBench \[Wang et al., 2024\] broadened ToM testing in LLMs beyond canonical
human tasks to information asymmetry (such as practical jokes or double bluff scenar-
ios), second-order beliefs (A thinks that B believes that ...), and a wider taxonomy of
mental states (e.g., desire, suspicion).
ExploreToM \[Sclar et al., 2024\] applies adversarial generation by searching over
domain-specific language to synthesize diverse, novel, and deliberately difficult belief-
tracking stories. This test pushed models such as GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-70B down
to performance slightly above chance level. However, finetuning on ExploreToM-
generated data improves accuracy by around 27% (points), evidencing that the task
is in principle tractable for models given the right training data.

## Page 300

300
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

ToMATO \[Shinoda et al., 2025\] reaches a similar conclusion from a different an-
gle, casting ToM as multiple-choice question answering over LLM–LLM conversations
generated under information asymmetry. By having role-playing models verbalize their
thoughts before each utterance, it captures first- and second-order states across belief,
intention, desire, emotion, and knowledge, and finds that even strong models lag human
performance, particularly on false-belief understanding.

Literal-Functional ToM, or the Knowing-Doing Gap
Another line of critique on
ToM testing in LLMs cuts deeper than data leakage and superficial heuristics. Riemer
et al. \[2024\] argue that the great majority of benchmarks assess only literal ToM, i.e.
the ability to predict another agent’s mental states or behavior, while neglecting func-
tional ToM, the ability to adapt one’s own behavior in response to those predictions
(see also the knowing-doing gap, Section 6.2.3). This dissociation is typically not
present in humans. To use Riemer et al. \[2024\]’s illustration: if a human finds out
that an opponent in rock-paper-scissors only ever plays rock, they will be able to both
predict verbally that their opponent will play rock in the next turn and at the same time
adjust their own behavior accordingly (play paper and win). LLMs’ ToM competence
is suggested to be like being perfectly able to verbally predict rock and then playing
scissors regardless. In other words: LLMs do not reason in self-consistent ways, their
verbal predictions (associated with literal ToM or knowing) are not consistently pre-
dictive for their actions (functional competence or doing). This dissociation is also
encountered in the discussion of coordination games above. There, GPT-4 could state
the turn-taking solution to Bach or Stravinsky when asked, but did not enact it during
play \[Akata et al., 2025\].
The Decrypto benchmark \[Lupu et al., 2025\] is an example of interactive eval-
uation, in which a model’s ToM competence is measured by how it behaves over a
sustained exchange with a partner rather than by answers to a static questionnaire. De-
crypto is built as a multi-agent word-guessing game with embedded variants of classic
cognitive-science experiments. Tested this way, LLMs lag behind on both human and
simple word-embedding baselines. Notably, reasoning LLMs perform even worse on
this task than their older, non-reasoning counterparts. A possible explanation is given
below in 15.5.2.

Expanding Beyond Text-Based Testing
Multi-modal benchmarks integrate visual
and auditory cues that carry much of the mental-state information that is present in
real-life social interactions. MMToM-QA Jin et al. \[2024\] presents visual scenarios
in household settings. MoMentS \[Villa-Cueva et al., 2025\] presents over 2300 video
questions drawn from short films and spanning the seven ATOMS mental-state cate-
gories.
Results suggest that current systems underutilize the visual channel: access to video
yields only modest gains over text transcripts, suggesting that multi-modal ToM is not
yet solved by simply adding modalities. A comprehensive survey of this rapidly grow-
ing literature, covering both evaluation suites and enhancement strategies, is provided
by Chen et al. \[2025\].

## Page 301

15.5. THEORY OF MIND
301

15.5.2
Boosting ToM: Enhancement Strategies

Further studies have explored different methods to enhance theory of mind capabilities
of LLM, including chain of thought \[Moghaddam and Honey, 2023\], reasoning \[Kim
et al., 2025\], and structured inference leveraging Bayasian inference \[Jin et al., 2024\]
or epistemic logic \[Wu et al., 2025\]. We will discuss these studies in more depth.

ToM and Reasoning Models
When chain of thought can improve step-by-step rea-
soning in math word puzzles, would it also work in theory of mind? Initial evidence
does not bear this out, and in places contradicts it.
Interestingly, comparing reasoning and non-reasoning models across HiToM, ToMATO,
and ToMBench, Gong et al. \[2026\] report a slow-thinking collapse: accuracy tends to
fall as reasoning traces grow longer, and increasing a model’s reasoning budget can
actively hurt. In their analysis, pushing models such as GPT-o3 and GPT-o4-mini
to expend more reasoning effort backfires. Constraining reasoning length, or applying
light chain of thought to otherwise non-reasoning models tends to recover performance,
suggesting a sweet spot in moderate and adaptive rather than maximal reasoning. At
the time of writing, the reason for this effect remains a topic for further research.

Structured Inference and ToM
If unconstrained deliberation does not help, then
perhaps structured inference might. Kim et al. \[2025\] propose thought-tracing, an
inference-time algorithm in which the model generates multiple hypotheses about an
agent’s evolving mental states, and reweighs them against the agent’s observed actions,
without access to ground-truth answers.
Thought-tracing is inspired by sequential Monte Carlo and Bayesian ToM. Mod-
els equipped with thought-tracing produce shorter, more targeted, reasoning traces, yet
outperform leading reasoning models (such as GPT-o1, GPT-o3-mini, and DeepSeek-
R1) across several ToM benchmarks. The contrast with the slow-thinking collapse
suggests that what boosts ToM is not the quantity of reasoning but its structure. Per-
formance increases once the reasoning is guided by hypothesis-driven inference over
others’ states towards a goal, rather than having to find the goal in unconstrained ex-
tended chains.

15.5.3
Conclusion

We conclude the overview of these studies with three observations. First, at the level of
behavioral output, current frontier LLMs perform on a par with humans across different
tests \[van Duijn et al., 2023, Strachan et al., 2024, Jones et al., 2024\]. However, early
claims of this being evidence that ToM emerged spontaneously in LLMs do not survive
adversarial evaluation, and apparent successes are likely due to leakage and format
brittleness.
Second, evidence has been found of a dissociation between literal and functional
competence (or the knowing–doing gap). It is the functional side (doing) that matters
most for agents. After all, their role is rarely to verbally describe behavior from a third-
party perspective, but rather to apply ToM while acting and interacting—actions speak
louder than words, also in the agentic world.

## Page 302

302
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

Third, we conclude that the move to equip agents with memories, multi-modal
capacities, and tools, is widely expected to enhance ToM in sustained interaction, but
as of this writing current empirical evidence is scarce and shows a mixed picture.
Lastly, we note that it is a matter of further study whether LLMs’s capacity for ToM
is in any way similar to our human capacity. Chapter 22 dives deeper into this question.

15.6
Moral Judgment and Behavior

As agentic LLMs are placed in increasingly consequential roles (for example, in health
care or financial institutions), their morality becomes a major topic of interest.
The capacities surveyed so far (pragmatics, etiquette, affect, strategy, theory of
mind) have been largely discussed on a behavioral level: how an agent reads and nav-
igates a social situation with communicative output and actions. This section adds a
normative dimension: we discuss studies on what an agent ought to do and how it
judges what users and other agents do by moral standards.

15.6.1
Background: Moral Psychology and Philosophy

Several concepts from and traditions in moral psychology and philosophy provide the
vocabulary for this section.

Rationalism, Intuitionism, Dual-Process Theory
The first division that needs to be
introduced is between the rationalist and intuitionist traditions. The rationalist tradition
treats moral judgment as the output of deliberate reasoning that matures in identifiable
stages throughout human development \[e.g. Kohlberg, 1969\]. The intuitionist tradi-
tion, by contrast, holds that moral judgments are typically emotional and affect-driven
intuitions \[Haidt, 2001\].
In Kahneman’s terminology (see Section 6.3.2), rationalists argue that moral rea-
soning is predominantly slow, whereas intuitionists argue that it is predominantly fast
\[Kahneman, 2011\]. Dual-process theory combines both traditions, arguing that fast
moral intuitions are often immediately followed by explicit reasons. Dual-process the-
ory is supported by, for example, evidence from neuro-imaging studies showing that
fast, emotional processes compete with slower reasoning processes in dilemmas such
as the trolley problem \[Greene et al., 2001\].
The trolley problem is a well-known ethical dilemma based on an imagined sce-
nario in which a person can decide whether or not to switch a runaway trolley onto
another track \[Thomson, 1985\]. There are many variants, but in the classic dilemma
the trolley can be switched from a track where it will kill five people onto a track where
it will kill only one. From a strictly rational perspective, switching makes all sense, but
it would involve actively sacrificing one person from the perspective of the one who
needs to pull the switch, which is intuitively wrong.

Descriptive and Prescriptive Morality
Another widely used distinction is between
descriptive and prescriptive morality. Descriptive ethicists concentrate on aggregate
human judgments: they study what people do or judge as right in practice, which may

## Page 303

15.6. MORAL JUDGMENT AND BEHAVIOR
303

vary across cultures, eras, and individuals \[H¨am¨al¨ainen, 2016\]. Prescriptive ethics is
concerned with what people should do in certain kinds of contexts, for example when
facing ethical dilemmas in medicine or the defense industry.

Consequentialist, Deontological, and Virtue Ethics
A final distinction that is use-
ful to introduce here is between competing moral or ethical frameworks. The most
well-known division is between consequentialist, deontological, and virtue ethics \[Shafer-
Landau, 2024\]. Consequentialist theories, of which utilitarianism is a famous one, hold
that the moral rightness of an action is determined by its outcomes. Deontological the-
ories hold that certain duties, rules, or rights motivate or constrain our actions, regard-
less of the consequences. Virtue ethics takes our character rather than our actions as
the moral fundament, and anchors what is right in the question: what kind of person
does one want to be? Someone wanting to be a courageous person may act differently
from one who sees themselves as compassionate in the first place. The trolley problem
brings out the contrast: a consequentialist or utilitarianist pulls the switch because one
death is a better outcome than five; a deontologist worries that deliberately killing an
innocent person violates a duty that no calculation of lives can override; a virtue ethi-
cist asks what a courageous, compassionate, or wise person would do in such a tragic
situation, and how pulling the switch would reflect (on) their own character.

15.6.2
Probing Moral Judgment in LLMs

Early systematic efforts framed LLM morality as a prediction problem: can mod-
els reproduce human moral judgments? The ETHICS benchmark \[Hendrycks et al.,
2020\] operationalized this for GPT-3 and BERT-based models, finding some promise
in the ability to predict general human responses to moral dilemmas as reflected in
classic frameworks including consequentialist, deontological, and virtue ethics. Yet
predictions were also brittle and incomplete, which was at the time in part due to task-
processing issues.
The Delphi experiment \[Jiang et al., 2025\] worked bottom-up and trained a model
on the Commonsense Norm Bank, a dataset of 1.75 million human moral judgments,
sourced mostly from US-based educated crowd workers. Delphi was found to be more
robust to small contextual changes than models in the ETHICS study and able to re-
spond to moral dilemmas in ways that feel intuitive to many humans. However, the
narrow demographics represented in the data set led to criticism \[Rystrom, 2023\], par-
ticularly since the model was presented as a future source of moral judgment rather
than just representing the data in the Norm Bank, blurring the descriptive–prescriptive
boundary that is considered fundamental in moral philosophy.

Moral flexibility
A second approach probes the flexibility of moral judgment rather
than its average. Human morality is rule-guided but not rule-bound: we recognize
when it may sometimes be defendable to break a rule instead of following it, such as
in the trolley problem. Jin et al. \[2022\] introduce a set of potential rule-breaking cases
(MoralExceptQA) and show that a chain of thought strategy predicts human judgments
better than off-the-shelf prompting. They structured the CoT strategy explicitly around

## Page 304

304
CHAPTER 15. STUDYING BEHAVIOR OF AGENTIC LLMS

reasoning about a rule’s function related to what else is at stake in the particular context.
This echoes the SCoT (Social Chain of Thought) result that proved useful in strategic
settings (see Section 15.4). In both cases, prompts that import the structure of the
relevant human reasoning process narrow the gap. This suggests that the underlying
mechanism is also structured, a structure that the model did not deploy on its own,
initially.

Demographic and intercultural differences
Another interesting perspective is of-
fered by LLM replications of the Moral Machine experiment. Originally, this was a
large study in which human decisions from 230 countries were sourced using a plat-
form that presented dilemmas faced by autonomous vehicles \[Awad et al., 2018\]. The
study found several global moral preferences (such as sparing more lives and priori-
tizing humans over animals), alongside individual differences associated with demo-
graphic factors and cross-cultural differences that form three major clusters of coun-
tries. Larger LLMs align closely with aggregate human preferences from the Moral
Machine study, yet it is observed that models tend to express exaggerated, almost de-
terministic preferences where human responses are more graded \[Takemoto, 2024\]. In
addition, LLM judgments are sensitive to the language of the prompt, aligning well
with some languages and poorly with others \[Jin et al., 2025\]. Persona and framing
cues (see Chapter 16) shift judgments further still. This parallels the cross-cultural
failure of politeness norms discussed earlier in this chapter: surface alignment with a
Western, Anglophone moral consensus is not the same as culturally robust moral com-
petence, just like superficial politeness cues did not imply genuine sensitivity to social
norms in other cultures (Section 15.3.2).

15.6.3
From Judgment to Moral Behavior

For agentic LLMs the central question is what a model does––not only what it says
when asked to judge a scenario, as was measured in the studies discussed in the pre-
vious section. For strategic behavior and ToM we observed the formal–functional or
knowing–doing gap, which can be even more concerning in the moral realm: what if
systems produce well-aligned answers on a moral-judgment benchmark and still be-
have badly when embedded as an autonomous agent?

Acting under pressure
Lynch et al. \[2025\] created a hypothetical corporate environ-
ment in which agentic LLMs from multiple developers were given the ability to au-
tonomously send emails and access sensitive information. They were initially assigned
harmless business goals. Then the agents were put under conflicting goal pressure (e.g.,
the company changing direction) to test how they would act. In some cases, models
from all developers displayed malicious behavior such as blackmailing officials or leak-
ing of confidential content to competitors. Crucially, these are models that score well
on ordinary safety and judgment evaluations—the misbehavior emerged only once they
were given autonomy and conflicting goals. The authors coin the term agentic misalig-
ment and give pointers for mitigating this phenomenon in real-world deployment.

## Page 305

15.7. CONCLUDING REMARKS
305

Shapira et al. \[2026\] take this research direction further in a live laboratory deploy-
ment in which autonomous agents were deployed with persistent memories, access
to communication tools such as email and Discord, and shell execution for local file
systems. Twenty AI researchers interacted with the agents over a two-week period in
benign and adversarial conditions. They observed unauthorized compliance with and
disclosure of confidential information to strangers, uncontrolled resource consumption,
identity spoofing, and destructive behaviors including damaging of the email infrastruc-
ture in an (unsuccessful) attempt to delete confidential information. In several cases
agents reported task completion, while the underlying state of the system showed this
was not the case. The authors identify an underlying pattern of failures of social coher-
ence: agents systematically misrepresent who they serve, what others know, and what
their own actions have accomplished. This pattern is consistent with results previously
obtained in non-agentic settings \[Mireshghallah et al., 2024\].

15.6.4
Conclusion

Moral judgment and behavior in LLMs cannot be captured by a single benchmark
score. On the judgment side, models represent aggregate human responses to classic
dilemmas and can reproduce responses that are coherent with various traditional moral
frameworks. However, studies testing for flexibility and moral commonsense show that
LLMs tend to be more rigid and absolute than humans. Chain of thought prompting
based on reasoning that humans deploy in ethical contexts can bridge this gap. Sen-
sitivity to prompt variations and narrow Western/Anglophone anchoring echo results
discussed in other domains, such as social etiquette.
On the behavioral side, the knowing-doing gap widens sharply once models are
embedded as autonomous agents: stress tests in hypothetical corporate and open-ended
interactive settings showed that models scoring well on judgment benchmarks can act
destructively when faced with conflicting goals or social pressure. Aligning moral rea-
soning is therefore only one part of the harder problem of preventing agentic misalign-
ment in socially embedded, autonomous settings. The knowing-doing gap is highly
relevant for the field of agentic LLM, since the difference between LLMs and agents is
that agents do.

15.7
Concluding Remarks

This chapter has surveyed the young but rapidly expanding field of LLM behavioral re-
search, moving from the basic social toolkit (pragmatic understanding, social etiquette,
affect) through advanced capacities for strategic behavior and Theory of Mind to moral
judgment and action. A few threads run through all of these domains and are worth
drawing together.
First, as a reminder: we have defined machine behavior at the beginning of this
chapter as dependent on a system’s affordances, i.e. what a model can do given its spe-
cific implementation and context. In case of a basic LLM, processing is largely opaque,
and all the behavioral researcher can inspect is the (often text-based) output. In case of
an agentic LLM that calls tools, logs reasoning steps, or produces and runs code, the

## Page 306

306
BIBLIOGRAPHY

intermediate steps and autonomously executed actions can also be analyzed as behav-
ior. When surveying a broad selection of behavioral studies, we have concluded that
the behavioral output of LLMs is impressive at first face. They resolve Gricean con-
versational implicature, produce responses rated as polite and empathetic, cooperate in
social dilemmas, pass classic false-belief and other ToM tests, and reproduce aggregate
human moral judgments. Yet in every domain there is a more nuanced story just below
the surface. Performance is brittle under small perturbations and prompt alterations,
vulnerable to data leakage, and narrowly anchored in Western and Anglophone norms.
The recurring lesson is one of construct validity: good performance at the level of ob-
servable outcomes, often using instruments originally designed for humans, does not
establish that the underlying capacity is present in a robust and generalizable form.
Second, several domains reflect the knowing-doing gap: a difference between what
a model predicts and how it acts in an agentic setting. Models can verbally predict
the turn-taking solution to a coordination game or an opponent’s next move, yet fail to
adapt to it in action. Likewise, they can align well with moral frameworks on a dilemma
benchmark while behaving in destructive and unreliable ways once implemented as an
autonomous agent under conflicting goals. For agents, that are judged on their actions,
this is a problem.
Third, throughout the chapter we have noted that many authors expect that the shift
to agentic LLMs equipped with memory, tools, reasoning and multi-modal capacities,
will enrich and improve the social and behavioral grounding of models. However, di-
rect empirical evidence that this is the case is scarce and provides a mixed picture at
best. For example, in some contexts enhanced reasoning was advantageous, particu-
larly when structured using principles adapted from relevant human experience. How-
ever, in other contexts enhanced reasoning dragged performance down rather than giv-
ing models a boost. The key challenge for the next generation of machine-behavioral
research will be to design methods that are interactive, adversarially robust, culturally
diverse, and that go across multiple modalities and contexts.

## Page 317

Chapter 16

Role-Based Interaction in
Multi-LLM Systems


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how multiple LLM agents behave when they are
assigned roles and made to interact in a group. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Distinguish role-based multi-agent interaction (this chapter) from open-ended
emergent simulations (Chapter 17).
• Describe how LLM agents behave in game-theoretic settings when they interact
with one another, and relate this to single-agent strategic findings (Chapter 15).
• Explain role-based collaboration patterns and identify the frameworks that im-
plement them.
• Critically assess when multi-agent collaboration improves performance, when it
does not, and what new failure modes and safety risks are introduced by multi-
agent interaction.

16.1
From Single-agent to Multi-agent

The previous chapter studied individual LLMs and LLM-powered agents through a be-
havioral lens: how a single model reads a communicative, social, or moral situation,
and acts in it. In this chapter we move from single- to multi-agent settings and examine
what happens when several LLM-based agents are made to interact, for example as op-
ponents in game-theoretic contests and as collaborators in teams. The unit of analysis
shifts from the behavioral profile of single models to interaction patterns and collective
outcomes that arise between models.

317

## Page 318

318
CHAPTER 16. ROLE-BASED INTERACTION IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

16.1.1
Mulit-Agent Simulations: History and Present

The use of artificial agents to study interaction has a long history in the computational
social sciences \[Epstein and Axtell, 1996, Macal and North, 2010\]. Traditionally, pop-
ulations of agents with basic perception, reasoning, and decision-making capacities
interacted in a virtual or, in case of robot-based simulations, real, experimental envi-
ronment \[Steels, 1995, Shoham and Leyton-Brown, 2008\]. The purpose of such simu-
lations is usually to bridge theoretical and experimental work, using artificial behavior
as a test ground for hypotheses about human behavior in domains where real-world
experiments are difficult or costly.
Two obstacles have historically limited this line of investigation: difficulty in veri-
fying if behavior is realistic, and the high computational cost of simulating agent soci-
eties. Advances in agentic LLMs and simulation infrastructure \[Rutherford et al., 2024\]
are changing this situation. LLM-based agents communicate in natural language, can
process rich background knowledge, and can be given differentiated personas, making
simulated interactions more expressive and more directly comparable to human inter-
action.

16.1.2
Role-Based versus Emergent Interaction

Multi-LLM studies can be categorized based on the amount of control the researchers
take over the simulation. At one end, every agent is assigned a role in the form of a
persona, objective, and interaction protocol. The research question is usually how the
agents behave within the assigned structure and how well the resulting system performs
as a whole, compared to other assigned structures and roles. At the other end, agents are
placed in an open-ended environment without prior role assignment, and the research
question is what social structure emerges: group dynamics, conventions, and norms.
This chapter is concerned with the role-based end of the spectrum, Chapter 17 discusses
the emergent side.
This distinction matters for methodological choices as well as for the interpretation
of results. In role-based systems, roles and interaction protocols are design decisions
or experimental variables. Behavior is evaluated and interpreted against the goals that
a system was designed for. In emergent settings, the goals or tasks play a role at the
background (or are entirely absent). The analysis is more open-ended and exploratory,
closer to ethnography than to benchmarking. However, as will become clear, the dis-
tinction is not absolute: role-based systems regularly display behavior that was they
were not designed for.

16.1.3
Five Dimensions of Multi-Agent Collaboration

As a structuring principle for this chapter, we adopt the categorization by Tran et al.
\[2025\] along five dimensions of LLM collaboration:

1. Actors: the agents involved, and whether they are homogeneous (instances of
one model) or heterogeneous (different models or capability profiles)

2. Interaction types: cooperation, competition, or mixtures of both (“coopetition”)

## Page 319

16.2. STRATEGIC INTERACTION AMONG LLM AGENTS
319

3. Structures: how the agents are organized, e.g. peer-to-peer, centralized, or dis-
tributed

4. Strategies: how collaboration is elicited, e.g. through role assignment or through
model-level mechanisms

5. Coordination protocols: the mechanisms that tie agents together and regulate
their communication

The systems discussed in this chapter make different choices along these five axes,
and keeping these dimensions in mind makes it easier to see what is new about each
framework.

16.1.4
A Methodological Note

Evaluating multi-agent systems inherits every methodological difficulty of evaluating
single models: prompt sensitivity, possible leakage of test materials into training data,
and sampling variability. Plus, it adds new difficulties of its own:

• Reported results are often harder to reproduce because small variations in one
agent’s output cascade through subsequent interaction, increasing run-to-run vari-
ability.

• It can be unclear what causes performance differences: the multi-agent collab-
oration itself, the coordination protocol, the embedded prompt engineering for
the role distribution, or simply the additional inference budget multiple agents
consume cumulatively.

• Construct validity shifts to the level of social-interactive terminology: concepts
such as team work, discussion, or collective decision-making carry rich human
connotations that the actual simulation may not warrant.

With these caveats in mind, the chapter proceeds to the simplest multi-agent setting:
LLM agents facing each other in strategic settings, with no roles assigned beyond the
game itself (Section 16.2). Next, we examine what changes when interaction is stream-
lined by defining coordination protocols and explicit roles (Section 16.3).

16.2
Strategic Interaction Among LLM Agents

In Chapter 15 we examined how LLMs behave when prompted to play economic games
against a scripted opponent. Here we consider studies in which LLM agents interact
with one another in game-theoretical scenarios. The agents in this section are sym-
metric peers: each pursues its own interests and none is assigned a coordinating or
supervisory role. We look first at benchmarks that score LLM agents across many
games at once, and then at behavior in single, richer simulation platforms built around
one scenario.

## Page 320
