Figure 16.1: LLM’s Performance on various Metrics \[Xu et al., 2024\]

16.2.1
Benchmarking Strategic Ability Across Games

The MAgIC study \[Xu et al., 2024\] uses social deduction games (Undercover and
Chameleon) and game theoretic scenarios such as cost sharing, the multi-player Pris-
oner’s dilemma, and public goods games. The goal is to extract seven capabilities:
rationality, judgment, reasoning, deception, self-awareness, cooperation, and coordina-
tion, as shown in Figure 16.1. LLMs in off-the-shelf and enhanced forms are evaluated
on these capabilities in multi-agent settings.
GPT-o1 and GPT-4 score significantly better than the other models. LLMs gen-
erally score high on judgment, rationality and cooperation, some also on deception,
but lower on reasoning and all but one score low on coordination. The exception is
GPT-o1 enhanced with probabilistic graphical modeling, an implementation of a the-
ory of mind-like competence inspired by Koller and Friedman \[2009\]. The authors
show that probabilistic graphical modeling boosts LLM performance across the board.
This is consistent with the general evidence discussed in Section 15.5 that humans lean
heavily on theory of mind in strategic settings.
A benchmark that isolates coordination as the object of study, rather than as one
trait among several, is the LLM-Coordination Benchmark \[Agashe et al., 2025\]. LLMs
are evaluated on two distinct tasks: agentic coordination in pure cooperation games
and question answering about those games (see Figure 16.2). The experiments find
that LLM agents perform well as long as decision-making can rely on environmental
variables, but poorly when success requires actively reasoning about a partner’s beliefs
and intentions. Concretely, such environmental variables include elements such as
the game layout, locations of objects, where each agent is currently positioned, which
doors are open, and so on. The clearest illustration is Overcooked-AI, the game where
LLMs did best. This game is fully observable, and its action space consists of moves
such as pick up an onion from onion dispenser 1 and place onion on plate 0. Under
most scenarios and layouts, LLMs only need to consider the next best steps based on the
state of the game environment, without taking into account other agent’s perspectives.
This asymmetry becomes especially clear when comparing performance on Over-
cooked with scores in Hanabi, a game in which every action requires reasoning about

## Page 321

16.2. STRATEGIC INTERACTION AMONG LLM AGENTS
321

Figure 16.2: Illustration from the LLM Coordination Benchmark \[Agashe et al., 2025\],
which uses two types of measures to assess agentic coordination: behavior in pure
coordination games in which agents must cooperate to maximize gains (middle) and
detailed questions about those games (right)

the partner’s beliefs. On Overcooked, zero-shot LLM agents can match or outperform
specially trained reinforcement learning baseline models. On Hanabi, however, the
reinforcement learning baselines show near-perfect scores, whereas most LLM agents
barely score at all. The best LLM agent (based on GPT-4-turbo) reaches only about
half the maximum score, even when enhanced with explicit theory of mind reasoning
and self-verification steps. Without such enhancements, the scores of strong models
such as GPT-4-turbo collapses almost entirely, indicating that the measured ability is
partly a feature of the agent framework rather than the model alone. The LLM agents
did prove more robust in cross-play: reinforcement learning methods degrade sharply
when playing unseen partners, whereas the zero-shot nature of LLM agents facilitates
transfer to unseen partners without performance loss.
The question-answering component of the study (see Figure 16.2, right column)
breaks the problem down by targeting environment comprehension, ToM, and joint
planning, separately. They find that LLMs score generally high on the first category
(¿80% for the best model), lower on ToM, and worst on joint planning (¡40% for the
best model, below random chance for open-source models). This is consistent with the
observed difference in scores between Overcooked (environment-driven) and Hanabi
(ToM- and planning-driven).
The key characteristic of pure cooperation games is that agents must fully cooperate
with each other with no competitive incentives. In contrast, in competitive settings such

## Page 322

322
CHAPTER 16. ROLE-BASED INTERACTION IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

Figure 16.3: Alympics Water Allocation Challenge Game \[Mao et al., 2023\]

as the Prisoner’s Dilemma (or the mixed-motive games in benchmarks like MAgIC),
an agent faces a genuine tension between individual and collective payoff. In such
games, when an LLM fails to cooperate, the reason is unclear. The agent may be bad at
coordination or it might reason strategically about individual gains. In pure cooperation
games, there is never any reason to defect, so any failure to cooperate is a genuine lack
of coordination ability.

16.2.2
Strategic Interaction in Single-Scenario Platforms

Benchmarks aggregate over many small games. A complementary line of research
builds single scenarios and studies agent behavior in-depth.
Alympics \[Mao et al., 2023\] provides a controlled playground for simulating strate-
gic interaction among LLM-driven agents, illustrated by a multi-round water-allocation
challenge in which scarce survival resources must be distributed over time, see Fig-
ure 16.3.
AucArena \[Chen et al., 2023a\] simulates auctions, across LLaMa 2.13b, Mistral
7b, Mixtral 8x7b, Gemini 1.0, and GPT 3.5/4.0, finding that the most capable LLMs
such as GPT-4 possess skills for auction participation such as budget management and
goal-focus, though performance varies even for that model, and the authors point to
considerable room for improvement.

16.2.3
Conclusion

Across benchmarks and single-scenario platforms alike, coordination emerges as the
consistent weak spot of LLM agents. Stronger LLMs score well on rationality and

## Page 323

16.3. ROLE-BASED TASK SOLVING AND TEAMWORK
323

judgment in MAgIC, manage budgets sensibly in AucArena, and match trained RL
agents in environment-driven cooperation. However, all but the strongest and most
heavily scaffolded models fail when success requires reasoning about what a partner
believes and intends.

In other words, models fail to consistently integrate theory of mind reasoning with
their behavior. In Chapter 15, failures of this kind were referred to as the knowing-
doing or literal-functional gap: GPT-4 could respond accurately when prompted to
predict the alternating pattern in Bach or Stravinsky, but failed to enact it when play-
ing. However, the multi-agent studies reviewed here complicate that diagnosis. In the
question-asking section of the LLM Coordination Benchmark, the questions about joint
planning pose exactly the decision the agent faces at each step of the game play. It is
on these questions that the models perform worst (and on ToM questions not much bet-
ter). Question-answering scores correlate positively with agentic performance across
games. In other words, knowing and doing move together here: where models act
poorly, they also reason poorly when the action problem is posed to them directly. For
pure coordination tasks, the deficit thus lies in taking the partner’s perspective (ToM)
and joint planning itself, rather tan in translating reasoning into action.

On a different level, the knowing-doing gap reappears. In Hanabi, GPT-4-turbo
reaches reasonable performance only when scaffolded with explicit ToM reasoning
and self-verification steps. Without these in place, it commits fatal errors in every Han-
abi trial. In other words, it acts wrongly initially, but recognizes and corrects these
errors when prompted to check the reasoning and verification steps. Similar perfor-
mance boosts were caused by probabilistic graphical modeling in MAgIC and Social
Chain-of-Thought in strategic-behavior studies discussed in Chapter 15. The bound-
ary between LLMs cannot reason about others and LLMs do not spontaneously deploy
such reasoning is apparently thin, and agentic embedding in the form of structured
reasoning and verification steps can bring out the latter.

The next section examines a different, complementary response to the same prob-
lem: instead of upgrading the agents’ reasoning, one can structure the interaction itself,
by assigning roles.

16.3
Role-Based Task Solving and Teamwork

In the previous section, agents were symmetric peers and coordination had to emerge
from their own strategic reasoning (with limited success). In the studies discussed in
this section, coordination is designed-in using interaction protocols and assigning roles
with distinct objectives.

In terms of the five dimensions defined in Section 16.1.3, the studies vary the strate-
gies and structures while keeping the overall interaction type cooperative. We proceed
from the simplest to the most complex structure: complementary pairs, multi-party
debate, teams, and social role-play under pressure.

## Page 324

324
CHAPTER 16. ROLE-BASED INTERACTION IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

Figure 16.4: Role-playing in CAMEL \[Li et al., 2023\]

16.3.1
Complementary Pairs

LLMs can perform tasks in pairs where they are assigned complementary roles, such as
creator-critic or manager-worker. In these pair-wise setups, each LLM agent is given a
distinct role and objective, and they communicate to jointly solve tasks.
In the CAMEL framework (Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration) \[Li
et al., 2023\], two LLMs have predefined roles to perform, to work on a goal such as a
coding task (See Figure 16.4). Through cooperation, together they drive a conversation
without explicit continuous human prompting. CAMEL uses inception prompting and
role descriptions so that agents stay in character and collaborate towards the goal. The
agents are prompted to break down complex problems in manageable steps through
their dialogue. During each interaction step the LLM agents effectively generate their
own inference-time training data, making the cognitive process visible for human in-
spection, while at the same time enhancing autonomous task performance.
Other studies have paired an LLM creator (or generator) with an LLM judge (or
critic) in a self-reflective setting. In this way the generative power of LLMs is lever-
aged through one agent, while adherence to rules or quality guidelines is enforced by
the other. Constitutional AI \[Bai et al., 2022\] employs one LLM to critique another
LLM’s responses against a set of ethical or quality guidelines, suggesting revisions.
The authors show that this kind of two-agent feedback yields refined final outputs that
are aligned with the desired principles.
A third form of pair-wise interaction follows human tutoring dynamics: teacher-
learner or expert-novice. Chapter 19.2 discusses various examples of this structure in
the context of distillation.
All three pairings exploit the same idea: one agent’s oversight can correct the

## Page 325

16.3. ROLE-BASED TASK SOLVING AND TEAMWORK
325

Figure 16.5: Three Different Communication Strategies in ChatEval \[Chan et al., 2023\]

other’s mistakes, leading to more robust joint performance than either agent achieves
alone.

16.3.2
Debate and Discussion

Beyond pairs, a prominent example of role-based interaction is the use of debate and
discussion between LLMs to improve reasoning and task performance.

Du et al. \[2024\] demonstrated that when multiple LLM instances propose answers
and critique each other’s reasoning through several rounds of debate, they can reach
a more accurate consensus answer with higher factual correctness. This approach,
described in terms of Minsky’s society of minds \[Minsky, 1988\], significantly reduced
reasoning errors and hallucinations in tasks such as math word problems and factual
question answering.

Liang et al. \[2024\] propose a multi-agent debate (MAD) setup where two LLM
agents take opposing sides in, for instance, a tit-for-tat negotiation (see Section 15.4)
while a third agent acts as a judge. The role of the judge is to guide the discussion
towards a final solution. The structured debate encourages divergent thinking and can
push a weaker model enhanced with MAD (such as GPT-3.5) to outperform a stronger
model without MAD (such as GPT-4) on a challenging benchmark. The authors discuss
how their MAD setup overcomes a known problem in model scaffolding with self-
reflective steps. Self-reflection can induce so-called degeneration of thought: once a
model gains confidence in a certain solution direction, self-reflection can reinforce the
confidence even if the direction is wrong. In the MAD debating-setup, the other agent
can push towards a different direction direction to avoid thought degeneration.
ChatEval applies this debate pattern to text evaluation \[Chan et al., 2023\]. Noting
that the quality of human text assessment improves when multiple annotators collab-
orate, the authors create a multi-agent referee team with debater agents, diverse role
specifications, and different communication strategies (see Figure 16.5), moving be-
yond single-agent prompting strategies.
Another approach, also motivated by Minsky’s society of minds, is ReConcile,
a multi-agent framework designed as a round table conference among diverse LLM
agents \[Chen et al., 2023b\]. The framework enhances collaborative reasoning between
LLM agents via multiple rounds of discussion. The agents must try to convince one an-

## Page 326

326
CHAPTER 16. ROLE-BASED INTERACTION IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

other to improve their answers. Experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate that a
confidence-weighted voting mechanism significantly improves LLMs’ reasoning. Fur-
thermore, the authors find that diversity (using different underlying models) is critical
for performance.
MindStorms introduces an LLM-based implementation \[Zhuge et al., 2023\] on
the CAMEL framework \[Li et al., 2023\]. Extensive experiments are reported with
up to 129 agents solving common AI problems: visual question answering, image
captioning, text-to-image synthesis, 3D generation, egocentric retrieval, embodied AI,
and general language-based task solving. The authors find that, in specific applica-
tions, mindstorms among many members outperform those among fewer members,
and longer mindstorms outperform shorter ones.

16.3.3
Role-Based Software Teams

An interesting application of role-based collaboration is software development, where
simulated teams that are entirely staffed with LLM agents develop software.
Automated programming by LLMs has suffered from problems, such as logic in-
consistencies and hallucinations that cascade throughout a development pipeline. MetaGPT
\[Hong et al., 2024\] builds on workflows that have proven to be effective in human soft-
ware teams. The framework converts Standard Operation Protocols (SOPs) into prompt
sequences and assigns agents the roles of a software company: product manager, archi-
tect, engineer, QA tester. In this way, the agents pass structured intermediate artifacts
down an assembly line. The product manager makes a requirements document, the
architect turns this into a design, the engineers code. In this way, complex tasks are
divided into manageable subtasks and agents can verify the process step-by-step, sig-
nificantly reducing errors.
Similarly, Qian et al. \[2024\] have introduced ChatDev, a virtual software com-
pany in which agents collaborate through the phases of a development process: design,
coding, and testing. Collaboration is organized as a chat chain: each phase is decom-
posed into short conversations between an instructor and an assistant agent (see Figure
16.6). Using a communication protocol that makes agents ask for more details before
responding, leads to what the authors call dehallucination, increasing the reliability
of each step. The framework demonstrates how structured communication in natural
language can facilitate multi-agent collaboration.
Where MetaGPT and ChatDev hard-wire a particular organization structure, Auto-
Gen \[Wu et al., 2024\] provides a flexible programming framework based on conversa-
tions between customizable agents that can combine LLMs, tools, and human input. It
was designed as an open-source platform that enables developers to define agents and
interaction structures depending on the application. Experiments demonstrate effec-
tiveness in tasks across mathematics, coding, question-answering, entertainment, and
other domains.

16.3.4
Social Role-Play

The systems discussed above assign roles to solve tasks. A final line of work assigns
roles in order to study social behavior itself: what do LLM agents do when placed in

## Page 327

16.3. ROLE-BASED TASK SOLVING AND TEAMWORK
327

Figure 16.6: The Chain-Structured Workflow in ChatDev \[Qian et al., 2024\] based on
Multi-Turn Dyadic Communication between Agents Powered by ChatGPT-3.5

socially demanding or conflicting situations?
In SOTOPIA \[Zhou et al., 2023\] agents coordinate, collaborate, and compete to
achieve complex social goals. The SOTOPIA environment features a large and diverse
task space by sampling interaction episodes from 90 (automatically generated) social
scenarios with 40 characters with individual personalities, occupations, secrets, back-
ground stories, and relationships with other characters (Figure 16.7). The authors eval-
uate the social intelligence of agents based on different LLMs against that of human
participants, observing various trends:

• Models that perform well on static benchmarks involving social reasoning (such
as ToMBench, see Section 15.5) do not necessarily succeed in interactive sce-
narios, illustrating the knowing-doing gap once again (Section 15.4.

• Weaker agents weaken their conversation partners, which is the reverse effect
of the conversational advantages discussed above, where agents prevented each
other from thought generation and other errors.

• Divulging secrets and violating social norms is observed across all models, con-
sistent with observations discussed in the context of moral behavior (Section
15.6).

• Humans perform significantly better on the most challenging SOTOPIA tasks
compared to even the best performing model (GPT-4).

The authors argue that the dynamic and interactive nature of SOTOPIA poses unique
challenges for LLM agents that static benchmarks systematically fail to reveal.
Social interaction in an extreme setting was studied in \[Campedelli et al., 2024\].
Inspired by the infamous Stanford Prison experiment \[Zimbardo, 1972\], the authors
examine the emergence of persuasive and abusive behavior in a setting of prisoners

## Page 328

328
CHAPTER 16. ROLE-BASED INTERACTION IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

Figure 16.7: Illustration of a Scenario with a Conflicting Social Goal from SOTOPIA
\[Zhou et al., 2023\]

## Page 329

16.4. CONCLUDING REMARKS
329

versus prison guards. It was found that the assigned personality of prisoner and guard
impact both persuasiveness and the emergence of anti-social behavior. Crucially, this
demonstrates that anti-social behavior can emerge in LLM agents through role assign-
ment and a specific interaction environment. This reveals a striking parallel to the
original experiment with human participants, and reminds us once again of the gap
between how a model judges situations (generally reflecting population-average moral
norms) and how an agent can behave once it is employed in a specific context of ac-
tion (see also Section 15.6). This study also finds that role assignment is not a neutral
engineering instrument: it can shape behavior in untoward ways.
To simulate strategic decision-making in cooperative settings, researchers have in-
troduced GovSim \[Piatti et al., 2024\]. They study how ethical considerations, strate-
gic planning, and negotiation skills impact cooperative outcomes. Most LLMs fail
to achieve an equilibrium since they fail to understand the long-term effects of their
actions on the group. Interestingly, the introduction of a special universalization rea-
soning language \[Levine et al., 2020\] (prompting models to ask the Kantian question:
What if everybody does that?) allowed more models to achieve a sustainable outcome.
Related results were demonstrated in NegotiationArena, introduced by Bianchi et al.
\[2024\]. They showed how LLM agents can conduct complex negotiations through
flexible dialogue in negotiation settings. The flexible dialogues significantly improved
negotiation outcomes by employing different behavioral strategies.

16.3.5
Conclusion

The studies in this section respond to the coordination weaknesses identified in Section
15.4 not by making individual agents better reasoners (as in 15.5.2), but by structuring
the interaction around them. Complementary roles tell each agent what its contribu-
tion should be, while interaction protocols and SOPs regulate when and in what form
agents communicate. In some setups, a judge or voting mechanism can help to channel
disagreement to a productive resolution.
Roles and interaction protocols provide crucial scaffolding where internal coor-
dination would otherwise fall short. This can be seen as a multi-agent analogue of
the structured reasoning schemes discussed in Chapter 15, such as Social Chain-of-
Thought, probabilistic graphs, or deliberation around moral rules. Such schemes turned
out to boost performance where unconstrained reasoning did not. In both the single-
and multi-agent cases, the model’s latent (social, moral, etc.) knowledge and behavior
are real, but need to be activated through an explicit structure.

16.4
Concluding Remarks

This chapter moved from LLM agents facing one another in strategic games, through
role-based collaboration patterns and the multiple setups that coordinate them in prac-
tice, to a critical assessment of when multi-agent systems work or fail.
In Chapter 15 we found single models that coordinate poorly and that can formally
predict what a partner will do without acting on that prediction in an agentic implemen-
tation. Both these patterns transfer to the multi-agent setting. Across benchmarks and

## Page 330

330
BIBLIOGRAPHY

platforms (e.g. \[Xu et al., 2024, Agashe et al., 2025\]), interacting LLM agents could
reason about self-interest, yet failed to coordinate their behavior such that they could
turn this reasoning into a strategic advantage. A dominant issue is their ability to con-
dition their behavior on their partners’ perspective, a problem foreshadowed in the gap
between knowing-doing or literal-functional competence for theory of mind, discussed
in Section 15.5. This resonates with work that systematically identifies inter-agent mis-
alignment as a dominant failure category for multi-agent systems \[Cemri et al., 2025\].
This literal-functional problem, once again, links to construct validity: just as acing
a theory of mind test does not establish a human-grade capacity for social reasoning,
a multi-agent setup outperforming a single LLM query does not establish collective
intelligence. Strong baselines, matched inference budgets, and ablations of the col-
laborative structure and interaction protocols would be the mulit-agent equivalents of
the perturbed ToM testing discussed in Section 15.5. More research is needed in the
multi-agent field to establish a solid empirical picture of where agentic LLM interaction
stands.
Finally, the multi-agent setting adds new risk categories. Role-assignment turned
out to be capable of activating anti-social and even abusive behavior in a setting inspired
by the Stanford Prison Experiment \[Campedelli et al., 2024\]. In other studies, miscoor-
dination, cascading hallucinations, and mutual reinforcement of weaknesses, triggered
norm violations, divulging of secrets, and reduction of task performance. Where spec-
ifying roles and interaction protocols scaffolded behavior and boosted performance in
some cases, in other cases these were a hindrance or a source of risk.
In the next chapter we discuss studies in which roles and protocols are not assigned,
but emerge from the interaction itself.

## Page 335

Chapter 17

Emergent Behavior in
Multi-LLM Systems


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how multiple LLM agents behave when they are
not assigned roles, in order to study emergent behavior in open-ended systems.
Specifically, you will be able to:
• Distinguish emergent multi-agent simulations from role-based interaction and
explain why open-ended settings call for different research questions and eval-
uation methods.
• Describe the architecture of generative agent simulations and how simulation
infrastructure scales from a handful of agents to thousands.
• Explain how (global-scale) conventions, norms, and meta-norms emerge from
(local-scale) agentic interactions in natural language.
• Understand how multi-agent simulation is used as a scientific instrument in com-
putational social science.
• Understand the importance of Open World benchmark environments for data
generation.
• Critically evaluate the validity of claims about concepts translated from a human
context, such as emergence, self-organization, or collective intelligence, and as-
sess the safety risks that open-ended multi-agent systems introduce.

17.1
What Is Emergent Multi-Agent Behavior?

The previous chapter studied multi-LLM systems in which every agent was assigned
a role and interactions were guided by protocols. Research questions concerned be-
havior within an assigned structure, asking how well a team of agents solve a task in
a controlled way. In this chapter agents are placed in an open-ended environment, and
the research questions shift from How do agents behave and perform given a certain

335

CHAPTER 17. EMERGENT BEHAVIOR IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

Figure 17.1: Agent-based Modeling and LLM-agents \[Gao et al., 2024\]

Figure 17.2: Structure of LLM-agents for Multi-Agent Modeling \[Gao et al., 2023\]

global structure? to What global structure emerges out of local agents interactions?

As we have seen in this book, agentic LLMs have enhanced abilities for percep-
tion, memory, reasoning, decision-making, and adaptive learning, and they can display
heterogeneous personality profiles \[Gao et al., 2023, 2024\]. Such features make them
also suitable for interacting in open-ended multi-agent simulations without prior role
assignment, as a proxy for human behavior in a society. Because LLM agents commu-
nicate in natural language, the interactions in such simulations are readable and inter-
pretable by researchers. This gives access to intermediate steps and makes simulations
much more comparable to human interaction compared to simulations in classic frame-
works, meeting long-standing interests from the social sciences. The general structure
of LLM-based agents suitable for such simulations is illustrated in Figure 17.1 and
Figure 17.2.

## Page 337

17.1. WHAT IS EMERGENT MULTI-AGENT BEHAVIOR?
337

17.1.1
From Agent-Based Modeling to Generative Agent Societies

The study of populations of interacting artificial agents has a decades-long history. In
agent-based modeling, macro-level patterns and regularities arise bottom-up out of lo-
cal interactions of simple agents \[Epstein and Axtell, 1996, Macal and North, 2010\].
One of the most influential results in agent-based modeling was that cooperation and
norms can emerge in populations of self-interested agents \[Axelrod, 1986\]. Cultural
evolution theory formalized how behavior can spread through a population by means of
imitation, communication, and education \[Boyd and Richerson, 1988\]. Steels \[1995\]’s
naming game demonstrated that even shared vocabularies (which are also in essence
conventions) can come into existence from pairwise interactions without central coor-
dination.
In classic agent-based simulations, agents followed hand-coded rules and exchanged
abstract information, rather than using natural language like the agents in this Chap-
ter. Another key contrast is that classic agents possess no background knowledge of
the world in any sense comparable to what LLM agents have. LLMs allow for an
entirely different level of simulations in which agents with rich and diverse personas
gossip, persuade, misunderstand, and negotiate in ways that are directly recognizable
to humans. Advances in simulation infrastructure make it feasible to run such agents
at population scale \[Gao et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024\]. The result is a new generation
of generative agent societies that give a new impulse to the old agent-based modeling
research agenda, while also introducing novel methodological problems and consider-
ations.
In Section 16.1.3 we introduced a spectrum of five axes for research control over
multi-LLM systems \[Tran et al., 2025\]. The difference between role-based and open-
ended simulations is a matter of degree rather than kind. Open-ended simulations sit
at one end of the spectrum, opposite role-defined and protocolized interactions. Open-
ended simulations still involve design choices that seed the outcomes, but they do so
in a less deterministic way, purposefully leaving space for new patterns to emerge.
This shifts the focus of the research: instead of evaluating performance on a task or
clearly defined goal, studies have an open lens—the interaction pattern is the research
goal. Open-ended simulatinos observe and explore in a more ethnographical way how
agents behave and interact, which requires different methodologies, as we will now
discuss.

17.1.2
A Methodological Note

The methodological issues discussed in Chapters 15 and 16 all carry over to the open-
ended setting: prompt sensitivity, run-to-run variability, cascading hallucinations, mu-
tual reinforcement of weaknesses, and validity of terminology from the human context,
all pose challenges for open-ended simulations. We will see that this setting amplifies
some problems, while mitigating others. For example, in the absence of protocols that
apply every time agents interact, small variations at the level of a single agent may put
the entire simulation on a different track. This is what makes open-ended simulations
both interesting and brittle. An example of a new issue that the open-ended setting
introduces is that there can be a thin line between emergence and retrieval: when LLM

## Page 338

338
CHAPTER 17. EMERGENT BEHAVIOR IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

agents in an open-ended simulation converge on a norm, it is unclear whether this norm
emerges de novo from their interaction, or whether it was simply retrieved from their
pretrained world knowledge.
Extensive overviews of this emerging field are provided by Mou et al. \[2024\],
Savarimuthu et al. \[2024\], and Xi et al. \[2023\]. We will discuss infrastructure and
simulation platforms in Section 17.2, then go to the emergence of conventions and
norms in Section 17.3, and conclude by discussing the importance of open world en-
vironments in Section 17.4. Finally , we reflect on risks of the open-ended setting,
in Section 17.5. Then, Chapter 18, contains a practical case in which you will work
hands-on with an open-ended simulation.

17.2
Simulation Infrastructure

Open-ended simulations require infrastructures that, on the one hand, provide a plat-
form where research data is being recorded while agents sustain their interaction and
behavior over a longer period of time. On the other hand, those infrastructures should
allow for enough space for phenomena to occur bottom-up and unknown structure to
emerge, and as such not be limiting. In this section we focus on scale, going from a
single simulated community inhabiting a virtual town to societies of a million agents.

17.2.1
Small Worlds

A system called Generative Agents was introduced by Park et al. \[2023\]. Generative
Agents is an environment where users can interact with a simulated town populated by
25 LLM-based agents. Based on social simulacra techniques proposed earlier \[Park
et al., 2022\], each agent was initiated with a unique persona and memory. For each
agent, a record is kept of all the experiences and conversations in the simulation. This
record is used to synthesize higher-level reflections, and plan further behavior (see
Figure 17.3).
In Generative Agents, the agents behave somewhat like characters in the video
game The Sims \[Nutt and Railton, 2003\]: they initiate conversations, form relation-
ships, spread information, and coordinate ad hoc group activities (see Figure 17.4).
Note that the interactions are influenced by user input and are therefore semi-autonomous,
the simulation is largely unscripted, but not fully. How a simulation works is illustrated
by the example of a Valentine’s Day party: the plan for the party was initiated with a
user prompt, and subsequently multiple agents spread invitations to one another and
show up at the right time with coordinated plans (some are late, just as in real life).
The agents developed believable social routines (such as daily schedules, and gossip-
ing) and even exhibit human-like character traits (some agents demonstrated deception
or stubbornness, while others showed cooperation). These results show that, with the
right starting prompt, social patterns can emerge from dynamic, semi-autonomous,
LLM interactions.

17.2.2
Societies of Thousands to a Million Agents

Scaling the Generative Agents architecture beyond 25 agents raises questions about
inference cost and environments that are rich enough to occupy thousands of agents.1

A large-scale social simulation is a trade-off between available compute power, total
simulation run-time, number of simulated agents, and accuracy of individual agent
behavior. Several platforms address these questions.
AgentSociety is a simulation at a large scale, involving over 10,000 agents \[Piao
et al., 2025b\]. It couples LLM-driven agents with a realistic urban environment with a
focus on mobility, employment, and consumption. It aims not only to study everyday
social dynamics (as in Generative Agents), but also offers a testbed for computational
social experiments. To allow for the required scale, the simulation runs on a distributed
inference backend, with stricter control of agent behavior.
OASIS is a scalable social media simulator for Twitter/X and Reddit \[Yang et al.,
2024\]. It supports modeling of up to one million LLM-agents. It is built on CAMEL
\[Li et al., 2023\] and has role-based agents as its starting point. In OASIS, not ev-
ery agent action involves an LLM-call, and not all agents are active all the time. At
its large scale, OASIS shows various social group phenomena, including spreading of
(mis)information, group polarization, and herd effects. OASIS is built upon an environ-
ment server, recommender system, agent module, time engine, and scalable inferencer
(see Figure 17.5).
Project Sid \[Ahn et al., 2024\] places up to 1000 agents in a Minecraft world and re-
ports a striking emergence result: agents are observed to develop specialized economic
roles (farmers, miners, guards), adhere to collectively adopted rules such as taxation,

and transmit cultural and even religious memes across settlements. However, even
though the interactions were not scripted, the emergence–retrieval caveat formulated
above applies here: the observed roles and behaviors can be expected to be abundantly
described in the training data of the LLMs powering the individual agents.

17.2.3
Simulation as a Scientific Instrument

In addition to being impressive showcases of scalable LLM technology, when used
carefully, these platforms can be used for intricate computational social experiments.
Simulated generative agent societies have been used to study long-standing research
questions from the social sciences (Section 17.1). AgentSociety, for example, has been
used for various case studies including the spread of inflammatory messages, polariza-
tion, the effects of universal basic income policies, and the impact of external shocks
to a society such as hurricanes \[Piao et al., 2025b,a\]. Such experiments would be un-
ethical, impractical, or outright impossible to run on human populations. The authors
argue that in simulations they can be repeated and changes to the experiment can be be
made at every step.

Li et al. \[2024b\] further illustrate the approach for misinformation. Their agents
exhibit diverse profiles in terms of gender, age, and the big five personality traits.2 One
of the findings is that encouraging comments does not significantly reduce the spread
of misinformation, whereas publicly labeling information with accuracy scores and
blocking specific influencers proved to be effective strategies, particularly in scale-free
networks \[Barab´asi, 2009\]. The pattern of such studies is characteristic: a candidate
intervention is implemented as a change to the simulated platform, and its macro-level
effect is measured over many runs. Whether these effects transfer to human populations
is precisely the validity question of Section 17.1.2; simulations of this kind are best read
as hypothesis generators and pre-tests, not as substitutes for field experiments.

A Borderline Case: AgentVerse
AgentVerse \[Chen et al., 2023\] is, strictly speak-
ing, a role-based system of the kind studied in Chapter 16. In AgentVerse problem
solving is split into four stages of expert recruitment, collaborative decision making,
action execution, and evaluation, iterated until the result is satisfactory (Figure 17.6).
We mention it here because of what happened beyond the design: agents manifest
emergent behaviors such as volunteering, characterized by agents offering assistance
to peers, and conformity, where agents adjust deviated behaviors under the criticism
of others. Destructive behaviors were also observed, occasionally leading to unde-
sired and detrimental outcomes. The fact that macro-scale behavior emerged in a role-
scripted simulation, illustrates that the role-based/emergent distinction is a spectrum:
even tightly protocolized systems regularly display behavior that nobody purposely
designed. We return to the risks associated with this observation in Section 17.5.

2Also known as OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.

17.3
Emergent Conventions and Norms

Authors have observed emergent patterns in several open-ended multi-agent simula-
tions. In this section we shift focus from the level of infrastructures and interactions to
the level of the conventions and norms.
EvolutionaryAgent \[Li et al., 2024a\] studies agent alignment in a multi-agent sys-
tem, with evolutionary methods that go beyond Reinforcement Learning from Human
Feedback (see Figure 17.7). EvolutionaryAgent follows a controlled approach to norm
emergence: it does not permit the evolution of social norms to be disorderly or ran-
dom, but it also does not intervene in each step of their evolution. The authors define
the initial social norms and a desired direction of evolution. Agents with higher fit-
ness (more norm-conforming) are more likely to reproduce, leading to the diffusion of
their strategies, gradually stabilizing and forming new social norms. Defining a com-
plete, realistic, and complex virtual society is challenging. The purpose of the work
is to study how, if such a virtual society existed, a system could further enable intri-
cate behaviors of agents, and how this would lead to the emergence of new dynamics.
The system provides a sandbox for investigating the safety of AI systems before they
impact the real world.
Based on Steels \[1995\]’s naming game, different approaches were implemented,
using agents powered by LLaMa 3 and Claude 3.5 \[Kouwenhoven et al., 2024, Ashery
et al., 2024, Baronchelli, 2023\]. These studies find that globally accepted conventions
(or norms) can spontaneously arise from local interactions between communicating
LLMs. The authors also demonstrate how strong collective biases can emerge during

## Page 343

17.3. EMERGENT CONVENTIONS AND NORMS
343

Figure 17.7: Overview of EvolutionaryAgent \[Li et al., 2024a\]

this process, even when individual agents appear to be unbiased, and how minority
groups of committed LLMs can drive social change by establishing new social conven-
tions that can overturn established behaviors.
The emergence of norms is studied at another level by Horiguchi et al. \[2024\], who
explore the potential for LLM agents to spontaneously generate and adhere to norma-
tive strategies, building upon the foundational work of Axelrod’s metanorm games.
Metanorms are norms about enforcing norms: the punishment of those who do not
punish agents that are breaking norms \[Axelrod, 1986\]. Controlling for the personal-
ity traits vengefulness and boldness, they find that through dialogue, LLM agents can
form complex social norms, such as metanorms, purely through natural language inter-
action. A related study by He et al. \[2024\] evaluates the capability of LLMs to detect
norm violations. Based on simulated data from 80 stories in a household context, they
investigated whether 10 norms are violated, and found ChatGPT-4 being able for detect
norm violations, with Mistral some distance behind.

Qiu et al. \[2024\] go a step beyond norms, and study the cultural and social aware-
ness of LLM agents. They introduce CASA, a benchmark designed to assess LLM
agents’ sensitivity to cultural and social norms across two web-based tasks: online
shopping and social discussion forums. (CASA is based on WebArena \[Qi et al.,
2024\].) Current LLMs perform significantly better in non-agent than in agent web-
based environments, with agents achieving less than 10% awareness coverage and over
40% violation rates. However, using prompting and fine-tuning on specific datasets,
cultural and social awareness can be improved.
Inspired by Minsky’s Society of Mind \[Minsky, 1988\], cooperation mechanisms are
explored in Zhang et al. \[2023\]’s agentic LLM simulation. This simulation consists of
four different societies of LLM agents, where each agent is characterized by a specific
trait (easy-going or overconfident) and engages in cooperation with a distinct thinking
pattern (debate or reflection). They find that LLM agents manifest human-like social
behaviors, such as conformity and consensus reaching, mirroring foundational social
psychology theories. Figure 17.8 illustrates the societies with different types of agents.
The question whether groups of LLM agents can successfully engage in cross-
national collaboration and debate is studied by \[Baltaji et al., 2024\]. Multi agent dis-

17.4
Evaluating Agents in Open World Environments

One of the main drivers of agentic LLM research is the problem of plateauing LLM
performance due to limited training data. Open World multi-agent interaction aims to
address this problem, generating data with multi agent simulations. Machine learning
can learn no more complexity than what is present in the dataset (or environment). The
idea of an open world model is that it can create infinite datasets or environments, in
which agents can continue to learn, to keep improving their intelligence. How should
such unlimited challenges be created? The advent of LLMs has given a new impulse to
this research question. This idea is followed, for example, in the multi agent finetuning
approach \[Subramaniam et al., 2025\].
Current agents are primarily created and tested in simplified synthetic environ-
ments, leading to a disconnect with real-world scenarios. Zhou et al. \[2023\] build
an environment, WebArena, that is more realistic and reproducible. WebArena is an
environment with fully functional websites from four common domains: e-commerce,
social forum discussions, collaborative software development, and content manage-
ment.
Games are also often used as benchmarks for interactive behavior. Real-world tasks
require handling intricate interactions, advanced spatial reasoning, long-term planning,
and continuous exploration of new strategies. BALROG \[Paglieri et al., 2025\], the
system that we used for Case Study 2, incorporates planning environments of varying
levels of difficulty, ranging from tasks that are solvable by non-expert humans in sec-
onds to challenging ones that may take years to master (such as the NetHack Learning
Environment). They find that while current models achieve partial success in the easier
games, they struggle significantly with more challenging tasks such as vision-based
decision-making.
Progress in machine learning depends on the availability of benchmarks. As models
evolve, there is a need to create benchmarks that can measure progress on new gener-
ative capabilities \[Butt et al., 2024\]. BENCHAGENTS decomposes the benchmark
creation process into planning, generation, data verification, and evaluation, each of
which is executed by an LLM agent. These agents interact with each other and utilize
human-in-the-loop feedback to explicitly improve and flexibly control data diversity
and quality. BENCHAGENTS creates benchmarks to evaluate capabilities related to
planning and constraint satisfaction.
AgentBoard provides an evaluation of the breadth of existing benchmarks \[Ma
et al., 2024\]. Benchmarks should have task diversity. It is necessary to cover various
agent tasks such as embodied, web, and tool tasks. Additionally, multi round inter-
action is important, to mimic realistic scenarios. Existing benchmarks typically adopt
single-round tasks. Furthermore, agents should be evaluated in partially-observable
environments, to test if they can actively explore their surroundings. Existing agent

## Page 346

346
CHAPTER 17. EMERGENT BEHAVIOR IN MULTI-LLM SYSTEMS

benchmarks fail to satisfy all of these criteria \[Ma et al., 2024\].
Research on Open World environments is related to curriculum learning. Pre-LLMs
work already shows that agent societies may create an automated curriculum of ever in-
creasing difficulty \[Elman, 1991, Bengio et al., 2009, Silver et al., 2017, Soviany et al.,
2022\], requiring increasing levels of intelligent behavior from the agents \[Racaniere
et al., 2019\]. Similar results have been observed for LLMs \[Feng et al., 2023\]. For
example, WebArena is used to study self-evolving curricula \[Qi et al., 2024\], which
can also help robot training \[Ryu et al., 2024\] or to mitigate hallucination \[Zhao et al.,
2024\].

17.5
Risks of Emergent Behavior

Chapter 16 closed by noting that role assignment introduces risk, since agents may
display unintended, even anti-social, behavior simply by playing a part too well. The
open-ended setting arguably raises the stakes, since fewer safeguards are built in, and
undesirable behavior can arise bottom-up from interaction dynamics. In a sense, this
anti-social behavior should not be too surprising, when we remember that the goal of
the earliest multi-agent simulations was to find out if cooperative behavior could ever
emerge out of the interaction between self-interested agents—which, to the surprise
of the researchers, happened, but only under the right circumstances \[Axelrod, 1981\].
The line between cooperative behavior and competitive behavior is thin.
AgentVerse observed destructive behaviors emerging alongside cooperative ones,
occasionally leading to detrimental outcomes \[Chen et al., 2023\]. The naming-game
studies showed that strong collective biases can emerge from populations of individ-
ually unbiased agents, and that small committed minorities can overturn established
conventions \[Ashery et al., 2024, Kouwenhoven et al., 2024\]. These mechanisms are
neutral in themselves, but could be exploited by agents that are not well-intended. At
platform scale, OASIS and AgentSociety reproduce misinformation spread, group po-
larization, herding effects, and the propagation of toxic content \[Yang et al., 2024, Piao
et al., 2025a\]; the same fidelity that makes these simulations scientifically useful makes
them in principle rehearsal spaces for manipulation strategies.
The constructive response is to turn this risk around. EvolutionaryAgent frames
its virtual society explicitly as a sandbox for investigating the safety of AI systems
before they impact the real world \[Li et al., 2024a\]. If norms among agents can be
steered toward a desired direction in simulation, then the same machinery can be used
to stress-test alignment approaches under population dynamics rather than in isolation.
Open-ended simulation can be used to understand the circumstances when risks first
emerge, and to cheaply study defenses against these risks.

17.6
Concluding Remarks

We have covered open-ended multi-LLM simulations without prior role assignment.
These simulations give a new impulse to long-standing interests in the social sciences to
model self-organizing behaviors, collective intelligence and the development of social

## Page 347

BIBLIOGRAPHY
347

conventions and norms. The scale of such simulations varies from a few interacting
agents up to a million.
The availability of infrastructure that supports large scale simulations enables fur-
ther studies. However, an open question is to what extent autonomous simulations
are truly open-ended, and not influenced by the LLM prompts and agent scaffolding.
Furthermore, although the purpose of open-ended simulations is to observe emerging
behavior, one has to be careful in interpreting behavioral outcome patterns. All LLM
agents are pretrained on human-generated data. It is difficult to distinguish which ele-
ments of behavioral patterns emerge out of agent-agent interaction, and which elements
are merely the result of retrieved pretrained behaviors.

## Page 353

Chapter 18

Case Study 4: Simulating
Societies with LLM Agents


What You Will Learn

In this case study you will familiarize yourselves with agent-based social simula-
tions through the lens of the widely adopted Generative Agents framework \[Park
et al., 2023\]. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Run and configure a multi-agent social simulation powered by LLMs.
• Work with a structured machine-psychological experiment.
• Compare two cognitive architectures: a standard memory system and one with
a negativity bias.
• Investigate how personality descriptions and architectural choices shape emer-
gent agent behavior.
• Critically reflect on prompt fragility, model dependence, and the limits of LLM-
driven simulations.

18.1
Social Simulation

In social simulations, generative agents are LLM-driven characters that interact with an
environment and with one another. The agents may plan activities, maintain memories,
or reflect on their experiences. The Generative Agents Framework, introduced by Park
et al. \[2023\], showed that LLM-powered characters together can produce believable
daily routines, social interactions, and even coordinated group activities—all emerging
from a relatively simple and elegant cognitive architecture.
The twist in this case study is that you will work with two cognitive architectures
for your agents, run the same scenario with both, and compare the emergent behavior.
One architecture treats all memories equally. The other introduces a negativity bias:
negative experiences are encoded more strongly and are more likely to be retrieved and
reflected upon. We will observe that this asymmetry, inspired by findings from cogni-

353

## Page 354

354
CHAPTER 18. CASE STUDY 4: SIMULATING SOCIETIES

tive psychology \[Baumeister et al., 2001\], has measurable effects on our experimental
agents.
The goal of this chapter is to understand how architectural choices—in our case,
small changes in the internal processing of an agent—lead to emergent consequences.
You will also see how fragile agent personas can be: a single word in a personality
description, or a subtle change in memory weighting, can fundamentally alter how an
agent acts, plans, and reflects.

Course Materials

You can find the course exercise materials here:
https://github.com/DorotaMoravcikova/agentic-llm-course-excercises

18.2
Background

18.2.1
Generative Agents

The generative agents framework, introduced by Park et al. \[2023\], showed that LLM-
powered characters can produce believable daily routines, social interactions, and even
coordinate group activities.
Each agent has three core components:

1. Memory stream: a timestamped log of everything the agent has perceived, done,
and thought.

2. Retrieval function: when the agent needs to act, it retrieves relevant memories
based on recency, importance, and relevance to the current situation.

3. Reflection mechanism: periodically, the agent synthesizes higher-level insights
from its raw memories.

The agent’s personality is defined by a short natural-language description—a scratch
file that specifies the character’s name, age, learned and innate traits, and their lifestyle.
This description is included in every LLM prompt, anchoring the agent’s behavior.

18.2.2
Bad is Stronger Than Good

When an LLM-powered agent embedded in the original Generative Agents simula-
tion receives criticism, it forms a memory. When praised an hour later, it forms an-
other memory. Generative agents retrieve the two memories—one negative and one
positive—with identical priority, as long as they are equally recent, equally relevant,
and equally important.
In general, cognitive architectures for agent-based social simulations draw on cog-
nitive science to produce believable behavior. The recency, relevance, and importance
variables are loosely inspired by insights about memory retrieval in humans. The im-
portance variable captures something akin to the arousal or salience of an event. How-
ever, in the original simulation \[Park et al., 2022\] the memory system is effectively

### Page links

- [Link 1](https://github.com/DorotaMoravcikova/agentic-llm-course-excercises)

## Page 355

18.3. IMPLEMENTATION
355

valence-blind: all memories—positive, negative, neutral—are encoded and retrieved
with equal weight. If the agent were human, it would treat the negatively valenced
event differently: encoding it with sharper sensory detail, retrieving it with greater
vividness, and rendering it more likely to resurface in subsequent thoughts. Psycho-
logical studies find that people remember insults longer than compliments. A single
bad interaction with a colleague can outweigh weeks of pleasant ones. In other words,
in our psychology bad is stronger than good \[Baumeister et al., 2001\], and this asym-
metry is nowhere more consequential than in memory.
In this case study, we test the effect of implementing the NEVER (Negative Emo-
tional Valence Enhances Recapitulation) model, a more human-like mechanism for
memory retrieval. In the NEVER-augmented agent, negative memories receive higher
importance scores at encoding time. As a consequence, they are more likely to be
retrieved and more likely to trigger reflections.
The architecture remains identical in every other respect. This allows for a con-
trolled machine-psychological experiment in which the effects can be compared of an
architectural choice: valence-blind versus valence-sensitive memory. In addition, you
will use the structured setup to test the effects of adapting the agent initialisations in
terms of their personality descriptions and system prompts.

18.2.3
Why This Matters for Agent Design

This case study illustrates two important lessons:

1. Architectural choices have emergent consequences: A memory weighting pa-
rameter that seems innocuous at the component level can produce dramatic changes
in the agent’s social behavior, emotional tone, and decision-making over time.
These emergent effects are difficult to predict from the architecture alone.

2. Prompt fragility: Agent behavior is highly sensitive to the contents of personal-
ity descriptions and system prompts. Small perturbations can produce large be-
havioral shifts—a phenomenon sometimes called prompt sensitivity in the LLM
literature.

18.3
Implementation

18.3.1
The Simulation Environment

The simulation uses the Smallville environment from Park et al. \[2023\]: a small town
rendered as a 2D tile map, where agents move between locations, interact with objects,
and have conversations.
Our simulation features a simplified scenario: a cafe with three agents. Please
meet:

• Dolores: A barista. Warm, empathetic, detail-oriented. The experimental agent—
the one who will receive the negativity bias.

## Page 356

356
CHAPTER 18. CASE STUDY 4: SIMULATING SOCIETIES

• Maeve: A barista with a matched personality profile. The control agent—standard
architecture, no negativity bias.

• Bernard: The cafe manager.
Unpredictable, moody, occasionally confronta-
tional. Bernard serves as a naturalistic stressor: a source of social friction that
both baristas are exposed to.

This setup with three agents of which two have a similar role and position (barista
working under supervision of Bernard), allows for a controlled experiment with agent
architectures and initializations. In our first step, Dolores and Maeve are given the same
personality traits and are exposed to the same environment. The only difference is in
how Dolores processes her memories: using the NEVER implementation that encodes
negative memories with higher importance.

18.3.2
Agent Architecture

Each agent maintains:

• A personality description (the scratch file): a short text describing the agent’s
name, traits, occupation, relationships, and goals.

• A memory stream: a list of timestamped observations, actions, and reflections.

• A current plan: a short description of what the agent intends to do.

18.3.3
The Cognitive Loop

At each simulation step (representing 10 seconds of in-game time), each agent executes
the following cycle:

1. Perceive: Observe the current state of the environment—what other agents are
doing, any ongoing conversations, changes in the surroundings.

2. Retrieve: Query the memory stream for relevant past experiences.

3. Plan: Given the personality description, retrieved memories, and current obser-
vations, use the LLM to decide what to do next.

4. Act: Execute the planned action in the environment.

5. Reflect (periodic): Every few hours of in-game time, synthesize higher-level
reflections from recent memories.

Each of these steps involves an LLM call. The prompt is constructed from the
agent’s personality description (which remains constant) and the relevant retrieved
memories and current observations (which are dynamic).

18.3.4
Two Architecture Variants

You will work with two variants of the retrieval function:

## Page 357

18.4. DISCUSSION
357

Variant A: Baseline memory retrieval
Retrieval is based on a weighted combi-
nation of recency, relevance, and importance. This is the standard generative agent
architecture as described by Park et al. \[2023\].

Variant B: Negativity-biased memory retrieval
When a new memory is created, its
emotional valence is assessed. The retrieval function is extended with a valence term.
Absolute valence is normalized to \[0, 1\] and multiplied by 1.5 for negative memories,
producing a retrieval hierarchy (negative > positive > neutral). The retrieval score
becomes:
score = 𝛼rec · 𝑅+ 𝛼rel · 𝐿+ 𝛼imp · 𝐼+ 𝛼val · 𝑉
(18.1)

with all 𝛼= 1. Thus: the only difference between the two variants is the addition of
the valence term; everything else is identical.

18.3.5
Setup and Installation

Clone the repository and follow the instructions in the README:
https://github.com/DorotaMoravcikova/generative_agents/tree/
course-exercises

18.4
Discussion

Having run your experiments, reflect on the following questions:

1. Prompt versus Architecture: You have seen that both the personality prompt and
the memory architecture influence agent behavior. Which lever is more power-
ful? Which is more predictable? If a simulation were to be used for consequential
applications such as modeling policy adoption, which would you prefer to use to
shape agent behavior, and why?

2. Emergent Behavior: Did you observe any agent behaviors that surprised you—
things that were not explicitly specified in the personality or architecture? What
mechanisms produced these emergent behaviors in your view?

3. Evaluation Challenges: How do you evaluate whether a generative agent is be-
having well? The valence score is one metric, but it is itself an LLM judgment.
What are the limitations of using an LLM to evaluate the output of another LLM
(or the same LLM)? Can you think of alternative evaluation approaches?

4. Cognitive Realism: The negativity bias is one example of a finding from cog-
nitive psychology. Can you think of other cognitive biases or memory effects
that could be implemented architecturally? What would you expect their emer-
gent effects to be? (Consider, for example: confirmation bias, the availability
heuristic, recency bias.)

BIBLIOGRAPHY

18.5
Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have familiarized ourselves with a generative agent simulation and
used it to explore two important phenomena in agentic AI: the emergent effects of
cognitive architecture choices (the negativity bias) and the sensitivity of agent behavior
to prompt content (prompt fragility).
We have seen that a small change in how memories are weighted—negative mem-
ories receiving higher importance scores—can produce measurable shifts in agent be-
havior over time. We have also seen that agent personas are fragile: small changes
to personality descriptions can produce large and sometimes unpredictable behavioral
effects.
These findings have practical implications for anyone building LLM-driven agent
systems. The persona is not a reliable anchor for behavior. The architecture—how
memories are stored, retrieved, and reflected upon—shapes behavior in ways that may
not be apparent from reading the code.
The field of generative agent simulation is young and evolving. The exercises in
this chapter have given you hands-on experience with the core mechanisms and the
core challenges. As the field matures, the problems of prompt robustness, cognitive
architecture design, and emergent behavior evaluation will remain central.

Bibliography

Agentic LLMs are new, and there is much research activity, on many topics. In this
part we have selected four research areas where important developments are under way.
These are: synthetic data generation, advanced architectures, mechanistic interpretabil-
ity, and perspectives on the cognitive architectures of agents. There are certainly many
more interesting research directions in agentic LLMs; we have selected these topics
because they connect to important points that were raised earlier in the book.
Note that the purpose of the previous chapters was to explain matters as clearly as
possible—suitable for a master’s course. The purpose of the next chapters is to cover
more advanced material—suitable for a master’s thesis. Of course we still try to be
clear, but the speed will be higher, and the depth will be deeper, with more references
to research papers. We encourage you to look up these sources. If you are looking for
inspiration for your own further research, we hope that these chapters will be of help.

## Page 363

Chapter 19

*Synthetic Data Generation for
Training Agentic LLMs


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn the role that synthetic data can play in the develop-
ment of agentic large language models. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Characterize the importance of data in the LLM training pipeline.
• Explain the general loop of distilling knowledge from stronger models for
weaker students.
• Describe the pipeline components for which synthetic data is being used as an
alternative to human-generated content.
• Outline the various strategies for curating and evaluating synthetic data.
• Contrast the advantages and disadvantages of using synthetic data by describing
the risks of using artificially generated data.

19.1
The Importance of Data

The rapid scaling of LLMs has led to a significant demand for training and evalua-
tion data. Some have coined training data the digital oil, reflecting the importance as
primary ingredient for AI development. Furthermore, data is increasingly becoming a
differentiating factor since other components of the pipeline, such as model architec-
tures, are homogenizing \[Kim et al., 2025a\]. As models continue to scale, they require
trillions of words of human-generated text scraped from the internet; however, there
is only a limited amount of human-generated data available, which raises the question
of whether training data could become the main bottleneck to scaling, see Figure 19.1
\[Villalobos et al., 2024\]. Moreover, as data requirements grow in scale, the acquisi-
tion of data becomes increasingly prohibitive in terms of cost and time, since most of
the straightforward sources are becoming exhausted. Furthermore, issues with privacy,
copyright, and bias cause the field to be looking beyond the curation of web-based

Figure 19.1: Projections of the available human-generated public text and dataset sizes
to train LLMs \[Villalobos et al., 2024\]. The intersection of the stock and dataset size
projection lines indicates the median year (2028) in which the stock is expected to be

human-generated data, and instead turn towards synthetic data generation \[Liang et al.,
2022\].
LLMs increasingly generate the data that trains the next generation of LLMs them-
selves: models are prompted to produce instructions, dialogues, reasoning traces, and
even entire training corpora that are then used to finetune, distill and evaluate other
models \[Long et al., 2024\]. This self-reinforcing loop lowers the cost and effort of data
collection compared to sourcing and annotating human-generated text, while also offer-
ing fine-grained control over style, difficulty, and coverage of the resulting datasets. By
now, this approach has drawn significant industrial \[Kapania et al., 2025\] and academic
interest \[Viswanathan et al., 2025, Alismail and Lanquillon, 2025\], spanning applica-
tions from general-purpose instruction tuning to the more specialized data needed to
train agentic behaviors such as tool use, planning, and multi-step reasoning (illustrated
in Figure 1.1 on page 17).
The growing reliance on model-generated data has also introduced a new term in
the scaling laws (Chapter 4), one that accounts for the proportion of synthetic data
present in a pre-training corpus. Recent work such as SYNTHLLM \[Qin et al., 2025\] il-
lustrates why this matters: by automatically extracting high-level concepts from source
documents and recombining them through a graph-based algorithm, it generates syn-
thetic corpora diverse enough to follow a predictable, rectified scaling law across model
sizes. In this version of the scaling laws, the gains taper off earlier (before other token
budgets typically used in pretraining), and larger models reach their optimal perfor-
mance on comparatively fewer tokens than smaller ones. This suggests that synthetic
data can be tuned not just for volume, but also for the shape of the scaling curve it
produces.
Beyond scaling behavior, generating data for agentic capabilities—tool use, plan-
ning, and multi-step reasoning—increasingly depends on coordinated multi-agent work-

19.2
Distillation Loop

Using synthetic data in the agentic LLM training pipeline follows the overall distilla-
tion loop, as shown in Figure 19.2. A generator (a strong model, or an orchestration
of several agents) uses a small amount of seed or real data to generate a large pool of
raw synthetic data. That pool is then curated (Section 19.4) before being used to train
or distill a model. Crucially, the resulting model can itself become the generator for
the next iteration. This closing of the self-reinforcing loop brings considerable risk to
training stability and downstream performance (see also the discussion of stability in
metalearning, Chapter 8).
Distillation is the special case of synthetic-data generation in which the generator is
a stronger model whose capability we are trying to transfer. In knowledge distillation,
a compact student model learns to copy a more capable teacher \[Hinton et al., 2015, Hu
et al., 2022\]. It can do so by directly optimizing against the teacher’s output predictions,
or it can do so by simply training on synthetic data emitted by a teacher. The goal of
distillation is to get a more efficient version of the teacher, both at inference time and
in terms of data cost, without sacrificing too much task performance. Distillation has
been applied widely, including in agentic settings \[e.g., Li et al., 2025a, Du et al., 2025\].
Distillation can also be used to derive preference data for instruction tuning. Zephyr
\[Tunstall et al., 2024\], for example, was trained with AI feedback, where outputs are
generated and ranked by strong teacher models, aligning a small model with user intent
at minimal data and training cost.

## Page 366

366
CHAPTER 19. *SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION

Four axes of distillation
Concrete distillation methods can be organized along four
axes. (1) The signal: whether the student imitates teacher logits, full output sequences,
or a scalar reward derived from the teacher. (2) The data source: whether the sequences
being scored are generated by the teacher or sampled from the student. (3) The timing:
whether that data is produced once up front (off-policy) or continuously as the student
changes (on-policy). (4) The teacher identity: whether the teacher is a stronger separate
model or the student itself.
We will now discuss these four axes of distillation.

19.2.1
Signal: The Distillation Objective

When we have white-box access to the teacher’s (𝑞) probabilities, the student 𝑝𝜃is
trained to make the student’s next-token distribution match the teacher’s. In distillation,
we often soften the distributions with a shared temperature 𝜏(so 𝑞𝜏(·) ∝exp(𝑧/𝜏) for
logits 𝑧). A generic distillation loss over a corpus of sequences is

L(𝜃) = E𝑥

"∑︁

𝑡
𝐷␀𝑞𝜏(· | 𝑥<𝑡) ∥𝑝𝜏
𝜃(· | 𝑥<𝑡)
#

,
(19.1)

where the sum runs over token positions 𝑡, 𝐷is a divergence (most commonly the
KL divergence), and the temperature 𝜏> 1 flattens both distributions so that the stu-
dent also learns from the teacher’s relative confidence. When only the teacher’s text
is available (black-box distillation, the usual case when distilling from a proprietary
API), we no longer observe 𝑞but only some tokens that we sample from it. The soft
target 𝑞𝜏(· | 𝑥<𝑡) then collapses to a one-hot vector on the sampled token, the diver-
gence 𝐷becomes the token-level cross-entropy, and Equation 19.1 reduces to ordinary
supervised fine-tuning on the teacher’s generations. In Section 19.3 we discuss the
Self-Instruct technique \[Wang et al., 2023b\]. This methods perform distillation from
the data side, and is therefore a black-box approach.

19.2.2
Data Source: Teacher-Student Paradigm

In distillation, the intuitive assumption is that a bigger, stronger teacher is always better.
However, there are exceptions \[Xu et al., 2025a, Li et al., 2025b\]. A capable teacher
may produce traces that are too long, too complex, or stylistically mismatched for
a small student to absorb. This phenomenon is known as the small model learnability
gap. Figure 19.3 illustrates a situation where small students learn more from the shorter
reasoning of a weaker teacher than from the elaborate chains of thought of a frontier
model. The practical implication is that the teacher should be chosen relative to the
current capabilities of the student rather than maximized in isolation \[Zhang et al.,
2026a\].

19.2.3
Timing: Off-policy versus On-policy Distillation

The third axis concerns timing. The most common recipe in distillation is off-policy
distillation. Here we sample a fixed dataset of completions from the teacher and then

## Page 367

19.2. DISTILLATION LOOP
367

Figure 19.3: Visualization of the Small Model Learnability Gap, where small student
models do not consistently benefit from long CoT reasoning and instead perform better
when fine-tuned on shorter CoT reasoning from smaller teachers \[Li et al., 2025b\]

fine-tune the student on them (as in the black-box case above). This is a simple and
parallelizable approach, but it suffers from a train/inference mismatch. The student is
only once shown teacher-generated token sequences at training time, yet at deployment
time it must continue its own, possibly flawed, sequences, which may be different
than the ones it has been trained on. This exposure bias compounds over long agentic
trajectories.
On-policy distillation addresses this by sampling sequences from the student itself
and having the teacher score them, all within the loop. Generalized Knowledge Dis-
tillation (GKD) trains the student on its self-generated output sequences using teacher
feedback on those sequences \[Agarwal et al., 2024\]. The student is corrected exactly
on the distribution of the states that it actually visits.
This on-policy view makes the connection to reinforcement learning through im-
itation learning explicit. The per-token teacher divergence in Equation 19.1 acts as a
dense, token-level reward. Distillation is turned into a form of reinforcement learning
where the teacher, rather than a sparse outcome checker, supplies the reward signal
\[Lu and Lab, 2025\]. Hybrid schemes push this idea further by selectively imitating
the teacher only where it helps during a reinforcement learning phase \[Zhang et al.,
2026b\].

19.2.4
Teacher Identity: Self-Distillation and Self-Improvement

The teacher and student model do not have to be different. When the teacher and stu-
dent model are the same, distillation becomes self-improvement: the model generates
candidate solutions, keeps the ones that pass a check, and trains on them. STaR \[Ze-
likman et al., 2022a\] bootstraps reasoning in this way, iteratively generating rationales,
retaining those that reach the correct answer, and finetuning on them.
Another approach is Self-Play Finetuning (SPIN) \[Chen et al., 2024\].
In this
method the model distinguishes its own generations from reference data across iter-
ations, improving alignment without any external teacher. Perhaps surprisingly, even
repeated self-distillation, with no new data source, can yield measurable gains, up to a

## Page 368

368
CHAPTER 19. *SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION

point \[Pareek et al., 2024\].
Self-improvement is most powerful when candidate outputs can be verified cheaply.
In such cases, an external signal can still be incorporated effectively. This is the case for
problems defined in code and math, as solutions are easy to execute and check. CURE,
for example, is a reinforcement learning framework whose reward co-evolves a model’s
coding and unit-test-generation abilities from their interaction outcomes. There is no
ground-truth code as supervision. Since code is easy to execute and check, the coder
and the test-writer act as mutually adapting agents, enabling long-horizon optimization
on hard problems. The same principle underlies self-challenging and self-evolving
agents, which propose their own increasingly difficult tasks and update their generation
policy over time \[Zhou et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025b\].

19.3
Simulating Human-generated Content

The move away from naturally occurring human-generated text, either directly ob-
tained or scraped from the web, is perhaps best seen in the evolution from curated
human-generated instruction data towards datasets where synthetic generation plays a
more central role. We will now discuss these methods, where datasets are, in their core,
still based on human-generated data.
As an example of a resource where humans still underpin most of the data, Natural
Instructions \[Mishra et al., 2022\], contains 61 distinct tasks, their human-authored in-
structions, and 193k task instances (input-output pairs). The instructions were gathered
from instruction documents for existing NLP datasets, all mapped to a unified schema.
Experiments with LLMs indicate that models benefit from observing the instructions
alongside examples, although these models have remained far behind an estimated per-
formance upper bound.
Subsequent work focuses on increasing the number of unique tasks and task types
\[Wang et al., 2022\], varying the length of the instructions \[Bach et al., 2022\], or in-
cluding particularly difficult tasks \[Srivastava et al., 2023\]. Importantly, all these meta-
datasets (datasets of datasets) are still ultimately built from human benchmarks: every
sample they contain is authored by a person. Therefore, there is a practical limit to how
much of this data can be freely found online.
Because these approaches rely on large amounts of human supervision in the form
of crowd-sourced datasets, recent work focuses on generating synthetic data that fills
the same role. Here, we see the creation of datasets such as Unnatural Instructions
\[Honovich et al., 2023\], which contain creative and diverse instructions collected with
little human labor, instead relying on prompting various LLMs. Experiments indicate
that training models on the somewhat noisy Unnatural Instructions dataset yields re-
sults comparable to those trained on high-quality, human-curated data, as shown in
Figure 19.4. This result suggests that machine-generated data offers a cost-efficient
alternative to human labor for expanding and diversifying training datasets.
The simulation of human-like text, code, and reasoning by generative models has
unlocked new methodologies for both training and evaluating machine learning sys-
tems. By prompting strong models, researchers can generate highly diverse and com-
plex datasets that mimic human content generation. For example, PersonaHub \[Ge
