Similar to self-improvement, training on synthetic data has shown much promise in
domains where model outputs are relatively easy to verify, such as mathematics \[Yang
et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2023\], programming \[Haluptzok et al., 2023\], and games \[Wang
et al., 2023a\].

19.3.1
Generating Training Data

We will now focus on generating training data. The use of synthetic data for training
has transitioned from a niche data augmentation technique to a core component of mod-
ern model alignment and reasoning pipelines. Techniques such as Self-Instruct \[Wang
et al., 2023b\] have demonstrated that smaller, open-weight models can be instruction-
tuned using data generated entirely by a stronger, proprietary model. The process, as
shown in Figure 19.5, involves seeding an LLM with a small set of human-written in-
structions and prompting it to iteratively generate novel task descriptions, inputs, and
outputs. The simulated human content allows models to acquire complex zero-shot
capabilities without the need for large groups of human annotators.

Leveraging existing data
Other approaches combine curated human data with syn-
thetic data, instead of replacing one with the other. Gunasekar et al. \[2023\] show
that training on a mixture of human-written textbooks and synthetically generated
text yields highly capable language models, suggesting that curated human data and
machine-generated data are complements rather than substitutes. One challenge is that
synthetically generated data tends to lack diversity and inherits errors and hallucina-
tions, even when it is seeded with human-generated data. Subsequent improvements
use a generation process that is based on ground truth documents \[Lupidi et al., 2025,
Yue et al., 2024\].

## Page 370

370
CHAPTER 19. *SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION

Figure 19.5: Self-Instruct pipeline \[Wang et al., 2023b\].

A complementary way to amplify a limited seed set is backtranslation. This ap-
proach was originally introduced in machine translation to synthesize parallel data by
translating sentences from a source language to a target language, and then back into
a source language \[Edunov et al., 2018\]. The same principle can be repurposed for
reasoning tasks: instead of only generating specific solutions for a single problem,
we generate new problems that are consistent with an existing solution. MathGenie
\[Lu et al., 2024\] applies this idea to mathematical reasoning by taking a seed set of
question–solution pairs. It augments the solutions, and then back-translates them into
new questions. Because each newly generated question is grounded in a verified so-
lution, this approach expands both the size and the diversity of the training data while
reducing errors and hallucinations.

Human-in-the-loop approaches
Fully automatic generation pipelines are not al-
ways sufficient. Models can struggle to generate specific scenarios or domain-relevant
cases. The reason for these failures is usually that the generating LLM has specific
blind spots, which can also make it difficult to generate genuinely informative data
\[Lippmann et al., 2024\].
Such problems motivate human-in-the-loop approaches, in which people steer, fil-
ter, or revise machine-generated content rather than authoring it from scratch.
WANLI \[Liu et al., 2022\] pairs a language model that proposes challenging natu-
ral language inference examples with human annotators who filter and relabel them,
combining the scalability of automatic generation with human quality control.
EvalAssist \[Santill´an Cooper et al., 2025\] applies a similar principle to evaluation
tooling, using synthetic data to support and accelerate human judgment. A related
strategy is to prompt the language model to produce an initial seed text, which human
raters then edit before the result is used to bootstrap a larger fully-synthetic dataset. In
this way, the human effort is spent on correcting the model rather than on authoring
every example.

## Page 371

19.3. SIMULATING HUMAN-GENERATED CONTENT
371

19.3.2
Generating Evaluation Data

Beyond training, synthetic generation plays a critical role in evaluation. Traditional
static benchmarks suffer from rapid data contamination, where test sets inadvertently
leak into the pretraining corpora of modern LLMs. To mitigate this, dynamic evaluation
frameworks \[Kiela et al., 2021\] increasingly rely on synthetic data generation to create
bespoke, single-use test cases.
Furthermore, the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm \[Zheng et al., 2024\] simulates human
evaluation by prompting a strong model to grade the outputs of other models, highly
correlating the models with human preference and significantly reducing the latency of
evaluation cycles.
Further creation of dedicated hard benchmarks for LLMs can once again be done
with human-in-the-loop approaches, such as the MATH2 benchmark. For this bench-
mark, multiple LLMs are used to iteratively generate and adjust mathematical questions
and solutions through multi-turn prompting. Human annotators then further expand on
the questions and check the answers, again aided by LLMs in the process \[Shah et al.,
2024\]. Other approaches to efficient generation of synthetic evaluation data shift the
task for annotators from coming up with new samples, to editing samples to be harder
for the LLM \[Yuan et al., 2021\].

Automated red teaming
One specific use case for machine-generated evaluation is
through the safety-oriented evaluation by means of automated red teaming. In this
approach, one LLM generates adversarial prompts to probe a target model for vulner-
abilities before deployment \[Ganguli et al., 2022\]. By synthesizing many potentially
malicious prompts, researchers can stress-test and harden models against toxic outputs,
jailbreaks, and misalignments at a scale that human red teams cannot match \[Perez
et al., 2022\]. Because the same generated prompts can subsequently be used to fine-
tune the target model against those failures, red teaming sits at the boundary between
synthetic evaluation and synthetic training data.

19.3.3
Generating Agentic Data

In agentic settings, data must be synthesized for an entire trajectory (and not just in
single instruction-response pairs). As the agent is interacting with its environment, a
full sequence of tool calls, observations, and decisions is produced \[Kang et al., 2025\].
This goes beyond data that trains or evaluates a regular LLM operating on a single
input-output pair. Generating agentic data is a more complex problem than generating
data to instruct the underlying LLM itself, even though the same generative models are
typically used to produce it. Let us look at an example.

Example 2. Consider synthesizing a single training trajectory for a tool-using
agent, roughly following the two-phase recipe of APIGen-MT \[Prabhakar et al.,
2025\].

## Page 372

372
CHAPTER 19. *SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION

First a task proposer invents a plausible user goal and a set of available tools,
together with a ground-truth answer:
User: “What will the weather be in Leiden this weekend, and should I bring
an umbrella?”
Tools: get forecast(city, days).
An actor model then rolls out the interaction, emitting the intermediate tool
call and consuming its (simulated) observation before answering:

get forecast("Leiden", 2) →{sat:
rain, sun:
clear} →“Rain
on Saturday, clear on Sunday—bring an umbrella for Saturday.”

Finally a verifier checks that the emitted call is well-formed, that its argu-
ments match the request, and that the final answer is consistent with the obser-
vation. Only trajectories that pass verification are kept.
Note what had to be synthesized: not just a single input–output pair, but the
goal, the tool schema, the call, the observation, and a checker that verifies the
whole trace.

Methods for agentic generation usually involve entire orchestrations of agents for
multi-turn conversations including human inputs and tool use \[Wu et al., 2024\]. APIGen-
MT \[Prabhakar et al., 2025\] exemplifies this shift with a two-phase framework that
generates verifiable and diverse multi-turn agent data. TOUCAN \[Xu et al., 2025b\]
pursues a similar goal at a larger scale, simulating realistic tool calls to construct a
large tool-agentic dataset. Beyond generating trajectories for a fixed skill, some work
synthesizes data explicitly to transfer a new skill or behavior from a strong model to a
weaker one, a process referred to as Generative Teaching \[Crispino et al., 2024\]. Fur-
thermore, agentic synthetic data is not limited to text, analogous generation pipelines
extend to images, tabular data, and other forms of interaction or behavioral data.
For the generation of agentic synthetic data, controlling the task complexity is a re-
curring challenge. Deep-research agents, for example, aim to solve complex question-
answering tasks through long-horizon interactions with online tools, but the data typi-
cally used to train them lacks fine-grained control over difficulty and quality, yielding
synthetic data that falls short of capturing sufficient complexity. Pandit et al. \[2025\]
address this issue with a pipeline that synthesizes question-answer pairs that progres-
sively increase task complexity until a frontier baseline web agent fails. This curricu-
lum learning approach calibrates task-difficulty directly against agent capability rather
than a fixed heuristic.
AReaL-SEA \[Gao et al., 2026\] addresses reliability from a complementary angle.
Here, a multi-agent engine synthesizes tool-grounded dialogues in combination with
executable per-instance checkers. Next, a closed-loop self-evolving process updates
the prompts over time to improve reliability.

19.4
Data Curation

Once synthetic data has been generated, we need to check it for quality and curate it.
Usually, this means filtering, scoring, and selecting samples so that only the examples

## Page 373

19.4. DATA CURATION
373

that are useful are retained. Evaluating synthetic data usefulness can be approached
in two complementary ways: extrinsically, by measuring its effect on a downstream
task, or intrinsically, by examining properties of the generated data (or the generative
process) directly.
In practice, curation is implemented as a multi-stage filtering pipeline in which cri-
teria that we will discuss below are turned into concrete operators. Typical stages in-
clude semantic deduplication (removing near-duplicate examples via embedding simi-
larity to preserve diversity), perplexity filtering (discarding incoherent or off-distribution
text using a reference model), rule-based or format checks, and reward-model or judge
scoring to retain only high-fidelity samples. The seminal Textbooks Are All You Need
paper \[Gunasekar et al., 2023\] is a reminder that this curation step often matters as
much as the volume of data: aggressive filtering for quality can outweigh sheer quan-
tity. Without it, models readily learn the generative artifacts and statistical anomalies
of their teachers.

19.4.1
Extrinsic evaluation

Extrinsic evaluation answers a simple question: does the synthetic data actually help
on a downstream task? This topic is also referred to as utility. In practice, utility is
measured by training or finetuning a model on the synthetic data (alone or mixed with
real data) and evaluating it on a held-out, real-world test set. Extrinsic evaluation is
the most direct measure of whether synthetic data is useful. For example, if the per-
formance (e.g., in terms of perplexity) of a pretrained model increases when synthetic
data is included, we can conclude that the data is useful. However, it is also the most
expensive: it requires a full training run before any signal is available. If we make
changes to the generation process or select a different set, we need to retrain and eval-
uate our model. This makes the extrinsic evaluation a poor fit for filtering or selecting
individual examples during generation.

19.4.2
Intrinsic evaluation

Intrinsic evaluation instead looks at characteristics of the generations themselves, with-
out the cost of a downstream training run. A number of quality aspects have been pro-
posed for evaluating synthetic text \[Ramesh et al., 2025\]. Rather than evaluating at the
output level, it is also possible to benchmark the language models of the generative
process directly \[Kim et al., 2025b\]. This can give an earlier and cheaper signal than
inspecting the generated data.

Data correctness
A generated example is only useful if its content is factually and
logically sound. Since synthetic data often comes from other LLMs, it inherits the gen-
erating model’s failure modes. This includes hallucinated facts, inconsistent reasoning,
or labels that do not match the content. These errors can subsequently propagate into
models that are trained on them. Correctness is typically checked by comparing genera-
tions against human-generated labels \[Long et al., 2024, Chim et al., 2025\], performing
verification (e.g., a rule-based checker or a separate judge model) \[Chen et al., 2025a,

## Page 374

374
CHAPTER 19. *SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION

Yang et al., 2025, Setlur et al., 2024\], or through consistency checks across multiple
generations for the same input \[Zelikman et al., 2022b, Seegmiller et al., 2025\].

Data diversity
A key problem in creating synthetic data is maintaining diversity.
Logit suppression and temperature sampling can improve data diversity but come at
a cost of data correctness \[Chung et al., 2023\]. Diversity is also difficult to measure:
lexical heuristics (e.g., ROUGE) or neural heuristics (embedding-based similarity) are
commonly used as proxies, but each captures only a fraction of the possible variation
in the data.
MetaSynth addresses this problem by generating synthetic data that enhances di-
versity through meta-prompting, where a language model orchestrates multiple expert
LLM agents to collaboratively generate data \[Riaz et al., 2025\].

Data contamination
A serious risk for synthetic data is contamination \[Deng et al.,
2024, Balloccu et al., 2024\]. The generating LLM is pretrained on large, imperfectly
filtered web datasets, and can memorize benchmarks and reproduce or closely para-
phrase them when prompted to generate new training examples. After many steps,
synthetically generated data converges to that of existing benchmarks. This inflates
evaluation scores artificially, for example in the case of code generation benchmarks
\[Matton et al., 2024\]. Solutions for this type of leakage should go beyond simple
exact-match filters, and requires n-gram overlap search against known benchmarks,
membership-inference-style probing \[Puerto et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2026\], or dy-
namic dataset construction pipelines \[Chen et al., 2025b\].

Fairness and biases
LLMs inherit and amplify social biases from their own training
data. If we, in turn, use the LLMs to generate synthetic corpora, we risk further per-
petuating stereotypical associations, skewed demographic representation, or unequal
generation quality across social groups \[Gallegos et al., 2024\]. This is of particular
concern for synthetic data because it is produced at scale and often consumed directly
as training material for new LLMs.
Finally, intrinsic metrics are only proxies for usefulness. A dataset can score well
on diversity or pass correctness checks while failing to improve, or even harm, extrin-
sic evaluation. Lexical and neural diversity heuristics measure surface-level variation
and can fail to spot redundancy in ways that matter (e.g., repeated reasoning patterns)
or overestimate diversity. Correctness checks further depend on the availability of a
trusted reference, rule-based verifier, or judge model, which for open-ended or sub-
jective generations may not exist, or may be unreliable. For these reasons, intrinsic
evaluation is best treated as an additional check rather than a true replacement for ex-
trinsic evaluation.

19.5
Risks

As should be clear by now, using synthetic data for training agentic LLMs is a solu-
tion that is not without problems. We will discuss several more risks associated with

## Page 375

19.5. RISKS
375

synthetic data, including model collapse, bias amplification, security and privacy vul-
nerabilities, and legal and ethical concerns.

19.5.1
Model Collapse

The defining risk of the loop in Figure 19.2 is that it feeds on its own output. Model
collapse is the well-documented phenomenon where training successive model gener-
ations on recursively generated AI data causes the diversity of the original distribution
to disappear \[Shumailov et al., 2024\]. Rare events and low-probability linguistic nu-
ance are sampled less often, so each generation forgets a little more of the distribution’s
long-tailed behavior until the model converges to a repetitive, high-probability model.
Some experiments show that repeated training on purely synthetic data yields diminish-
ing and eventually negative returns \[Singh et al., 2024\], and concentrating a corpus on
a few synthetic sources, rather than many, increases the fragility of the resulting model
\[Schaffelder and Gatt, 2025\]. Similarly, small students distilled from a teacher are
prone to hallucination and often fail on long-tailed knowledge \[Kandpal et al., 2023\].
More subtly, imitating a teacher can produce a student that matches the teacher’s style
while lagging on factuality, a gap which is usually only revealed by targeted capability
benchmarks \[Gudibande et al., 2023\]. The standard mitigation is to keep anchoring the
corpus with real human data rather than training on synthetic data alone.

19.5.2
Bias Amplification

Because generative models over-represent the majority modes of their training distri-
bution, synthesizing data tends to cut off the diverse, long-tail perspectives found in
natural human discourse \[van der Meer et al., 2024\]. A student trained on such data
can therefore exhibit an amplified, caricatured version of the teacher’s social biases.
The student model reproduces stereotypical associations, skewed demographic repre-
sentation, or unequal generation quality across groups \[Gallegos et al., 2024\]. This
concern is larger for synthetic data than for original model outputs because the data is
produced at scale and consumed directly as training material, and each round of the
loop compounds the previous round.

19.5.3
Security Risks

There are also security risks associated with synthetic training data. Relying on gener-
ated data introduces new attack vectors for maliciously polluting training data. If the
teacher model or any stage of the generation pipeline is compromised, an adversary
can mount a data-poisoning attack. Because synthetic corpora are typically too large
to audit exhaustively, subtle back doors or malicious instruction–response pairs can
be inserted, which remain dormant until triggered in the deployed student. Poisoning
even a tiny fraction of a web-scale corpus has been shown to be practical and cheap
\[Carlini et al., 2024\], and the risk is heightened when the “teacher” is an uncontrolled
third-party model whose training data and alignment are opaque.

## Page 376

376
CHAPTER 19. *SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION

19.5.4
Privacy Preservation

Synthetic generation is frequently mentioned as a solution for data privacy. The idea
is that synthetic data does not contain personally identifiable information (PII) \[Dwork
and Roth, 2014\], yet is able to reflect the statistical properties of private data (such as
medical records).
However, in this type of data there is a substantial risk of memorization. Without
strict privacy guarantees during the generation phase, generative models can uninten-
tionally reconstruct and therefore leak exact snippets of the sensitive human data on
which they were originally trained \[Carlini et al., 2021\]. Privacy evaluations show that
off-the-shelf privacy-preserving methods can fail \[Ramesh et al., 2024\].
Common privacy approaches rely on differential privacy \[Dwork et al., 2006\], a
guarantee on the generative process that bounds how much the output distribution can
change when a single individual’s record is added to or removed from the dataset.
This bound is controlled by a privacy budget, where smaller values enforce stronger
protection at the cost of greater utility loss \[Yue et al., 2023\].

19.5.5
Copyright and Terms of Use

Part of the appeal of synthetic data is that it sidesteps the unclear legal status of scraping
internet-scale human text, which has already produced copyright litigation. The 2025
Bartz v. Anthropic settlement in the US is illustrative. A district court found LLM
training itself exceedingly transformative and thus a candidate for fair use, however,
liability still arose from how the underlying corpus was obtained, namely the ingestion
of hundreds of thousands of pirated books, and Anthropic settled at roughly $3,000 per
work (about $1.5 billion in total), with parallels in other legal cases such as Kadrey v.
Meta. This shows that to an increasing degree the data underlying training is scrutinized
for copyright and terms of use.
Synthetic data does not fully escape this issue. Distilling from a proprietary model
raises a distinct issue: the terms of service of most commercial LLM APIs explicitly
forbid using their outputs to train competing models. Data generated by a black-box
teacher may therefore be legally problematic regardless of copyright. Such a tension
surfaced publicly in 2025 amid accusations that competing systems had been trained
on the outputs of frontier APIs. For practitioners, this means that the licence of the
generator is as important to check as the licence of any human data it replaces.

19.6
Concluding Remarks

Synthetic data has moved from a niche augmentation method to a central ingredient
of the LLM pipeline (Chapter 3), driven by the prospect that human text becomes
a scaling bottleneck (Chapter 4). Strong models and multi-agent orchestrations can
simulate instruction data, evaluation benchmarks, and, more recently, whole agentic
trajectories of tool calls and decisions (Chapters 9 and 11).
Because raw generations are noisy, curation, extrinsic utility together with intrinsic
checks on correctness, diversity, and contamination, are as important as generation

## Page 377

BIBLIOGRAPHY
377

itself. The various setups can be considered forms of knowledge distillation organized
along the axes of signal, data source, timing (off- vs. on-policy), and teacher identity.
Reusing synthetic data from the same model for self-improvement has promises for
enabling verifiable reasoning (Chapter 6). However, in all these pipelines we need to
be careful about what data these models are consuming: without real-data anchoring
and careful auditing, model collapse, bias amplification, security, privacy, and licensing
risks all compound with every iteration.

## Page 391

Chapter 20

*Advanced Transformer and
Agentic Architectures


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn about advanced transformer and agentic architectures.
Specifically, you will be able to:
• Understand the concept of Turing-completeness, and learn that transformers are,
in principle, Turing-complete.
• Understand that transformer models can perform planning, when we train them
on decision traces, instead of on natural language.
• Describe how embeddings can be connected directly to other embeddings, in
looped language models, skipping tokenization layers.
• Describe how agents can perform reinforcement learning in-context, by storing
a history of state-action-reward triples.
• Describe the advantages and disadvantages of self-modifying agents.
• Understand how metalearning can be applied to harness design, to create a meta-
harness that improves the basic harness.

20.1
Transformer Architectures

The success of large language models has spawned interesting new research avenues
into transformer architectures. LLMs were good at language, but not at other problem
types such as reasoning and planning. This caused researchers to explore the limits
of the types of computations that transformers were able to do, and we will discuss
some of the topics in the following sections. Specifically, they asked the questions
whether transformers were Turing complete (Section 20.1.1)? The weak performance
on planning problems prompted studies that trained transformers directly on decision
traces, to see if that allowed them to be able to plan and backtrack (Section 20.1.2).
Next, we will look at looped language models, where multiple models are connected

391

## Page 392

392
CHAPTER 20. *ADVANCED AGENTIC ARCHITECTURES

directly at the level of the embeddings.

20.1.1
Transformers are Turing-complete

The difficulty of LLMs to manage state at inference time suggests that LLMs are lim-
ited in the type of computations that they can perform. In theoretical computer science
the concept of Turing completeness indicates whether a certain model of computation
is powerful enough to be able to perform any type of computation of a certain category
(which includes being able to manage state values correctly). This concept was intro-
duced in a famous paper by Alan Turing in 1936, in which he proved that a certain type
of machine would be powerful enough to do so \[Turing, 1936\]. To be called Turing
complete, a system must be able to simulate any other computational device and be
able to process any problem that can be expressed in an algorithm (but perhaps take in-
finite time and memory to do so). It turns out that it is not too difficult to achieve Turing
completeness; most general purpose programming languages are Turing complete.1

The difficulty of LLMs—and of transformer-based models in general—to manage
state would suggest that the transformer architecture may not be Turing complete. In-
terestingly, already in 2021 P´erez et al. \[2021\] have studied this question, and have
proven that the transformer architecture is able to simulate a Turing machine, and is
thus Turing complete.
This is an encouraging result, since it indicates that there is no fundamental reason
why transformers would not be able to manage state correctly. It may well be a matter
of finding the right prompt, or finding the right pretraining and finetuning dataset.
Unfortunately, the fact that something is theoretically possible, does not mean that
achieving it will be easy, or that it can be done efficiently. For example, it might be
that certain architectural extensions to the transformer architecture would enhance the
ease with which efficient state management can be achieved. We will now discuss
methods that have been developed so that LLMs can efficiently solve decision making
and planning problems.

20.1.2
Pretraining Backtracking on Decision Traces

The finding that transformers are Turing-complete encourages research in planning
and decision making. In this section we will discuss studies that pretrain a transformer
architecture on decision traces, to good results. Note that this section is not about
transformers that are trained on natural language—LLMs—but on transformers trained
on decision traces.
First we discuss pretraining transformers directly on decision traces: sequences
of state-action-reward triples, not language tokens. Several works study whether trans-
former networks can be trained to perform reinforcement learning—to learn from feed-
back, to perform learned policies, and to explore to learn better actions. Chen et al.
\[2021\], Lee et al. \[2023\], Wang et al. \[2024\] showed that basic transformer architec-
tures can indeed be pretrained and finetuned on decision traces from typical planning

1For example, the Python programming language is Turing complete, but simple regular expression
matching, without backreferencing, is not.

## Page 393

20.1. TRANSFORMER ARCHITECTURES
393

Figure 20.1: The Cartpole Problem: Balance the Pole just by Moving the Cart Left or
Right

problems. When an empty (non-language trained) transformer is pretrained on deci-
sion traces, it can exhibit in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL). So far, this has
been shown using toy problems such as Boyan’s chain and Cartpole (see Figure 20.1).
Furthermore, in the games of Chess and Hex encouraging results were achieved by
pretraining the decision transformer on minimax \[Markeeva et al., 2024, Knuth and
Moore, 1975\] and MCTS \[Browne et al., 2012\] search traces \[Schultz et al., 2024,
Kempinski et al., 2025\]. Transformers were able to learn to lookahead and search a
few steps. Other works report encouraging results in the game of Othello \[Li et al.,
2023, Kempinski et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025\].

A further work that studies how transformer architectures can be trained to perform
decisions is self backtracking \[Yang et al., 2026a\]. In this approach the model is again
trained on decision traces. However, a new kind of token is introduced, <backtrack>,
that prompts the model to perform explicit backtracking at inference time. The model
is trained on a dataset of decisions, and when an error is encountered during training,
the <backtrack> token is learned, to find an alternative solution. At inference time,
then, this backtracking is performed. A mechanism that consists of expansion/back-
tracking/selection is executed by the model, so that alternative solutions for the state in
question are examined.

The self backtracking approach reports good results on typical planning problems
such as the 24-game and maze navigation, compared to standard baselines on small
versions of DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3. Through the introduction of a new type of to-
ken and new backtracking-functionality in the model, this approach allows enhanced-
transformer models to perform search, blurring the line between training and inference.

These are encouraging results, although it is still an open question to what extend
the weakness of transformers in managing state has been solved. Performing inference-
time ICRL on larger problems is an area of active research.

## Page 394

394
CHAPTER 20. *ADVANCED AGENTIC ARCHITECTURES

20.1.3
LoopedLLM and Recursive Multi-Agent Systems

Improving the expressive power of transformers brings them closer to a general purpose
programming architecture. We will discuss two other developments: looped language
models and recursive systems.
It is easy to connect LLM agents at the language level: just let them speak to
each other in natural language, on which they are all trained. However, this necessi-
tates many (de)tokenization steps, which take time and introduces differences between
embeddings. Can we directly connect embeddings, bypassing the tokenizers, and do
training and inference at that level?

Giannou et al. \[2023\] show how looped transformers (transformers whose input
neurons are directly connected to transformer output neurons, either from the same or
from another model) can emulate a basic calculator, a basic linear algebra library, and
in-context learning algorithms that employ backpropagation. Looped transformers are
a powerful architecture, see for example Yang et al. \[2023\], Saunshi et al. \[2025\], Zhu
et al. \[2025\].
A further development of direct embedding-to-embedding connections is recur-
sive multi-agent systems \[Yang et al., 2026b\]. This approach connects heterogeneous
agents in a collaboration loop, enabling in-distribution latent thought generation and
cross-agent latent state transfer. An inner-outer loop learning algorithm (metalearning,
see Chapter 8) performs whole-system co-optimization through shared gradient-based
credit assignment across recursion rounds. Experiments with four agents over bench-
marks from mathematics, science, medicine, search, and code generation, showed sta-
ble multi-agent training. In comparison with other single/multi-agent and recursive
baselines, accuracy is improved by a few percentage points, inference is twice as fast,
and token usage is reduced by comparable ratio.
An innovation of RecursiveMAS is the introduction of a two-level recursive-link.
Training a multi-agent system is difficult because gradients must flow through multiple
models, and this process can become unstable. RecursiveMAS improves this process
by freezing the parameters of the underlying LLMs and only training the lightweight
RecursiveLink modules. The training occurs in two stages.

20.2
Agentic Architectures

In addition to new transformer architectures, the work on agentic LLMs has also led to
advanced agentic architectures. First, we will look at in-context reinforcement learning,
where we will see that LLMs are able to perform policy improvement when the prompt
is given a history of state-action-reward triples. Second, we will look at self-modifying
agents, and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this approach. Finally, we will
look at meta agents.

20.2.1
In-Context Reinforcement Learning

Recall from Section 2.2.3 that the goal of reinforcement learning is to compute a pol-
icy that has an optimal action for each state \[Sutton and Barto, 2018\]. As the agent

Figure 20.2: For reference, the standard reinforcement learning loop where the agent
learns a 𝜃-parameterized policy 𝜋𝜃from feedback rewards 𝑟from the environment
upon its actions 𝑎, selected from policy 𝜋𝜃, etc. \[Sutton and Barto, 2018\]

converges towards this policy, in each timestep, the agent learns these actions from
feedback from its environment, the rewards. These rewards reinforce the confidence
of the agent in the policy’s actions in each state (see Figure 20.2). The self-reflection
approaches from the previous section borrow many ideas from reinforcement learning
for the agentic harness. We will now discuss related methods that optimize prompts by
in-context reinforcement learning, where the LLM performs prompt improvement.
Reinforcement-type learning mechanisms have been observed to emerge directly in
LLMs, when environment histories were provided to the LLM by an external prompt
optimizer: the LLM in certain self-reflection loops can perform policy-improvement.
This phenomenon is called in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) \[Song et al.,
2025\], see Figure 20.3.

Krishnamurthy et al. \[2024\] asked the question whether generic LLMs that are
trained on language can explore in-context, and whether they can learn in-context from
feedback. This question has since been answered positively by various studies \[Demir-
can et al., 2024, Song et al., 2025, Moeini et al., 2025, Monea et al., 2024, Nie et al.,
2024, Wang et al., 2024\].
In ICRL, an external harness iteratively calls the LLM, feeding it a sequence of
action, state, and reward triples, in-context (Figure 20.3). The history of triples grows in
each iteration. The LLM reacts by improving its implicit policy, providing increasingly
good action choices in each iteration, thus we conclude that it performs the essence of
reinforcement learning inside the LLM.
In ICRL, the agent-algorithm selects an action, to sample a step and get an answer
(a state, reward pair) from the environment, see Figure 20.3. A Markov decision pro-
cess, or MDP, is a process in which all relevant information to calculate the next state
is contained in the previous state and the action taken. Therefore, the prompt for the
policy-LLM contains all relevant information, it accumulates the history of (𝑠, 𝑎, 𝑟)-
triples, which the LLM can use to improve the policy of the best action for each state.
For state, the history of answers is a natural choice, but, in general, how to best model
LLM prompt improvement as an MDP is still an active area of research.
In ICRL the agent uses the LLM for the policy-function. The LLM can also be
used (with a different prompt) to play the role of environment, as in a self-reflection
harness.
In-context reinforcement learning occurs in a multi-round prompting harness, where,
after the environment-LLM generates a response at the current round, a numerical re-

Figure 20.3: ICRL: Prompt Optimization with Reinforcement Learning

ward is calculated by the LLM for the response that the LLM just calculated. At the
next round, the agent-LLM is prompted again with the same task and a context that
now consists of the previous responses and rewards. The quality of the agent-LLM’s
response increases as the context becomes longer. Just like a reinforcement learning
algorithm, the LLM is able to maximize the numeric reward, at inference time. Song
et al. \[2025\] report how the ICRL approach was validated on the applications of tree of
thoughts (Game of 24, creative writing, and ScienceWorld), outperforming self refine
and reflexion.
How does the ICRL process work, inside the LLM? At inference time the LLM per-
forms a forward pass through the transformer network, computing the inference token.
This forward pass has been found to implicitly perform reinforcement learning \[Wang
et al., 2024\]. In other words, in-weights learning is where the model has learned the
right answer from its trained weights, at training time; in-context learning is where the
model has learned the right answer at inference time from few-shot examples provided
in its context; and in-context reinforcement learning is where the LLM has learned
the right answer using (apparent) reinforcement learning on a growing sequence of the
state-action-reward triples that it produced itself through inference. Thus, the rein-
forcing algorithm, optimizing the policy, is done implicitly by the LLM forward pass
(inference step) when a sequence of prompts or history is given in the context.
Note that the LLM can be used for the agent, as a policy optimizer, and for the
environment, to calculate the next state and reward. To ensure that the agent is learning
without accidentally benefiting from the environment’s knowledge, it is better to use a
separate LLM. This, too, is an active area of research.

20.2.2
Self-Modifying Hyperagents

In this book, we have discussed self-reflective prompt improvers that are based on
search algorithms and reinforcement learning. The code for these external algorithms
is written by human researchers, and does not change as the agent is learning. The
approach by which the prompt is improved is limited by these static algorithms.
LLMs excel at manipulating and judging computer code \[Zhuge et al., 2024\]. We
could, in principle, easily ask them to generate code for an agentic prompt harness, or
for an in-context reinforcement learning harness. We could even ask the LLM to run the
code on a particular problem instance, and, based on the outcome of the experiment,
ask for an improvement of the prompt-improver code. If the LLM is good at using
experiment-results for writing prompt-improvement code, this approach could work

## Page 397

20.2. AGENTIC ARCHITECTURES
397

better than standard approaches from the published literature.
Self-modifying code (computer programs that alter their own instructions while
they are being executed) has a long history in computer science \[Cai et al., 2007\], as
an alternative to conditional branching statements. Many computer languages support
it, from assembly languages, to Lisp \[Abelson and Sussman, 2022\] and Python. It
is a powerful method that can be used for performance improvement, for example in
just-in-time compilation \[Ansel et al., 2011\]. However, programs become less pre-
dictable, which may cause problems in finding errors in the program, and raises secu-
rity concerns. For this reason the use is sometimes discouraged when predictability of
programs is important.
An advantage of self-modifying agents is open-endedness: they can continuously
improve themselves, without fixed boundaries set by static algorithms \[Schmidhuber,
2007\].
A challenge is to do this safely \[Zhang et al., 2026b\].
In Darwin-G¨odel-
Machine-Hyperagents the authors integrate (1) an agent to solve the target task with (2)
a meta agent to modify itself and the task agent, into a single (editable) program. Note
that the meta-level modification procedure is itself editable, enabling self-modification.
This allows, in principle, not only improving the task-solving behavior, but also the
mechanism that generates future improvements \[Zhang et al., 2026c\]. The experi-
ments, however, do not achieve full openness, as they use a fixed task distribution, as
well as fixed parent selection and evaluation protocols.
As approaches become more open-ended, paradoxically, a challenge becomes to
control the process of improvement, to ensure that it does not degenerate, but keeps
improving \[Cemri et al., 2025, Ecoffet et al., 2020\]. In general, the problem of powerful
metalearning approaches is to ensure stable learning processes. Powerful generation
requires powerful evaluation—adaptation to fit the environment.

20.2.3
Meta Agents

The two-level optimization process of metalearning that we have seen in many self-
reflection approaches, can be applied as an explicit design principle in harness design
for agents. Recently, several such architectures have been published. In these designs,
the inner learning loop is formed by the harness and the LLM, and the outer learning
loop improves the configuration of this inner harness. The inner harness configuration
typically performs prompt management, memory management, tool use, and security
and control, and can be represented as language or code. The outer loop analyzes
execution traces of the inner loop, to improve the configuration or code of the inner
harness. We will briefly describe some of these approaches.
Self improving coding agent \[Robeyns et al., 2025\] is based on the idea of self-
modifying agents. They demonstrate that an agent system, equipped with basic coding
tools, can autonomously edit itself. Their approach improves performance on software
engineering benchmark tasks, achieving substantial performance gains from 17 to 53
percent.
Meta harness \[Lee et al., 2026\] also achieves good results, using external memory
and text optimization. Figure 20.4 illustrates how meta harness works. (1) A filesystem
has all prior candidates’ source code, execution traces, and scores; the agent reads
this, and generates code for a new harness. (2) The proposed harness is evaluated on

evaluation tasks. (3) All proposed code, reasoning traces, and evaluation scores are
stored in the filesystem in a new directory, and the loop repeats.
Self harness \[Zhang et al., 2026a\] and Agentic Harness Engineering \[Lin et al.,
2026\] further explore harness design, achieving substantial improvements on software
engineering tasks. Recursive self-evolving agents \[Nguyen et al., 2026\] focuses on the
selection aspect of self-improving agents.
Another use case is described by Luo et al. \[2026\]. They use a meta harness to
design a harness for turning a scientific paper into a conference-poster. This work thus
has contributions on two levels: a method for making a meta-harness, and a concrete
harness for designing posters—which the authors, obviously, use on their own paper.
The Shepherd system \[Yu et al., 2026\] provides a functional meta agent program-
ming environment.2

Concluding Remarks

In this chapter we have discussed some advanced architectures, at the level of the trans-

## Page 403

Chapter 21

*Mechanistic Interpretability
for LLM Agents


What You Will Learn

In this chapter you will learn how to look inside the black box of large language
models using tools from explainable artificial intelligence and mechanistic inter-
pretability. Specifically, you will be able to:
• Distinguish between the four main interpretability paradigms: behavioral, attri-
butional, concept-based, and mechanistic interpretability.
• Explain how hallucination relates to faithfulness, and describe how mechanistic
methods can identify the internal circuits responsible for model failures.
• Describe the residual stream formulation of the transformer and explain how
information is iteratively refined across layers.
• Apply the logit lens and tuned lens to visualize how a model’s predictions evolve
through its layers.
• Explain polysemanticity and superposition, and understand why individual neu-
rons are poor units of interpretation.
• Use sparse autoencoders for dictionary learning to decompose model activations
into monosemantic, human-interpretable features.
• Perform circuit analysis and activation patching to identify and causally verify
the internal algorithms responsible for specific model behaviors.

21.1
Opening the LLM

How do LLMs work inside? Opening up the black box of large neural architectures
is an important topic of research. We wish to understand how the billions of neurons
embed representations, how they reason and how they come to conclusions. The field
of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) provides many different methods to do so
\[Minh et al., 2022, Rios et al., 2020, Van Stein et al., 2022, Selvaraju et al., 2017, Ali

403

## Page 404

404 CHAPTER 21. *MECHANISTIC INTERPRETABILITY FOR LLM AGENTS

et al., 2022\].
Static XAI methods from the classical machine learning community have been
quite successful \[Molnar, 2020\]. Methods exist to relate how input pictures map to
output classes, for example using feature maps \[Ren et al., 2016, Kohonen, 1982, Red-
mon et al., 2016\]. Counterfactual analysis \[Karimi et al., 2020, Huang et al., 2024\],
LIME \[Ribeiro et al., 2016\] and SHAP \[Lundberg and Lee, 2017\], among others, help
understand how inputs map to outputs for structured data. These methods belong to
the behavioral and attributional class of explainability algorithms, where the model
is seen as a black-box (Figure 21.1). Attribution methods such as SHAP and LIME
approximate the contributions of different input features to the final output. Behavioral
analysis such as achieved by using counterfactual methods provide insight into which
features matter (but not perse how much they matter).

Figure 21.1: Taxonomy of Interpretability Paradigms.
Behavioral interpretability
treats the model as a black box, mapping input-output relations ( 𝑓(𝑥) = 𝑦). Attri-
butional methods quantify the influence of specific input features on the final output
using gradients or saliency. Concept-based interpretability employs probes to identify
high-level, human-understandable representations within hidden layers. Mechanistic
interpretability aims to reverse-engineer the specific causal circuits and internal algo-
rithms that govern model behavior.

Moving beyond surface-level input-output correlations, concept-based interpretabil-
ity seeks to identify whether specific, human-understandable information is encoded
within the model’s internal states. This is primarily investigated through linear prob-
ing, where a simple supervised classifier is trained on frozen hidden activations to
detect the presence of particular semantic concepts—such as parts of speech, senti-
ment, or factual entities \[Alain and Bengio, 2016, Belinkov, 2022\]. While attribution
methods highlight which parts of the input are influential, probing allows researchers
to verify what knowledge the model represents at different layers (Figure 21.1). How-
ever, a known limitation of probing is the causal gap: discovering that a concept is

## Page 405

21.2. HALLUCINATION AND FAITHFULNESS IN MODEL REASONING
405

represented in a layer does not necessarily mean the model uses that information for its
final prediction.
More recently, dynamic methods have been developed to uncover patterns under
the hood of large transformer models. These belong to the sub-domain of mechanis-
tic interpretability (MI). The goal of MI is to uncover the mechanisms by which the
model dynamically comes to conclusions \[Nanda et al., 2023, Bereska and Gavves,
2024, Ferrando et al., 2024, Rai et al., 2024\]. In other words, MI seeks a low-level,
causal explanation of a model’s behavior in terms of its internal activations and con-
nections, analogous to decompiling a program’s binary into readable code. Methods
such as sparse autoencoders \[Cunningham et al., 2023, Makelov et al., 2024\], neural
lenses \[Black et al., 2022\] and circuit discovery \[Conmy et al., 2023\] are being used to
successfully enhance insight into how LLMs work, for example, in chess \[Davis and
Sukthankar, 2024\].
XAI and MI in particular are active areas of research that will allow us to better
understand how LLMs reason and come to conclusions \[Sharkey et al., 2025\]. Once a
better understanding is reached, LLMs can be improved accordingly, for example, to
reduce hallucinations.
This chapter will dive deeper into the many facets of MI.

21.2
Hallucination and Faithfulness in Model Reason-
ing

A significant barrier to the deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments is the
phenomenon of hallucination: the generation of syntactically plausible but factually
incorrect content. From an interpretability perspective, the challenge lies in distin-
guishing whether a model’s output is the result of a robust internal computation or a
post-hoc justification. This distinction is formalized as the study of faithfulness, the
degree to which a model’s stated reasoning (e.g., in chain of thought prompting) is
causally responsible for its final output.
Mechanistic interpretability (MI) provides the tools necessary to move beyond be-
havioral metrics of accuracy and toward a causal understanding of model failure modes.
For instance, research using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) has identified specific hon-
esty or knowledge-retrieval circuits \[Lindsey et al., 2025\]. In these studies, researchers
identified latent features that activate when a model encounters unfamiliar entities; a
failure in the inhibitory logic of these circuits, where the model proceeds to gener-
ate tokens despite low activation in the relevant knowledge feature, directly results in
fabricated answers.
Furthermore, MI allows us to investigate the causal necessity of intermediate rea-
soning steps. While a model may produce a convincing chain of thought (CoT), it
remains possible that the model has already calculated the final answer via a separate
internal shortcut and is merely generating the CoT as a stochastic parrot.
To test this, Chen et al. \[2026\] utilized causal mediation analysis combined with
SAEs to intervene on the latent thought process during arithmetic tasks. By inject-
ing the latent activations from a CoT-enabled run into a standard zero-shot run, they

## Page 406

406 CHAPTER 21. *MECHANISTIC INTERPRETABILITY FOR LLM AGENTS

demonstrated that in sufficiently large models, these intermediate thoughts significantly
boosted solution confidence. This provides empirical evidence that for larger architec-
tures, the CoT is not merely cosmetic but represents a faithful causal link in the model’s
reasoning chain.
Conversely, the absence of such causal links in smaller models suggests that faith-
ful reasoning may be an emergent property of scale, appearing only when the model
possesses sufficient parameters to represent complex, multi-step algorithms. Devel-
oping robust metrics to quantify this faithfulness is a critical frontier in AI safety; by
peeking into the model’s activations, we can potentially develop hallucination detectors
that trigger when a model’s internal confidence features do not align with its external
verbosity.

21.3
The Residual Stream and Iterative Refinement

Before exploring specific MI methods it is necessary to establish a formal mental model
of the transformer architecture. Unlike classical feed-forward networks where each
layer replaces the representation of the previous one, modern transformers operate on
a residual stream \[Elhage et al., 2021\].
Formally, let ℎℓ∈R𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙be the state of the hidden representation after layer ℓ.
The Transformer architecture is defined by the recurrence:

ℎℓ= ℎℓ−1 + Fℓ(ℎℓ−1)
(21.1)

where Fℓrepresents the computation performed by the ℓ-th layer (comprising multi-
head attention and feed-forward blocks).
This structure implies that the final representation ℎ𝐿is a cumulative sum of the
initial embedding 𝑥𝑒𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑑and the contributions (Δℎ) from every subsequent layer:

ℎ𝐿= 𝑥𝑒𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑑+

𝐿
∑︁

ℓ=1
Δℎℓ
(21.2)

In this view, the residual stream acts as a high-dimensional communication channel.
Individual layers do not transform the entire state; rather, they read information from
the stream, perform a local computation and write their results back into the stream via
vector addition. This additive nature ensures that information can persist across many
layers, and more importantly, it justifies the linear decomposition of the model’s final
output.

21.4
Polysemanticity and Superposition

A primary bottleneck in reverse-engineering neural networks is polysemanticity (Fig-
ure 21.2): the empirical observation that individual neurons frequently activate for
multiple, semantically unrelated concepts. This phenomenon is deeply linked to super-
position, a regime where a model represents 𝑛features in 𝑚dimensions, where 𝑛> 𝑚.

Polysemanticity in Neuron Activation Space

Figure 21.2: The concept of polysemanticity in LLMs and other transformer based
models

Under the linear representation hypothesis, models exploit the high-dimensional ge-
ometry of activation space to store features as almost-orthogonal vectors. While this
allows for efficient information compression, it results in a basis mismatch where the
fixed neuron basis does not align with the true feature basis.
A formalization was provided by Elhage et al. \[2022\], who demonstrated using toy
models that superposition is a mathematically principled strategy for models to maxi-
mize information density when features are sparse. They identified phase transitions
in feature encoding: as the sparsity of a concept increases, the model can pack more
features into the same number of dimensions, albeit at the cost of interference or noise
between those features.
To resolve this entanglement, researchers have turned to dictionary learning, most
notably via sparse autoencoders (SAEs). The objective is to learn a linear transforma-
tion that maps the tangled neuron activations into a much higher-dimensional, sparse
latent space. Bricken et al. \[2023\] successfully applied this to small-scale transform-

## Page 408

408 CHAPTER 21. *MECHANISTIC INTERPRETABILITY FOR LLM AGENTS

ers, demonstrating that the resulting SAE features are significantly more monosemantic
and human-interpretable than the original neurons. This suggested that models are not
inherently uninterpretable, but rather that we have been looking at them through the
wrong coordinate system.
Subsequent work has explored whether architectural modifications can mitigate the
emergence of polysemanticity. For instance, Liu et al. \[2023\] and others have investi-
gated how different activation functions or regularization penalties (e.g., 𝐿1 sparsity)
can pressure the model into adopting a more aligned, interpretable internal basis. De-
spite these advances, polysemanticity remains a pervasive challenge in state-of-the-art
models. The current consensus in MI is that interpreting a model requires moving be-
yond the “neuron-as-a-unit” paradigm and instead identifying the underlying sparse
feature basis in which the model’s causal logic is actually computed.

21.5
The Logit Lens

A fundamental intuition in mechanistic interpretability is that a transformer model does
not compute its output in a single leap at the final layer. Instead, it iteratively refines a
representation within the residual stream. The logit lens1 provides a window into this
process by decoding the hidden states of intermediate layers directly into the output
vocabulary space.

21.5.1
Formal Mechanism

Consider a transformer with 𝐿layers. Let 𝑥0 be the initial embedding of a token, and
ℎℓbe the state of the residual stream after layer ℓ∈{1, . . . , 𝐿}. In a standard forward
pass, the final hidden state ℎ𝐿is converted into logits 𝑦via the layer norm (LN) and
the unembedding matrix 𝑊𝑈∈R𝑑𝑚𝑜𝑑𝑒𝑙×|𝑉|:

𝑦= Softmax(LN(ℎ𝐿)𝑊𝑈)
(21.3)

The logit lens generalizes this by applying the same unembedding transformation to
intermediate states ℎℓ:
ˆ𝑦ℓ= Softmax(LN(ℎℓ)𝑊𝑈)
(21.4)

where ˆ𝑦ℓrepresents the model’s tentative probability distribution at layer ℓ. By visu-
alizing these distributions across all layers, researchers can observe the evolution of
belief as the model moves from vague semantic clusters to specific token predictions.

Direct Logit Attribution
While the logit lens provides an aggregate view of the
residual stream ℎℓ, we often wish to isolate the contribution of a single layer or head.
Because the final logit 𝑦is a linear function of the cumulative sum of layer outputs,

21.5.2
From the Logit Lens to the Tuned Lens

While the initial logit lens is highly informative for the final third of a network, it often
yields gibberish or high-entropy distributions in early layers. This occurs because the
residual stream at layer 2, for example, is not yet formatted for the output distribution;
it may be storing low-level positional information that is mathematically orthogonal to
the unembedding matrix 𝑊𝑈.
To bridge this gap, Belrose et al. \[2023\] introduced the tuned lens. Instead of using
the static 𝑊𝑈, the tuned lens trains a layer-specific affine transformation 𝜙ℓto map ℎℓ
to the logit space:
𝑦𝑡𝑢𝑛𝑒𝑑,ℓ= Softmax(𝜙ℓ(ℎℓ))
(21.6)

early layers into the output vocabulary, revealing that factual information often emerges
much earlier in the network than the naive logit lens would suggest.

21.5.3
Applications and Interpretations

Lenses serve as a critical diagnostic tool for identifying early exit candidates and locat-
ing specific knowledge neurons. For instance, if the logit for a specific fact (e.g., Paris)
jumps from the 100th to the 1st rank at layer 14, it suggests that the attention heads or
MLP sub-layers in layer 14 are responsible for the factual retrieval.
Variants such as the attention lens \[Sakarvadia et al., 2023\] apply similar logic to
the outputs of individual attention heads, allowing us to see what each head contributes
to the prediction in isolation. Collectively, these tools shift our view of the transformer
from a sequential pipeline to a cumulative iterative refiner of latent information.

21.6
Circuit Analysis

A central objective of MI is the identification of circuits: minimal subgraphs of a
model’s computation graph that are both necessary and sufficient to implement a spe-
cific high-level function. Unlike behavioral analysis, circuit discovery seeks to explain
how information is transformed step-by-step, from input embeddings to the final logit.

## Page 411

21.6. CIRCUIT ANALYSIS
411

21.6.1
The Prototypical Circuit: Induction Heads

The discovery of the induction head represents a landmark in transformer interpretabil-
ity \[Olsson et al., 2022\]. Induction heads are a specialized circuit consisting of at least
two attention heads that implement a prefix-matching algorithm. Formally, given a se-
quence \[𝐴\]\[𝐵\] . . . \[𝐴\], an induction head at the current position \[𝐴\] attends to the pre-
vious occurrence of \[𝐴\] and copies the subsequent token \[𝐵\] into the residual stream
(Figure 21.5).

The Mechanism of Composition
To understand how the two heads in an induction
circuit communicate, we must define the three types of attention composition \[Elhage
et al., 2021\]:

• V-Composition: The output (Value) of a previous head is used as the input to a
subsequent head.

• Q-Composition / K-Composition: The output of a previous head affects where a
subsequent head looks by writing into the Query or Key vectors of a token.

An induction head typically relies on K-Composition: a previous token head in an
early layer writes information about the preceding token into the residual stream. The
induction head in a later layer then uses this information in its Key vector to match the
current prefix, allowing it to attend to the correct historical token \[𝐵\].

Figure 21.5: Mechanics of an Induction Head Circuit. Induction heads implement a
prefix-matching algorithm where the model identifies a previous occurrence of the cur-
rent token (the prefix) and attends to the subsequent token to predict a repeat sequence.

Olsson et al. \[2022\] observed that these heads emerge during a specific phase tran-
sition in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in the model’s in-context learning
capabilities. This was one of the first instances where a complex capability was traced
to a specific, discrete algorithm implemented across multiple layers.

21.6.2
Methodologies for Circuit Discovery

Manually identifying circuits is labor-intensive. The study of the indirect object iden-
tification (IOI) task by Wang et al. \[2022\] remains the standard for manual tracing. By
utilizing path patching, they identified a network of 26 attention heads (classified into

## Page 412

412 CHAPTER 21. *MECHANISTIC INTERPRETABILITY FOR LLM AGENTS

roles such as Name Movers, S-Inhibition Heads, and Duplicate Token Detectors) that
collectively perform coreference resolution. Coreference resolution refers to the pro-
cess of identifying when different tokens in a text refer to the same underlying entity.
For example, in the IOI task, the model must determine that a later mention of a name
(the indirect object) refers back to a specific person introduced earlier in the sentence,
a computation implemented by a specialized sub-network of attention heads.
However, scaling these findings to frontier models requires automated circuit dis-
covery (ACD).

• ACD: Conmy et al. \[2023\] introduced an algorithm that performs recursive ab-
lation to prune edges in the computation graph, preserving only those whose
removal significantly degrades model performance on a specific task.

• Sparse Feature Circuits: Moving beyond neurons, more recent frameworks in-
tegrate sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to trace circuits in feature space rather than
neuron space \[Marks et al., 2024\]. By treating SAE features as the nodes and
the weights between them as edges, researchers can build attribution graphs that
visualize the flow of human-understandable concepts (e.g., refusal, translation,
or grammar checking).

Evaluation: Faithfulness, Completeness, and Minimality
It is vital to distinguish
between a suggested circuit and a causal circuit. A circuit is considered faithful if the
model’s performance is preserved when all components outside the circuit are ablated.
It is complete if it captures all pathways the model uses to solve the task.
As models scale, we find that algorithms are often represented redundantly or in a
distributed manner across the residual stream. Therefore, circuit tracing is not merely
a search for a single wire, but an attempt to map the causal mediation of information
through the high-dimensional latent space of the model.

21.7
Activation Patching and Causal Interventions

While observational tools such as the logit lens or probing can identify correlations
between internal states and outputs, activation patching (also termed causal tracing or
interchange interventions) allows researchers to make definitive causal claims. This
technique is a practical application of causal mediation analysis \[Vig et al., 2020\],
designed to isolate the effect of a specific model component on a downstream behavior
(Figure 21.6).

Formal Framework
The procedure involves two distinct forward passes:

1. Clean Run (𝑥𝑐𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑛): An input that produces the target behavior (e.g., The Eiffel
Tower is in Paris).

2. Corrupted/Counterfactual Run (𝑥𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑟): A modified input where the target behav-
ior disappears (e.g., The Colosseum is in Rome or adding Gaussian noise to the
embedding of Eiffel Tower).

Figure 21.6: Activation Patching. Activations from a clean run (where the model suc-
ceeds) are swapped into a corrupted run (where the model fails). By observing whether
this interchange intervention restores the correct output, we can causally verify if the
patched component is responsible for the specific reasoning task.

Let 𝑧𝑖,ℓbe the activation of component 𝑖at layer ℓ. In activation patching, we com-
pute a patched run by replacing the activation 𝑧𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑟
𝑖,ℓ
with 𝑧𝑐𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑛
𝑖,ℓ

forward pass. We then measure the probability recovery:

Effect = 𝑃(𝑦𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡|patched) −𝑃(𝑦𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡|corr)

𝑃(𝑦𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡|clean) −𝑃(𝑦𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡|corr)
(21.7)

An Effect score near 1.0 indicates that the patched component is a sufficient causal
mediator for the information being studied.

Locating Knowledge and Circuits
Activation patching has led to significant archi-
tectural insights. Meng et al. \[2022\] utilized massive patching sweeps to demonstrate
that factual associations are often localized within specific MLP blocks in the middle
layers of a model. They found that patching these knowledge neurons could force a
model to output a specific fact even when the input context was corrupted.
Beyond localization, patching is the primary tool for path patching, which identifies
interactions between components. In the indirect object identification study mentioned
before, Wang et al. \[2022\] patched specific attention heads to trace how information
flows from duplicate token detectors to name movers. This reveals the computational
graph of the model, moving beyond simple localization to understand the internal al-
gorithm.

## Page 414

414 CHAPTER 21. *MECHANISTIC INTERPRETABILITY FOR LLM AGENTS

Scalability and Attribution Patching
A major challenge of activation patching is
its computational cost, as a full sweep requires a forward pass for every component in
the model. To mitigate this, researchers use attribution patching \[Syed et al., 2024\],
which uses gradients to linearly approximate the effect of a patch. This allows for rapid
hypothesis generation, where the most promising causal candidates are later validated
with exact (but slower) activation patching. This surgery-like precision makes patching
an indispensable part of the MI toolkit for moving from speculative interpretation to
rigorous causal proof.

21.8
Sparse Autoencoders: Dictionary Learning for Fea-
ture Discovery

As discussed in the context of superposition, neural networks often represent more
features than they have dimensions (𝑛> 𝑑). To resolve this tangled representation,
we utilize sparse autoencoders (SAEs), a form of unsupervised dictionary learning
designed to project activations into a higher-dimensional sparse latent space where
features are approximately monosemantic.

The model projects lower-
dimensional input activations (𝑥∈R𝑑) into a much higher-dimensional latent space
(𝑐∈R𝑁, where 𝑁≫𝑑). A sparsity penalty (e.g., 𝐿1 regularization on 𝑐) forces most
hidden units to be inactive (grey), resulting in a sparse set of active, interpretable fea-
tures (teal) that are used to reconstruct the original input.

## Page 415

21.8. SPARSE AUTOENCODERS: DICTIONARY LEARNING FOR FEATURE DISCOVERY415

Formal Architecture and Training Objective
An SAE consists of an encoder that
maps a model activation 𝑥∈R𝑑to a high-dimensional hidden state 𝑐∈R𝑁(where
𝑁≫𝑑), and a decoder that attempts to reconstruct the original activation (Figure
21.7).
The encoder is typically defined as:

𝑐= ReLU(𝑊𝑒𝑛𝑐(𝑥−𝑏𝑑𝑒𝑐) + 𝑏𝑒𝑛𝑐)
(21.8)

And the reconstruction is given by:

ˆ𝑥= 𝑊𝑑𝑒𝑐𝑐+ 𝑏𝑑𝑒𝑐
(21.9)

To ensure the model learns a sparse dictionary rather than a simple identity map-
ping, we optimize a loss function combining reconstruction fidelity with a sparsity-
inducing penalty:
L = ∥𝑥−ˆ𝑥∥2 + 𝜆∥𝑐∥1
(21.10)

where 𝜆controls the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and feature sparsity.
Recent advancements, such as JumpReLU SAEs \[Rajamanoharan et al., 2024\], utilize
a thresholded activation function to achieve near-binary on-off feature behavior, which
more closely aligns with the theoretical ideal of discrete semantic features.

21.8.1
Monosemanticity and Shadow Models

The efficacy of SAEs has been validated across various scales. Cunningham et al.
\[2023\] demonstrated that SAEs could recover latent features in GPT-2 representing
specific grammatical concepts (e.g., numerical context), while Gao et al. \[2024\] suc-
cessfully scaled this to billion-parameter models, identifying features for programming
languages and sentiment.
A profound implication of this work is the ability to construct a shadow model:
by replacing a model’s polysemantic MLP layers with a sparse feature-based approxi-
mation, we can preserve model performance while rendering the internal computation
legible. Bricken et al. \[2023\] showed that these SAE features are significantly more
monosemantic than the original neurons, effectively untangling the superposed states
into a basis that humans can reason about.
In the context of circuit tracing, researchers have moved beyond simple autoen-
coders to transcoders \[Dunefsky et al., 2024\]. While a standard SAE reconstructs a
single layer’s activations (𝑥→ˆ𝑥), a transcoder is trained to map activations from layer
ℓto the output of layer ℓ(e.g., 𝑥→MLP(𝑥)). This forces the latent features 𝑐to
represent the actual computational transformation performed by the layer, providing a
direct map of how information is processed rather than just how it is stored.

Evaluation and Open Challenges
Evaluating SAEs requires metrics that balance
faithfulness (how much performance is lost when using features?) and interpretability
(can humans or automated LLM-probes reliably describe the feature?). Despite the
success of SAEs, challenges such as feature splitting, where a single semantic concept
is divided across multiple redundant features, and the difficulty of interpreting very rare
features remain active areas of research.

## Page 416

416 CHAPTER 21. *MECHANISTIC INTERPRETABILITY FOR LLM AGENTS

21.9
Concluding Remarks

21.9.1
Outlook and Emerging Directions

Mechanistic interpretability has transitioned from a niche curiosity to a rigorous dis-
cipline that seeks to bridge the gap between statistical performance and scientific un-
derstanding. As the field matures, several frontier directions are defining the research
agenda for the next decade.
The most pressing challenge remains the interpretability labor bottleneck. While
manual circuit discovery on GPT-2 was a breakthrough, the sheer number of features in
frontier models like GPT-4 or Claude 3 necessitates automated workflows. Automated
interpretability \[Bills et al., 2023\] utilizes LLMs to generate and test hypotheses about
the semantic meaning of millions of latent features discovered via SAEs. This recursive
loop—using a model to interpret its own predecessors—is likely the only path toward
the complete transparency of trillion-parameter systems.
To move beyond just-so stories, the field is adopting more rigorous validation
frameworks. Causal scrubbing \[Chan et al., 2022\] represents the current state-of-
the-art for hypothesis testing. By systematically replacing components of a proposed
circuit with their expected values under a specific hypothesis and measuring the per-
formance drop, researchers can quantitatively measure the faithfulness of their expla-
nations. This moves MI closer to a formal verification science, where one can prove
that a model uses a specific algorithm.
Mechanistic interpretability is increasingly viewed as a prerequisite for robust AI
alignment. By identifying the circuits responsible for deceptive alignment or situ-
ational awareness, researchers hope to build safety buffers that detect if a model is
merely producing a user-pleasing answer while internally calculating a different, po-
tentially harmful outcome. Furthermore, understanding the training dynamics, such as
the grokking phenomenon where a model suddenly moves from memorization to gen-
eralization \[Nanda et al., 2023\], allows us to intervene during the training process to
steer models toward more interpretable and safe representations.
While this chapter focused on language models, the principles of MI are being
rapidly extended to other domains, for example to time-series transformers \[Kaln¯are
et al., 2026\]. Time-series transformers present unique challenges, as the tokens lack
discrete human semantics, requiring the development of new dictionary learning tech-
niques for continuous signals. Similarly, interpreting vision transformers and multi-
agent reinforcement learning systems will require a synthesis of spatial, temporal and
social interpretability lenses.

21.9.2
Further Reading

The journey from post-hoc behavioral observation to mechanistic circuit diagrams rep-
resents a paradigm shift in AI research. We are no longer satisfied with models that
merely work; we demand to know how they work. By combining the microscope of
sparse autoencoders with the scalpel of activation (and attention) patching, the com-
munity is building a comprehensive map of the transformer’s mind, one circuit at a
time.
